From 2016-2020, my email marketing startup was stuck at $3M ARR. Literally *nothing* I did moved the needle. I was completely demoralized. 

Here's the story of how we hit $20M ARR (and my message to founders who feel like quitting):

BACKSTORY

In 2016, I hit $3M ARR in the highly competitive Email Marketing SaaS space.

To do this, we used a creative data mining/cold calling strategy.

It seemed like leads would flow forever.

Until they didn't...

Things got so bad I was forced to scale back the team. 

It was the hardest day of my life.

I tried to remain optimistic.

But I had no idea what to do.

No move I made worked.

As I scrambled, two unfortunate patterns emerged:

1. I would meet someone who did X and they would convince me that X was my problem and the reason I was stuck. So, I would spend thousands of $ on FB ads or a new website or SEO or a partner program, which never worked.

2. I would meet someone I saw as an expert and they would tell me to sell the company

The problem was no matter who I met, I took their advice WAY too seriously. 

That's how desperate I was.

I had constant anxiety.

I wanted to quit.

My dream-life was collapsing before my eyes.

Then one day I learned something new...

I heard you could resolve anonymous website visitors to an email address. 

This was mind blowing.

Our current customers biggest problem was shrinking email lists. 

"Damn," I thought.

If I can turn anonymous web traffic into emails, I can sell it to anyone. 

It took us 18 months to figure out how to do it. 

I thought it would be a cool feature inside our app.

But then we noticed something...

People were signing up for our app, using the new anonymous ID feature, downloading the data, and using it in another email app and saying it was amazing. 

I read once that if someone is willing to endure a brutal user experience and still give you a high NPS score, that’s an early sign of product/market fit.

So we made a major pivot.

We spun out the anonymous ID feature as its own product.

I got the UI and front-end of v1 done on Upwork. 

Then I ran a $5,000 Facebook ad campaign to promote it.

And something amazing happened...

We got $10,000 back in MRR!

That was the moment Retention.com was born.

Since then, we’ve had plenty of bumps in the road.

But it’s been mainly up-and-to-the-right.

Why am I sharing this?

Because when I was stuck, I would have done ANYTHING to hear from a founder who was going through the same.

To read their words, what they were trying, what was working and not. 

I would have done ANYTHING to learn how to get unstuck.

That's why I create all of this content on Linkedin about my business.

That's why I share about the journey.

I’m doing it for the founders who are stuck

I'm doing it for a younger version of myself.

If you're out there and you're stuck... 

Know this:

The breakthrough is around the corner.

It may not feel like it.

You may want to quit.

But just keep building.

45 days after launching RB2B our conversion rate (from free-to-paid) was a demoralizing 0.2%. Then we changed our pricing and our conversion rate jumped to 9%! Here’s what was WRONG and how we fixed it: 

BACKGROUND: 

- On Mar 1 we “accidentally” launched our Person-Level Identity tool
- We tried to give unlimited leads and a push to Slack for free
- We wanted to charge a tiny percentage for integrations 
- It didn’t work because people could parse the slack block with Zapier

Three major problems led to the 0.2% conversion rate: 

Problem #1: Our pricing was broken for the little guy

- Certain businesses just can’t pay $495 for something like this
- With a freemium offer, we learned that’s around 90% of signups
- We had around 100 people say they were dying to pay - just not $495
- Our LinkedIn community told us EXACTLY what we needed to do

Problem #2: Our product was broken for the big guy

- Our highest traffic customers needed an ICP filter
- We were also missing HubSpot and Salesforce integrations
- Capping our upside at $495 didn’t make sense either

Problem #3: Nobody knew what to do with the leads. 

- People wonder how soon they should reach out (ASAP)
- They also wonder if they should refer to the site visit (NO)

Here’s how we solved the three major problems: 

1. We changed our pricing (Thank You for the advice LinkedIn)

OLD PRICING - 0.2% conversion rate

$0/mo        unlimited leads/slack only
$495/mo   unlimited leads/everything

NEW PRICING - 9% conversion rate

$0/mo        200 leads, slack only
$99/mo      200 leads, everything
$149/mo    300 leads, everything
$249/mo    500 leads, everything
$349/mo    700 leads, everything
$499/mo    1,000 leads, everything 
...up to…
$949/mo   10,000 leads, everything

2. We built features. 

- HubSpot integration is LIVE and DOPE. It syncs w/ HS tracking cookie.
- ICP filter is coming next 30 days (I guess we didn’t need it)
- Salesforce integration next Q (we prioritized smaller co’s)

3. We created educational content, and are going to add a two-touch sales motion.

- We have over 25 pieces of “how to engage the leads” content
- We are creating more every day
- Our goal is to have every possible use case covered by the end of Q3
- 9% conversion is pre-sales (can't wait to see how the sales changes things)

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are hard.

A 0.2% free-to-paid conversion rate 45 days in is demoralizing. 

Luckily, no decision is permanent, and it’s VERY easy to pivot early on.

When something isn’t working, you can talk to your customers - or your LinkedIn community - and they’ll tell you why.

The hard part for most people is admitting that their “genius” idea was completely WRONG.

The longer I do this, the more I accept the fact that even though I’m SOOO much more experienced than I was 10 years ago, my intuition, most of the time, is still pretty bad.

There is wisdom in holding your own ideas very loosely. 

Because you don’t *really* know.

But your customers do.

I’ve talked to over 20 founders the past 4 weeks and every one of them is miserable.

They want me to be miserable too … but I’m NOT. 

11 years in, I’m more excited than ever. 

Here’s the top 5 reasons why I love my job and life (and how you can too):

1. I focused on profit from day 1. 

Nobody does this in tech, because VC is the “shortcut”. You go faster (and almost no founder makes money).

But - 10 years later, that profit has grown to a magnitude where we have the resources to pursue any opportunity we want to. 

2. I hired an incredible exec team. 

The longer we exist, the bigger we get, and the more credibility we have, the better the talent is that wants to join us on our journey. 

I love waking up every day to build with such smart and motivated people. 

3. That exec team lets me do what I want to do (and what I’m good at).

I love the early-early, really small, really lean team stuff. I love coming up with products and seeing if people like them or think they suck. 

I also love doing outrageous marketing stunts, and I have learned to love creating organic social content. 

But despite being the CEO of a $29m ARR company, I: 

a. I never interview, hire, or fire anyone

b. I don’t deal with any of the people opps in the larger part of our org

c. I only do internal meetings on Monday

I do content on Tuesday, have a marketing meeting on Wednesday, and by Friday most weeks my calendar is completely empty. 

(You 9-9-6 grinders out there will say I’m soft … But I’m optimizing for the energy to keep at this for DECADES)

4. My work rhythm gives me energy for my family life, and vice-versa. 

This is part of running my calendar how I do (which most CEOs would say is LIGHT). It creates a virtuous cycle in the two parts of my life I actually care about. 

5. On January 6 I was able to create my dream life.

I love Aspen and the mountain life it provides. 

On January 6, I was able to move my family a to a house a mile outside of downtown, and rent an office two blocks away from the gondola. 

When I am enjoying a powder day and walk two minutes to my office, I still cannot accept that this is now my permanent reality.

My wife loves it and my kids are going to grow up rippers…

All while I keep building this growing, profitable business, with people I love and respect. 

What’s the takeaway? 

You probably don’t have the patience to bootstrap, but you should. 

We all know bootstrapping gets you there slower. 

Nobody respects you for YEARS in the beginning… that SMALL thing you’re working on…

And worst of all you don’t have TechCrunch articles about how you raised at some dumb valuation to send your friends and family so they can think you’re rich (when you’re not).

But if you can just manage to do what we did…

Get something going…

Small at first…

Then keep doing it for a decade…

You’ll end up having the one thing that you actually wanted when you started this whole thing. 

FREEDOM ✌️

Four months ago, we launched RB2B and I shared my plans on how we are going to turn it into a $1B company (with less than 10 employees). Here is a mid-year review of where we are and an update to our projections:

BACKGROUND:

Originally, I said our first year goals were to get $4M in ARR with 5 employees. 

I received some flak for the audacious goals. 

You can read the post here: https://bit.ly/3YS2LZ9

We're 4 months in now, and we've learned a lot about the business.

Here's a breakdown of what we did well at, what we didn't, and what's next:

What we did well:

1. Revenues:

- Projected to achieve $5.4M ARR, surpassing the initial target of $4M ARR
- Already at $2M ARR post-churn with 5 more months remaining
- Likely to exceed our post-churn revenue target for year 1

2. Free to Paid Conversion:

- New pricing has significantly increased free to paid conversions.
- Achieved double the paid customers with 66% of the estimated signups.
- Expected 1040 paid customers from 30K signups in April.
- Achieved 720 paid customers from 11.5K signups in July.
- On track to end the year with over 2000 paid customers.

3. Support Automation:

- Providing effective support using extensive automation.
- Currently managing with just 1 employee and hiring another soon.

4. LinkedIn Game:

- Excellent performance on LinkedIn.
- Entire RB2B team contributed with engaging content.

What we didn't do well:

1. Annual Contract Value (ACV):

- Decreased from $500/user/month to $275/user/month.
- Experimented with different pricing strategies; $99/mo proved more effective than $500/mo.

2. Number of Employees:

- Originally estimated 5 employees for $4M ARR by December 2024.
- Currently anticipating 10 employees to achieve $5.4M ARR this year.

Here is how we get to our goals for 2025 ($16.6M ARR): 

- More signups : Will result in more revenues
- More organic traffic 
- More linkedin content
- More SEO
- Brand refresh
- UGC content
- Thought leadership ads
- Higher ACV per customer : Can improve our revenue profile
- New GTM Strategy (soon to be announced ***)
- New Products
- Sales assist PLG

From where I stand, I am confident of hitting $16.6M (post churn for 2025) or approx $1.4M month. I will provide far more clarity on the  2025 goals by the end of this year. 

Here are the major lessons learned : 

- Estimates are only directional but sometimes you can surprise yourself 
- It’s good to have goals but be willing to change variables
- You cannot always attribute to what specifically worked to get you here
- Continuous GTM experimentation is crucial for growth
- Hitting PM fit for a self serve B2B product is a beautiful thing
- With automation and modern business patterns you do not need to hire much
- To make more money, find a way to charge less

Keep Building, Keep Innovating. Keep Disrupting. 

Remember, only by striving for the unattainable.

We discover our true potential. 

Will provide another update in a few months.

Michael Kurson (CEO of First Touch) is booking 5 demos/mo using RB2B.  

Here’s his 9 step playbook ANYBODY can use to turn site visitors into pipeline:

1. Install RB2B, connect with First Touch via webhook.

- First Touch is a platform for research, enrichment, and activation

2. Filter down to the top 10% of site visitors who are perfect ICP.

- Most web traffic is noise - focus on the best to not waste time

3. Enrich with deep company and contact-level research. 

- Michael does this through First Touch, many accomplish it through Clay
- What if RB2B could do this for you in Slack?!?!

4. Identify others in the buying group. 

- Michael uses First Touch to do this, we will do this for you soon

5. Multi-threaded connection requests on LinkedIn. 

- Michael has several people at his company reach out to several people at the account for a very strategic outreach operation
- He believes “if you are putting a site visitor into a sequence, this will not work”

6. Post content, hope for engagement

- Accepted connect requests will get served your content

7. If engagement comes, reach out around that engagement on multiple channels.

- Michael uses First Touch to help stack the second signal on the site visit

8. If engagement does NOT happen, perform deeper company research to find a trigger. 

- Perplexity deep research can come up with a reason for you to reach out by searching the web and relating it back to your domain in any scenario

9. Start omnichannel outreach based on the deep research. 

- Rinse and repeat.

TAKEAWAY

As it turns out, it’s still quite difficult to turn a site visitor into pipeline. 

But here’s the thing… 

It’s still WAY easier than prospecting a cold lead.

There’s no doubt that the web signal is the most valuable signal there is… 

But in the age of AI, to make a signal work, you need to have a process.

I ask Diana all the time - “why does everything have to be so hard?”

It’s 2025, in the age of AI. 

That’s just the way it is. 

And it’s only getting worse.

Keep building.

I quit drinking alcohol five years ago.

Here's what my life looked liked then vs. now:

Me in 2019:

- Drinking 2-4 beers/drinks every night
- Getting hammered once/week w/ friends
- Smoking while I drank (sometimes w/o drinking)
- Drinking was 100% of stress relief AND social life
- Weighed 225 (20lbs heavier than now)
- Looked like I was 45, when I was 39
- Business was at $3m ARR for 3rd year in a row
- Single, chasing, bouncing around the world… lost

Me in 2025:

- Zero booze or drugs of any kind in 4.5 years
- Stress relief is sauna/cold plunge and wakesurfing
- Social life is hanging out with people w/ kids
- Weigh 205 (20lbs lighter)
- Look like I did when I was 34 (and I’m 44)
- Business over $25m ARR bootstrapped, personally making 10x
- Happily married, two young kids, deeply rooted in Austin

TAKEAWAY

If you ask me what the most impactful decision I’ve made over the past 10 years there is no question what I’d say… 

Quitting drinking.

For anybody who drinks every day, if you take three months off, you will notice an enormous difference in the quality of your life.

For me, I’d been drinking so much for so long that when I stopped it felt like I had a superpower.

You’ll feel like you got 25% of your life back.

You’ll be more present in all of your relationships. 

You’ll be far more intentional in everything you do. 

You’ll be much better at home, and at work.

There’s really only one thing I regret about the whole situation … 

Not quitting sooner.

This week Amos Bar-Joseph announced SwanAI raised $6m to take on Claude and Clay. When I told him I was sad to lose another bootstrapper to the VC dark side, he said something that totally dumfounded me. 

Amos: “We’re building a generational company and not planning on raising any additional funds.” 

Is anybody else confused by that statement?

I respect the hell out of Amos and his team. The guy joined my community last year, took my Linkedin course, and from zero created what I thought was a better version of both my Linkedin content AND my RB2B product! 

My absolute favorite thing he did was this forward looking statement that gave him MASSIVE credibility on every post … “When you’re scaling to $30m ARR startup with just 3 people …” and he had like 10 customers. Genius marketing. 

But people ask me why I hate VC so much and this is an example. 

Is it not common sense that you could not both create a generational AI company that fights against giants like Claude and Clay and only raise $6m? Didn’t Claude just raise $30 BILLION?

Here’s my question. Do these investors ACTUALLY think Claude and Clay can be taken down with $6m? I’m guessing they do not, and they liked Amos and his team so much that they would happily go along for the ride. I’m sure they also LOVE the ambition these guys have. I certainly do. 

But at the same time, I’m sitting here wondering what would have happened if they just bootstrapped $10m ARR with the three of them, and at that point, decided if they wanted to keep going or take capital. 

I wish these guys the best. As I replied to Amos, a long and prosperous journey. I hope most of all that these guys can keep enjoying it with the added pressure that they now MUST go very, very, very big. 

Amos, you’re a G. 

Keep building.

1/ Your DM’s are flooded every day with people asking for early access

2/ Industry experts are telling you that it’s going to be bigger than your last business in under 12mo (and the last biz is about to hit $10m ARR)

3/ Competitors in the space are trying to partner with you to power certain parts of your product

4/ Your pricing and offer are “oranges” in a world of “apples” - it’s high perceived quality at an incomprehensibly low price

5/ You are planning to dominate a small but exponentially expanding niche within an enormous addressable market

6/ You have unique distribution and cost advantages that you understand

7/ People who aren’t even your ideal customer profile say “I would buy that”

In 2 years, Retention.com grew from $6M -> $13M -> $21.5M. And then about 9 months ago, we stopped growing. Revenue stalled at $21.5M with no signs of growth, despite all our attempts to contain churn. 

If we were VC backed, we would have been forced into doing some unnatural things to force short term growth and create panic. 

But since we are bootstrapped, we did something unusual and now our overall business is back growing very nicely once again. 

And last month we grew by 8% MoM!

What VCs would have recommended we do?

- Solve this growth/churn problem with a sense of urgency
- Bring in experienced staff from larger competitors. VC backed companies are impatient. When they hit a wall, they are eager to bring in leaders that have seen similar growth before 
- Invest more in customer success. Possibly hire a CS leader from one of the competitors. 
- Switch our market segment. Since SMBs churn the most - find a way to go upstream into the enterprise market segment to reduce churn
- Secure additional funding to increase the runway
- If nothing works, sell the business to a competitor for pennies on the dollar

We did none of those. 

Instead we counted our blessings. 

We are still very profitable at $22M. 

We had time to pause and rethink.

While we were addressing the churn and growth issues, we launched a completely new product RB2B and our intention was to continue growing as a combined entity.  

- We minimized workflows and investments to retain profits from the business in case our top line dropped further
- We took the same solution (DTC) and applied it to a whole new market (B2B)
- We decided to do this with modern GTM (LLG) and with minimal hiring
- Now RB2B is bringing in over $500K in new ARR every month and growing rapidly

Business growth is back: 

It turns out the combined entity is growing very nicely! We will end the year at $25M ARR. Combined profits have risen and we have found a non disruptive and patient way to keep growing. We think we have found solutions to our growth and churn issues, the impact on revenue will become evident in the next several months. 

Takeaways: 

Sometimes it is OK to accept your TAM isn't big enough to support your ambition 

Or that it will take a much longer time to solve the problems in your business. 

But that is not a defeat. 

You can still grow your business and find new markets even if the one you selected seems to slow down on you. 

Work with your own timelines. Refuse to panic. 

Select strategies that provide you with more time to solve problems. 

Resist having a gun to your head when solving strategic growth problems. 

A sustainable solution is like good cooking. 

It takes time and patience. 

Focus on surviving and staying in the game. 

That itself is winning when others are folding up.

I sold my first startup for $10m cash. And immediately got scammed out of $1m in banker fees. If you're a founder thinking about selling your company, here's a step-by-step process for closing multi-million deals (w/ $0 in banker fees): 

BACKGROUND

- I had Aye Moah (CEO of Boomerang) on UnF*ck My Startup LIVE
- She bought GQueues for millions, but unlike me …
- She did the deal directly with the Founder, no banker, minimized legal expense
- Early stage SaaS buyers and sellers need to READ THIS POST 👇

Here’s Mo’s 8 playbook to close multi-million deals w/ ZERO banker fees: 

1. Don’t use a banker!

- Contrary to popular belief, if you have the buyer (or seller), you don’t need a banker.
- Lawyers can advise you and create all documentation to get a deal done

2. Hammer out main deal points w/ Founder on the other side.

- This is key for minimizing your LEGAL fees
- Don’t spend billable hours on points that don’t matter

3. Operate from a position of trust. 

- It’s VERY helpful to have a relationship with the counterparty years before
- This was Mo’s situation, my situation when I sold my co, and Jesse Stein’s situation on all 3 of his acquisitions
- You can tell lawyers to ignore inconsequential things… like a $9 payment that occurs after a cutoff time/date that could be wordsmithed infinitely to take care of edge cases

4. Be aligned with values and product philosophy.

- Cultural fit is the most important factor for making post-transaction integration successful
- Make sure both sides care about the “why”, both of the business, and product decisions

5. Find out what MARKET is.

- Tap into your network to figure out transactions that have CLOSED for deals like yours
- Ideas about what market might be (without closes) are not relevant
- You can get a business valuation if necessary

6. BUYERS: Figure out what you can afford to LOSE.

- “If this goes to ZERO, what can I afford to pay and still survive”?

7. Figure out deal structure. 

- Asset vs stock deal, cash vs. equity payout, holdbacks, earnouts, etc.
- Lawyers can help with what is possible, Founders can figure out if it’s appropriate

8. Sell to the RIGHT buyer. 

- These are our babies. You want to sell to the right person
- The acquirer of my business still had ALL employees after the 3 year non-compete

TAKEAWAY:

There are a few lessons here if you’re buying or selling an early stage SaaS.

1. Don’t pay bankers millions of dollars unless they are finding your buyer
2. You can minimize legal fees by hammering out major points w/ Founder
3. You should get to know potential buyers of your startup TODAY

Selling a startup is the ultimate reward for this journey we’re on. 

When you sell (or buy), keep as much money as you can. 

Don’t make the same mistake I did. 

You’ll regret it.

P.S.

Last month I got very offended by a comment that said I wasn’t REALLY a bootstrapper because I’m not eating Ramen in my parent’s basement. What makes a real bootstrapper? It’s not what you think: 

1. You love doing more with less.

Prioritizing efficiency and having insanely high standards for what you want to get back from what you’re doing (and spending) is what a bootstrapper lives and breathes. If you run your business this way but pay yourself $30m per year (like Ross Andrew Paquette), you are still a bootstrapper.

2. You love small teams.

You believe that companies should be able to get farther with fewer people (and the friction that comes with it) than the world believes - like Ryan Babenzien, who just made his 4th hire at $40m revenue.

3. You love running profitable, growing businesses. 

This is the anti-SaaS playbook, but if you’re wired this way, you’re a bootstrapper, Ramen or not.

4. You value freedom more than growth. 

Few understand the true deal with the devil that they enter when they take on VC money. Bootstrappers know that customers funding their growth is the only way to avoid becoming an underpaid, overworked salary man with the title “CEO”. 

5. You aren’t building for an exit.

Bootstrappers know that businesses get bought, not sold, and that creating a great business - that turns a profit in the meantime - creates something that a buyer will want someday.

6. You have ridiculously high standards for what’s “working”.

Some people call this capital efficiency, I call it having high standards. If you’re bootstrapping, you can only afford to do things that have a truly absurd return on your time and money because you need a quick CAC payback to keep growing.

7. You pursue ideas that are not venture fundable - but customers WANT.

If you are reliant on VC, you will only be able to pursue ideas that they approve of. This eliminates a massive amount of opportunity to pursue profitable, efficient, growing SaaS. You also eliminate the competing interest between what your customers want and what investors want to hear.

TAKEAWAY

I get offended when people say that I’m not a bootstrapper.

They say it’s not fair for me to say - mostly because I have resources.

I don’t believe bootstrapping is about the amount of resources you have … 

It’s about how you deploy those resources.

How you run your company.

And how you plan to grow.

Because it’s not about living in your parents’ basement…

Bootstrapping is a state of mind.

From 2016-2020, my email marketing startup was stuck at $3M ARR. Literally *nothing* I did moved the needle. I was completely demoralized. 

Here's the story of how we hit $20M ARR (and my message to founders who feel like quitting):

BACKSTORY

In 2016, I hit $3M ARR in the highly competitive Email Marketing SaaS space.

To do this, we used a creative data mining/cold calling strategy.

It seemed like leads would flow forever.

Until they didn't...

Things got so bad I was forced to scale back the team. 

It was the hardest day of my life.

I tried to remain optimistic.

But I had no idea what to do.

No move I made worked.

As I scrambled, two unfortunate patterns emerged:

1. I would meet someone who did X and they would convince me that X was my problem and the reason I was stuck. So, I would spend thousands of $ on FB ads or a new website or SEO or a partner program, which never worked.

2. I would meet someone I saw as an expert and they would tell me to sell the company

The problem was no matter who I met, I took their advice WAY too seriously. 

That's how desperate I was.

I had constant anxiety.

I wanted to quit.

My dream-life was collapsing before my eyes.

Then one day I learned something new...

I heard you could resolve anonymous website visitors to an email address. 

This was mind blowing.

Our current customers biggest problem was shrinking email lists. 

"Damn," I thought.

If I can turn anonymous web traffic into emails, I can sell it to anyone. 

It took us 18 months to figure out how to do it. 

I thought it would be a cool feature inside our app.

But then we noticed something...

People were signing up for our app, using the new anonymous ID feature, downloading the data, and using it in another email app and saying it was amazing. 

I read once that if someone is willing to endure a brutal user experience and still give you a high NPS score, that’s an early sign of product/market fit.

So we made a major pivot.

We spun out the anonymous ID feature as its own product.

I got the UI and front-end of v1 done on Upwork. 

Then I ran a $5,000 Facebook ad campaign to promote it.

And something amazing happened...

We got $10,000 back in MRR!

That was the moment Retention.com was born.

Since then, we’ve had A TON of bumps in the road.

But it’s been mostly up-and-to-the-right.

Why am I sharing this?

Because when I was stuck, I would have done ANYTHING to hear from a founder who was going through the same.

To read their words, what they were trying, what was working and not. 

I would have done ANYTHING to learn how to get unstuck.

That's why I create all of this content on Linkedin about my business.

That's why I share about the journey.

I’m doing it for the founders who are stuck

I'm doing it for a younger version of myself.

If you're out there and you're stuck... 

Know this:

The breakthrough is around the corner.

It may not feel like it.

You may want to quit.

But just keep building.

VC money might save your business, but VC advice could kill it. Here’s why we need to decouple capital and advisory in the startup ecosystem:

Being an early stage VC is a tough job. 

Managing other people’s money in one of the riskiest asset class is not easy. 

Most of their investments fail or barely make it. 

Deal sourcing is a nightmare and the bulk of the opportunities they run into are a complete waste of their time. 

Short fund cycle means they have a limited window to show success with their risky investments. 

All of this creates a high-pressure environment for investors. Many aren't experts in the domains they invest in, yet the environment makes it easy for them to give advice that both they and the founders may accept as expert guidance. 

Here are 4 ways investor advice can kill the venture... 

1. Insisting on tough decisions with little information: 

Many investors get impatient about growth during board meetings and start dispensing strong recommendations to their portfolio companies to hurry them up even when they do not have the full picture of the business. While this is done with good intent, it can easily destroy the venture or initiate a domino effect of negative culture that can get out of control.

2. Recency Bias: 

A lot of the advice or preferences early stage investors provide are rooted in “recency bias” and what they have seen work with other portfolio companies, hoping the same strategy will work elsewhere. VCs are in the game of pattern matching. They depend upon their cognitive bias to identify the next winner based on what they have seen in the past.

3. Misalignment on timelines: 

Building a successful, sustainable venture takes time and involves many nuances. Misaligned expectations for growth can derail the venture. It's important to have transparent conversations to align on expectations, milestones, and key metrics.

4. Misunderstanding the team’s strengths and weaknesses:

I have spent my entire career as an operator and I often take on advisory roles. I've learned that growth strategies must align with a company’s DNA and be rooted in the team’s super powers. What works for one company may not work for another, even if the strategy sounds solid. Successful growth is tied to understanding your team’s unique strengths and weaknesses.

TAKEAWAY: 

Despite best intent, bad investor advice has the potential to kill a venture.

Listen to your early stage investor, but recognize the limits of their operating experience.  

Don’t hold it against them—they’re doing their best to navigate the pressure.  

Work with them, not against them.  

Align on strategies, timelines, metrics and experiments to avoid unintentional setbacks.

Design experiments that generate the data needed to make informed decisions.

Always rely on Data. 

The right data and frameworks can drive clarity in decision making and cut through boardroom biases or opinions.

Last week I had coffee with a founder who's been stuck at $2.5-$3m ARR for 9 months, is burning $400k/mo, closing a TON of new business, but can’t get ahead of churn. He asked me what I would do, and was surprised by what I said: 

Founder: What would you do if you were me? 

Me: Before I tell you - what do YOU think you should do? 

Founder: I think we should run our SMB business as lean as possible, and focus on the Salesforce ecosystem.

Me: Why do you like the Salesforce ecosystem? 

Founder: Because NOBODY has anything like what we sell, unlike the SMB ecosystem, where there are several competing offers. The deals are larger - we have a few we’ve been working on - but they take forever to close.

Me: How do you get in front of those prospects? 

Founder: Our investors give us a couple introductions per month, which is cheap, and we exhibit at shows, which is expensive.

Me: Why is the SMB segment churning?

Founder: They don’t see the results they are looking for during the first several months, or they are just too small for us to move the needle. 

Me: I feel you there.

Founder: So what would you do if you were me?

_________

The advice I gave him was very similar to the path we chose a couple months ago at Retention.com

If you can’t stay in front of churn at $2.5-$3m ARR: 

- You have a product/market fit problem in SMB
- You need to prove out the upmarket segment
- You should definitely not be burning $400k/mo

I told this Founder that the only path forward was to acknowledge that there is a product-market fit problem, and until it was solved, $3m ARR was his ceiling.

When there is a product market-fit problem, there is only one way to handle it. 

The brutal reality is that you must get as small as possible. 

You need to completely wipe out this burn, because this model is unsustainable.

You need to do the things YOU KNOW you need to do to find PMF:

1. Try to talk to every churned customer yourself.
2. Slowly improve the product to eliminate churn reasons.
3. Learn about personas and who actually is and isn’t ICP
4. Keep pushing forward with the upmarket experiment 

When you find PMF, burning $400k/mo at $3m ARR COULD make sense. 

I mean, I hate it, but I can see how others would argue it’s the right move.  

Before then, it most certainly does NOT.

A critical mistake early stage founders make is trying to do ANYTHING to scale - and I mean ANYTHING - before they find PMF. 

Save yourself the agony. 

Before PMF, do things that don’t scale. 

PS.

I wrote #1-#4 as a reminder to myself. 
I’m guilty of the same thing at RB2B.

The spreadsheet that almost killed my company looked completely reasonable at the time. I built it in 10 minutes.

Sadly, I've watched dozens of founders make this same mistake.

After years of grinding, you've found early-product market fit.

Growing 20-30% month over month. Mostly inbound until recently. Then you hired 2 salespeople and had them start doing outbound.

And it's working!

More net-new demos than before. Truly incremental activity. And unlike inbound, you can actually MEASURE it. Full speed ahead!

So you open a spreadsheet.

If 2 reps are booking 10 demos a week… what if you had 10 reps doing the same thing? What if you had 20 reps?

You start extrapolating. Year-end revenue. Series whatever. Maybe PE interest.

Then you start hiring more.

(Even writing this is triggering some serious 2023 PTSD for me!)

If you have made this mistake - and I know many reading have - you know what happens next.

Your 10 new reps contribute ALMOST NOTHING to the overall demo booking.

You try everything from incentives, to power hours, to activity targets.

You're eventually forced to give their manager an ultimatum…

And it all blows up and ends in layoffs.

From 2012-2022, using the classic Predictable Revenue playbook, you could put a college kid in front of a laptop, call them an SDR, and they actually WOULD create demand. They would book demos. 

Not today.

Starting in 2023, outbound reps can only CAPTURE demand you've already created… they do not CREATE demand.

Repeat after me.

"Reps do not CREATE demand. They CAPTURE it"

I have the battle scars to prove it.

In order to avoid this painful outcome for your employees, sales leadership, and company, before you grow your sales org, you must do one thing...

You must PROVE that you can systematically expand your ability to generate leads through marketing before you make a single hire. 

Ask yourself:

1/ Are your reps' calendars completely full? If no... 
2/ Fill them without hiring. If yes..
3/ Figure out how to get more capacity by offloading admin.

Step 2 is where everyone skips ahead.

It feels slow and boring. Unsexy compared to building a sales org.

But your company has to learn to CREATE demand before you hire reps to capture it.

Over the past 9 months, RB2B's churn dropped from 'holy sh*t we're dying' (15%/mo) to 'still bleeding but breathing' (7.2%/mo). That's a 50% improvement that literally saved our company. Here are the 5 biggest mistakes I made in 2024... and how I fixed them in 2025:

1. I was delusional about product-market fit.

When we launched 18mo ago, person-level website ID was meant to close the loop on ABM, be a new source of meaningful pipeline, and completely transform GTM. We now know it’s not any of that, but it’s still by far the best source of intent, so people keep buying it.

2. I was optimizing the product for my ego, not customer happiness.

I resisted fixing certain things because I thought they would expose other problems that would ultimately lead to churn, in favor of bigger things I thought were transformational (like deeper Hubspot and Salesforce integrations). 

Turns out the integrations weren’t transformational, and fixing the little things has made people happier. Whooops.

3. I stopped talking to customers. Now, every Wednesday from 1-4pm I get my ASS handed to me by customers.

I do a rapid fire, back-to-back 15min customer calls for 3 hours every Wednesday afternoon. This has been revelatory. I know what people hate about RB2B, I know what we need to build. I also review EVERY Delphi chat that comes in, and get a ton of Intercom tickets.  This informs user pain and product dev.

4. We stopped trying to extract - and started trying to deliver - maximum value. 

We aren’t there yet in terms of pricing, but we now think the average $149/mo user is getting so much that they would keep the product even if there wasn’t hard-dollar ROI. 

5. I stopped LARPing as Russell Brunson/Gary Vee

Last year I was on a podcast tour, making courses, trying to create a youtube channel, doing one-to-many sales webinars, and making a docu-series … which was taking 60% of my time at least. Now I spend 1 morning a week writing LinkedIn posts, 1hr on “UnF*ck My Startup”, and the rest of my time goes to RB2B product (and a few one-on-ones and exec meeting for Retention.com).

TAKEAWAY

You can judge my churn all you want. 

Here’s the reality: 

5% churn = $15m ARR w/ 3 FTE’s.

I’m 90 days away from figuring out how to get there.

Stay tuned...

In 2016, I was stuck at $3M ARR with my Email Newsletter App for 36 months. Here's the best piece of startup advice I got during that period (and why it ultimately got me unstuck):

“Try to solve a problem in email that hasn’t been solved yet.”

When I was stuck, I was: 

- Building features my competitors had to catch up
- Trying to do growth marketing w/o product-market fit
- Frustrated that nothing I tried would work

Once I solved an unsolved problem, I was:

- Selling something new that my prospects hadn’t heard of
- Had inbound demand, so didn’t need growth marketing
- Excited to get out of bed because I was having a blast

Try to solve a problem that hasn’t been solved in your vertical. 

Don't just try to do what everyone else is doing better.

Do something different.

It’s the quickest way to get unstuck.

As I look at 2025 for RB2B, I hate all my options. If you’re an early-stage SaaS founder, and you're being 100% honest with yourself, you probably do too. Here’s why:

1. Anything we build (that works) will get copied in 1 second

I’m not saying we’re great at product, but if we were, and we did what it took to figure out how to actually get the person-level ID to work, people would just copy everything we did immediately, at a WAY faster pace than ever.

2. It feels like every SaaS is a race to the bottom price war

What’s the result? “More for less” offers, tangential competitors/partners all building everything, trend towards the marginal cost of distribution, which isn’t zero, but it’s still much lower than here.

3. I don’t like the idea of building everything under the sun

Everybody brings up Rippling for the example of what to do in this market, but I don’t think they realize how absolutely incredible the execution has to be across the board to pull Rippling off. Very, very few teams can actually do this. 

4. I don’t think users actually WANT another platform

There is a narrative that you need to be a supplier or a platform, even if workflows that you are enabling could be done in platforms that the customer already has. I don’t like this path, but VC-backed companies are forced down that road.

5. I haven’t spent enough time w/ AI to understand how it can help

This is my fault. I am a late adopter. We use Fin for support, and I get why LLMs are incredible at doing research, but outside of that, I really don’t know the use cases for AI, and as such, am probably being lapped by those who do.

TAKEAWAY

2025 will be a tough year for early-stage SaaS. 

On one hand, it’s amazing that it’s easier to start a SaaS than ever. 

On the other hand, that means you have 100 competitors the second you get something working.

What’s my plan for 2025? 

I’m trying to focus on things we can do that other people can’t. 

Can I get better at content? 

Can I get better at community? 

Can I build a brand that actually matters?

I’ve been thinking about these things a LOT recently. 

If the answer is “no, no, no”… 

Then here we go 2025. 

Let the Rat Race begin.

rows.content:
It’s almost 2025 and we’re *still* setting up young salespeople to fail.

99% of early-stage founders think their BDRs create demand (they're wrong).

This idea is leading to TERRIBLE outcomes for both companies and sellers: 👇

It looks like this...

- The “Predictable Revenue“ model (or what I call the Old Way) requires us to create a revenue goal based upon an arbitrary growth rate

- We then look at the BDR team’s productivity and fail to realize 90% of the demand they captured would have found its way to you through another channel (Yes, it’s really 90%)

- We then take the number of reps divided by the number of demos they booked per month and assumed that if we hire 4x more reps we'll have 400% more demos

- We then grow our BDR team by 4x with young reps, don’t train them how to sell, and teach them a playbook that literally does not work anymore

- We then layer on managers to help with the new headcount, add expensive tech, the whole nine yards

- Then nothing appears to be happen… but that’s okay, you just need to give it 6 more months (maybe more!) to actually start working

- Then 6-12-18 months goes by and EVERY WEEK the manager of the 400% bigger BDR team is asked by the executive team why they're missing their targets by 75% 

- Finally, either the manager quits or is let go, the BDR team shrinks to the size it used to be or smaller, pipeline remains unchanged, and you feel guilt/shame for having put everyone through it all 

Trust me, I know.

I went through this at Retention.com last year.

Here's the takeaway:

The Predictable Revenue model is broken.

If you're going to work for a company that still runs that playbook, be careful.

It fails to acknowledge:

- Cold outreach doesn’t work in 2024/25 like it use to
- BDRs in 2024/25 are capturing (not creating) demand 
- Growing teams won’t actually grow demand

And it puts salespeople and their managers in an impossible position.

Our young sellers deserve better than that.

Train them right.

Flood them with demos. 

Be content-led.

Capture demand through traffic to the website (both identified and anonymous) 

Use partnerships, influencers, and other ecosystem plays. 

And let sellers sell. 

Stop trying to replicate the Salesforce playbook.

It's not 2010 anymore.

Your salespeople (and your bottom line) will thank you for it.

CEO: My startup is at $2.5m ARR after 24mo, and it’s just me and my co-founder. We want to raise $5-7m at around $30m post. What do you think? 

Me: I hate that idea. 

CEO: Why? 

Me: What are you planning on doing with the money? 

CEO: We think we have pretty decent PMF, so we want to build out engineering, sales, marketing, and CS teams so we can speed up.

Me: The reason I hate it is because if it’s just you two right now you don’t have any repeatable processes. So, you’ll go hire all of these people, it will be a total mess, it will slow you down, and you’ll likely end up doing a large layoff to get small again. I’ve been there. Twice.

CEO: That makes sense. What would you recommend doing instead? 

Me: If you can, I’d recommend continuing to bootstrap it, hiring someone in each department first, start delegating, and see how that goes. As that starts to work, hire a couple people under them. 

CEO: I’m doing the math in my head - depending on how quickly that happens, I’ll probably need money for that.

Me: You will - but not $5-$7m. I had Ryan Allis (sold iContact for $169m) on our show. He said something I never heard before - NEVER raise more than 1x your ARR.

CEO: Why not?

Me: Because if you do raise 5-10x your ARR and you stall out, EVER, you will join the 80% of VC backed companies where investors get their money back but the founders get nothing. Keeping your raises to 1x your ARR dramatically lowers that risk, because you’ll be so far along when it comes time to deploy those large amounts of capital. 

CEO: Sounds like pretty prudent advice. But won’t my valuation be lower if I take less money? 

Me: Yes, but valuation is meaningless unless you are getting a chance to sell significant secondary. I’m talking many many millions. Raising as little money as possible maximizes your probability-weighted financial outcome.

CEO: Thanks for the advice. We’ll keep bootstrapping it for now, and only raise 1x our revenue if and when we need it. 

Me: And you will end up being much richer for it! 

CEO: AMEN

$10M ARR is the FU MONEY of SaaS.

Here’s the breakdown:

I think $10m ARR bootstrapped is the new unicorn.

Why?

Because if you can bootstrap $10m ARR in a lean way, all your wildest dreams will come true.

You will be able to do whatever you want with your life.

(I know because I’ve done it)

Not only that, I think bootstrapping $10m ARR is actually way easier than creating a unicorn.

And WAY less risky, with a FAR higher probability-weighted financial (and happiness) outcome.

Here’s 6 reasons why all founders should commit to bootstrapping $10m ARR:

1. You and your co-founder will be making over $1m/yr in salary and dividends.

This is simple math (another benefit of a small, efficient team). You and your co-founder can easily clear $1M each at $10M ARR, and probably more. With VC money, you have to be much, MUCH larger before you can take home that kind of money. It will be years later, if it ever happens.

2. You can sell your business in ONE SECOND for $30-$40m+

I’m sure you’ve all seen the math. Dilute yourself down to 5% on a 15 year run to $1B, and if you didn’t pull out HUGE secondary checks, you actually come out behind. Not only that - there are only a handful of buyers at $1b. There are hundreds - maybe thousands - of EBITDA buyers at $30-$40m.

3. You can hire a CEO to run your company, work 1 hour per week, and clip the coupon

4. You can work 100 hours per week and run yourself into the ground (if that’s your thing)

5. You can go raise $50m and build a unicorn

Your product and GTM will be so tight that if you want to hit a home run at this point, you can absolutely do it. And as a profitable company, you will have leverage to get good terms from growth equity funds. Many will put the money straight in your pocket.

6. You can keep running it lean, get to $25m ARR with 25 people and pay yourself $10-$15m per year.

This is a possibility that literally no one talks about. And again, I think it’s actually much easier and higher probability than creating a VC-backed unicorn. Exit or not, if you get here, game over. You get a decent exit every year!

TAKEAWAY:

If you can bootstrap $10m ARR, the options available to you are SO GOOD.

The harsh reality is that most companies never get there.

Why?

Because you get traction and VCs show up at your door.

They gas you up with hopes and dreams about how your SaaS will be a decacorn

They give you money that you don’t need, which you promptly turn around and spend.

All the while, it’s actually INTERFERING with the one thing that will make you great, capital or not.

Product-market fit.

If you can find PMF, bootstrapped, then use money from your customers to get to $10m…

You can do anything you want with your life.

Ross Andrew Paquette, who grew Maropost $0-$25M ARR profitably in 3 years, is the PERFECT example of this.

He's joining me on Tuesday at 3pm ET on UnF*ck My Startup LIVE to share how he did it and his growth playbook for 2026.

7 reasons why you should never take VC (explained in 60 seconds):

1. Dividends are good
2. Investor value prop is weak
3. A new seat at the table is net-negative
4. They’re in the portfolio game, you’re not
5. I want to do things investors won’t tollerate
6. I don’t believe in measuring things or sreadsheets
7. Large carrots in front of us make us make bad decisions

———

1. Dividends are good

If you create a successful early-stage startup, you should be rewarded by getting paid millions of dollars every year… Not just some *potentially* astronomical number at some point MAYBE in the future.

2. The investor value prop is weak (if you don’t need capital)

I listened to pitch after pitch of investors saying their “go-to-market advisory would be game-changing” for us. This pitch was weak and designed to get founders like me dreaming big dreams that if they panned out would largely be my team’s doing.

3. A new seat at the table is a net negative. Period

At best, investors will slow you down. At worst, they will ruin your life AND destroy your common equity if your business slows down for macro reasons outside of your control.

4. Investors are in the portfolio game. You’re not

Situations can emerge - FREQUENTLY - where what is best for your life and company can be usurped by a group of investors wanting a quick 2x. Even if they have a minority position, there are SO many ways they can exert influence and drive the outcome that is best for the fund.

5. I want to do things investors would not tolerate

My strategy for 2025 was to give away a super-valuable product using viral distribution strategies and do a lightning-fast PLG. I did it with a team that is unreasonably lean. I even let AI run RB2B for 7 days when the team went on vacation. THE SECOND any of this plan went sour, I would be told to stop, and if I didn’t, I’d be fired.

6. I don’t believe in measuring things or spreadsheets

I think almost all measurement (aside from top-line ARR) is garbage and leads to bad long-term decision making in favor of optimizing in the short term for whatever metric you’re going for.

7. Large carrots dangled in front of us make us make bad decisions

An investor’s job is to try to figure out what number will motivate the founder to transact, and once identified, get them to attach their identity to that number. We love validation that our beautiful business IS worth $100m, even if it actually lowers the probability-weighted financial outcome for the founder.

TAKEAWAY:

Last year I was seduced by the idea that I could take millions off the table.

After speaking to an investor a week, I realized that those millions would likely change the things about my life that I value most.

I’d sacrifice independence, freedom and it would slow us down.

That’s why I’m a bootstrapper at heart.

And I always will be.

25 things I wish THIS GUY knew about business (me, 25 years before $28m ARR bootstrapped):

1. Building things that make money is far more rewarding than making money itself.

2. Ideas don’t matter. Execution is everything. Learn how to execute.

3. YOU are going to have to do everything. No one will sign up to execute your “ideas”. (Why would they? You have never actually DONE anything.)

4. Your skills as an entrepreneur will compound over time. Start acquiring them NOW.

5. The quality of your product will dictate how much wind you have at your back.

6. The quality of your team will dictate how far (and fast) you can go. Great talent is everything.

7. You will NEVER regret removing a person from the wrong role. You will only wish you did it sooner.

8. To even have a shot at success, you need a great product AND great marketing. Don’t sleep on either side, or you will never get anything off the ground.

9. Brand is a very real - and very powerful - thing. Learn how to build aspirational brands.

10. Ignore what everybody else is doing. Startups don’t kill startups.

11. Don’t copy people. Figure out how to do SOMETHING new, even in crowded spaces.

12. You don’t actually want wealth. You want freedom, and control over your time and job.

13. Embrace the idea of years (maybe a decade of) “ramen profitability”. Being small will ultimately compound into huge profits (and the freedom you want). It just takes time.

14. The goal is to create the maximum amount of profit with the fewest number of employees.

15. Nobody who is ahead of you can actually give you good advice. They can only share experiences.

16. Set up your life and work so that you can do it for decades without burning out.

17. Learn how to build organic audience on social media ASAP. It will change the trajectory of anything you are doing.

18. Relentless focus on one thing over years and decades is what will make you successful.

19. Let go of the idea of a retirement “number” - because it will always change.

20. A truly great life partner and children will add more to your life than you could ever imagine.

21. Your life will someday be more expensive than you ever thought possible. Don’t fight it - it actually DOES make you happy. Just figure out how to make more money.

22. Consider sobriety. It will really help you, and you will wish you found it sooner.

23. Nutrition is actually far more important than exercise. But exercise > everything else.

24. Never take your foot off the gas. Innovate or DIE.

25. Everything is going to take way longer than you think. Never, EVER give up. 

Just keep building ✌️

Last month I spent $30,000 to share a room on Sir Richard Branson’s private Caribbean island. No oceanfront villa. No private suite. Just a twin bed… in a billionaire’s house. And the craziest part? I thanked him for it. Here’s how Branson turned Necker Island into the best “community business” I've seen:

1. Make a personal paradise that is so beautiful and inspiring that people are blown away by it.

- The topography, balinese architecture, chic interiors, views, food, service, and every water sport imaginable are this man’s paradise
- (Richard Branson’s paradise is paradise is ALSO your paradise)
- It’s also his home… And he and his staff makes people feel like they are guests at his home
- He has lemurs and baby kangaroos that I got to bottle feed, and over 3,000 flamingos
- You can drive golf balls into the ocean or sit in a hot tub on top of the great house, which is the highest point on the island

2. Make it so expensive that inspiring groups are the only people likely to go there (and so expensive that it funds this paradise).

- At $150k/night for 48 people max, I believe most people find themselves there with a group of very interesting people doing very interesting things
- I was invited by Brett Hurt, and we attended Alexander McCobin’s Principled Business Summit, put on by his fund, Liberty Ventures
- I met people doing all sorts of wild things like making tunnels with plasma guns, cross border payments for agriculture, building up a TopGolf empire
- I also got to have great conversations with John Mackey (founder of Whole Foods) and Brock Pierce (a true crypto OG who was literally involved in every single project) … Is anybody aware that Tether (he co-founded) generated $13b of profit in 2024 with 50 employees?!?!

3. Physically BE there - and ACT like you’re part of the group (even though you’re clearly not).

- Richard was on the dock when we arrived and pulled us off the boat from Tortola
- The second morning itinerary started with “Optional Hike with Richard Branson”
- He spent time sharing his epic stories - hot air balloon near death experiences, ALMOST avoiding the first gulf war entirely, virgin galactic and the dream of space
- He played chess during lunch with whoever wanted to take him on

TAKEAWAY

Sir Richard Branson has created a personal paradise. 

Not only that… 

People line up to pay him insane amounts of money to visit…  

And those people are the very people he’s interested in meeting anyway!

I don’t think I’ve ever seen a more incredible example of a community business.

7 days before they launched Jasper, they had been stuck for 2 years at $2m ARR and were planning on selling their prior business (Proof) for pennies on the dollar and starting a restaurant instead! 

This is my favorite “founder getting unstuck” stories of all time … 

And it was so impactful for me because I sat there and watched it happen from across the room, 15 feet away.

That's why I’m thrilled to announce that Dave is joining me tomorrow on our Inbound-Led Outbound Live.

Founder: I’ve got 35 AI agents making me 100x more productive!

Me: But you’re still on Zoom calls 9 hours a day...

Founder: [nods]

Me: You’re missing the point of AI

Founder: What do you mean?

Me: You’re trying to bend AI to fit into your existing business. And yeah, you will see some incredible gains come from that. But it's not enough.
 
Founder: So what’s the problem?

Me: If you rebuilt your product, pricing, and go-to-market around AI…
it could run your entire front line. Every customer conversation. Every interaction. You’d be free to focus on SUPER-high-leverage stuff. Product, brand, growth.

Founder: That SOUNDS nice, but our product requires a sales call to get people properly educated and onboarded.

Me: You’re still missing the point. If your product, pricing, and positioning is simple enough, AI can handle ALMOST every customer interaction. We proved that with RB2B.

Founder: But our product is more complex than yours. It has to be.

Me: That’s what every SaaS founder says right before they get out-executed by some YC kid with an AI-native business. Over the next few years, the old guard will stall out, while a new generation of truly AI-native companies emerge who design their product and go-to-market strategies in a way where every human minute spent ACTUALLY gets amplified by 100x.

Founder: What does that even look like?

Me: AI has made the 3-man, $10m ARR SaaS a reality. How? If you’re not on calls all day, you can spend your time on MUCH higher leverage activity like product, pricing, and growth.

Founder: Yeah, but we aren’t RB2B. So what should I do?

Me: Stop asking, ‘How can AI help us do more of what we already do?’ Start asking, ‘What would my business look like if AI could do almost all of it?’ Design that version. Then build toward it.

Founder: That’s kind of terrifying.

Me: It should be. Because if you don’t, you’re screwed.

Founder: And if I do?

Me: You win. $10M ARR. A couple FTEs. The FU money of SaaS.

Last Wednesday I gave up on my new startup MoltSets entirely. I was devastated. Today, I think it's a $10m ARR biz because of ONE CHANGE we made to the offer. Here's what happened:

To Set The Stage:

- Seven weeks ago Robb, Tate and I stopped working on RB2B
- We are focusing on MoltSets - unlimited contact data APIs
- Hopefully we’ll be in closed beta next week - waitlist below

My original hypothesis for MoltSets is that a large number of Clay Agencies (maybe 200?) would pay $495/mo for MoltSets.

That alone isn’t an attractive business.

But I hoped how loud they were would pull in growth marketers and Founders at $199/mo, and individual reps who wanted to do sales in Claude at $19/mo.

Then I had 3 of the biggest Clay Agencies say the same thing last week:

“There’s probably 10-30 people who would pay $500/mo for that.”

FACK!

But then one of them suggested something WILD.

What if instead of trying to get HUNDREDS of people on $497/mo…

You tried to get THOUSANDS of people on a $97/mo plan that was unlimited and STILL had huge rate limits???

As I continued my conversations with GTM nerds, the enthusiasm for the $97/mo offer became palpable.

So much so, that a few people said words that are music to my ears:

“How can you run a profitable business with a $97/mo truly unlimited offer?”

When I explained it to them, it clicked:

1. We have incredibly cheap, massive awareness through LinkedIn
2. We are already using our database and data team (profitably) to serve three other business lines
3. MoltSets piggybacks on those two “moats” for another path to monetization of both of them, and
4. We will do this without humans, like RB2B

“Ah, I see.” (they said, nodding)

TAKEAWAY

Customer Discovery is more important than ever.

I’ve never sent a cold email or made a cold call, and I’m trying to design a product for people who are the best in the world at it.

Vibe-coding makes you think you should just throw a product out there and see what happens.

But unless you are LITERALLY eating your own dogfood and solving a PAINFUL PROBLEM that you actually have, there’s no way your vibe-coded slop will be disruptive.

Going $0-$1 quickly requires two things:

1. A disruptive product
2. Disruptive marketing

If you don’t have both, you’ll get stuck. I know because I’ve been there.

There’s only ONE WAY I know of to create both those things …

CUSTOMER DISCOVERY.

The market knows. You just have to ask.

Two weeks ago I went to a CEO dinner at SaaSOpen where the cumulative revenue of the 9 CEOs was over $1B ARR. Here were my 7 most interesting takeaways:

(In attendance: Chili Piper, Apollo.io, Clay, Justworks, HootSuite, the ZoomInfo of China, Pavilion, and Ebsta)

1. Without making it a rule, for 4 hours, only one person spoke at a time, at a table of 12 people. The level of intense focus and attention was incredible.

2. The CEO’s that had hundreds of millions of ARR and thousands of employees set so much better of an example than I do. Just the way they speak. They are playing the game at such a higher level than I am. You can tell they are used to having thousands of eyes on them at all times. It was admirable, that level of poise. Yes, I have thousands of people watching my every move I make too, but it's different...

3. We talked about the nature of reality and the way people interpret it for like 30 minutes. I never thought that would have been a topic of discussion for a bunch of SaaS people.

4. Nobody could decide if we were more or less politically divided than the past, and there was a 50/50 split between people who thought tech was responsible for it vs. didn’t contribute at all. 

5. The Justworks CEO had a cool way of getting buy in from employees. They articulate a super hi-res vision of the future, where we are today, the gaps that needed to be closed, and WHY it was so important to close them. Every executive and manager could recite it word for word! That was so motivating. I want to be able to articulate that clear of a vision to our people.

6. I walked around the room thanking everybody, feeling so humbled to be able to participate in such a fabulous conversation, and surprisingly they said my zone of genius (which I see as these weird social media pranks) was equally enthralling.

7. Sam Jacobs said everybody he’s speaking to had a much better '24 than they were expecting … and were optimistic about 2025. I was surprised by this because I think it’s actually HARDER for my audience, which is 50% $0-1m ARR.

TAKEAWAY:

Why was this dinner so cool for me? 

I’ve never sat at a table where every single attendee has been ahead of me. 

I’d love to re create that somehow, more often. 

Thank you Alina for putting this all together.

As the Founder of Y-Combinator, Paul Graham has invested in 4,000 startups (including 85 unicorns) and helped create over $600B in enterprise value. When he was asked how he would fund a startup if he were starting TODAY, I was shocked by what he said:

PAUL GRAHAM: “I would raise maybe $500k, keep the company small for the first year, work closely with users to make something amazing, and otherwise stay off SV's radar.”

(So the guy who has seen more VC deployed than any human being alive says he basically wouldn’t use VC!)

PAUL GRAHAM: “Ideally I'd get to profitability on that initial $500k. Later I could raise more, if I felt like it. Or not. But it would be on my terms.”

(…Get to profitability?!?!?! Why does no one take his advice?)

PAUL GRAHAM: “At every point in the company's growth, I'd keep the company as small as I could. I'd always want people to be surprised how few employees we had. Fewer employees = lower costs, and less need to turn into a manager.”

(…I have said these exact words over and over to our team … We always want to be the smallest version of ourselves that we can be)

———

I have never felt so validated for the path we have chosen at Retention.com. 

$25m ARR, 40 employees.

I love how people always seem surprised by how small our team is.

I just NEVER would have guessed that Paul Graham - who has seen more intergalactic successes than literally anyone - would share my business building beliefs. 

These are the words of a bootstrapper at heart! 

What’s the takeaway? 

The fundamentals of business are pretty simple. 

Rule #1: Make things people love
Rule #2: Make more money than you spend

The crazy thing is that we exist in the one space in the world where rule #2 not only does not apply … 

The whole VC machine is set up to get young founders excited about how “rich” they are going to be (but most likely not) and have them do the exact opposite. 

I always loved reading Paul Graham’s essays. 

I love them even more now… 

Because he’s got the heart of a bootstrapper.

YC’s best advice is “default alive” - have enough cash to survive without the next raise. Great advice… nobody f*cking does it. 

Paul Graham (the founder of YC) once said he’d raise $500K, get ramen profitable, and probably never raise again. 

The guy who’s seen more VC deployed than ANY human alive basically says he wouldn’t use it more than he absolutely has to. 

But the reason no one listens to this advice is because founders are delusional about their own companies. 

We think what we have is better than what it actually is, and we can’t help ourselves. 

Our startups are our babies. We have a totally unrealistic and out-of-touch view of them. 

It’s way too easy when you have a little bit of traction to go out there and raise way too much money.

Then you’re set on a path to burn forever. 

“Default alive” is a great concept.

Maybe 1/100 YC companies actually do this. 

YC knows it, and they fund them anyway.

I’ve scaled 3 sales organizations in 13 years. These are the 7 BIGGEST LIES I hear about scaling up sales teams at early stage startups:

1. Bigger teams mean faster growth

The opposite is true. The “Old Way” of building sales teams is a large internal org pushing on a string that appears to be “profitable-ish” but is really losing money. Why? Because it forces reps to use a prospecting playbook that doesn’t work in 2024 and is capturing (rather than creating) demand.

2. You can scale reps linearly and maintain productivity

This never works. In 2024, prospecting activity doesn’t CREATE demand, it CAPTURES it. Ask anyone who has rapidly grown a BDR org, only to see pipeline numbers unchanged. Most of the time unmeasured (thus unscaled) activities like brand and podcast are actually creating demand.

3. It’s good to have your AE’s prospect

Wrong. What works is to have your AEs calendars so full of demos that they have to stay up until 9pm every night dealing with follow-up but they don’t mind because they are making SO MUCH money.

4. You need to compete on expensive perks to attract top talent

Not true. Great reps don’t care about your kombucha machine or unlimited PTO. The best reps want to work for a highly-ambitious company in a fast-paced environment that has a reputation for flooding reps with GOOD leads they can close.

5. "Predictable Revenue" is the goal

This model is predicated on building a massively inefficient assembly line of reps who execute a playbook that 100,000 other SaaS companies are also running. It creates a massive amount of waste in the name of "predictability" that wont come.

6. Ecosystem plays are for the big boys

Part of the “new way” of building hyper-lean sales orgs is to create/capture demand through developing agency/partner/influencer type ecosystems the second you hit PMF and use them to funnel low-in-funnel, declared-intent leads into your small team of highly-trained, senior reps to close with incredible velocity.

7. Founder brand isn’t important for me and my space

DTC ecomm really wasn't on Linkedin and yet I spent 9 months posting daily and creating video content. And it worked! Then we created a B2B product and it worked even better because my ICP lived on Linkedin. Downside: It’s *very* hard work and takes tons of time. But, there’s nothing like it. It’s the future.

TAKEAWAY

Most folks think scaling sales teams is about creating Predictable Revenue.

They think sales creates demand and the more muscle they put behind it the faster they will grow.

Because of this they hire too fast, don't train enough, and force salespeople to live and die (mostly die) by a playbook that doesn’t work anymore.

They have no idea that they can set up an ultra-high-velocity sales machine that creates low-in-the-funnel leads from months and years of content that cuts through and indirect channels.

Yesterday, Klarna’s CEO announced they were firing several SaaS providers (including Salesforce and Workday). This is just the start of a long, painful trend. Many SaaS companies will soon miss their targets and lose top accounts.

Here’s why and how SaaS teams can prepare to avoid this cold winter:

BACKGROUND:

For those unfamiliar, Klarna offers flexible payment plans for online and offline purchases. With $2B in revenue and a $7.8B market cap, Klarna is a profitable company—a dream client for any enterprise SaaS vendor.

Yet, Klarna does not see the need for many SaaS tools. Why?

They’re not replacing Salesforce or Workday, but instead reimagining their entire workflows using AI. They’re realizing that many SaaS tools designed for old workflows are now obsolete. They may end up developing some in house AI tools to serve their proprietary workflows.

Klarna is setting new benchmarks for AI-driven organizations, and their approach is likely to become mainstream within 18 months. As more companies adopt this model, the TAM for SaaS will shrink dramatically. SaaS vendors that quickly adapt to AI use cases will survive and thrive, but many will fade away as the market contracts.

Additionally, Klarna recently announced it would cut over 50% of its workforce, reducing staff from 5,000 to under 2,000, driven largely by AI integration in marketing and CS. This will naturally lead to a reduction in SaaS spend, but the layoffs aren’t the cause—it’s Klarna’s AI-centric organizational design that’s causing the decrease in spend.

Mark my words.

SaaS vendors must evolve to stay alive.

If you are a SaaS vendor, how do you cope with this? 

1. Cannibalize your own business:

Just like Netflix shifted from DVD rentals to streaming, SaaS companies must embrace AI and be willing to disrupt their own offerings. Those who don’t evolve will face the fate of Blockbuster.

2. Identify your AI use case:

Look for adjacent areas where AI can bring quantum leaps and major productivity gains, not incremental improvements. Don’t just build another system of record—focus on real innovation that pushes boundaries and transforms your space.

3. Reduce Costs:

The era of zero-interest rates led to bloated processes and structures. Now is the time for SaaS companies to learn to do business with lower costs and operate more efficiently.

4. Prepare for Price Pressures:

Expect downward pricing pressure as AI-driven enterprises like Klarna redefine efficiency. Expensive SaaS solutions will struggle, while lower-priced alternatives will thrive in this new wave of innovation.
 
5. Go Global:

In the past, selling in the U.S. alone was enough for a series A/B companies. But as competition in the US intensifies, expanding internationally with competitive pricing will offer much-needed room for expansion.

SaaS vendors do have choices, but they ain’t pretty.

They can disrupt themselves in the next 12 months, or...

They can wait to be disrupted by others later.

CEO: My startup is at $2.5m ARR after 24mo, and it’s just me and my co-founder. We want to raise $5-7m at around $30m post. What do you think? 

Me: I hate that idea. 

CEO: Why? 

Me: What are you planning on doing with the money? 

CEO: We think we have pretty decent PMF, so we want to build out engineering, sales, marketing, and CS teams so we can speed up.

Me: The reason I hate it is because if it’s just you two right now you don’t have any repeatable processes. So, you’ll go hire all of these people, it will be a total mess, it will slow you down, and you’ll likely end up doing a large layoff to get small again. I’ve been there. Twice.

CEO: That makes sense. What would you recommend doing instead? 

Me: If you can, I’d recommend continuing to bootstrap it, hiring someone in each department first, start delegating, and see how that goes. As that starts to work, hire a couple people under them. 

CEO: I’m doing the math in my head - depending on how quickly that happens, I’ll probably need money for that.

Me: You will - but not $5-$7m. I had Ryan Allis (sold iContact for $169m) on our show last week. He said something I never heard before - NEVER raise more than 1x your ARR.

CEO: Why not?

Me: Because if you do raise 5-10x your ARR and you stall out, EVER, you will join the 80% of VC backed companies where investors get their money back but the founders get nothing. Keeping your raises to 1x your ARR dramatically lowers that risk, because you’ll be so far along when it comes time to deploy those large amounts of capital. 

CEO: Sounds like pretty prudent advice. But won’t my valuation be lower if I take less money? 

Me: Yes, but valuation is meaningless unless you are getting a chance to sell significant secondary. I’m talking many many millions. Raising as little money as possible maximizes your probability-weighted financial outcome.

CEO: Thanks for the advice. We’ll keep bootstrapping it for now, and only raise 1x our revenue if and when we need it. 

Me: And you will end up being much richer for it! 

CEO: AMEN

The only metrics that matter at each stage of SaaS:

$0-500K ARR: Weekly MRR growth rate
$1-5M ARR: Weekly MRR growth rate
$5-10M ARR: Churn + Top of funnel growth

Yes, it’s the same metric twice, but weekly MRR growth rate is the ONLY thing that matters from 0-$5M.

Are you growing week over week? If so, by how much?

Keep it simple. Track the number that tells you if you're moving forward or not.

Churn doesn't matter until $5M+. Before that, you don't have enough customers for the data to mean anything. 

Once you hit $5M, churn starts eating you alive if you ignore it. That's when it matters.

Top of funnel growth becomes the game at $5-10M. You've got the product, you've got retention. Now it's about feeding the machine.

But before $5M…

Weekly MRR growth rate ONLY.

I think building in public worked for me to the extent that it did because nobody at my level was doing it when I started.

When I first decided to do it, we had $13M ARR with 6 people at Retention.com

Now I’m doing it with RB2B, which has $7M ARR with 3 employees. 

Those numbers are unique, which is one of the reasons people pay attention to them.

But it's not even just about numbers. I'm way more credible than someone building in public for the first time. I've been doing this for over a decade. 

That credibility is what makes people listen.

While most people don’t have those numbers, and it won’t work nearly as well as it did for me, I still believe building in public can be incredibly valuable. 

When you're starting from zero, everything is working against you. Anything you can do to get attention is an edge you should jump on. 

But you don't have to do it forever.

Get off the ground, get some traction, then stop if you want. 

No one's got a gun to your head saying you have to “keep building in public” once you start.

Are there founders with no personal brand pulling way more revenue? Obviously.

But telling a founder at zero with no budget and no audience that building in public doesn't work is just bad advice.

- In the 19th century, companies that refused to adopt machines and industrialization failed

- In the 1990’s, companies that were slow to adopt technology and IT faded away 

- In 2004, cloud companies took on premise software and rebuilt it for the cloud. Those that did not migrate to cloud surrendered their market share to more modern technologies

- In 2024, AI companies are taking cloud apps and making them AI-native. Cloud companies that do not migrate to AI fast enough will lose market share to those that do. 

Don't listen to the naysayers.

Business is rapidly evolving. 

In the next few years, every single business will undergo AI transformation. 

And new technology trends generates chaos, hype and confusion. 

Not all initiatives during this time will be successful.

In fact, many will fail. 

But not trying is not an option. 

If you want to be one of the winners in the next wave of transformation, stay in the game. Don’t miss this wave. 

Learn to survive amidst this chaos. 

The world is changing and so must we.

Let me be clear here - If you are leaving AI comments on my posts, I don’t blame you, because someone dumb told you this is how you grow a linkedin following and you have no idea how to think for yourself or get anything to actually work.
