Taylor Haren just told me he generated $8m in pipeline for Fyxer by sending 4mm emails this month, and he’ll send 8mm next month! Here’s 5 things Taylor is doing in cold email that you’re NOT: 

1. 1x Email Every 2 Months to EVERYBODY

No sequences. No segmenting. The entire TAM gets 1 email every 2mo, unless they unsub.

2. Short and Punchy Copy

Clear and concise works for the internet. So do free things, and most importantly, have an offer that slaps. (See image below for the copy 👇).

3. No links - ESPECIALLY on the First Email 

Phishing is actually the problem here. If you don’t have a link, there is 0% chance a spam filter thinks you’re phishing. Ask for replies, spell out domains [fyxer(dot)com].

4. Automated Positive Reply Script

Use AI to read replies. If interested, respond with how to set up an account - WITH a link. Add “this inbox isn’t monitored for further replies”. Fyxer sees no drop off.

5. Don’t use AI to over-personalize. 

Taylor thinks the perfect balance is dropping in something that references their job title or industry, not that you read a case study on their website and think XYZ… 

TAKEAWAY

Is cold email dead? 

Taylor Haren certainly doesn’t think so… 

Neither do Fyxer Co-Founders Richard and Archie. 

They just went from $1M to $10M in 5 months.

And cold email is alive and well at RB2B as well!

Want to know something crazy? 

Over the past 30 days at RB2B, Taylor has sent: 

- The same copy, to
- The same list, with
- The same exact result

As 14mo ago when we launched. 

Our best campaign gets 1 positive response for every 9 emails sent!!!

Want to see our RB2B copy? 

Comment RB2B and I’ll DM it to you. 

(make sure we're connected)

I have some bittersweet news. Yesterday, RB2B hit $4M ARR (just 40 weeks post-launch). Sounds great, right? Wrong. Churn has gotten so out of control that I’m officially declaring RB2Bv1 dead. Here’s what comes next:

Here’s what RB2Bv1 was: 

- Person-Level Website Visitor Identity
- Free push to Slack

Churn is higher than new business for four reasons: 

- People need to filter out the noise
- People need to route the signal to a rep
- Reps want to be told what action to take
- And there are now 3,247,892 copycats

Luckily, we’ve solved the first 2 problems, and the 3rd is coming soon.

How? 

We completely rebuilt our Hubspot integration 

We believe it solves the filtering and routing problem. 

Here’s the 5-Step RB2B >>> Hubspot Setup: 

1. Make sure your TAM is in Hubspot 
2. Send the RB2B Lead to Hubspot 
3. If the lead is an named account in Hubspot, HS tags a rep
4. Hubspot either alerts the rep in HS, who lightly tailors a message, or
5. Hubspot sends a slack message with the rep tagged, who gets alerted

There are a few key differentiators from our last HS integration: 

- Repeat signals (which for larger deals are very valuable)
- You don’t get charged $0.50 for a marketing contact
- We are passing LI URLs to the record and pageviews to timeline
- This allows filtering IN HS, and POWERFUL workflows to be built

We believe we’ve solved the filtering and routing problem for HS users, but we still have one more problem to go until we’re at RB2Bv2. 

The “what now” problem. 

Soon, RB2B will tell a rep exactly what to do when a signal comes in from a named account, based on context from the CRM and pageviews. 

“Connect on LinkedIn, and send the following message …” etc

While RB2Bv1 is completely dead, filtering, routing, and “what now” is what our customers are telling us they need. 

(in addition to solving the broken link problem, which should happen this week)

We’re also looking at adding reverse IP lookup for companies (which is worldwide), and adding several other identity vendors for higher coverage. 

That should give us a push to $10-$15m ARR … at which point we’ll probably stall out again and have to re-invent ourselves yet once again.

… RB2Bv1 is dead …

Longlive RB2Bv2!

You don’t need 100,000 followers to be WILDLY successful on LinkedIn. Here are my 3 favorite stories of people who had their mind blown by the power of LinkedIn:

1. Curtis Matsko, CEO of Portland Leather Goods

Curtis is a good friend and loyal customer of Retention.com.

/// Curtis's LinkedIn process ///

Once per week, he opens his laptop, hits record, and creates 7 videos in a 30min sitting with his coworker, Mariana (who LinkedIn believes is his wife … but is not).

Zero planning. They just talk about what they are working on and thinking about. His assistant then posts the videos daily.

/// The Results ///

His last 3 major hires have come INBOUND from people who have watched his Linkedin videos. They showed up and said, "I love what you’re doing, I know EXACTLY what you’re all about, and I want to get involved. I’m all-in!"


2. Megan Bowen, CEO of Refine Labs

Megan is business partners with one of LinkedIn OG’s - Chris Walker - but set about building her following very differently.

She surgically connected to every single member of her ICP with a consistent connection request campaign over years. Her content then warms them up, and gives her the ability to open conversations with them.

/// Megan’s LinkedIn Process ///
 
2020-2021: 
- 5X / week LI posts 
- Co hosted DGL with Chris
- 5-10 connection requests / day

2022-2023: 
- 2-3X / week LI posts
- Took a step back from podcast focused on running biz
- Continued 5-10 connections requests 3x / week on average

2024: 
- Became CEO, bumped activity back up to 3-5X / week
- Got back into podcasting for Stacking Growth
- 5-15 new connection requests / week

This is the playbook Alec Paul advocates, and would run with someone if they were just starting out.

The true power of LinkedIn is getting connected to your ICP, then having them see your content for a few months. As Alec once told me, “You literally become a celebrity in their eyes by the time you ask them if they want to chat.”

/// The Results ///

Demo book rates through the roof!


3. Robb Clarke, Head of Technical Ops at RB2B

Robb runs our entire support effort at RB2B. I encouraged him to make himself a LinkedIn creator when we launched. He committed to posting 3x per week.

/// The Results ///

With only 1,800 followers, Robb has been featured on multiple pieces of high-reach content, webinars with brands like Intercom, and was flown to attend the Pioneer conference in London!

TAKEAWAY:

LinkedIn is the most powerful networking vehicle on the planet.

Even if your goal isn't to generate leads, you can quickly and efficiently create content that will benefit you.

If you’re CEO, every person who: 

- Wants to work for you 
- Wants to invest in your company
- Wants to partner with your company

Will check out your LinkedIn profile.

Why not turn that profile into a trust-building machine?

Curtis, Megan, and Robb sure have…

They all understand that trust = brand.

And in 2024, brand is built one post at a time.

You’re not Steve Jobs. You’re not Travis Kalanick. You’re not Parker Conrad. And that’s OK. Instead of wasting years chasing VC funding and "massive" exits, most founders should focus on one goal: bootstrapping to $3M ARR. Here’s how I grew my first $3M ARR startup into a $25M ARR SaaS with $12M in profit (without giving up control):

Company 1: Robly Email Marketing

My first startup was a bootstrapped email newsletter app. We got it to $3m ARR by going after Constant Contact customers with a cheaper/better offer (for a $40/mo product!). 

That only got us about 1% of their revenue, but fortunately we kept the team tiny, and were left with positive cashflow to keep building.

Company 2: GetEmails (now Retention.com): 

Started as a feature in Robly. People were using the feature (called RoblyID), downloading the file, putting it in Klaviyo, and said it was awesome. 

We spun it out, funded it with the cash coming off Robly, and despite being stuck several times along the way, it’s now over $20m ARR… And we ended up selling Robly for $10m to private equity.

Company 3: RB2B 

RB2B was the result of Santosh pushing me to create a GetEmails for B2B. Before RB2B, company-level ID existed, but not person-level. Now, we have around 20 competitors, including ZoomInfo. 

We used the cashflow from Retention to get it off the ground, went $0-$4m ARR in 40 weeks, and it’s nicely positive cashflow (albeit stuck).

When you stack RB2B on Retention it’s a 40 person team with $25m ARR and $12m run-rate profit. 

Sounds like a dream business. 

Except that we’re stuck again...

TAKEAWAY:

I don’t know why more people don’t follow the path I took.

Start small and profitable, then take bigger and bigger swings.

You’ll learn valuable lessons and become incredibly skilled when the stakes are low, so that when the stakes are higher, you can swing that much harder.

Remember:

You're not Steve Jobs.
You're not Travis Kalanick.
You're not Parker Conrad.

Neither am I.

That's OK.

Start small.

Then go bigger and BIGGER as the journey progresses.

My biggest takeaways from Peter Walker (Head of Insights at Carta):

1. 70% of VCs are net negative to the companies they fund. Vinod Khosla said it. One of the most respected investors alive openly admits that most of his peers actively hurt the companies they back.

2. Venture capital has killed more good businesses than it has created great ones. Perfectly profitable $5-10M ARR companies got pushed past their natural ceiling and ended up worth nothing.

3. Your valuation is not your self-worth. Founders are treating paper numbers like real money and building their identity around it. Most of it will never materialize into actual wealth.

4. Bootstrapping has a marketing problem. Venture is incredible at talking about itself (funding rounds, unicorn status, Wall Street Journal profiles, etc). Bootstrappers just build profitable businesses and nobody covers it.
 
5. The "I'll just sell for $50M" exit fantasy is almost never real. Only 2-3% of seed and Series A companies get acquired in any given year, and most of those are just acquihires (aka glorified job offers).

6. Taking VC money is a 10-year marriage that's harder to exit than an actual marriage. Founders treat fundraising like a milestone. It's actually a decade-long legal and financial entanglement with someone whose incentives don't fully align with yours.

7. The pre-seed bar has doubled. A few years ago you could raise on an idea and a founder. Now more than half of pre-seed rounds involve companies that already have revenue. The rules changed and nobody announced it.

8. The Series A markup is theater. When Sequoia leads your Series A, your seed investor looks like a genius on paper. But it means nothing about whether your company will ever return real money. It's optics designed to help VCs raise their next fund.

9. Sam Altman says take the 1% shot at a billion. But nobody talks about the 99%. The Silicon Valley narrative is built entirely around the outliers. The bodies left behind (good founders who destroyed profitable businesses chasing unicorn status) never get a profile in TechCrunch.

10. If you're building a software company without AI today, you need an extraordinary reason why. VCs aren't debating this anymore. Non-AI software companies are functionally locked out of institutional capital right now, and the founders who don't adapt are playing a different game entirely.

One of my CEO friends raised over $100M. His startup had a $1.2B unicorn valuation in 2021. I always thought he was CRUSHING IT on every observable metric. So did he. 

Then last week we went jogging and he started venting... 

He’s 13 years in, and the last two have been excruciating.

Rocketship to $50m ARR, almost no growth since 2022. 

He told me: “The only choice we have is to try to build literally everything, pitch tool consolidation to our biggest customers, and pray for expansion. The problem is every company in our space is doing it too”.

A few minutes went by before either of us said anything. It was just depressing.

Four years ago, he was running every day, eating well, looked great. 

Today, he’s rocking a chubby face and dad bod.

He broke the silence. 

“We’re completely stuck. IPO is off the table, I don’t know how we could ever get back to $1.2b valuation let alone a 3x from there. Nobody ever told me this was a possibility.”

This is the biggest reason I talk about bootstrapping so much.

So many founders are trapped in the hype-cycle, drowning in VC money, still burning epic amounts of money trying to figure it out.

But for most of them, there’s no way out.

I've been stuck before. I talk about it all the time.

Sometimes you get unstuck, find that killer product and before you know it you're everybody’s darling again.

But most of the time you're not. You're just treading water.

And then you wake-up, you're 50, dad bod, trying to internalize the idea that the likely outcome for your life’s work is selling your baby for less than the VC you raised.

Maybe you took life-changing secondary, and you’re fine with the situation. 

But maybe you didn’t, and you’re sitting there, anxious about how you’re going to get out of this situation, and even more anxious about what’s next.

My CEO friend isn’t unique. 

There’s a whole class of companies that raised at huge valuations, are stuck, and have no idea what to do.

They’re underwater, they know their plan is terrible, yet they can’t admit it to themselves… The consequences are too just too dire. 

This is what no one ever thinks about when they get on the VC treadmill. 

And that’s why I always say…

If you can bootstrap, bootstrap.

1,850 paying customers, 13 months, $5m ARR, 5 employees. How did we get so far so fast at RB2B? Here's our 6-step startup playbook (and my message to founders who feel STUCK):

1. We created MASSIVE awareness.

Santosh and I spent the six months prior to launch building an audience of buyers. And doing discovery with over 300 of them to validate that what we had was worthwhile.

2. We threw a terrible MVP out there and got feedback.

We set people up with a pixel and emailed a spreadsheet to people and tried to charge them $495/mo. It didn’t work. Some said “I’d pay $199.” Others said “meh”. We kept throwing spaghetti against the wall. 

3. We found a magic moment - the Slack App.

Tate built a beta that pushed site visitors into Slack, with a headshot. I started showing people at dinners and parties on my phone, and saying “this person is actually ON our website right now”. I had never experienced this type of positive reaction to anything I had built in the past. I knew we were on to something.

4. We made that magic moment FREE.

I believe in the immense power of free, ESPECIALLY if you have a magic moment that you can make free. We screwed up on many things related to pricing along the way, but I think we got this one correct. I do not think we would be anywhere near where we are if Slack wasn’t free.

5. We listened to customer problems. But didn’t actually fix much.

If you’ve been following from home, you probably know that we have a churn problem. You may even be thinking “they really haven’t built much over the past year”. Customers gave us tons of feedback on the product and user experience, but I viewed the solutions they were asking for as the first steps to causing other problems. We have much better solutions now (on their way) so I’m glad I waited.

6. We stopped all marketing (besides me posting on LinkedIn). 

I thought the product and experience was so bad that we were just burning leads. I killed every channel but posting - which I’m able to do because we don’t have investors. We are starting to ramp other channels back up. We slowed down, to speed up.

TAKEAWAY

For anybody but an AI coding company, $0-$5m ARR in 13mo with 5 people is exceptional. 

Especially because it’s not just something we’re SAYING we’re doing… 

We actually DID it.

What’s the flip side? 

We’re stuck until we provide an experience that is different than today.

I’ve been stuck 6 times in my career. 

It feels just as bad at $25m ARR as it did when I was stuck at $3m. 

But here’s the good news… 

1. We have gotten unstuck 5 of the 6 times
2. I know how to get RB2B unstuck 

The anxiety of being stuck and the satisfaction that comes from getting unstuck is probably why I like the game so much in the first place. 

If you’re stuck, just know that you CAN get unstuck. 

I was right where many of you were 5 years ago, stuck at $3m for 3 years. 

And I got to $25m. Bootstrapped. Thanks to my lean, hungry team.

You can get there too.

Just keep building.

Over the past 6 weeks, I’ve done 15min calls with 72 customers and over 20 of them asked me how the most successful people use RB2B. I had no answer, but now I do. Here’s the email copy I used to book these calls + the questions and tools I used to get incredible testimonials:

1. Do 12 x 15min customer calls every Wed afternoon. 

These are valuable for so many reasons. I now know why people hate and love our product, and what we need to build. Here’s the copy I use, sent to every +$249/mo user after 30 days: 

==================

Subj: Can we hop on a quick call?

Body: 

Adam Robinson here, founder and CEO of RB2B.

First off - thank you.

You’re one of our most valued customers, and I’d love the chance to personally learn from you.

I’m setting aside time over the next few weeks for short 15-minute conversations with a handful of our top users. I want to understand exactly how you're using RB2B, what’s working well, what’s not, and how we can improve the product to serve you even better.

If you're up for a quick call, you can grab a time that works best here:

[CALENDAR LINK HERE]

I genuinely appreciate your time.

Your feedback will directly influence where we take RB2B next.

Looking forward to connecting,

Adam

Founder & CEO

RB2B

================

2. Ask happy customers if they will do “workflow testimonials” 

I use Simple Testimonial for this. It makes it VERY easy for users with two clicks to answer a series of question on video. Mine are: 

- What is a 10sec summary of who you are, what your company is, and what you do?
- How are you actioning RB2B data, step-by-step?
- Can you share the message copy you using to reach your site visitors?
- Are you reaching out to other people at the visitors’ company, or just the visitor?
- What is the tangible result you’re seeing from RB2B?
- What would you say to a friend about why they should choose RB2B?

3. Edit each testimonial separately, and make one large mash-up. 

John Eley is helping me out here.

4. Send the long mashup to customers who ask how people are winning w/ RB2B.

5. Make posts and put adspend behind each of the short testimonials. 

Understory is running these to our founder, marketing, and sales personas. The customer wins because they get visibility from my account, we win because people are learning how to use RB2B. 

TAKEAWAY

Six weeks ago I had no idea how our best customers were winning. 

Now I have a 47-minute video compilation of them telling me exactly how they are crushing it (below is a shortened version).

I guess sometimes being clueless is the best starting point.

Last quarter Dave Gerhardt told me to let Eli Rubel re-do our RB2B website and branding. The current version is a $79 webflow template called “SaaS”. When I spoke to Eli, I told him I only care about one thing:

Give me ugly, shocking branding that at least 80% of people in SaaS will hate.

Why?

Here are the 5 reasons I want RB2B to have hideous branding that makes peoples’ skin crawl:

1. I hate the sterile, inauthentic typical Silicon Valley SaaS branding.

Take a look at 6Sense’s website and you’ll know exactly what I’m talking about. The soft color palette, the politically correct stock photos, the stupid robot, the endless buzzwords … It all makes me want to vomit.


2. I believe that pattern interrupt is the best marketing strategy.

Nails on a chalkboard will make people stop and pay attention.

And we are in an attention war, full stop.


3. Two years later, people start copying you.

We rebranded Retention.com in late 2022. I loved it. It was weird, aggressive, strange colors, it didn’t look like any SaaS site I had ever seen. We did a poll when we were picking brands and it was dead last of the four options. That was a signal.

I was not surprised to see that a wannabe competitor OpenSend copied us nearly identically 18mo later (seriously, go look at it).


4. I remember how weird Mailchimp’s 2018 rebrand was, and how it made me feel.

Does anyone else remember looking at that yellow website and just thinking “what am I looking at?”

This was after everyone and their mother in SaaS copied their prior branding.

They are legends.

Then Intuit bought them, and made them look like 6Sense :/


5. Russell Brunson is my hero.

I first saw the Clickfunnels site in 2017 and had no idea what I was looking at.

It seemed like a kindergartner got ahold of a website builder and slapped something together in 1 hour

I couldn’t figure out how he found people that looked like the actors in the explainer video. They looked so unapologetically “normal” … I had never seen anything like it.

But they were actors (I think).

I dismissed it as garbage, just like everybody else in B2B.

But as I dug deeper, I realized that he was in the process of growing the fastest growing bootstrapped SaaS ever.

Still, everyone wrote them off, nobody has tried to do what he has done since…

Mostly because of who he is and who he was selling to.

____

TAKEAWAY

Eli loves the fact that I want branding that is different from anything that has ever existed.

Something that will make people FEEL something…

Instead of this drab, bland, sterile, inauthentic crap that everyone else makes.

Designers LOVE working on projects like that.

He was like...

“We could do the standard agency onboarding… or you could let us wing it”.

I chose the latter.

Last week we had our first call where he revealed the branding...

I absolutely LOVED it.

Below is my reaction as we went through what they put together. 👇

Want to see what’s behind the curtain???

Stay tuned…

Most first-time startup founders I talk to set themselves up to fail. Here are the 7 biggest mistakes I see nearly EVERY founder make (myself included):

1. You spend too much money on things you don’t really need

People love getting offices, hiring salespeople, getting VA’s, expensive video equipment, software, and even setting up an entity pre-revenue. In 2013, I bought a VOIP phone system a year before we had a customer! Cash will be EXTREMELY tight at some point, even if it’s not now. Remember that.

2. Hiring people before $1m ARR

This is a hot take. I think there should be a technical co-founder building and a business co-founder doing sales, marketing, and support until $1m ARR - just like Klaviyo did. If you have that discipline, you will be profitable, control your destiny, and emerge with product-market fit.

3. Thinking you are an “ideas guy” and can find an operator

I spit out my drink when I hear this. Just like when I hear someone talking about “stealth mode”. Thinking someone will do the hard work for you at this nearly impossible stage is delusional. Once you get to $10m ARR with under 10 people, you earned it, but until then, no way.

4. Not “doing things that don’t scale” under $1m ARR

First-time founders don't understand how manual getting to $1-$3m ARR is. It’s face-to-face conversations, however you can get them, taking the feedback, and improving product as quickly as possible. Nothing will work until the product is great, so all that “growth hacking” will be a waste of time and money.

5. Thinking seed funding means you have a good business

If you were able to raise money for your idea pre-revenue, it means nothing more than you could sell a vision to investors. The hard part is making a business out of it. Keep that in mind and avoid funding at all costs. You’ll thank me later.

6. Not posting on organic social media starting TODAY

This one took me a decade to realize, and a year after I started to master. Nothing is more powerful in today’s world than being able to create great organic social media content that your prospects have demand for independent of what you’re selling. If you start today, you’ll get zero engagement, followers, or leads, but that’s not the point… You’re one day closer to finding your voice.

7. Thinking you’ll be in and out in 3-5 years

Founders should have a decades long time horizon when they start. People wildly overestimate what they can accomplish in a year, but wildly underestimate what they can accomplish over a decade.

TAKEAWAY:

Being a first-time founder is hard.

Literally everything is working against you.

If we knew how hard it was, most would never start.

But here’s the good news...

As Alex Hormozi so elegantly put it:

Every successful person started with:

0 revenue
0 subscribers
0 customers
0 fans

And the only difference between them and everyone else is they actually start.

But that’s not REALLY the secret.

The successful ones not only start…

They keep building.

It's almost 2026. If you're a SaaS founder, you're probably screwed. Anything you do that works gets copied, CAC is up, LTV is down. Here are the 7 things I see that ARE working - in a world where most things are NOT:

1. Creating a TRULY AI-first startup

I'm not talking about slapping some LLMs on top of your old-school workflows and calling yourself "AI-native." I mean creating products on top of LLMs that increase productivity by 10x or more. Companies like Cursor and Fyxer aren't using AI as a feature - they're using it as their foundation.

2. Word-of-mouth

This has always been true, but it's more critical than ever. With word-of-mouth, anything works. Without it, nothing does. Costs are up, attention is fragmented, and buyers distrust everything. The startups that are growing have products so good that users can't stop talking about them.

3. Personal brand

The ability to create organic content that your target market has demand for - completely independent of what you're selling - is the most efficient GTM motion that has ever existed. It's an automated trust-building machine, and trust = brand. In 2026, brand is built one post at a time.

4. Cold email ... in specific contexts

Enterprise buyers? Jesse Ouellette  says they're blocking it completely. But SMB and VC-backed startups? Blast away, but do it correctly. Most founders sending to an audience where it WOULD work can’t get it to work because of bad messaging.

5. Thought leadership ads

If you know how to create bangers on LinkedIn, pick the best ones and put some $$$ behind them. Promoting a post you know LinkedIn already loves is one of the cheapest sources of eyeballs you can get.

6. Cold calls

We had Kevin "KD" Dorsey on UnF*ck My Startup this week and he told us the EXACT cold call script that was generating a 12%-13% rate of accepting the pitch on 200 dials/day/rep that is booking him 20-25 meetings/week per rep. Today. Calling works.

7. Staying ridiculously lean

I’m seeing startups winning that are running with tiny teams, staying profitable, and controlling their own destiny. Getting to $10M ARR with 10 people is now the gold standard… Not raising a $100M round at a unicorn valuation.

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are hard. They always have been. 

But in 2026, everything will get harder.

Most SaaS founders are going to fail because they're running playbooks that worked in 2020.

But if you focus on these seven things, you might have a shot.

I just have one question for YOU LinkedIn… 

Did I miss anything?

We used to spend $875,000 every year on our BDR team. Here's the uncomfortable truth about that rate of spend:

BDR teams, scaled up “the old way”, have stopped working.

Our outbound response rates have plummeted over the last 12 months.

Just like everyone else’s.

Why?

Because buyers’ inboxes are ruined.

99% of tech companies:

- Use the same automation tools
- Send the same email cadences
- Contract the same data vendors
- Message the same prospects

Which is bad, but...

Then AI tools came and made it 100x worse.

Here's the “old way” of running a sales organization:

- Pick a revenue target for the end of the year
- Model out how much manpower it’s going to take to get you there
- Hire, hire, hire, and then... hire some more

I made this mistake in 2023 at Retention.com.

Then our VP of Sales resigned.

Of course, it was a surprise at first.

But it caused me to rethink how we run our business.

I had read a few posts from Sam Jacobs about the “new way” of running sales.

Where $30M ARR companies were doing MORE sales with 2 reps than 25.

I spoke to founder friends and investors who were seeing the same.

When it became time to design the GTM strategy for RB2B (a completely different product in a totally different market), we decided to create one of these “new way” super-light, super-lean sales machines.

What’s shocking about it is that we’re better on every metric than any business we’ve ever run.

Here’s what we’re doing at RB2B to generate pipeline: 

1. We’re leveled up our Founder Brand content.

- Our goal is to be undisputed #1 at LinkedIn thought leadership content 
- It’s creating a huge amount of trust in the market and informing buyers of our solutions
- It’s the most efficient awareness-generating machine that has ever existed.

2. We went with a low-touch “freemium” pricing model.

- A viral content strategy benefits heavily from a viral pricing strategy
- If traditional outreach doesn’t work, free (but valuable) software will sell itself
- Our price points are way too low - people buy without thinking about it

3. We’re keeping the internal team as small as possible.

- We have five team members and have gone $0-1.5m ARR in 19 weeks
- Robb has done a fantastic job at creating a self-serve support experience
- We want to scale to $15-20m with under 10 people, then see where we’re at

This isn’t “predictable”, but it’s the most efficient way to scale up a SaaS that exists.

Will this work for everyone?

Probably not.

But the next generation of unicorns will look more like us than Salesforce.

Running as lean as possible.

And leading with great content.

I f*cking hate trade shows. Why?

Here’s my life at trade shows in 2019:

- Buy a ticket for large industry show “X” for me and Diana
- Have zero pre-arranged meetings or any kind of plan
- Sit at lunch tables attempting to peddle our 8 week old startup, no one cares
- Look at other vendors who have killer booths in both envy and awe
- Feel stressed and anxious because I’m afraid of talking to people
- Drink way too much bad coffee, eat horrible food, sleep terribly
- Leave deflated, telling myself that if I made 1 connection it’s worth it

I still have PTSD.

Here’s my life at trade shows now:

- Lobby show owner in advance for a keynote, hopefully land one
- Figure out if I want to meet any of the other speakers in advance
- Post that I’m speaking, arrange a bunch of meetups in advance
- Show up two hours before my keynote, stand there
- Have inbound convos with people who know me from my LI stuff
- Connect with the 10-20 people who go to all of these who are now friends
- Try not to drink too much coffee (but fail, because I have a keynote and need energy)
- Give keynote and get 100x more exposure in 45min than I did in all of 2019

TAKEAWAY

Even though I hate them, they are a necessary evil.

The value of in person interaction is irreplaceable.

I acknowledge that my experience at shows today is unique … 

But I’ve been there, with no plan, no resources, and no chance of success.

You are going to have to learn how to navigate the hell that is tradeshows.

Why?

You HAVE to get in front of people and tell them your story.

You CAN have a plan, even if you don’t have resources, or a big LinkedIn following. 

Figure out who you want to meet. Meet them. 

Tell them what you’re doing. 
Show them a diagram. 
Ask them if they’d pay for it.

What they say back to you (and how they say it) will tell you a lot about the journey that lies ahead.

Last week a founder friend was in town and I had him over for coffee. He's been stuck at $2.5-$3m ARR for 9 months, is burning $400k/mo, closing a TON of new business, but can’t get ahead of churn. He asked me what I would do, and was surprised by what I said: 

Founder: What would you do if you were me? 

Me: Before I tell you - what do YOU think you should do? 

Founder: I think we should run our SMB business as lean as possible, and focus on the Salesforce ecosystem.

Me: Why do you like the Salesforce ecosystem? 

Founder: Because NOBODY has anything like what we sell, unlike the SMB ecosystem, where there are several competing offers. The deals are larger - we have a few we’ve been working on - but they take forever to close.

Me: How do you get in front of those prospects? 

Founder: Our investors give us a couple introductions per month, which is cheap, and we exhibit at shows, which is expensive.

Me: Why is the SMB segment churning?

Founder: They don’t see the results they are looking for during the first several months, or they are just too small for us to move the needle. 

Me: I feel you there.

Founder: So what would you do if you were me?

_________

The advice I gave him was very similar to the path we chose at Retention.com

If you can’t stay in front of churn at $2.5-$3m ARR: 

- You have a product/market fit problem in SMB
- You need to prove out the upmarket segment
- You should definitely not be burning $400k/mo

I told this Founder that the only path forward was to acknowledge that there is a product-market fit problem, and until it was solved, $3m ARR was his ceiling.

When there is a product market-fit problem, there is only one way to handle it. 

The brutal reality is that you must get as small as possible. 

You need to completely wipe out this burn, because this model is unsustainable.

You need to do the things YOU KNOW you need to do to find PMF:

1. Try to talk to every churned customer yourself.
2. Slowly improve the product to eliminate churn reasons.
3. Learn about personas and who actually is and isn’t ICP
4. Keep pushing forward with the upmarket experiment 

When you find PMF, burning $400k/mo at $3m ARR COULD make sense. 

I mean, I hate it, but I can see how others would argue it’s the right move.  

Before then, it most certainly does NOT.

A critical mistake early stage founders make is trying to do ANYTHING to scale - and I mean ANYTHING - before they find PMF. 

Save yourself the agony. 

Before PMF, do things that don’t scale.

Microsoft started sending out fake auths to people who weren’t actually sending, and Google has made things similarly difficult in different ways. 

What’s the end result? 

A larger percentage of “valid” emails are hard bouncing, and a MUCH larger percentage of invalids are ACTUALLY VALID. The first problem jacks up your deliverability, the second is straight-up leaving money on the table. 

The reason MoltSets beta is seven weeks late is because we’ve been trying to figure out the best way to maximize email coverage and minimize bounces, which is what we think our audience will ultimately want. It’s not an easy problem, but we think we’re on to something.

We’re going to validate every email we deliver (as part of the $27 unlimited plan and up) append an “email grade” or “confidence score” to every email we return. 

The grades are going to look like this: 

A: Validated in the last 30d, with date attached
B: Known positive email activity (from our proprietary signal network)
C: Catch-all
D: Known negative email activity (soft or hard bounce) 
F: Hard invalid, spam trap, abuse, do not mail, or no known activity

A: SEND IT
B: SEND IT
C: whatever you what to do 
D: we wouldn’t send, but it delivers like a catchall 
F: don’t even think about sending it

Nothing will work until the product is great, so all that “growth hacking” will be a waste of time and money.

5. Thinking seed funding means you have a good business

If you were able to raise money for your idea pre-revenue, it means nothing more than you could sell a vision to investors. The hard part is making a business out of it. Keep that in mind and avoid funding at all costs. You’ll thank me later.

6. Not posting on organic social media starting TODAY

This one took me a decade to realize, and a year after I started to master. Nothing is more powerful in today’s world than being able to create great organic social media content that your prospects have demand for independent of what you’re selling. If you start today, you’ll get zero engagement, followers, or leads, but that’s not the point… You’re one day closer to finding your voice.

7. Thinking you’ll be in and out in 3-5 years

Founders should have a decades long time horizon when they start. People wildly overestimate what they can accomplish in a year, but wildly underestimate what they can accomplish over a decade.

TAKEAWAY:

Being a first-time founder is hard.

Literally everything is working against you.

If we knew how hard it was, most would never start.

But here’s the good news...

As Alex Hormozi so elegantly put it:

Every successful person started with:

0 revenue
0 subscribers
0 customers
0 fans

And the only difference between them and everyone else is they actually start.

But that’s not REALLY the secret.

The successful ones not only start…

They keep building.

In 44 months, I grew Retention.com from $0-$20m ARR. Here are the 8 biggest mistakes I made along the way (and the revenue levels where I made them):

1. We sold to anyone who showed up at our doorstep

Revenue Level: 0-$12M ARR

Not focusing on an ICP and running a self-serve app was the story of our first 2.5 years. I didn’t realize how wrong this was until later. Now I know we would have gone *farther, faster* if we sold only to big Shopify stores.

2. We wasted 6 months and $300k working towards a sale that didn’t happen

Revenue Level: $5-$8M ARR

We attempted to sell the entire business in late 2021. Such a waste of time and money. Thankfully we didn’t sell. We’re much more valuable now.

3. I got major FOMO
 
Revenue Level: $14-$17m ARR

I felt like if we didn’t go as fast as humanly possible we were going to miss the opportunity. This led to panicked hiring, a horrible corporate spending culture, and a bunch of wasted time and money trying to “be everywhere”.

4. I thought our sales and onboarding was easier and less complex than it was

Revenue Level: $12-$18m ARR

We thought we could have inexperienced AEs closing 5 deals per day with a 7 day sales cycle and rush people through onboarding. As you can imagine, that wasn't true! We needed alignment on expectations and what success looks like.

5. I set a FY23 revenue target that was 50% too high
 
Revenue Level: $13-$18m ARR

My idea of “We have to get to $50m” led to over-hiring before we truly had a repeatable sales model. Empty AE calendars led to turning everyone to hunters, which didn't work (because most demand is created elsewhere in 2023). Then our VP sales resigned and we shrunk from 15 to 4 reps.

6. I assumed other vendors’ playbooks would work for us

Revenue Level: $12-$18m ARR

Because Klaviyo and Yotpo had a large agency partnership sales motion, I thought we needed one too. We have a great opportunity in the partnerships space, but it doesn’t look like either of their motions. We had to figure out what works for us.

7. We created a $5k/mo unlimited pricing tier
 
Revenue Level: $12-$19m ARR

This just didn’t work to capture mid-mkt market share. Pricing is relatively less important to those companies. What it did create was existing customers contracting down to 5k, capped our upside, made overage impossible to capture, and upgrading non-existent.

8. We oversold people and didn’t realize it for 5 months

Revenue Level: $12-16m ARR

This was my fault for not seeing it coming. The consequences were horrible. It created a euphoria about the opportunity that led to over-hiring and overspending, then on the back-end led to a massive wave of dissatisfaction, contraction, and opt-outs at 60 days. We're doing the opposite now.

TAKEAWAY:

Growing a startup is hard.

I hope I don’t make these mistakes again. 

What I do know is that I’ll continue to make mistakes...

Just new and different ones!

Here's the trick:

Make sure you’re doing 9 things right for every 8 you do wrong.

The biggest mistake I see at $10m ARR - and I see it ALL the time - is Founders getting caught up in the unavoidable euphoria of real traction and raising VC money for a business that is actually sub-VC scale. It happened to me too.

If you take that money thinking you will be the next unicorn and you are not, you are relegated to a decade of a low paying job, when you could have been a bit more cautious/responsible/whatever you want to call it and preserved a life-changing outcome for yourself no matter what happened. 

You only need to get rich once. I’m begging you to maximize the probability of that before you swing for the fences. 

Just my two cents ✌️

I hit rockbottom February 26, 2018. It was midnight and I was lying in bed with my wife, having just left the Traffic & Conversions trade show, and I remember saying to her... “We're screwed. Nobody cares what we built.”

I had just spent a year of my life and $1M building a newsletter platform called Lead(.)com in stealth.

The plan was to “launch” it at the Traffic & Conversions Summit.

The day of the event we collected some leads, but when I started talking with people face-to-face I saw their reaction. All they were thinking was, "How do I get this guy to stop talking to me about this lame product?"

What I was selling was just not interesting. 

They had already solved THAT problem.

When we hit up the leads it was absolute silence.

That night I could barely sleep.

I was miserable.

Totally defeated.

The following morning I had to figure out how to salvage it.

I remembered once hearing it was possible to have an anonymous visitor hit a website and you could resolve it to a deliverable email address.

I thought I could sell that to anybody.

So on the second day of the trade show, I closed every conversation with:

"By the way, what if I could get you the email addresses of people who visited your website and didn't fill out a form?" 

BOOM!!

People's eyes lit up.

"What did you just say???"

Those conversations inspired the next 6 years of my life.

Here's the origin story of Retention.com and RB2B and WHY the hardest lesson for founders to learn is that they need to do customer development at the same time (or BEFORE) they build their product.

Building in "stealth mode" is the DUMBEST thing a startup founder can do. Here are the top 6 reasons why building in stealth mode is a rookie mistake (and why I won't sign your NDA):

1. No one is going to steal your idea.

Anybody who is capable of executing your idea is already busy doing something else that they believe is more valuable than whatever you share with them. Don’t make people sign NDA’s to talk to you. It makes it clear that you don’t know what you’re doing.

2. You NEED feedback.

People farther along in their journey can often help you avoid mistakes that all entrepreneurs make (and you will make, too!). More importantly, you need to be speaking to your ideal customer profile to figure out if your product is even valuable.

3. Ideas are like assh*les. 

Everybody’s got one. Furthermore, this is hard to believe, but someone is definitely working on whatever your idea is already (if it’s even a halfway-decent idea). That’s just the world we live in.

4. Ideas are just multipliers of execution.

Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk created trillion dollar companies through being the best at execution. Many others had the ideas of online bookstores, electric cars, and rich guys have been trying to go to space (unsuccessfully) forever. A great idea makes great execution go even faster, but is worth nothing on its own.

5. Building in stealth increases the risk of your startup to a point where you will almost certainly fail.

Please read “Four Steps to the Epiphany” by Steve Blank. The ONLY shot a startup founder has is to follow the method in this book. You must be developing the customers for your product simultaneously with the product itself. If no one will buy what you are building, you must stop and start over. The sooner you find out the better. There’s no way to find that out in “stealth mode”.

6. Our intuition is a terrible indicator of market viability.

You simply have no idea what the market is going to want, with the one exception of you building something to solve your own problem. However, that is still a market of one, and you need to go out and validate that others have the same problem to even have a SHOT at succeeding. 

TAKEAWAY:

Don’t build in stealth mode. 

Go get feedback from your ideal prospects.

Talk to founders who are more experienced than you.

Build up your customer base before you start building your product. 

Read “Four Steps to the Epiphany”, and treat it as Gospel. 

But please, pretty please, above ALL ELSE…

Don’t ask me to sign an NDA to hear about your “idea”.

On November 22nd, I declared RB2B dead. I cut $100k/mo in marketing spend (cold email, ads, UGC, SEO). Then in January we grew 10% to $4.5m ARR. Here are the 5 changes we made that led to our biggest ARR gains yet:

1. Cut all marketing spend - over $100k/mo

I went from thinking we had PMF in July to thinking we absolutely did NOT in November. When you fall out of PMF, there is only one thing to do - get as small as humanly possible, and find a new PMF.

2. Brought in Diana Ross to help with sales, onboarding, and enablement

Diana has been a part of two journeys to $10m ARR as the only rep (once with me), and her contribution was far beyond just selling. We have a hypothesis that this and other signals can be filtered by accounts in the CRM, they can trigger workflows in the CRM, and sales and marketing teams would rather action these signals from there than build in another platform.

We realized the workflows we sold last year were either put a human in front of a noisy Slack channel, or run leads through Clay as an ICP filter and shoot them out the SPAM cannon.

Slack is hard to action. Clay --> Instantly/Smartlead works GREAT if you’ve got a ton of traffic and a large TAM. But... ABM? Forget about it.

3. We stopped selling “leads” and “demos” as success

I got this REALLY wrong. Traffic is not leads. Demos are not the only measure of success of knowing a named account is on a high intent page. Orienting people towards that in the beginning led to disappointment.

4. We rebuilt our Hubspot integration

We realized in this new world, we needed to integrate w/ Hubspot CRM (not Marketing), we needed to add more fields, and most importantly, we needed to improve our documentation to show people how to alert reps, add to lead scores, trigger automations, all from site visitors, all in Hubspot.

Do you have a sales team that would like to know when a named account is on a high intent page and trigger HS workflows? DM me.

5. We built a Salesforce integration

Similar to #4, we believe that teams who use Salesforce CRM want to have their CRM filter the signal and reps alerted when a named account is on a high-intent page. And that signal can trigger workflows in the CRM.

Not just the first time… Every time the account comes back.

DM me if you want to route the signal into your CRM and alert your reps of a named account on a high intent page… and/or trigger automated outreach.

TAKEAWAY:

If I look back at what we did in Dec and Jan, I still don’t understand why we grew so much.

Maybe it was just that churn took a breather.

But if that’s not the case…

And the Startup Gods allow us to be correct about our CRM hypothesis, that…

1. Marketers want their reps to know when a named account is on a high-intent page
2. They don’t want to have to adopt another platform to build out workflows you can build in the CRM

...we might actually be able to get this thing moving again!

Here’s where I turn to you LinkedIn:

Is that hypothesis crazy, or not?

1) Tommy Clark, B2B SaaS CEO Ghostwriter Extraordinaire
 
October – Jan 2022
 
19 months ago I decided we needed to hone in on an ICP – large Shopify stores – and within that ICP we had zero competition, low penetration, and an awareness problem.
 
I read "Founder Brand" by Dave Gerhardt, but I was afraid to get started.
 
- I didn’t want to start posting against the best in to world
- I didn’t want to get on the Social Media treadmill
- I didn’t want to be famous (so I told myself)
 
I met Tommy, who convinced me that I should start on LinkedIn because the ecosystem was there(ish), and there was a creator/user imbalance still in favor of creators.
 
So, we started.
 
I remember coming home from an event and writing my first post.

It took 2 hours.

The results?

12 likes. 3 comments.
 
The next day, Tommy posted a screenshot of a tweet of someone I had never heard of before.
 
2,750 likes, 450 comments.
 
I sat back and observed for a while.
 
I had this feeling I heard other CEOs articulate after they start posting:

January – June 2023

I was willing to share financials, be transparent about our journey – ups and downs, and my company was at $12m ARR with 6 FTE when I started… All of which was unique.

Melissa Kwan is a 3x bootstrapper. Here's what she said are the 11 most shocking surprises on her way to $1m ARR (everyone disagrees with #10 but I swear by it):

1. Everything they thought would make a huge impact, did not.

They got 1 customer from being top 3 on Product Hunt. 18 trials from a 250k person newsletter. Spent 7 months on a huge design update, zero lift.

2. Product-led is 10x harder than sales-led.

PLG is the hardest nut to crack. Getting someone to find you, sign up, try the product, then convert all on their own is HARD.

3. The market wasn't as ripe as they thought.

Given live webinars (her product) have been widely adopted, they thought automating them would be an easy sell. Turns out, it wasn't a concept most people could grasp without a demo.

4. Consumers are more discerning and less forgiving than ever.

Doesn't matter how great your product is and how many features you have, users will find the fringe case you can't solve and bounce.

5. The amount of time they spent on content creation.

LinkedIn, blogs, backlinks, templates, customer stories, podcasting, videos, guest posting, webpages, help articles, workshops, thought leadership.

6. A single user can cause scaling issues and uncover system flaws.

One user sent so many webinar attendees in 10 days into their system that it was 400x the average user. They never imagined a user like this could exist and was unprepared.

7. Plan limitations are for not losing money (not just making money).

Since they didn't have usage limits, they lost $8k in streaming costs due to the incident in #6. They had to put limits in to restrict similar power users.

8. Pricing strategy can be the difference between profit and loss.

They grandfathered existing customers when they increased prices against the advice of our peers. That could have been $30k/m to invest towards platform costs and hiring.

9. Incremental growth month over month amounts to meaningful revenue.

They grew 10-20% MoM in the 1st year, 5-10% MoM in the 2nd, 1-7% MoM in the 3rd. It often felt too slow and was discouraging, but they got there.

10. You don't need all the fancy metrics to know what to prioritize.

The only thing they obsessed over was the voice of customer through support tickets. Issues, requests, feedback and suggestions. Their roadmap was designed accordingly.

11. $83k/month is not a lot.

There always seemed to be another expense, another hire, another investment. They're capital efficient with outsourcing and contractors. CEO/CTO/COO make salary concessions, and they were still below break even.

In March of 2021, two weeks before we were supposed to be wired $10m for selling my first bootstrapped startup, one of our engineers accidentally deleted the entire code base - and WE DIDN’T HAVE A BACKUP!!! 

Here’s the full story and how NOT to run your IT at a tiny startup: 

March 26, 2021 was a day like any other. 

I woke up, went for a run, made some coffee, and plugged in for the day.

At around 10am, I got a text from Tate, our CTO.

Tate: “Something really bad just happened.” 

This wasn’t immediately alarming. 

It's a startup. Things always go wrong.

Me: What happened?

Tate: Gustavo (name changed to protect the innocent) deleted the entire code base. 

Me: WHAT?!?!?! How did he do that?

Tate: One of our four nodes crapped out, which has been happening all the time. I taught the guys to go into Amazon and 'reset' it. The problem is there is an option to 'stop' the node directly below the 'reset' option. He chose to 'stop' that one, and just then, by chance, a second node crapped out. He stopped that one two. When you stop two nodes on a 4 node distributed database, it’s all gone.

Me: Well, that sucks, but I guess he didn’t mean to. We have a backup, right?

Tate: No, because to save money, I wasn’t writing a brand new backup file every day because I didn’t want to store two 1TB files. Instead, I would update the old file with the new backup information. There is a two hour window every day where it was writing where if the code base was deleted we wouldn’t have a backup.

I finally began to internalize the meaning of what I was hearing.

My heart started to accelerate and my palms began to perspire.

_____


TIMELINE:

10am: Find this out. 

10:02am: Call co-founder, James, we panic.

10:15am: Call Amazon, they say there is nothing they can do. Ask for someone 
higher up, tell them millions of dollars are on the line.

10:30am: Speak to the higher up person at Amazon, they tell us there is nothing they can do.

10:32am: Tate attempts to reach out to the backup company.

11:00am: Acquirer reaches out and says “your website has been down for a couple hours. Do you know what’s going on?”

11:30am: Tate makes contact with the backup company. They tell him he is an idiot and pennywise and pound foolish for having any time exposed without a complete backup file. Say they can’t help.

11:45am: Tate explains that we are about to sell this for $10m - in literally two weeks - and is able to convince them to connect him with a very senior engineer who actually built the product to see if they can dig into the file somehow. But they had never done this before, so they had no idea. They gave it us a 20% shot they would be able to get the code base back. 

12:00pm: I go to my friend Brad’s house - a VC - who says he has never heard anything like this ever in 30 years of tech, and that Tate had to be plotting something. I said he had 25% of the equity. No way.

***Ran out of space!!

Post continues in the comments 👇

Only 4% of startups make it to $1m ARR. Why? 

Because Founders who FAIL do it backwards.

Founders who fail: 

1. Come up with an idea
2. Build way too much product
3. Try to find buyers post launch through growth hacking

Founders who succeed:

1. Find their buyers BEFORE they start building
2. Build as little as humanly possible to get a feedback loop
3. Ignore growth hacking and focus on doing 1-to-1 things that don’t scale

The problem with the first approach is:

- Software is INCREDIBLY slow and expensive to build
- Our intuition is a bad indicator of market viability
- Nothing works when you don’t have word of mouth

The reason the second approach works is:

- They don’t spend dev resources until they know people will buy
- People are literally telling them (with their wallets) what they need to build
- They don’t do ANYTHING 1-to-many until they have strong word of mouth

______


My favorite “founders who succeed” story of all time is BarkBox. 

In 2012, Matt Meeker had a great dane in Manhattan. 

He thought it sucked that you couldn’t buy toys for big dogs on the island. 

What did he do? 

1. He made a photoshop doc of a website for a monthly box of dog toys
2. He walked around NYC asking big dog owners if they’d buy it
3. He charged 50 people $30 before they started building anything

What happened to BarkBox?

It IPO’d in 2021 and it’s listed on the NYSE.

______


Startups are HARD. 

It's the MOST risky career path you could ever choose… 

But you can reduce risk with three simple steps:

1. Sell before you build
2. Build as little as possible
3. Do things that don’t scale 

That's the formula for the 4% club.

99% of startups think they need to maximize predictable revenue. They're wrong. The next crop of $1B unicorn startups will solve for sales velocity above all else. Here's 9 reasons why velocity will define the new world:

1. Revenue was never actually predictable

Everybody underestimated their revenue in 2021-2022 and overestimated their revenue in 2023... 2024 seems to have either surprised people negatively or positively but certainly hasn’t been what most predicted.

2. Prospects do their own research

The best GTM motions touch the prospects early and often in the research process with timely and relevant content that helps them on their buying journey. Making it easy for prospects who aren’t ready to buy to access and consume your content to wins deals down the road.

3. Outbound channels are maxed out

Automation overwhelm has led to response rates being cut in half over the last 36 months. Inboxes are ruined, LinkedIn is worse, and AI tools will increase problem 100x.

4. The world is set up for a new GTM model

As cold outreach becomes more difficult, the model of the future will be one that warms prospects up through brand, innovative marketing strategies, UGC-generating machines, small events, indirect channels like partner and affiliate, and captures demand VERY low in the funnel. Close rates are 2-3x, sales cycles are 60% less and sales teams will be smaller.

5. “Influencers” will become more powerful

As the era of AI content unfolds, the best, most authentic content coming from the most trusted voices will become even more powerful. Social continues to become the primary method to create awareness, even for SaaS.

6. High-Velocity environments attract the best talent

The best people want to be on teams that prioritize moving FAST. The antithesis of this is a bloated GTM org that values head count above all.

7. You can be profitable (at the expense of predictability)

Running a lean team that captures demand at the bottom of the funnel (and resists the temptation to layer on outbound reps who will simply capture the demand that you are creating elsewhere) will increase focus on capital-efficiency, reduce system-wide dependence on external funding and create a less volatile ecosystem in the long-term.

8. Massive user acquisition sets you up for global domination

Santosh always says that 100,000 users is the equivalent of a $1B/yr marketing budget. I have yet to hit it, but we’re going to try.

TAKEAWAY:

It’s almost 2025.

The Predictable Revenue model is VERY dead.

The next great startups will sacrifice predictability for velocity (and profitability).

Not only is it what our buyers want, but...

It will create healthier companies with happier employees.

Everything is setting up for this to be the next great GTM motion…

How do I know?

If I were a 22-year-old Stanford grad who wanted to work 9-9-6 in the hopes of making life changing money, I WOULDN'T sell my soul to Y-Combinator and try to create the next OpenAI. I would do the opposite: 

1. Before I founded ANYTHING, I would first achieve mastery at engineering or product or sales and marketing. 

You could either do this by getting a job at high quality startup where you will both acquire skills AND learn what excellence truly is, or…

2. Start a company, but if it’s your first swing at it, AIM LOW.

Try to get something small and profitable working, where you gain the skill of creating and marketing a product, billing customers, and making them happy. 

On one end of the spectrum is a one-man consultancy or agency, on the other is sending humans to the moon. SaaS is in the middle.

Start simple.

3. Learn from your mistakes in a low-stakes, low pressure environment.

Entrepreneurship is a skill like anything else, and there are fundamental things like hiring and managing that are critically important to making something succeed that you need to master. 

It really helps to not have VCs breathing down your neck as you mess everything up the first few swings you take.

4. Start aiming higher as you become more successful and gain entrepreneurial prowess, and keep growing that stream of profits.

Take that slowly growing stream of profitability and start making larger, more complex bets that have asymmetric payoffs. 

Think SaaS, marketplace, vertical AI companies. 

5. After a decade or two, take the tens of millions of profits you are making, and go BIG.

At this point your skill as an entrepreneur is so much greater than when you were 22 and wanted to 9-9-6. 

In fact, you can probably execute a vision of the scale you wanted when you graduated from Stanford with a fraction of the capital and a normal work schedule. 

———

But you probably won’t do that. 

Why? 

Because it feels too good to go big (even though the stats show you are more than 80% likely to either fail or make no money).

And it feels better to send your mom a TechCrunch article about how your fledgling company is worth $100m+.

And what feels the best… Which you CAN’T let go of…

Is bragging to all your SF friends about how your team is doing 9-9-6.

Business is about two things. 

1. Making your customers happy
2. Making more money than you spend

If you keep doing that longer than anybody else, you win. 

Slow and steady wins the race. 

Not 9-9-6.

I just hit 150,000 followers on LinkedIn. It took 700+ posts, 55M+ impressions, but it transformed my life and business. Here are the 9 biggest lessons I learned after 36 months of posting on LinkedIn:

1. You can actually make money by posting on LinkedIn

RB2B would not exist, be at ~$8m ARR in 24mo (run by 3 people), and be growing at 7%/mo if it were not for posting on LinkedIn. We literally launched the product because of how viral my B2B posts were going.

2. Storytelling is everything

One of my competitors posts a monthly build in public that talks about what happened that month at the company. When I give a monthly update, I talk about my emotional journey being at the head of a $30m ARR company … with very little mention of what we actually did. Guess which one does better. Story > Everything.

3. Hook, Hook, Hook

The best post idea doesn’t get written unless there is a great hook. If you don’t get people to click “see more”, you wasted your time writing that post. I will die on this hill.

4. Your credibility is everything

Treat every post as though nobody has ever heard of you before. Why will they keep reading? I say things like “I bootstrapped $0-$1m ARR 3x, and ______”, or my personal favorite, Amos’s line … “when you’re scaling a $30m ARR company with 3 people” … when he had less than $1m ARR!

5. You should study the greats, and pattern match

I most closely mimicked Chris Walker’s playbook, back when talking heads were still popping. But the video wasn’t the only thing I copied … I patterned matched his ideas, which were CRUSHING, but adapted them to my subject matter. I wish I did this sooner.

6. Haters are good

If you actually break out, there will be a majority who love your stuff and a minority who absolutely hate it and you. It pays to have thick skin and not give a shit … and even wind those haters up when you can.

7. Punching up is a good thing

Recklessly attacking 6Sense changed the course of RB2B, and while they would likely not agree, them serving me that cease and desist probably accelerated their demise.

8. Always wrap it up with a TAKEAWAY

If you’re posting on LinkedIn, you’re in the edu-tainment business. Equal parts “edu” and “tainment”. Every post needs a lesson, and you should wrap every lesson with something coy that gives the reader a dopamine hit, which gets them to engage.

9. If you can, ride the wave

Last year I noticed AI was sucking all the air out of the room. While I knew nothing about AI and wasn’t using it, I crafted a story about RB2B that we were leaving for a week and our entire business would be run by AI, and that stunt worked.

Let’s go over what I did in this post.

- I dropped a big hook
- Established credibility
- Told you a bunch of stories
- And (am currently) wrapping it up

Go forth and pattern match!!  ✌️

P.S.

I got VERY offended by a comment that said I wasn’t REALLY a bootstrapper because I’m not eating Ramen in my parent’s basement. What makes a real bootstrapper? It’s not what you think: 

1. You love doing more with less.

Prioritizing efficiency and having insanely high standards for what you want to get back from what you’re doing (and spending) is what a bootstrapper lives and breathes. If you run your business this way but pay yourself $30m per year (like Ross Andrew Paquette), you are still a bootstrapper.

2. You love small teams.

You believe that companies should be able to get farther with fewer people (and the friction that comes with it) than the world believes - like Ryan Babenzien, who just made his 4th hire at $40m revenue.

3. You love running profitable, growing businesses. 

This is the anti-SaaS playbook, but if you’re wired this way, you’re a bootstrapper, Ramen or not.

4. You value freedom more than growth. 

Few understand the true deal with the devil that they enter when they take on VC money. Bootstrappers know that customers funding their growth is the only way to avoid becoming an underpaid, overworked salary man with the title “CEO”. 

5. You aren’t building for an exit.

Bootstrappers know that businesses get bought, not sold, and that creating a great business - that turns a profit in the meantime - creates something that a buyer will want someday.

6. You have ridiculously high standards for what’s “working”.

Some people call this capital efficiency, I call it having high standards. If you’re bootstrapping, you can only afford to do things that have a truly absurd return on your time and money because you need a quick CAC payback to keep growing.

7. You pursue ideas that are not venture fundable - but customers WANT.

If you are reliant on VC, you will only be able to pursue ideas that they approve of. This eliminates a massive amount of opportunity to pursue profitable, efficient, growing SaaS. You also eliminate the competing interest between what your customers want and what investors want to hear.

TAKEAWAY

I get offended when people say that I’m not a bootstrapper.

They say it’s not fair for me to say - mostly because I have resources.

I don’t believe bootstrapping is about the amount of resources you have … 

It’s about how you deploy those resources.

How you run your company.

And how you plan to grow.

Because it’s not about living in your parents’ basement…

Bootstrapping is a state of mind.

If you’re in SaaS you may not recognize this guy, but every serious entrepreneur needs to study him. Why? Because he bootstrapped his SaaS startup to $100M ARR in just 36 months.

Here are 8 lessons I’ve learned from Russell Brunson and Clickfunnels that you should implement in everything you do, starting today: 

1. Start posting content every day

Russell started a daily podcast in his car on the way to work where he published experiments he was doing, what was working, and what wasn’t. He stuck with it for years and woke up to thousands of fans saying they binged every episode. 

Slowly becoming an “expert” over time created the possibility of $100m ARR.

2. Deeply understand the psychology of your prospects

If you understand the deepest fears and biggest dreams of your prospects, you can create messaging that pierces the hearts of your target audience.

3. Make sure your offer ISN’T incremental

People are not looking for a better version of what’s not working for them. You need to offer a new vehicle.

4. Master one-to-many selling

This was the true unlock, and something no one else has done. Russell was spending $3K driving traffic to a weekly webinar that made on avg $50k in yearly subscriptions. Not kidding.

The secret: he bundled/value stacked info products WITH his SaaS (and positioned the subscription to the SaaS as “free”).

5. Create a category

Russell created a website builder when there were 100s of them, but positioned it as a “sales funnel builder” and had zero competition (for a bit) in that new category.

6. Have ugly branding

The first time I saw the Clickfunnels website, I couldn't believe it. It looked like a kindergartener made it. Like everybody else in SaaS, I blew them off, only to find that it was the fastest growing bootstrapped SaaS ever.

7. Start a movement

Russell studied the biggest movements in history - good and bad - and dialed them down to 3 key components: A charismatic leader, a new opportunity and a future-based cause.

Russell created a tribe called Funnel Hackers and his 2 Comma Club to celebrate the most successful members. He’s a religious-level figure to many.

8. Stay bootstrapped!

Infusionsoft tried to acquire Clickfunnels for $35m early on and VCs were beating the door down. Russell wanted to stay bootstrapped.

TAKEAWAY:

Russell Brunson would crush anything he set out to do

Even so, it’s SHOCKING he could bootstrap $100m ARR selling a $97/mo product to vSMB.

What’s even more insane is that it’s been almost 7 years and no one has tried to replicate his playbook in SaaS.

I believe that Russell’s go-to-market strategy:

1. Driving people to a live event
2. Using an influencer to do one-to-many selling
3. Value-stacking tech with info, tools and templates

…is the future of GTM.

I’m sure sellers of $1M unbudgeted tech will push back and say “no way”.

And maybe for complex and expensive enterprise tech, it's true.

But for everybody else, I have just one question:

Why not?

What Acquirers/Investors Want to See

1. Predictable Revenue Machine: Buyers pay a premium if your revenue can be forecasted accurately. A systematic ABM + outbound + inbound machine that you can demonstrate on a slide deck is insanely attractive.

2. Growth Rate: 30%+ YoY growth is the benchmark for a “hot” SaaS. The faster you’re growing, the higher your multiple.

3. A “Rule of 40” Company - If you’re at a firm with 30% annual rev growth rates and 10% EBITDA then you’re at a Rule of 40 company. That or higher and you’ll find interest.

4. Healthy NRR: Annual net revenue retention of 110%–130%+ is a green light. It shows your existing customers stick around and expand.

5. Profitability (or a Path to It): Depending on the macro environment, many buyers want to see that you’re not burning cash unsustainably.

Valuation Multiple Benchmarks:

1. Revenue Multiples: In private deals, 4–6x revenue is common for mid-market SaaS with decent growth. However, if you’re at high double or triple-digit growth (and a large TAM), 8–10x or even higher multiples can happen.

2. EBITDA Multiples: Some private equity buyers focus on EBITDA multiples, often 10–20x, depending on growth and profitability.

3. Exceptional Cases: If your product is in a hot niche (like AI, cybersecurity, or a sector with network effects), multiples can go even higher.

A CEO friend of mine raised $40M at $400M valuation. Two years later? The money’s gone and his ARR is flat. If you asked him the biggest mistake he made he would tell you: hiring salespeople. Here's why:

To be clear, it wasn’t JUST hiring salespeople… It was HOW he hired them.

Another founder buddy of mine recently did a Private Equity (PE) round.

His investors were pushing him to grow his team of reps from 5 to 20.

Fortunately, my PE backed friend talked to my CEO friend first.

Here's how that conversation went:

PE Backed Friend (PBF): We just raised $25m and they want us to hire a bunch of salespeople.

CEO: Of course they do. But don’t do it yet. That pressure is EXACTLY what smoked me, wasted 2 years and $40m, and very likely shaved 10 years off my life.

PBF: Ok… well… what do I do?

CEO: Are all of your reps at 100%?

PBF: Not really. One might be, the rest aren’t.

CEO: Do not hire ONE MORE REP until ALL of your reps are at 100% capacity. If you build a machine that has slack in it already, you will experience all sorts of cultural and motivational problems. The same amount of demos your marketing machine is creating and reps are capturing will go to even MORE people. Your team will miss numbers week in and week out. You will attempt to solve that problem by demanding reps you hired to be AE’s do more and more outbound. That will not work. Your sales leader will probably either quit or be fired, because you’ll have the exact same productivity on 4x the team size.

PBF: That’s terrifying. Especially now that we’re PE backed.

CEO: Tell me about it.

PBF: What do I do instead?

CEO: Before you hire a SINGLE REP, make sure all of your reps are at 100% capacity. Make sure your marketing machine can actually produce more pipeline. If and when you can actually flood your reps with activity and the entire team is at 100%…

PBF: Then I hire reps?

CEO: NO!!!! Absolutely not. You work on raising the 100% higher. Figure out how you increase the capacity of the existing team to handle the increased pipeline generation. Can you create AI agents that save account research and follow up time? Can you hire sales assistants to do some of the unavoidable repetitive work? ANYTHING to get your already 100% capacity reps more productive. THEN… AND ONLY THEN… Do you start slowly adding reps onto the team.

PBF: I am so glad I spoke to you before I did anything.

CEO: Me too.

TAKEAWAY

Institutional capital still wants to push founders into rapidly hiring reps to accelerate growth.

While that sometimes works, it’s VERY easy to do it the wrong way.

What’s the RIGHT way?

1. Make sure your marketing machine can grow
2. Get all your reps to 100% capacity
3. Raise that capacity as much as possible
4. Slowly add reps to THAT machine

Build your team that way and you can’t lose.

Just 6 months after launch, RB2B hit $2.9m ARR but our churn rate is 15.6%/mo and it’s getting WORSE! Here are the 4 biggest mistakes I made so far and how we plan to fix them:

1. I didn’t realize how big the “WHAT NOW” problem would be

There's an emotional euphoria when people see their site visitors flowing into Slack. However, there is an (almost) universal lack of understanding about what to do next. We’ve provided how-to content, but our customers are putting the burden of coming up with a playbook on themselves… So they either don’t know it’s there, or it’s not good enough.

POTENTIAL SOLUTION:

Make content that answers the question “what - EXACTLY - is another business like me doing that is working?” persona-by-persona, and figure out how to get it into onboarding.

2. We don’t REALLY understand why people are churning.

The hypothesis is people are getting stuck in the “what now” stage, not getting value out of the leads, not getting ROI, dissatisfied with data quality, or going to a competitor.

POTENTIAL SOLUTIONS:

We have implemented Churnkey, but I want to hear it from the horses’ mouth. After I get back from paternity leave, I’m going to speak with customers >$300/mo as they leave and will post about it.

The Clearbit team also said Reveal had a nasty churn issue and that getting other teams within the company using other products was the thing that helped the most. So, we’re on it. Building two more solutions.

3. We need more than just one feature

I alluded to this in the previous section. I was convinced that a point solution with a clear value proposition and a monster free offer had the best shot at growing in 2024. While that may be true, it’s also an unbelievably high churn scenario.

Providing more sources of value for different uses of the tech and different people at the org should have been a more obvious thing to me.

I also believe we can provide info products/coaching for our $0-$1m ARR community that will not only be value-add to the RB2B deployment...

But that can help founders get unstuck and get to the next rung in a scalable, efficient way.

4. I didn’t realize how enthusiastic people monitoring their traffic would be.

We’re not sure whether or not it’s because of who we’re selling to - SMB and VSMB - or because of the nature of our product.

But people LOVE seeing visitors come into Slack, seemingly even more than the people who are creating business outcomes with the data.

Appreciating this, the emotional journey of it, the customer journey built around the emotional journey, and products built to help people monitor traffic better are where we need to go. 

TAKEAWAY:

Simply put, at 15% churn we aren’t going to grow ARR much more.

If we can cut churn to 8%/mo, I believe we’ll get to $10m ARR in 12mo.

If we can’t, we’ll get stuck at $5m.

So Linkedin… This post is a cry for help.

I'd LOVE to know for all you churned RB2B users...

1. Why did you actually churn? 
2. What could we have done to save you?

145 slides of artisanal, hand-crafted data on US startups and venture capital. Here are the top 5 trends Peter Walker says founders need to know as we get into 2026:

1. AI ate 44% of invested capital (slide 10)

And that share climbs to 61% if you just look at software startups. If you are building a startup and not using AI, you should have a damn good reason why.

2. Founders sell wildly different amounts of equity for the same $ at pre-seed (slide 32)

Lots of capital sloshing around at the earliest stages of company building - but that capital is mostly chasing the same deals/founders. Meaning those in demand get to set their own prices and those in the cold scrap for attention. 

3. ARR at Series A is ~3x higher than in 2021 (slide 52)

Call it a $3M median for Series A B2B companies these days. And $7M is now 75th percentile. These are not inflation adjusted, but even so the pace seems to be getting faster by the day. 

4. The average new hire receives 50% less equity today than in 2022 (slide 84)

Startups are building with fewer employees than ever - meaning the leverage in hiring conversations is on the side of the employer. Salaries haven't kept pace with inflation and equity has been halved in 3 years. The only employee group bucking this trend are AI/ML engineers. 

5. Some venture funds can get better terms than the typical 2 and 20 (slide 134)

About 10-15% of the funds raising last year received carry of 25%-30% and some of them also grabbed management fees above the blended 2% benchmark. Just like with founders, certain GPs have a special allure. We'll check back in a decade to see if those higher fees resulted in better returns. 

----------

Now more than ever, Peter says (not me! Peter) founders should do some SERIOUS INTROSPECTION about whether to take VC money at all. If your ambition requires a $1B exit or an IPO — go meet some VCs. 

But you can build a fabulous business without any venture money. Picking the right capital game can make all the difference!
