99% of salespeople think the next generation of $1M/year earning AE’s are current entry-level sellers at top-tier startups learning the ropes as BDRs. They’re wrong. The next generation of 7-figure sellers are aspiring YouTubers:

Here's the breakdown:

1) We’re moving into a sales world where the best “influencers” will have incredible power

Generative AI will increase the amount of content created by a factor of 100x over the next several years. Fewer voices will break through, but those who do will break through so spectacularly because we will crave authenticity and perspective that great thought leaders bring. The POV that the leader brings is what makes great content… AI doesn’t have perspective.

2) Few on LinkedIn understands how powerful video is

I’ll make two exceptions - Chris Walker and Morgan J Ingram. The talking head itself is completely hypnotic. Anybody who says anything even semi-intelligent and can get people watching them talk every day and will have a power over their audience that text simply cannot create. It’s a weakness that we have as humans.

3) “Influencer Selling” is infinitely more capital efficient than sales teams

Whether it be with founder brand or a non-founder becoming an influencer, you can create and capture WAY more demand with WAY less time and energy than a traditional marketing and sales motion. That’s in addition to the insane top-of-funnel awareness you create for you and your company.

4) Aggregating audience (which really means BUILDING COMMUNITY) through video is a learned - and INCREDIBLY valuable - skill

This is MOST VALUABLE thing any company can be doing over the next decade. Community and brand are the only two moats that exist in a world where competitors can ask ChatGPT to copy your entire website and product and spit it out in 5 minutes.

5) Sales teams will have 5% of the headcount, 50x the overall follower count.

Assembling and managing a sales team will be more like putting together a team of elite athletes. But, unlike sports, there isn’t a fixed amount of players that can be on the field. I think we’re going to see some crazy new playbooks built during the next VC bubble when money is flowing freely.

6) This new generation of rep is going to be PAID.

As eyeballs on the social platforms continue to grow, so does the value of the athletes (or sellers) who know how to attract the most eyeballs. Will these types of reps be paid multiples of what today’s highest paid reps are being paid? Definitely. Will we hear about insane “contracts” that these types of reps move jobs for? Without a doubt. Will these reps be paid more than CEOs? 100%. They will make or break a business.

TAKEAWAY:

The next generation of $1M W2 sellers won't follow the SDR to AE path.

They’ll be YouTubers who decide they want to make REAL money.

When this happens, sales teams are going to get smaller.

But much, much more powerful.

Want to be a “super-rep” paid millions?

Start sharpening your video skills.

I hit rock bottom Thanksgiving 2017. I was sitting in my brother’s living room watching a Digital Marketing 101 course on my laptop. 10 minutes in I started to panic... "There is NO REASON anyone would buy us over MailChimp."

TO SET THE STAGE:

- I was 4 years into building my startup Robly Email Marketing
- We had been stuck at $3M ARR for 2 years
- We got to $3m ARR sales-led, ran out of leads
- I thought I needed to learn about marketing
- I went to DigitalMarketer(.)com and started taking courses

So I sat there on the couch, listening to Ryan Deiss talk about marketing. 

A few minutes in a bright yellow card filled the screen.

At the top it said STATEMENT OF VALUE.

Ryan said, “If you cannot fill out this card for your business, do not do ANYTHING else.” 

He said that if you cannot articulate a clear statement of value for your business… who you serve, how you help them, and why your customers should choose you… Nothing else will work.

So like any bright-eyed founder in their 20’s, I set out to conquer the card. 

60 seconds later I felt a wave of panic in my body.

My face turned red, my heart raced, my breathing accelerated.

As I looked at this VERY simple fill-in-the-blank card… 

“[PRODUCT NAME] enables [CUSTOMER] to experience [OUTCOME]”

I realized I couldn't answer it.

There was nothing I could write down for Robly, my stuck $3m ARR startup.

There was not a single reason ANY group of people would choose us if they knew about Mailchimp. 

1. We weren’t any less expensive. In fact - Mailchimp would have been FREE.
2. We were WAY behind on features, and they were building faster than us. 
3. We had no integrations, and they had over 1,000 of them.

I sat there for an hour, thinking about every customer I had spoken to over the prior 3 years, comparing what we offered them to Mailchimp.

Then a wave of nausea came over me.

Nothing had been working for me because nothing was GOING to work for me.

I didn’t sleep much that night.

At around 2am, I had an epiphany.

One that many startup founders had before me.

“I need to do something COMPLETELY different than what I’m doing right now.”

There was no way we were going to catch up to Mailchimp in the email space.

I woke up with the naive optimism that only a Founder in their 20’s can have.

I was strangely at peace with the fact that what I was working on was dead.

I needed to make a product so differentiated I could fill out this simple card.

At the time, I had no idea how long it would take…

Nor did I realize that the answer would come almost two years later, when I launched GetEmails (now Retention.com).

TAKEAWAY

Go fill out that statement of value card for your business.

Be as brutally honest with yourself as possible.

If you do not have a compelling answer.

More ads and cold email aren't going to help.

P.S.

I started a private community to help $0-1M founders find PMF. Almost everyone is struggling with the “statement of value” problem. If you want to join us, DM me.

Here's how to raise $25M in VC, get acquired and make no money (a startup case study):

YEAR 1: Initial Success and Seed Funding

John and Amy, decide to start Acme, Inc., in a niche vertical SaaS market. 

Within four months, they develop the initial software and gain early traction. 

By month six, they accept a $500K seed investment. 

Competing against a billion-dollar company with an outdated solution, they see an opportunity for disruption.

Year 1 Metrics:

- Customers: 25
- Average Revenue per Customer: $20K/year
- Total Revenue: $500K ARR
- Employees: 5 (plus contractors)
- Total Funding: $500K
- Total Expenses: $90K/month

At month 12, facing the end of their initial funds and contemplating a Series A, Amy suggests focusing on revenue growth to $1M before further funding. However, their lack of GTM experience and advice from their seed investor, lead them to pursue a Series A round...

____

YEAR 2: Growth and Series A

By month 14, Acme, Inc. secures a $6M Series A at a $40M valuation. 

The founders spend the next year building their team to drive growth.

Year 2 Metrics:

- Customers: 175
- Average Revenue per Customer: $16K/year
- Total Revenue: $2.8M ARR
- Employees: 24 (plus contractors)
- Total Funding: $6.5M
- Total Expenses: $380K/month

While they grow, they face hiring mistakes and struggle with PMF.

____

YEAR 3: Growth with Significant churn and Series B Funding

They raise an additional $18M at a $150M valuation, but are unable to accept an acquisition offer due to their high valuation.

With the new fund raise, Acme is instructed to go enterprise, compete with the larger vendors and increase their prices.

With a total of $24.5M in funding in 3 years, Acme is everyone’s favorite.

Year 3 Metrics:

- Customers: 350
- Average Revenue per Customer: $24K/year
- Total Revenue: $7.8M ARR
- Employees: 68 (plus contractors)
- Total Funding: $24.5M
- Total Expenses: $1.5M/month
- Churn: 30%

The timing is unfortunate; price increases and low end competition leads to rising churn (30%), threatening the business.

On the board’s advice, they hire a Director of CS and a 15-person CS team.

However, cost increases and churn continue to grow...

____

YEAR 4: Market Challenges and Leadership Changes

Acme, Inc.’s revenue hit $10M in its fourth year, but growth stalls shrinking their TAM. 

New competitors and a price war increase churn to 45%. 

Despite hiring a CS team to tackle churn, costs soar and churn worsens. 

Board brings in a new CEO, replacing the founders. The new CEO in turns brings in a new management team. 

____

YEAR 5: The End

None of this helped and the company accepted an offer to sell to their largest competitor for $35M that barely paid the preference shares. The founders make no money.

The investors and founders congratulate each other on Linkedin for a successful exit!

Where did the founders go wrong?

Did they raise the $6M too early?

Should they have pushed back on price increases or move to enterprise?

In 7 months, we grew RB2B to $3.5M ARR with only 5 full time employees. Here’s the new Linkedin-Led Growth startup playbook we used to grow 23% MoM (explained in under 2 minutes):
 
1. Product:

Instead of getting caught in an endless cycle of product development, we built a thin slice of value that was truly differentiated. By avoiding what existed in the market, we stayed focused on solving real problems. Unlike many other vendors, we are NOT trying to become an "all-in-one" platform.

2. Pricing: 

We wanted to build a large brand. One of the reasons we chose a self-serve GTM model is because both free and enterprise users have the same power to boost brand presence in social media. Because of our free users - we have already built a brand of over 20,000 users; generating as much UGC content/week as some of the largest brands in our space.

3. Visibility:

We prioritize GTM innovation over product innovation. We want to ensure that we stand out in the market by HOW we deliver value and not just WHAT we deliver. We prefer to make more investments into generating market visibility than into building a product. We do not believe “If you build, they will come”.

4. Product Launch:

We went from being unknown to widely recognized in a matter of weeks. Adam and I connected with over 300 decision makers in 6 weeks through 20 min credibility calls generated from Linkedin engagements. These calls weren’t for selling - they were about building trust.

5. Integrations:

Integrating with other systems is a key growth flywheel. We’ve already built 25 integrations and are adding more each month. Every new integration drives valuable user-generated content and brand impressions on social media causing demand for more integrations.

6. Team:

Our team has stayed small and focused, excelling at a few things rather than being mediocre at many. We’ve leveraged bots and one-to-many strategies. We have said no to unnecessary tasks and simplified workflows to stay lean and efficient.

7. Saying NO to revenues:

We’ve turned down customers who require extra hand-holding or support. Saying no to revenue is a secret superpower many venture-backed companies overlook—better to decline than hire a large team to fulfill revenues.

8. Community:

We have created a community around Inbound-led Outbound and bootstrapped ventures. Our growth has been driven by our community. We aim to work in public and grow alongside our community.

9. Content:

Beyond products, we’re committed to helping our community through content and coaching. We’ll openly share our learnings to help others grow. We want to see 1000+ ventures that can replicate the RB2B growth model.

P.S.

We (of course) LOVE Linkedin, but there’s only so much I can pack into a single post. That's why next week Adam Robinson hosting a live workshop with an inside look at every tactic, strategy and tool we've used to grow to $3.5M ARR in 7 months. Register here: https://lnkd.in/gwir8KHp

rows.content:
I completely butchered 2024 and nearly killed RB2B.
How? I didn't talk to customers for over 15 months.
I was too busy trying to become an "influencer".

I became everything I hated about founders building a personal brand.

I completely lost touch with the customer, and our product suffered.

Our MONTHLY churn rate hit 15% last Thanksgiving… and I celebrated that as great content 🤦

How badly did I mess up?

- 15% monthly churn = 99% of customers gone within 12mos (we could be at $10m ARR!)
- I was spending 4+ hours daily on content vs 0 minutes with customers
- I had 47 podcast appearances scheduled but couldn't name our top 3 customer pain points
- I spent Q3 + Q4 creating courses/community instead of going deep with our 1,500 paying customers on how to be better

———

My come-to-Jesus moment was in June at our quarterly planning in Toronto.

I was asked to give a resource audit on RB2B.

I realized that MOST of what I was spending my time on was working AGAINST the only thing that would get us to $10m ARR.

I wasn’t talking to customers.

I was posting hot takes and going on podcasts…

Then trying to get intel from team members who were talking with customers.

Here’s the problem with that strategy:

If you’re not PART of the conversations, hearing the frustration in people’s voices, observing the micro-expressions on faces as they say what they say…

- You’re out of touch
- You miss a HUGE amount of meaning
- You can’t make the call on what to build or fix next

———

That night in Toronto I was sick to my stomach.

The way I was spending my time and running my org was wrong.

I couldn’t sleep - regret, anxiety, shame overwhelmed me.

I was making such a basic error for such a long time, unable to see it.

Our product was suffering, and our churn was so bad that it would be borderline IMPOSSIBLE to grow any more.

I knew I had to make BIG CHANGES:

1. We shrunk the team and removed the layer between me and the customers
2. Robb and I created an onboarding flow that asks tier 1 users on the 21st day if they’d like to have a 15min call (see template below)
3. I spend 30m/day reviewing support tickets with Robb (and improving Finn’s responses)

THE RESULT:

- My Wednesday afternoons are packed with video calls with REAL tier 1 customers explaining REAL pain that I want to fix
- I’m reviewing 100s of support tickets every week with Robb

But the biggest difference?

I now have an EMOTIONAL connection with the pain are customers are experiencing when they use our product.

Which is the driving the total product transformation we’re undergoing.

TAKEAWAY

If you're a SaaS Founders reading this, don't make the same mistake I did.

Don't optimize for vanity metrics (followers, likes, podcast appearances).

Focus on the only metric that matters: customer retention.

Jason Lemkin has said this before…

Your LinkedIn engagement is inversely correlated with your product quality.

Stop posting. Start talking to customers.

Your business depends on it.

The future of high-growth startups isn’t Product Led or Sales Led.

The best companies will need to find a way to combine BOTH.

I have had the fortune of developing GTM teams that leveraged both PLG and SLG capabilities.

Here are 5 tips if you want to do the same:

BACKGROUND:

There are several reasons why you may want to add PLG capabilities to your enterprise sales team or add an enterprise sales team to your Product Led sales process. 

1. Why PLG - PLG is not just an inexpensive GTM strategy deployed by startups, many large enterprises use PLG as well. PLG is how modern buyers want to buy software. PLG revenues are prone to churn and in attracting low quality customers.  

2. Why SLG - Sales led growth on the other hand can lead to much higher quality revenue with lower churn. If a company has both these strategies, it is likely that sales team will also close far more revenues than the PLG team. 

3. Org Design - I have seen PLG teams reporting into Growth or Marketing given the need for constant growth hacks and product changes to keep growing. It has never worked out well. All revenue should report into VP of Sales or CRO irrespective of whether it is sales led or product led.

4. Land and Expand - With PLG, you land into the company with individual bottoms up adoption. The goal is to keep expanding into that organization with PLG nurture. Once you get 10-15% adoption, it’s time to go after the team leader/manager and do top down selling to expand. If there are multiple teams signed up than it is time to have a conversation with the VP and go after a MSA.  

5. Brand - Vendors with Freemiums and Product led sales often results in a much superior brand than their counterparts. The reason is simple. It’s much easier to get 100,000 freemium or $50/mo users than 1000 users paying $500/mo. This creates immense brand heat on social media if the PLG users are incentivized to create UGC posts. 

TAKEAWAYS:

Most successful PLG companies also have enterprise sales teams. 

(just look them up on Linkedin) 

So, stop asking yourself PLG or Sales led?

Just do both

If possible try to have pricing that goes all the way from freemium → $99/mo → $1000/mo → $250K+ annual 

Most revenue will come from higher end pricing but a bulk of the brand (and pipeline) will be built by self-serve pricing 

Land and Expand GTM strategy can be used to systematically penetrate and grow in large enterprises.

The HARDEST thing about being a founder is that you need to maintain absolute conviction, while keeping an open mind that you might be 100% wrong. Last quarter, I bet RB2B’s entire future on a new idea. “This is it. This is how we’ll get to $20M ARR. Nobody else is doing it.” Then two months later, I abandoned it completely. Here’s what happened:

RB2B churn is mizz.

It needs to be something very different than it is to grow past $5m ARR.

Nick Weldon (Founder of 5x5) and I came up with the idea of always-on display ad product for SMB B2Bs.

AI-generated ads that marketers KNEW were being shown to rep’s target accounts. 

Kind of like a person-level Demandbase for the little guy.

We spent all morning on it, and celebrated with some steak tacos. 

I scootered back to my office and could hardly contain my excitement.

“THIS is going to be my path to $20m ARR," I told myself.

I spent the next week mapping out the details of what I was trying to create. 

MORE importantly, I made a list of people to speak to who were EXPERTS on the ads ecosystem. 

The biggest names out there. 

Gabe, the CEO of Demandbase. Chris Walker. Dimitri, CEO of Influ2. Gil, CEO of Metadata.

I was flying high into my first conversation, which was with Chris Walker. 

I pitched him my entire walk home from my office, and as I walked into my back yard, I finished, and waited for him to respond.

There was an uncomfortable pause.

“I really just DON’T like the idea at all.” 

I felt like I got punched in the gut. 

I respect Chris’s opinion A LOT, but he’s not the end-all-be-all, so I went on with my calls the next two weeks. 

What happened?

I have NEVER had that universally NEGATIVE feedback about a product idea.

––––

So, I decided to kill the idea.

The same idea that was my ENTIRE WORLD for the prior month or so. 

All my hope, all my inspiration, all my dreams.

Here’s the crazy thing… I felt real loss when I killed it.

A light sadness in my chest for about the next week or so… As if a thing I had before was gone.

I had internalized the success of the product - and what it would have added to my life - even before we started building anything. 

Startups are so hard. 

I think you have to internalize success before you start to have CLOSE to enough energy to do what it takes to get something off the ground.

But at the same time, you have to be willing to change your mind completely if the world tells you it doesn’t want what you’re making.

Average founders aren't willing to accept that nobody wants what they’re building. 

They push out a product nobody wants, and their entire life is a grind. 

The best founders do the opposite. 

Strong convictions, loosely held. 

And you just keep swinging.

Founders think the biggest risk of VC money is running out of cash and making nothing. It’s not. It’s getting trapped—stuck running a successful business into the ground, chasing an exit that will never come. And making nothing. Here are two $50-100M examples that prove it:

This company ACT-ON (see below) raised $53m:

- 17 years later they sold for $53m to a SPAC 
- 20% was cash, the rest was stock
- 2x Revenue multiple

As Jason M. Lemkin said the other day… 

"Just plain tough."

Now, let's look at Keap (formerly Infusionsoft).

- Raised $100m
- Acquired 23 years later for $80m 
- Under 1x Revenue 

Rough. 

Why do I advocate for bootstrapping? 

Compare those two outcomes to another startup...

Maropost - bootstrapped by Ross Andrew Paquette in the same marketing automation space - but he did it right.

Check out these Maropost stats: 

- Founded 2011
- $0-$30m ARR in 5 years 2011-2015
- $20m+ EBITDA 2015-2022 (Straight to founder)
- 2022 Roll-up strategy >>> more EBITDA (to founder)

The first time I heard what Ross had done seven years ago, I made it my goal in life to accomplish something like it.

The idea of generating massive amounts of cash and answering to nobody was so appealing for so many reasons.

And we’re not quite there yet, but we’re getting close. 

TAKEAWAY

Nothing is more exciting in the life of a young founder than closing a huge round at a monster valuation. 

It’s impossible to not feel rich, even if you didn’t take secondary (and most don’t).

Let me tell you what no young founder ever thinks about… 

The ACT-ON/Infusionsoft outcome.

You work for 20 years, sell for less than you raised, and walk away with nothing.

And for every ACT-ON and Infusionsoft that hit the tape, there are another 1,000 zombies … 

Who have raised WAY too much with no way out. 

I would love to ask the founders of either company one question and one question only…

“Wouldn’t you have rather done it like Maropost?”

“SEO takes 12 months to show results.” That’s the lie every marketer tells themselves. I asked our new SEO hire Sam Dunning what he’d do if he had 90 days to start CRUSHING competitors with organic search. Here's his 7-step plan:

1. Start where we win already

Drill down into the top aspect of your product & industries you serve best and use cases that you have sold well into historically, solve expensive problems for and have demand for.

2. Build a moat like no other

Map out every way that a prospect could search for your offering, compare vendors/alternatives, look for use cases/integrations etc. when they are in buying mode for our solution.

3. Craft and improve

Build pages for each of the above. Look what type of page (article, listicle, landing page) ranks already and blow it out the water. Fuel your page copy with customer research, unique stats product visuals, proof points, or reporting and address tough questions from sales calls. Ensure each page goes into detail and is chunked up (e.g. for use case or industry pages to serve up niche specific content that can be served in LLMs). 

4. The cheat code for LLMs (listicles)

Find every website “Top X software” listicle for your niche. Reach out to the author of each and offer them a sweetener to include your brand (and a backlink is a bonus).

You could offer to have them on your own listicle, offer a podcast slot, service exchange, social shoutout, etc. Some are pay to play. Many are up for value trade.

Make sure you build your own listicles for each competitor alternative term, best X software term, etc. Again craft yours to blow current pages out the water and chunk up to be easily digestible for LLMs on searches into offering/use cases etc.

5. Leverage past media

Find an exec from your team that’s done a lot of press, podcasts etc. Put their Linkedin profile url into an SEO tool. Reach out to all relevant sites citing them that did not give you a brand mention or backlink to amend article. This is a huge quick win.

6. Control the narrative

Google & LLMs love to cite Reddit and Quora. Start being helpful on relevant threads. Only mention your brand where it’s relevant. Start guesting on the top podcasts in your industry. Focus on a useful show for your ICP. Ask hosts to mention your brand and a backlink in the published article. If you can do all this and have resources for your own YouTube channel and podcast great, if not, prioritize the above tasks.

7. Speed beats slow moving giants

Do all the above with speed and you will chip away at giant slow-moving competitors. They have slow approval processes with layers of management, legal etc. Speed will be your unfair advantage.

Join us tomorrow on Unf*ck My Startup LIVE (3pm ET) and Sam will give you the exact blueprint for optimizing your content, technical foundation, and link-building efforts for rapid SEO results.

We just spent $150k to fly 38 employees out to NYC for a 72 hour AI hackathon. Why? Because I’m terrified the AI-native 2027 version of Retention.com ($20m ARR, 35 FTE) looks nothing like the business today and if I don't build it we're screwed.

As Diane from ApplyAI so elegantly put it: 

“If you do not build the AI-native version of your business, some young, hungry founder will… and they are out there trying as we speak.” 

Yikes.

———

I believe all mature SaaS with people and processes have to completely transform themselves, else they will die a slow death (as MANY SaaS are right now, some know it, some don’t).

I also believe the effort has to be grassroots. The totalitarian approach won’t work because people at the top are out of touch with the actual work that gets done. 

I thought going into this that a year ago most of our team probably wasn’t using AI for anything. 

By mid-2025 they had become fluent with ChatGPT, but most weren’t building agents to automate repetitive work. 

And most of us are unaware of what’s possible… me included. 

I’m not sure exactly how long we all have, or if there is a definitive moment where if you haven’t achieved transformation you will suddenly implode. 

The more likely scenario is the mature companies stall-out and enter a slow melt phase, while super-lean, AI-native startups solving overlapping problems flatten every market with point solutions that collectively solve the incumbents whole problem for 1/50th of the cost (and 1/1000th of the team).

———

How do you level up your team? 

I’ll tell you how we’re trying to do it. 

BEGINNER PHASE: 

- Understanding how to prompt effectively and the contrast between good and bad prompting
- Familiarity with types of work LLMs are well suited for and what they’re not
- The limitations of LLMs, how confidently they can be wrong, how to check them

INTERMEDIATE PHASE: 

- Time audits identifying work that is both repetitive and aligns well with LLMs strength
- Familiarizing team w/ workflow builder that meets their technical appetite (zapier/n8n)
- Getting them comfortable trading imperfection for 100x efficiency

ADVANCED PHASE: 

- The design (but not necessarily development) of increasingly complex workflows
- Every task and process gets the same scrutiny - “can AI handle this”
- All roles evolve from doing things to monitoring and improving machines

Most people get tripped up between intermediate and advanced because they go down rabbit holes of a 20 part course on how to use n8n rather than understanding what’s possible, designing, and getting someone else to build.

———

TAKEAWAY

If I don’t build the 2027 AI-native version of my business, I’m screwed. 

If you don’t do the same with yours, you’re screwed too. 

What’s the only difference between you and me? 

I realize there’s a dozen YC kids working 9/9/6 trying to eat my lunch. 

Do you?

You just have to keep building.

Last week I was at an 8-person founder breakfast in Aspen. Guy goes around the table and asks everyone how they're using AI day-to-day. I was super embarrassed to answer the question, but I did.

Me: “I don’t.” 

Everybody looked at me like I had five heads. 

The guy sitting next to me said he uploaded his DISC personality test to Claude and used it as a thought partner to identify blind spots on his way to work, someone else stacked agents on agents to run their entire GTM…

You get the point. 

I mean I’ve tried. I try to use Claude to help me with posts for a while, then I stop. I try to use it as a thought partner to help me with strategic things, then I stop. I read an article about how if you just use it for 1h/day for a year you will understand the gravity of what’s coming. I’d do that for two days, then stop. 

When I walked out of that breakfast, I shared my embarrassment with one of the Founders at the table. 

He posed a pretty interesting question. 

“Maybe we should all be asking ourselves how you are running your life in such a way where you can be super high leverage WITHOUT using AI.” 

I thought about that for a while....

Many people think it’s nuts that I’m a CEO of a $30m ARR SaaS and don’t have an executive assistant. But I ask people why they have them: 

“They book my travel” (well I don’t travel much)
“They schedule my meetings” (I use Calendly)
“They do my personal errands” (I don’t even know what this means)
“They handle my email” (I don’t want someone to handle my email) 

I think I’ve managed to simplify my work life to the point where I feel like I don’t need much help or many more tools. 

On Monday, I’m in internal meetings all day. 
On Tuesday, I write posts and make content. 
On Wednesday morning, I have a marketing meeting. 

The rest of the week is trying to figure out what’s next. 

What’s the takeaway? 

That guy who asked me what I was doing different may have been on to something. 

What if half the things people use AI for never ACTUALLY needed to be done in the first place? 

Maybe the best tool is a simple life.

Sam Parr: My friend sold his startup for $1b and only cleared $3m (pre-tax). 

Me: What?!? How???

Sam: He raised $400m of VC from Seed to Series E and had 4 co-founders. 1.2% total founder ownership after employee options.

Me: And he didn’t take any secondary? 

Sam: Nothing meaningful. He didn’t have the leverage.

Me: That sucks. 

Sam: Tell me about it.

Me: You talk to TONS of wealthy entrepreneurs about how they did it. How do you avoid having this happen to you? 

Sam: The problem with VC is that you are signing up to ultimately own 10% or less of something that has a 70% or greater chance of failing. If you just don’t raise, or raise as little as possible, the odds that you will have something smaller, own most or all of it, that has a much higher chance of succeeding… And be wealthy… are much higher.

Me: Have you ever taken VC? 

Sam: Nobody would invest in The Hustle, which felt horrible at the time, but ended up being incredible for me personally. I sold it for more than what you see on the internet (which is high 20mm’s FWIW), bought the S&P index with the money (which is up 45% since I sold), and didn’t have to give anything to any investors. So I look like a genius compared to my $3m friend.

Me: Would you take VC now? 

Sam: Now I would use VC money, but I’m post liquidity. I would want to really try for something big, and it wouldn’t really crush me if I wasted a decade on something that failed. Pre-liquidity it would have.

Me: What does “post-liquidity” mean? 

Sam: I asked a bunch of wealthy friends how much money they spent. One guy who I really respected said $600k. I divided that by 3%, and it gave me $20m. After The Hustle, I cleared $20m and then some. So, that, for me, is “post-liquidity”. 

Me: So you think no VC until post-liquidity? 

Sam: Some businesses absolutely require VC. I invested in a robotics company that used a TON of capital and made the founder a billionaire. But, in general, if you want to get wealthy, use little or no investor money.

Me: Fair. One more thing. 

Sam: What’s that? 

Me: Asking for a friend… How does someone who bootstrapped $25m ARR and going to do $14m in profit this year get on My First Million? 

Sam (smiling): email me … and come up with the angle!

In 27 months, we grew Retention.com from $1M-$13M ARR with only 1 salesperson (me) doing 1,000's of sales calls. Here are my 10 biggest pieces of advice for any startup who wants to book and close more sales calls:

1. Ask for 15 mins, but book 30

When booking a meeting outbound, you have a better shot at getting a meeting by asking for 15 mins than 30. You may have piqued their interest but with a busy schedule, they are going to weigh learning about your business vs their time. Ask for 15 but send a meeting invite for 30.  If they can’t do the full 30, they will let you know, but from my experience, this rarely happens.

2. Tell your story

People remember a story more than a product  Figure out your short story that you can tell prior to getting into the product pitch. How does your story connect to your business / product? 

3. 5X5 Pitch

Keep your product deck for your initial call to 5 slides / 5 minutes and make sure you answer any of the common questions you get from prospects. You can always book a follow up call to share more detail once you hook their interest.

4. Always Be Pitching

Take control of the call and the sales cycle. You will only learn what does and doesn’t work by actually pitching.  

5. Tell a customer story

Again, people remember stories more than they do stats. Tell a story of a customer before implementing your product and the business outcome after implementing it. Don’t just talk numbers. Talk about how people felt, what they said, etc.

6. Create Urgency

Attach an incentive if the deal is done by the end of the week or month.  (Example: 20% more credits or a 15% discount)  This also sets you up well for follow up as it now makes them feel like you are on their team to try and help them get the deal in for their benefit.

7. Land and expand

We all want to close the big ACV deals, but the truth is most buyers don’t want to make a big commitment without seeing how your product works. Find a way to get them on for a small $ amount, with the plan to expand if the product meets their expectations.

8. Opt-Out Period

Reduce buyer friction by offering a 90 day opt out period if you are trying to close 12 month agreements. It shows confidence that your product will drive the results you say it will.

9. Deck Recap

Create a 1-2 pager highlighting the most important parts of your sales deck that you can send via email after every call (even if they don’t ask for it). The prospect won’t remember all details from the call, so this gives them something to look back on and will help sell internally if other stakeholders are involved.

10. Video for FAQs

Create short form talking head video answering all FAQs. This will add value in your follow up, show you listened to the questions they had and that you care about making sure they understand the answers. It also helps internally as others will likely have the same questions as the person on the phone.

Have questions about how to book/close more calls?

AMA anything 👇

We used Clay + Claude Code + Apify to launch a multi-channel outbound system that self-improves over time. Here's the actual process Alex Fine🌲 and Understory built for us:

Step 1: They fed 569 demo call transcripts into Claude Code via the Fireflies API to extract competitive signal: which tools kept coming up, what specific language frustrated prospects used, what objections stalled deals, and what made someone stay on the call.

Step 2: Claude analyzed all 569 calls and built a competitor displacement map. Nine competitors ranked by how often they appeared and how dissatisfied those prospects actually were, based on the exact words they used. 

Step 3: Every transcript, intake form, strategy session, and past campaign result got indexed into a structured knowledge base. It updates automatically every time a new call comes in. The system gets smarter with every interaction.

Step 4: They connected Apify directly into Claude Code via MCP. Claude identified the right actor, pulled unique data on decision-makers at companies actively using those high-displacement competitor tools, and pushed 9,000+ contacts to a webhook automatically. Absolutely no manual list building.

Step 5: That webhook dropped everything straight into Clay. They enriched, validated, and segmented by firmographic signals and intent data.

Step 6: They wrote the copy based on everything the knowledge base surfaced. Messaging built around the exact language our target prospects use when they're unhappy with a competitor. Every version synced live to Google Docs via the Google MCP so we could see and edit in real time.

Step 7: Campaigns launched via Instantly for email and HeyReach for LinkedIn. Every reply, positive, negative, or neutral, gets analyzed and fed back into the knowledge base. Every LinkedIn response. Every new demo call that books. Claude re-analyzes what resonated, what didn't, and why. The brief updates automatically. The next campaign starts with sharper targeting, better messaging, and fresher signal than the one before it.

Campaign 2 starts smarter than Campaign 1. 
Campaign 3 smarter than Campaign 2. 

The results already prove it!

Most agencies finish a campaign and start the next one from scratch.

In the last 30 days, RB2B’s churn has gone from 9.1%/mo to a STILL HORRIBLE 8.8% (down from 15%/mo last September). I’m incredibly confused about what to do next. Here’s why:

1. RB2B is a high-churn product category with a high-churn persona and a high-churn GTM motion (freemium, no sales, no onboarding, etc)

2. The category is also plagued with issues:

- You can’t book a demo by spamming a site visitor
- You can’t book a demo from a site visit if you can’t outbound in the first place
- A low % of traffic is ICP, for most people it’s not a channel on its own

Product improvement is the only REAL way to reduce churn.

So we need to keep improving.

But, how?

———

Product improvement for RB2B is what I’m confused about.

There’s an obvious feature set that the product person in me wants to build:

It’s “RB2B handles the whole site visitor workflow”.

Meaning - someone hits the site, we:

1. Filter for ICP using AI
2. Provide additional qualified contacts at the account
3. Do AI research for personalization
4. AI writes the copy for the sequence
5. We send the LI connection and messages

And if we built that, it would be better to rebuild RB2B from scratch.

———

I think it’s easy to understand why I think that’s what RB2B “should” be.

Here’s why I’m confused:

If you properly filter for ICP, it will eliminate 90% of site visitors.

For MOST of our customers, that would cut lead count.

For the few who are larger, the workflow described above COULD work…

But high-traffic sites want a bunch of OTHER signals to get demos.

Then once we added the OTHER signals and a workflow builder, we would be in direct competition with (and trying to sell to the same GTM teams as) Common Room, Unify, Warmly…

…and the scariest of all, Clay.

No thank you.

———

So what are we going to do?

Rather than compete with the companies who are owning workflows, we are going to try to power them.

1. We’re creating an OEM product where you can put our pixel inside your own and have RB2B’s identity inside your own app

I’ve bootstrapped $0 to $1M ARR three times. If I had to start over with no money and no personal brand, here’s how I’d hit $1M ARR in under 12 months:

1. Hunt whales in their natural habitat.

Alina Vandenberghe told us on UnF*ck My Startup that she went to sales meetups and showed the people in the room who looked like they knew everybody a diagram of what she wanted to build (now $40m ARR Chilipiper). She asked if they’d buy, if not, what else would they need. Then she built it.

2. Turn your journey into content.

The indirect benefit of an audience rooting for you comes in the form of “pull” (rather than push) recruiting, a customer base who are also fans, and improved content creation skills as time goes on. B2B companies are transitioning to a Kardashian era. You may think it's cringe, but it is the future.

3. I’d test different offers with cold email. 

My good friend Nick Weldon loves to say 5x5’s product was not great, but their offer was incredible. High response rates to cold email - even if you don’t have the product yet - can help you nail your packaging and messaging.

4. Obsess over word-of-mouth like your life depends on it (because it does).

If you have word-of-mouth, everything you do will work. If you do not have word-of-mouth, nothing you do will work. How do you get word-of-mouth? Product-market fit. Deliver more value, quicker, for less money, with less friction, until you have a wave of inbound. 

5. Ignore every “growth hack” until step 4 is bulletproof.

This is where I see founders waste the most time and energy. “Growth hacking” works for companies with product-market fit ONLY BECAUSE they have product-market fit. Save yourself the heartache. Stop focusing on button colors and 30 part email flows. Focus on giving more, better, faster.

6. Don’t hire ANYONE.

Most software businesses are capable of getting to $1m ARR with the founders alone, ESPECIALLY with AI. RB2B is currently at $6.3m ARR - we only have 3 FTE’s. You absolutely can do this too.

TAKEAWAY

I’ve gone $0-$1m ARR 3 times.

Each time twice as fast with half the resources. 

It’s not because I got smarter… 

It’s because I learned what NOT to waste time on. 

The fastest path to $1m ARR isn’t a secret framework.

It’s being 1% better - at the RIGHT things - every single day.

Massive success is inside of you. 

You just need to find it.

Keep building.

One year ago our churn was over 15%/mo. I was focused on Founder Brand, one-to-many selling, and building a community. Jonathan Shuster, DM’d me and said there was one OBVIOUS thing I was ignoring completely:

Actually talking to my customers. 

(This seems so idiotic in hindsight I’m embarrassed to be even write this)

I finally linked up with Jonathan this summer.

He helped me put together a low-lift churn study and set up a regular cadence of customer interviews. 

While it hasn’t come close to solving the churn problem, it has helped churn, and made me feel much better about the direction we’re going with RB2B. 

Here’s Jonathan’s 5-step guide on who to interview and what to say: 

1. Find your BEST customers. 

- Dig into intercom, stripe, baremetrics, or whatever else you have to find your longest-standing, high LTV customers.
- Pull 35-50 people out of that segment to ask for an interview
- Send them a one-to-one email asking them if they’d talk to you (the CEO) about the product for 15min
- Line up 5 interviews. More than 5 and you will start hearing the same thing over and over again.
- See my copy below (image)

2. Find a few of your your churned customers who you THOUGHT should be high-LTV.

- Enrich your customer list by revenue, industry, employee count, web traffic, and whatever else you use to determine ICP fit
- Find 35-50 churned customers that match your ICP
- Send them an email that says “I am the founder of RB2B and I really, really, really want to understand why you churned. Would you be willing to hop on a 10 min call to discuss?”
- Line up 5 interviews (you only need 5)

3. Ask your best customers five questions like these (modify them for your product)

-  Why did you choose us versus the other solutions out there? What's the rest of your stack look like?
- If we were to disappear tomorrow and you couldn't have us, what would you do?
- When you find a good lead/visitor, how do you know it's a good match?
- What do you do when you find a good lead? How do you route it?
- What do you do when you find a bad lead?

4. Ask your churned customers the following q’s (modified for your biz): 

- How'd you choose to evaluate us? Where'd you hear about us?
- Do you use anyone else to solve this problem now?
- Be brutally honest, what didn't work?
- How do you figure out what is a good vs bad lead
- What would make it so you could use us again?

5. Determine your product roadmap based on what you’re not doing that people want, and your marketing message based on what you ARE doing that people love. 

TAKEAWAY

Most founders will read this, nod along, and never actually do it. 

They'll tell themselves they're too busy building, or that they already 'know' their customers.

Don't be that founder.

Block off 2 hours this week, send those emails, and have those conversations.

Your solutions to churn are hiding in plain sight. 

You just need to ask.

We’re launching a new brand for RB2B in January. My whole team hates it. Here’s why they’re wrong:

To set the stage: 

- Eli Rubel asked to redo our $79 webflow website that is full of typos
- I told him “nah, this thing is all we need, and I am too lazy to fix things”
- He did one for Dave (which I like, even though it’s not ugly)
- DG told me I should let him do my brand
- So we’ve been on a journey, that started off with me saying... “I want NAILS ON CHALKBOARD”

Here are the 4 things most people in SaaS get wrong about brand:

1. The best branding is about pattern interrupt. 

Seth Godin said that Silk (non-dairy milk) wasn’t selling until they put it in the refrigerator section next to milk. Why? Because on the shelf it was “milk alternative, milk alternative, milk alternative.” In the refrigerator section, it was “milk, milk, milk, NOT MILK.” 

This is how people are wired. 

2. Everybody tries to copy whatever the hottest VC-backed SaaS brand just did. 

The easiest way to not be remembered is to copy - or emulate - branding that is prevalent at the time. It’s tempting to do - and maybe I’d think about it if I knew I had to raise money - but the MOST impactful thing is to be MEMORABLE, and the way you become memorable is to look like nothing before you. 

Anybody remember Mailchimp’s yellow rebrand in 2018? Legendary.

3. It’s OK if the brand image makes you feel uncomfortable or icky inside.

New things don’t feel good. Most of us love more of the same, even though we think we do not, because there is great comfort in familiarity. My team hates the fact that I seek a brand that puts you in a place of unease when you see it for the first time (or second, or third).

4. Your brand story is critically important (but it’s not the story you think it is)

Brand isn’t the story that Oatly writes on the back of their milk carton. Brand is the story that gets told about your company, behind your back, when no involved party is around. Earlier today I got forwarded a text from a founder that said he LOVED both my content and how I was creating a whole new generation of bootstrapped founders. 

RB2B’s REAL Brand Story? That.

TAKEAWAY:

During our first call, the NoBoringDesign team asked me what I was looking for. 

I said, “I’m not sure … but I’ll tell you what I want the OPPOSITE of.” 

…then I shared my screen and typed www(.)6sense(.)com

So where did we end up? 

Time will tell. 

But - this is the logo. I think it’s badass. 

But… like I said earlier… My team hates it. 

Which makes me love it even more.

Nails. On. Chalkboard.

Stay tuned…

There's a new gold rush in SaaS and it’s happening now. Here's the new AI playbook for building SaaS startups to $5M in ARR (with 5 FTEs):

Take a legacy SaaS tool, add a layer of AI, slash the price and run it lean. 

The founders who do this will cause MAJOR DISRUPTIONS next year.

Here's the 9 steps to follow:

1. Find a legacy SaaS app with the following characteristics: 	

- Workflow automation, business process management, customer engagement
- Preferably in a market niche
- High Margin/Expensive

2. Find a way to inject AI:

- Improve data collection using AI
- Automate repetitive tasks and optimize workflows
- Enhance personalization, improve analytics, enable predictive decision making
- Identify new revenue opportunities using customer data
- Automate mundane tasks using RPA or better information extraction 

3. Build the app in weeks

- Use rapid app development environment or AI code generators to create your app in weeks not months
- I recently caught up with Jason Masciarelli from Pega Launchpad. Sounds like a terrific opportunity to cut down on dev time and cost to build a workflow automation tool. 

4. Innovate on Pricing

- Significantly lower SaaS pricing
- Explore usage based pricing or outcome based pricing

5. Content and Thought Leadership

- Position your app as a modern and efficient market substitute to legacy apps
- Highlight the AI related optimizations and demonstrate
- Mention the lower price and it’s impact on ROI
- Ensure your buyers are receiving your content on Linkedin

6. Design efficient GTM

- Don’t plan on hiring an enterprise sales team
- Consider self serve GTM
- Get early customers via Linkedin content and prior relationships

7. Don’t hire a large Support or CS team

- Use as much automation as possible for support and CS
- Try to serve 1000+ paid accounts with just 1 support staff  
- Say NO to revenues that dont fit your initial business model

8. Org Design

- Keep the team as small as you can
- Don’t hire any VPs or senior folks for a long time
- Hire a lot of fractional contractors, advisors or ICs

9. Capitalization

- Bootstrap if you can, but you don’t have to
- If you raise capital, find investors that care about efficiency and small exits
- Do not take on the burden of large exit until you know that’s possible
- Prioritize revenues. Pursue lean and profitable growth strategies 

By executing on this playbook, you could achieve a few million in revenue profitably with a lean team (<5 FTEs) in a year or two and possibly even an acquisition offer from a legacy app vendor. 

If you choose to scale further, you will have the option to secure a large investment from a growth fund to embark on your journey to scale at your terms.

CEO Friend: My bootstrapped healthcare startup just crossed $3M ARR. We’re still only the 4 co-founders. I think we can raise $10m at $70-80m valuation. Should I do it?  

Me: What are you going to do with the money? 

CEO: We are getting our asses kicked by our heavily funded competitors who all have 30-50 person sales teams. We’re just grinding right now and getting out-sold … So, we were thinking we’d just hire a bunch of salespeople as fast as possible.

Me: I don’t hate using external funding with strong PMF - which you clearly have - to accelerate growth. But if you do what you’re planning to do, you’ll get smoked.

CEO: Why do you say that? 

Me: Two main reasons. One is there is a big difference between a product that sells and a sales machine. Hiring, training, and retaining productive reps is a totally different business than you 4 pushing product out the door. 

CEO: That makes sense. What’s the other reason? 

Me: Everybody underestimates the magic of the Founder Selling. It’s impossible to quantify until you get other people in there doing the job instead. 

CEO: You’re probably right. But we need to figure it out, and we need some money.

Me: Yes - but do you need THAT MUCH money? To let’s say … create a small pod and at least start to figure out what it looks like to hire a rep and ramp them to productivity.

CEO: No … not $10m. I could probably do it with $500k or so. But I still need the $500k. 

Me: If that’s the case, I’d use non-dilutive funding from someone like Nathan Latka at Founderpath, and stay bootstrapped. Flesh out your repeatable sales model, get to $10m ARR, then if you want to do a big raise, go even bigger than $10m. Or, if you’re growing fast enough, stay bootstrapped!

CEO: That sounds like a pretty good option. Hook it up!

1. Go to EVERY industry event

Alina’s co-founder (and husband) Nicolas went to every single B2B event they could find in the NYC area.

Pro Tip: After a certain amount of times that someone sees your face, people will feel like they know you. So just keep going to events in your industry.

2. Target influencers in advance

If you can get a list of attendees, figure out who has large, engaged followings, and make sure you speak to them before you leave the event. 

3. Identify influencers at the event. 

Observe the event attendees. Find the people who always seem to have people around them, no matter where they move in the room. Is someone hugging people more often than anyone else? Go talk to them. They are a hyper-connector.

4. Show them your doodle and ask for feedback. 

Before they had ANYTHING Nicolas was holding up a notepad with a drawing of what Chili Piper was planning to build, and asking if the influencer would buy it, and most importantly, if they wouldn’t, why not. 

Pro Tip: Alina said she asks as many questions as humanly possible, which informs what they are doing, or plan to do.

5. Once you have a product, get the influencer to use it. 

It is far better to get them to buy it, but if they won’t, free is better than nothing. Your product HAS to be valuable and different, but if it is, and it works, these people will talk about it, which is the entire strategy. 

BONUS: People lie on Zoom calls, so you need in-person meetups.

Alina prefers this in-person strategy because she believes that because of the camera or recording, people are unwilling to deliver the brutal truth necessary to create great products. 

Yes, it takes time to go to events, but it saves SO MUCH TIME getting to the core of what you need to be building.

________

Here's a real-world example of how this worked:

Kevin "KD" Dorsey was one of the early influencers that used Chili Piper, he saw immediate value, and talked about it to everybody he knew just because he thought it was awesome. Since then, more influencers in the ecosystem have adopted Chili Piper, and this strategy continues to drive their acquisition engine.

________

I'm sure many of you are thinking... 

“I could NEVER walk up to someone like that at an event”. 

I know how you feel. 

I felt the same way.

I used to go to events and be TERRIFIED of speaking to people.

Alina said she felt the same until she read a book called "Non-Violent Communication", which flipped her from an introvert to an extrovert. 

After I heard her that, I immediately went out and bought the book.

Because I think we all need to be implementing her playbook.

It's timeless and will work forever (no matter your product).

Cold emails and social media will only get you so far.

Build relationships IRL.

Most first-time startup founders I talk to set themselves up to fail. Here are the 7 biggest mistakes I see nearly EVERY founder make (myself included):

1. You spend too much money on things you don’t really need

People love getting offices, hiring salespeople, getting VA’s, expensive video equipment, software, and even setting up an entity pre-revenue. In 2013, I bought a VOIP phone system a year before we had a customer! Cash will be EXTREMELY tight at some point, even if it’s not now. Remember that.

2. Hiring people before $1m ARR

This is a hot take. I think there should be a technical co-founder building and a business co-founder doing sales, marketing, and support until $1m ARR - just like Klaviyo did. If you have that discipline, you will be profitable, control your destiny, and emerge with product-market fit.

3. Thinking you are an “ideas guy” and can find an operator

I spit out my drink when I hear this. Just like when I hear someone talking about “stealth mode”. Thinking someone will do the hard work for you at this nearly impossible stage is delusional. Once you get to $10m ARR with under 10 people, you earned it, but until then, no way.

4. Not “doing things that don’t scale” under $1m ARR

First-time founders don't understand how manual getting to $1-$3m ARR is. It’s face-to-face conversations, however you can get them, taking the feedback, and improving product as quickly as possible. Nothing will work until the product is great, so all that “growth hacking” will be a waste of time and money.

5. Thinking seed funding means you have a good business

If you were able to raise money for your idea pre-revenue, it means nothing more than you could sell a vision to investors. The hard part is making a business out of it. Keep that in mind and avoid funding at all costs. You’ll thank me later.

6. Not posting on organic social media starting TODAY

This one took me a decade to realize, and a year after I started to master. Nothing is more powerful in today’s world than being able to create great organic social media content that your prospects have demand for independent of what you’re selling. If you start today, you’ll get zero engagement, followers, or leads, but that’s not the point… You’re one day closer to finding your voice.

7. Thinking you’ll be in and out in 3-5 years

Founders should have a decades long time horizon when they start. People wildly overestimate what they can accomplish in a year, but wildly underestimate what they can accomplish over a decade.

TAKEAWAY:

Being a first-time founder is hard.

Literally everything is working against you.

If we knew how hard it was, most would never start.

But here’s the good news...

As Alex Hormozi so elegantly put it:

Every successful person started with:

0 revenue
0 subscribers
0 customers
0 fans

And the only difference between them and everyone else is they actually start.

But that’s not REALLY the secret.

The successful ones not only start…

They keep building.

If I were starting an AI company, I would not aim for a $1B exit. VCs will hate this, but I think the new startup model looks like this:

In this 1,000 word post I’m going to cover:

1. Bootstrap vs Venture Capital
2. The 4 skills that matter now
3. Where the biggest opportunities are
4. How you should go to market
5. What success looks like

INTRODUCTION

In 2025, what should be the goal of starting a new venture?

Simple.

Generate +$10m ARR with less employees than fingers on one hand.

Either sell that company, or replace yourself, take some time off, and do it again. And again. 

Why?

Because the relative attractiveness of a business like RB2B… 

…which LITERALLY RAN ITSELF as a $6m ARR company as the 3 FTE’s went off the grid for a week…

vs a VC-backed startup is GREATER than it’s ever been. 

We sat here and proved that it’s simultaneously possible to: 

- Hit $6m ARR in 18mo
- Have only 3 FTE’s, and
- Be AI-native enough to leave for a week

And today we’re growing FASTER, from a 50% HIGHER BASE, than we were six months ago.

———

BOOTSTRAP VS. VC

The risk-adjusted financial outcome of bootstrapping has always been far greater than VC. 

Most VC founders don’t make money. (The few that have will comment that I don’t know what I’m talking about. Hi guys 👋)

At my other business - Retention.com - we were able to DISTRIBUTE $5m in cash to the founders on our way to $10m ARR. 

And we haven’t sold, and yes, that business is stuck right now, but the reality is that it generates $9m in profit and we find ways to fight the churn and reinvent ourselves.

Meanwhile, almost all of the venture-backed vendors in the Shopify space (with a few exceptions) are suffering a similar fate while burning large amounts of capital every year.

Yes, Klaviyo is worth $10b. 

Yes, there are 1-2 other potential epic success stories. 

But for the most part, I think if the founders of the other 80% of companies could turn the clock back, they would have probably chosen to do it more like we were doing it. 

And it’s not just about the money the founders make. That’s just a nice perk. 

Inevitably most founders stall out and are required to reinvent their businesses completely.

The stress of having to do that when you owe someone $100m and your equity is FOR SURE worth less than that, vs. experiencing a mini-exit once a year while you’re doing it, is a night-and-day difference.

I can’t imagine how miserable I would be if we’d raised $50-$100m in 2022.

If I’m honest, I probably wouldn’t be around anymore.

———

THE 4 SKILLS THAT MATTER NOW

I believe that an entire internet will be built on top of the current version of LLMs, with little incremental improvement of the base layer necessary.

It can already do an incredible amount of things unbelievably well…

IF AND ONLY IF you know how to prompt well. 

Realistically, the average joe will NEVER be able to prompt well.

And there is a multi-100-trillion-$ opportunity in that fact.

Last week I was on a podcast with Amit Vasudev (VC + Founder of Clearbit) and one of the things we discussed was whether INFORMATION ASYMMETRY in tech investments can incentivize bad actors to the point where good investors and good founders simply exit the market.

BACKGROUND:

In 2001, George Akelorf received a Nobel prize for his work on markets with information asymmetry. Most economic theories are based on the buyer and sellers having access to the same information. In his paper “The Market for Lemons”, Akelorf presents a powerful model to explain how the used car market behaves under information asymmetry wherein buyers and sellers do not have access to the same level of information.

Used Car Market:

Imagine a market with two types of cars: high-quality cars and “lemons.” Buyers are willing to pay $20,000 for a high-quality car and $10,000 for a lemon. But due to information asymmetry, buyers can’t tell the difference, so they’ll pay an average price of $15,000 for a car. For sellers with HQ cars, $15,000 is too low, so they leave the market, while sellers of lemons receive $5,000 above their target price and stay. This results in a market dominated by LQ cars, as poor quality gets rewarded while high quality exits—all because buyers lack key information.

Founders & Investors :

Founders have an incentive to present themselves better than they actually are and some may indulge in “Signal Inflation” and “Fake it till you make it”. In the process they may share all the right signals with the investors - that are temporarily managed to make themselves look better. 

Early stage ventures have no track record making it difficult for investors to assess quality. VCs face the challenge of distinguishing companies that are "actually good" versus the companies that only "look good". 

This information asymmetry creates an investment risk. 

To address this risk, VCs may expect all founders to inflate signals and include it into their discounting and risk models thereby rewarding lemons and punishing great companies. 

Conclusion:

Good founders that are focusing on actually building their business and not on how they signal progress, may lose out on the investments and give up. 

Good VCs that are not interested in marketing themselves may also lose out to other investors that focus more on marketing than helping their portcos. 

In short, the information asymmetry can potentially lead to bad behavior or lemons.  

Do you agree such an information asymmetry exist with early stage investments? 

What have you seen work to reduce Information Asymmetry between VCs and Founders?   

Please Share in Comments.

Two weeks ago I was having a drink with John Mackey (Founder of Whole Foods), and I nearly spit out my drink when he turned to me and said, “VC’s RUIN great businesses.” Wait… WHAT?!!?

Me: Tell me exactly what you mean by that, John.

Mackey: VC’s need to shoot for the moon. There are a LOT of great businesses that aren’t meant to be trillion dollar company.

Me: But didn’t Whole Foods do $22b in sales last year? 

Mackey: I’m not talking about Whole Foods - I’m talking about the MANY other Founders I’ve watched get on the VC treadmill, only to waste money trying to push a business farther than its natural state, ultimately destroying a huge amount of value.

Me: Funny enough - I see the same thing all the time. With software in particular.

Mackey: Tell me what you mean by that.

Me: I always thought that software businesses had the characteristics to be INCREDIBLE small-to-medium sized cash generating businesses. I’m talking - $50m ARR with $25m profit. We don’t have to move physical goods, so with a good enough product, we should be able to be WAY more profitable. 

Mackey: I agree with you there. 

Me: Yet, I don’t see anybody doing that. I only know of a few examples - Ross Andrew Paquette from Maropost being one of them, who has been generating over $20m profit for more than a decade. Nobody in our ecosystem even knows it’s possible, so they all head down the VC route as soon as they get any traction. Most fail, but even worse, some spend a decade or two creating businesses that are quite valuable, but not actually valuable to THEM.

Mackey: That’s one major problem. The problem I had at Whole Foods was that I needed VCs to fund my acquisitive growth strategy, but after seven or eight years they needed OUT. It forced me to IPO well before I otherwise would have.

Me: You’re a billionaire now - would you ever use VC money again? 

Mackey: If I get Love Life scaling, and I’m trying to ramp thousands of physical locations in a short period of time, I definitely will, because I don’t see a better alternative. 

Me: What will you do differently? 

Mackey: I’ll be planning for their exit from Day 1.

TAKEAWAY

John Mackey thinks VC ruins great businesses. 

Yet, he’s very open to using VC money again. 

But only using it under the following conditions: 

1. Proven product-market fit of his retail business
2. He’s ready for rapid, international expansion
3. The exit (IPO) is planned from Day 1

Until then… 

He’s a bootstrapper.

Marty Kausas: Why do you hate VCs so much?

Me: How much time do you have?

BACKGROUND:

Marty is a young-buck YC-founder with early traction.

Ed Hallen is the co-founder of Klaviyo, an IPO’d decacorn.

Every Marty is hoping to become Ed someday. Ed has reached the endgame of the life the VC/YC path is selling, he's worth $100’s of mm now, and I spoke to him the other day about this.

Ed: “Most VC-backed founders end up failing. That just sucks for Founders.”

He told me about an article he wrote for the Harvard Business Review about what he calls the “Mighty Middle”.

He concluded sub-VC scale, bootstrapped companies in niche markets had far higher probabilities of creating life-changing outcomes for founders than the VC track...

And therefore are better for the Founders!

But that wasn’t the most interesting part.

When you talk to Ed about Klaviyo, you can tell he doesn’t think of himself and his co-founder as any more capable than their VC-backed peers.

You get the sense that he believes Klaviyo is where it is because of a few breaks that were totally out of their control. Things they NEVER saw coming.

1. Linking themselves with Shopify when it was a $50m valuation, now it’s $150b (a 300x!)

2. Mailchimp got in a fight and killed their integration w/ Shopify in 2018

3. Email is the one positive NRR product in SMB

What would have been the fate of Klaviyo if none of this was true?

We will never know, but my guess is it would be MUCH smaller than the $1.3b run rate (or whatever Klaviyo is now).

The last point Ed made on our call was my favorite.

“Hundreds of millions of dollars has zero utility beyond a number MUCH smaller.”

His point is that most Founders want the freedom to build cool shit, and live the life they want.

A huge amount of money in the bank, and the huge company that young founders think they want, can work AGAINST those goals.

But good luck trying to explain that to a 25yr old paying $3k/mo rent in SF. 'I'll find that out for myself', says the young Founder. Touché.

Last but not least, I always point out the VC path is dependent on transactions with volatile valuations for the Founder to realize the fruits of his labor. 

A decades-long effort of creating a VERY good business most of the time ends up in a very low-paying job with a boss (your investors). Why? Because if you're VC-backed and your business stops growing, your equity is torched. 

Klaviyo was the exception.

Is Pylon?

Only time will tell.

Marty and YC types make the mistake of bucketing Ed’s “Mighty Middle” in the “lifestyle business” category and dismissing us as “playing small”.

It’s not about playing small.

It’s about freedom, and making sure if Marty were to create a great business (and he probably will), the fruits of that labor accrue to Marty (which is unlikely).

So to answer your question, Marty.

Why do I hate VC’s so much?

Because I want YOU to win. And I want you to be free.

But I think by taking $50m, you minimized the odds of both.

Last night I had a chat with a SaaS founder who raised $60M for his startup. The latest round was a $40M Series B at a $400m valuation at the end of 2021. 
He thought he was on the unicorn path, but now it's a VC nightmare.

After the latest raise, he went on a hiring and spending spree, built out a half-baked “platform”, spent boat-loads on go-to-market.

In the beginning, it all looked like it was working. 

For six months revenue spiked and they were closing deals left and right. 

But the last 18 months have been brutal.

Massive layoffs, horrible churn, sprinting to profitability.

Before that series B - even though they were venture backed - they were focused, lean, profitable, and actually had decent retention.

Here’s the bombshell...

What’s their ARR 3 years after the deal?

About the same as it was BEFORE the Series B.

Except instead of being profitable, now they are burning.

Instead of a core product suite of high-retention products, they have a leaky platform.

And the STRESS LEVEL of the last three years… 

He didn’t even want to talk about it.

The problem is, for this founder, there’s no way out.

It’s a zombie company that raised (and burned) way too much capital. 

There’s not a clear path to an exit with a 1-3x return for investors.

The truth is I’ve been stuck like this a bunch of times.

In fact, I did something very similar in 2023… 

I hired up for massive growth, and spent a boat load on GTM, and instead of 9-figure ARR, I got a bunch of churn.

But unlike this founder, who is stuck trying to move this zombie forward …

As a bootstrapped founder, I was able to pivot, and focus on efficiency.

We got a lot smaller.

We started a new business (RB2B), and found two new TAMs in two totally different markets. 

And even though we also failed at the unicorn dream, we fell back on a massively profitable $25m ARR company.

So what’s next for my founder friend?

Thinking about it is anxiety-inducing.

What’s next for us??? 

Anything we want.

If you can bootstrap… 

Bootstrap.

Last week I saw several Linkedin posts recommending SDRs do 5,000+ units of outbound/month and maximize sales channel activity. This is bad advice. The brute force approach is short sighted and will kill your credibility and annoy your buyers.

There’s a reason why those are upper limits.

We don’t need to hit them every week.

I don’t understand why Sales leaders constantly suggest hitting those limits to meet goals. That’s such an old-school approach. It may have worked when the market was not saturated.

But not anymore...

Here’s the Model they're recommending:

Model 1: Maximize Channel Activity

- Maximize Linkedin connects (200/week)
- Maximize dials (500/week)
- Maximize emails/account (1000/week)

This may have been OK when you didn’t have to create demand.

When demand already existed and you could capture it through rapid conversations.

Increasingly, this transactional approach has only suited high-velocity, low ACV SaaS products with short sales cycle and quick onboarding.

But with sustained use, you risk losing trust and credibility with your buyers in the long run.

Here’s the model you should instead opt for:

Model 2: Maximizing Trust

- Research and Understand Pain Points
- Find context
- Present yourself as a resource to the buyer
- Build relationship
- Solve relevant and targeted problems
- Don’t maximize outbound

This approach can be slower and more expensive.

While we historically saw this approach followed by ABM marketers for large ACV, high margin products - now it is increasingly relevant to all solutions.

This leads to more strategic conversations and allows an AE to create an environment where demand creation or demand inception can happen. 

TAKEAWAY:

Don’t maximize your channel outputs with relentless Calls, Inmails or Emails.

Do your research.

Use Signals, Content and AI Agents.

Use Inbound-Led Outbound.

What’s good for the industry and buyers is also good for you.

We are all in this together.

Everybody wins or Everybody loses together.

3 ways I’m NOT using AI at RB2B (and 5 ways I am):


1. I’m NOT using AI to write LinkedIn posts

Call me old fashioned, but I think if you’re trying to create THE BEST art, the best art is valuable because of the perspective of the artist. I still write it all.

2. I’m NOT using AI as a SPAM cannon

Despite the promise of the category, I haven’t heard of a single person that has been satisfied with an engagement with an outbound AI SDR.

3. I’m NOT using AI to do sales

I’m second guessing this one after we had Kevin "KD" Dorsey on Unf*ck My Startup yesterday. He said the only reason AI hasn’t taken over SDR is because it’s illegal, and you have to say you’re an AI. But he said inbound is 100% there.

——————

I AM using AI to:

1. Handle 8,500 support requests/month

Robb Clarke has done an incredible job at molding Intercom’s Fin into something that works very well. Not perfect, but very well. Only 3% of our support requests involve a human.

2. Filter, tier, and route our PLG signups

Brendan Short created a Clay table that sorts our 1,500+ signups per month by traffic, industry, company size, sales team size, CRM used, location and routes them accordingly.

3. Create scorecards for AE’s and CS reps to evaluate calls

This is a new one for us, and what I believe is the most impactful but hardest to measure. Did the rep hit all of the areas of a discovery call? How was their tone in a CS call? What objections did they handle poorly?

4. Come up with an excuse to reach out to prospects

My brother Anthony showed me a research AI he created with Make using perplexity deep research that is SUPER expensive (~25c per domain) but can manufacture a relevant reason to reach out for any large retailer. The output is incredible and his team loves it. We ran our list through it. Our team loves it too.

5. Be my business coach

After Sam Parr told me he has made a custom GPT coach for every key pillar of his life and he’s fed them TONS of context and engages with them many times per day. I made a business coach. I asked it to ask me every question about my business. And I agree w/ Sam - LLMs as any kind of coach, especially once given a bunch of context, are amazing.

TAKEAWAY

AI is incredible, and getting better every day.

But I don’t think the best application is replacing people doing the same “old way” tasks that people did to sell “old way” products, services, and software.

We’re trying to jam it in that box right now because it’s how we all make money.

And in many cases, it’s doing those things pretty well.

But, I’m most intrigued by the “always on coach” application.

Our basic humanity - the lizard brain, our heuristics - is our worst enemy.

ChatGPT - especially with context - allows you to rise above it, with little effort.

All of our lives are the decisions we make.

Those decisions compound.

What would life be like if every decision you made over decades was 5% better?

There’s only one way to POSSIBLY find out…

Ask ChatGPT.

———

I haven’t been as excited about our business as I am now for a long long time. 

RB2B is exciting because we’re showing you how far you can get in 2025 with a combination of a Founder-Led Freemium GTM, entirely AI customer interaction, and a tiny core team.

(We’re shooting for $7m ARR by year-end and $10m ARR year-end 2026, with 3 FTE!)

Retention is exciting because if this product reinvention works, we’re incredibly well positioned to experience another S-curve of growth in the Shopify ecosystem. 

TBD there … but we’re seeing very encouraging signs.

———

I was speaking to a founder friend this morning about how when you’re really excited about your business, everything else in your life is so much better. 

It’s an energetic tailwind. 

The same is true for the other way … 

When things suck (and they have for us, many times)…. 

It’s a cloak of anxiety that’s impossible to get out from under. 

But man… 

What a gift - to have something so interesting and dynamic to work on every day. 

And with such talented people.

Entrepreneurship is truly the greatest, most interesting game in the world. 

The sad thing is that some day the music will just stop. 

For me, for my biz, for you, for all of us.

At that point, I’m only have one regret… 

That I couldn’t just do it all over again.

So I’ll just keep building.

Every time I feel bad about my business - which is often - I get dinner with a VC backed Founder in the $20-30m ARR range who has raised over $50m. I share my complaints, then they share theirs👇

- They are unprofitable
- They’re either stuck or not growing fast enough for their investors
- Their investors send them all the Clay and AI financing news weekly
- They have 5x the team size I do (and execs)
- They are on planes at least 1x/week (I hardly travel)
- They are being forced to add product complexity
- They face intense new-entrant competition despite superior product
- They are under an incredible amount of stress and don’t see a way out

After they are done… it always kicks off the same dialogue:

CEO: “But you’re making money, right?” 

Me: “Yea, we will probably do $12-14m profit this year."

CEO: “That sounds like the absolute dream.” 

To which I always get reminded that... Yes, it actually is!

But when you’re in the middle of it all, it’s so easy to lose sight of.

Startups are hard. 

Some things get easier, but in my 12 years of experience, it almost always feels like shit.

But if you can last long enough as a bootstrapper: 

1. You will end up being enormously profitable (mini exits every year)
2. You will have total freedom to design the life you want for yourself

Raising money is exciting and validating, but most of the time you end up stuck with no way out.

The reality? 

$10m ARR is the FU Money of SaaS. 

In 2026, it takes fewer FTE’s than ever before.

At RB2B we’re about to cross $9.6m ARR with a team of 3. 

99% of VC backed founders would kill for that business.

If you can bootstrap, bootstrap.
