RB2B’s 6 month birthday was September 1st. We hit $2.6m ARR in 184 days (WOW), but have 14% monthly churn (OUCH!). Here’s a detailed breakdown of the metrics, my 3 biggest takeaways, and what comes next:

180 DAY METRICS:

REVENUE

$2.63m ARR
809 paying customers
$271/mo avg subscription price

ACTIVATION

14,338 company signups
81% of users have received at least 1 contact
10%+ free-to-paid conversion
800+ Hubspot integration connections

CHURN 

14.1% User Churn (more like 10%, agency canceled 80 accounts, came back under 1)
15.5% Revenue Churn (see above)


MY 3 BIGGEST TAKEAWAYS:

1. Top-of-funnel coming from LinkedIn has been incredible

I’ve never done this before, so it’s unclear how deep the well is. Santosh HAS done it before, and insists the well is very deep and we have a long way to go before it dries out. I also think we are getting even better on the content side, which I think is our ace-in-the-hole here.

2. Our activation metrics are great

From conversations I’ve had with others, most people struggle for a 30% script install, while we’re above 80%. I think the quality of the traffic coming from LinkedIn is responsible. Free-to-paid is also great. It’s not entirely zero-touch, since we hired Ilija, but we are still trying to figure out the motion, so it’s close.

3. Churn is the VERY obvious problem

Jason M. Lemkin would say this isn’t even a SaaS. I can’t say that I’m totally surprised - we are selling leads to SMB and VSMB in a hard environment. Santosh again is unsurprised by this 9 month LTV out of the gates. We have started down the long road of adding products and features to increase stickiness. 

Our first attempt is a traffic insights product that tells you ICP visitors by page. The alpha version a couple weeks ago was a miss. Working on 2nd now.

Curious as to what the product people on Linkedin think. Your feedback helped a ton with our first six weeks pricing dilemma (when we had 3000 signups and only 13 paying customers).

I talked to people on the original Clearbit Reveal team and churn was always a nightmare - for the same reasons we’re seeing it, and we are selling to on average much smaller companies - and the only way they reduced it was users from different departments using different products within their product suite. 

TO SUM IT UP:

It’s really awesome to see $2.6m ARR in 6 months. 

That’s where my first startup was after 4 years.

However, I’ve been at this long enough to know this churn number will start haunting us pretty soon.

I feel like we know what we need to do. 

This product may not be low enough churn to ever be a massive company … 

But I do think we can meaningfully reduce churn by creating great solutions for other departments. 

WHERE WILL RB2B BE IN 12 MONTHS?

If you tell me where our churn rate will be, I’ll tell you our ARR. 

I know one thing for sure… 

We know EXACTLY what we need to focus on. 

Better onboarding. 

More “wow” products. 

Lower churn.

We’ll just keep building.

If I was a first-time startup founder, I would not aim to build a $1B unicorn. VCs will hate this, but here's why you should think SMALLER and try to create a $3m-5m ARR profitable SaaS instead:

1. It’s relatively easy to get a small, profitable SaaS working.

One extreme of entrepreneurship is the solo consultant, the other is sending people to Mars. SaaS is somewhere in the middle. Smaller goals mean smaller teams and less complicated products, probably no management layers, no big expensive tech, no SOC2, etc.

2. It’s much easier to bootstrap a small, profitable SaaS.

If all you’re trying to do is get to sub-$5m ARR, you can very likely build a solution that exploits a small hole in a very large market, and do it quite profitably. You won’t need VCs to sign off on your idea, which means far more ideas are available to you.

3. Your odds of success are much higher if you are aiming lower.

According to Notion Capital, 3% of startups make it to $100m ARR, whereas 60% stall out between $3m-$10m ARR. You are 20x more likely to be successful if your endgame is single-digit ARR.

This might be a hard pill to swallow, but as a first-time founder you are probably not skilled enough at execution to pull off a unicorn. I never have, and I’m 12 years in.

4. You will learn VERY VALUABLE lessons as you fight to $3-$5m ARR.

Just because you aren’t shooting for the moon doesn’t mean you won’t learn many of the exact same lessons you’d learn if you were playing much bigger. I learned SOOO many things about teams, product, sales, and marketing being stuck for 4 years at $3m ARR.

5. You will be able to start a bigger, better startup with the free cash.

GetEmails (now Retention.com) was the result of 3 years of experiments inside of Robly and currently has 7x the revenue and 4x the free cash. RB2B was funded by Retention’s free cash.

6. You will eventually enter the Bootstrapper’s “Promised Land”.

While you and your co-founders may not be excited about $4m ARR with $1.5m of free cash, if your second startup is 3x bigger and your next is 3x bigger than that, you will be in a position where you are being paid the equivalent of a small exit EVERY YEAR with resources to do whatever you want.

TAKEAWAY

Starting a SaaS startup is hard.

Especially as a first-time founder.

Lowering your ambition will increase your chances of your success.

And smaller successes in the short-term can compound into much larger successes down the road.

VCs will try to interfere with this restrained ambition.

They want you to aim higher, grow faster, build more complicated products, and hire more people.

All while incinerating capital as quickly as you are willing to tolerate.

That won’t maximize your probability-weighted average of long-term success.

The most important rule of the game is simple:

Stay alive so that you can keep playing.

Over the past 10 years I’ve read over 250 books about startups. Here are the 8 books that got me from $0-$25m ARR with zero funding (in order of impact) and what I learned from each of them:

1. Four Steps to the Epiphany by Steve Blank

I re-read the first half of this book each time I start a startup. It’s dense, but there is no better description of the steps to take to reduce your chance of failure to ZERO. Takeaway: Build your audience of buyers before you launch, or you’re screwed.

2. Founder Brand by Dave Gerhardt

This has been more impactful than anything I’ve ever done in business. Yes, I have magical alignment in that I am my ICP and my ICP lives on LinkedIn. Even if you do not have that alignment, Founder Brand content creation is an automated trust-building machine and will pay dividends.

3. ReWork by 37 Signals

The OG SaaS bootstrappers have great takes on the benefits of creating a business outside of the VC ecosystem. You should read this book, then immediately do Y-Combinator’s Startup School, and land somewhere in the middle.

4. Y-Combinator Startup School

These guys understand the importance of pursuing growth as a key metric, but can skew towards making you think you should try to go big (because many of the biggest went through YC). As I said, land between here and ReWork.

5. The Hard Thing About Hard Things by Ben Horowitz

Such an incredible articulation of the things that make the CEO job difficult. Must-read for any aspiring Founders to know what you’re getting yourself into.

6. The Great CEO Within by Matt Mochary

Excellent description of how your journey and experience will change if you achieve product-market fit. I have read this book many times, and each time a different part resonates with me. Most recently: “Find a mentor, find a therapist, find a group of peers.”

7. $100m Offers by Alex Hormozi

“Have an offer so good your prospects will feel stupid not doing it.” Read, and re-read again. Then look yourself in the mirror and ask yourself if that statement is true for you. If not, make it true… And when you do, everything will change.

8. Purple Cow by Seth Godin

Nothing describes the necessity of being different better than this book. Make yourself a Purple Cow so you get talked about. It’s within your control, do it!

TAKEAWAY:

These books have formed my beliefs about how successful startups happen.

You reading this today - and RB2B going from $0-$3m in 30 weeks with 5 people - is the result of me picking up Founder Brand by Dave Gerhardt two years ago.

It planted a seed that led to a rabbit hole that kept giving me enough back that I just kept digging.

But should you spend a bunch of time and money building your Founder Brand?

When should you? When shouldn’t you?

What if you could ask DG - the guy who LITERALLY wrote the book on it?

Well…

You can.

Tomorrow (at 3pm ET) Dave Gerhardt is joining me on Inbound-Led Outbound LIVE to talk all things Founder Brand.

Join here: https://events.rb2b.com/

I’m the CEO of a $28m+ ARR SaaS. 
How did I do last year? Grade me - A to F. 
(real metrics below)

1. TOP LINE: $28.2m Run Rate (+11.2%) 

- The story here is Retention.com was flat and RB2B grew from 4 to 6.5m ARR.
- I take full responsibility for not investing in innovation on the Retention side (we have changed that this year)
- We need to add a LOT to RB2B in 2026 to not experience a similar plateau
- If I’m being honest I get massive FOMO when I see AI startups going $0-$100m ARR in 2 years or less

2. BOTTOM LINE: $1m/mo 6mo Average Profitability (+45%)

- Our goal in running this metric is to substantially grow this metric over time
- We chose looking at the 6mo average
- Our goal is to continue to grow without adding meaningful headcount, so profitability growth will continue to outpace revenue growth

3. CHURN: 5%/mo for Retention, 9%/mo for RB2B 

- We sell a high churn product to an even higher churn buyer persona
- I have spoken to many founders of similar businesses - nothing helped until they added completely different tangential products
- In 2025, we acknowledged the solution, but have not shipped it yet

4. HEADCOUNT: 33 FTE, flat

- We love running lean, and growing without adding headcount
- We are not in a hyper-growth situation at the moment … if we were, I would feel differently about managing to a flat headcount

5. INNOVATION: Hired Phil, put 5 FTE’s on something COMPLETELY new

- I believe my biggest mistake of 2023-24 was not doing this sooner
- I now realize that growth is about “S-Curves”
- If you hit PMF once, you better be working on your next PMF, or you will slide

6. CULTURE: WAY better than 2023, LOTS of room to improve

- Quarterly employee surveys indicate we are managing better and communicating clearer
- We prioritize delivering financial, intellectual, and interpersonal capital to our team
- Our goals seem attainable, we focus on doing fewer things, but better
- Voluntary churn is near zero

7. VISION: $28m >> $33m ARR in ‘26, Retention2.0 MVP in-market, RB2B multi-product

- This is not as exciting as sending humanoid robots to Mars (which is happening)
- It’s very exciting to me - we have a bunch of irons in the fire, and some might work!
- If we can nail 2026 and 2027, this business will be completely transformed

TAKEAWAY

All you armchair quarterbacks out there…

As a CEO, how did I do last year? 

Give me a letter grade, A through F, but most importantly … 

TELL ME WHY!!! 

I need feedback.

Last year Diana Ross spent $50,000 on a Taylor Swift box, then 3 hours manually building a prospect list, and ABM’d 100 highly personalized emails to female CMOs… and we got ZERO responses back. WHAT?!?!?

She was devastated.

What CMO wouldn't want to go to see the Taylor Swift Eras concert…

In a box, with free champagne, a custom Taylor Swift cocktail, and some free Swifties Eras swag?

It didn’t make any sense. 

But then she reached out to this same group of “Dream 100” CEO’s on LinkedIn. 

And she got a VERY different response...

All of a sudden, she was getting “YES” from CMO’s of massive ecom brands… 

She asked them why they didn’t respond to the email. 

It turns out ALL of them received the email… 

And they all read it. 

But they didn’t write back because the event sounded too good to be true!

The show was a hit, and we’re now in conversations with a handful of CMOs that we wouldn’t have even DREAMED of pursuing 12 months ago.

What’s the lesson here?

I think it’s two parts. 

1. Create events that are so good that people don’t believe they’re real, because in 2025, that’s what it takes to break through the noise.

2. Make sure they know you’re a human and that you’re for real. Linkedin is the best place for this.

Who’s in for the next Taylor Swift box with the Retention.com team?

I could retire. I could sell my companies. So why do I still do this? When it’s so fucking hard and I don’t have to anymore.

I build startups because it’s the most true expression of who I am. And I believe we are in an age where AI has enabled builders to build whatever they want to give them whatever life they want, in a way that was never before possible. 

For me, I have a COMPULSION towards building insanely lean businesses. Maybe you don’t. But I do. In 2019 Tate, Diana, and I bootstrapped $13m ARR with six people PRE-AI. I am not bragging, I am stating that journey was one of the most fulfilling things I have ever gone through as a human being, BECAUSE it was so authentic to who I am and we created something that I believed was the most beautiful business I could imagine at the time.

With RB2B, AI made even MORE insanely lean possible, and I believe one of the most amazing things I have ever seen on this planet. We’ll hit $10m before the end of the year and it’s run by 1 FTE and a handful of part time people a few hours per week. Haters would say “you had more than 1 FTE in the beginning”, “it’s about to stall”, blah blah blah and they would be correct. But when we started RB2B in 2023, people were extolling the virtues of a 10 man $10m ARR business. The idea of a 1 man $10m ARR business was completely absurd and had not yet happened. Now it’s a reality, and the growing cash flow from RB2B and Retention.com are funding our next venture, MoltSets, which we’re going to build in the same way as we built RB2B. 

So why do I do what I do? 

Because I am expressing my creativity by building what I consider to be extraordinarily beautiful machines, and they deliver to me (and my team) the life we want. I am so grateful for Tate, Diana, Michael and Keleigh for being so values-aligned, and supportive of the often insane ideas I have, and going along with me as we see how far we can push this pathologically lean philosophy. I hope I am lucky enough to keep building elegant, cash generating companies with a calm schedule and energized, long-term team for decades to come. 

But it wasn’t always this way. The only way to describe the first seven years was “terrible”. I posted a while ago a letter to myself that I wrote in 2015 when I was stuck at $3m ARR about how I wanted to get to where I am today in five years … and it’s heartbreaking imagining telling that guy who wanted it SO BADLY that he would make ZERO PROGRESS for the next three years. 

I never gave up, and eventually I got one thing to hit, and then another. 

And now, this is my art.

I am so grateful for having this endless canvas to express myself. 

And I hope I never run out of paint.

In less than 8 years, the best salesperson I ever met went from an intern at Xerox, to closing $1M enterprise deals to becoming the co-founder and CRO of a Unciorn-bound tech startup.

Here are the 9 things that made her a top 0.1% seller:

1. She truly believes what she sells is best for the customer

Call it drinking the KoolAid. The best salespeople are the best because they believe their customers will be far worse off without the solution.

2. She hits her activity goals every day (no matter what else is going on)

Traveling to NYC for meetings? Wake up early and prospect to hit your activity goals. Have a company-wide offsite all week? Stay up late and hit activity goals. Have to work the booth at a trade show? You get the point.

3. She generates her own leads, even when it’s "not her job"

She was always a “full-stack AE”. Even when her job involved a large amount of inbound, she took it upon herself to build systems that were automating outbound for her.

4. She intimately understands what customers care about

She doesn’t just talk, she listens. Over time she develops a deep understanding of who the customer is, what matters to them and what doesn’t. She’s able to cater the pitch to who she’s talking to, and has a deep intuition for personas.

5. She understands the product better than anyone

She developed a unique understanding of what her product does, relative value of its component, and what features should be built. This allows her to emphasize and de-emphasize certain parts of the product depending on the situation.

6. She has a Kobe Bryant-like commitment to excellence

She doesn’t understand when people don’t do things completely and correctly, because that’s what she would do if she were doing it. She expects the same out of the people who work for her.

7. She knows where to spend her time and the company’s money

You only get to #1 if you figure out how to get the maximum amount of revenue from the minimum amount of money and energy spent. Then do it all over again as fast as you can, every single day.

8. She is extremely focused on her craft

Her whole life is family and work. This type of focus is necessary to be successful in anything you do. This may sound depressing, but it’s the reality of what it takes to be #1 in anything. You need to decide if that’s actually what you want.

9. She’s never complained about anything, ever

This quality is present in truly elite sellers that often goes unmentioned. Great sellers don’t have time to complain. They are too busy making sh*t happen.

...

So who is this Hall of Fame seller?

Her name is Diana Ross.

My good friend and CRO at Retention.com + RB2B.

The playbook for sales success isn’t complicated.

Selling tools is a $1M business. Selling dreams is a $1B business.

There's no better example than Sam Brannon:

In 1847, Sam Brannon opened a store by the American river to sell tools to gold miners. He prominently displayed a jar of gold with signs to the river saying “Gold found here”. His first store did about $5,000 in revenue per day and in just a few years, Brannon became the richest person in California. 

Here's 4 examples of how this applies to SaaS:

1. Before you sell your tools, Sell a dream. 

By promoting the discovery of gold in the river - Brannon first provided a dream and a vision that matched with what people wanted anyways. And then he pointed them to his store to buy the tools needed to fulfill their dream. 

Brannon famously ran through the San Francisco streets announcing the discovery of gold sparking a frenzy in the population. 

Most SaaS companies have the tool but they refrain from selling the dream or vision that matches with what the customer is looking for or creating a frenzy and buzz around their market demand. 

2. How Hubspot (with Inbound Marketing) sold a dream before selling tools

Hubspot pioneered the term Inbound Marketing. They promoted this vision to their users which created a category and a market for the Inbound Marketing tools from Hubspot.  

At RB2B we are promoting the Inbound-Led Outbound concept and to those that buy this concept we point them to RB2B as a tool that delivers on this concept. 

3. Charge prices that are aligned to value delivered

The perceived value of Sam’s dream was so high that he could charge $15 for tools that he sourced for only $0.20.  

In small pockets and market niches, there may exist opportunities to deliver high impact while charging a significantly high premium for SaaS tools.

4. Leverage the entire Ecosystem

Brannon didn't just sell supplies. He became a key part of the entire gold rush ecosystem. He provided instructions, maps and advice to the miners. In doing so he became indispensable to those seeking fortunes. This also provided him with the needs and requirements of his target market. 

SaaS companies need to do the same and attempt to expand their footprint across their entire ecosystem. This will give them an opportunity to influence the buyer across the entire value chain and get a good understanding of what their buyer wants. 

What SaaS companies do you think are selling dreams/vision the best?

Share below in the comments.

“It's never going to work”. That's what a billionaire CEO told me as I was explaining my vision for the next 24 months of my startup. And not only was he right, but it led to me getting sued.

BACKGROUND:

In the spring of 2017, I was sitting on the couch in my New York apartment, sending emails to wrap up my day.

My startup, Robly Email Marketing, had grown from $0-$3M ARR, but got stuck, and at this point, had been stuck for a year.

Looking for answers, I popped over to LinkedIn.

I saw a message that was so intriguing I read it twice.

An employee of the pioneer in Email Marketing messaged me…

This company HATED me because the way I got to $3M was by calling their customers and offering them a better deal.

What intrigued me so much about the message?

The end of the message was this:

“They put $50m into their in-person selling program, and when we got acquired they just chopped it. You’re the perfect guy to swoop in and take it over.”

This was it!

This was how I was going to get unstuck!

I agreed to wait until his non-compete expired and hire him.

___

A few days later, one of my mentors connected me with a billionaire CEO, who agreed to meet with me as a favor.

I was excited to bound my new idea off a legend.

But half way through our meet, the CEO stopped me.

“It's never going to work,” he said.

“Why not?” I asked, flustered.

“I’ll show you.”

He then started writing numbers on a legal pad.

“How many customers do these agencies have, on average, and how much would they charge?”

“Maybe 10-20, and they charge around $1-2k/mo” I said.

“And what does your software cost?”

“$60/mo,” I replied.

“And what affiliate commission do you pay?”

“40% for life.” I proudly said, because it was HIGHER than most.

The CEO laughed and shook his head.

“If you get 100% penetration into the agency’s accounts, you will make them a total of $24 for each account they bill $2k to their agency for. They aren’t going to care about you or your software.”

What did I do?

Did I listen to the most successful founder I had ever spoken to?

Of course not.

Not only did I proceed, I ended up hiring the guy early because the perfect time presented itself to strike, and “non-competes aren’t enforceable in California”.

Fast forward 12 months...

After the initial excitement, the program got zero traction.

Then the competitor sued me and dragged the lawsuit out for a year.

Eventually we settled, and the employee informed me that by California law, I was obligated to pay his legal fees too.

What a kick in the nuts.

TAKEAWAY:

Should I have listened to the billionaire CEO?

Maybe.

Maybe not.

I think many first-time founders fail because they haven’t learned what only being in the game can teach you.

Those hard lessons shape the founder you become.

Total failure, wasting a year of my life, burning several hundred thousand dollars, and a lawsuit were awful…

But I’m a stronger founder for having gone through it.

The key is living to fight another day.

In the past 24 months, I’ve spoken to hundreds of $0-1M ARR startup founders and 99% of them are STUCK. Here are the 5 biggest mistakes they're making that prevent them from finding Product-Market Fit:

1. They can’t clearly articulate what they do. 

This seems pretty basic, but under 1% of founders I speak to have nailed this. Why is it so important? A clear one-liner is what you use to get people to talk to you, and conversations (customer discovery) is what gets you from $0-$1.

2. They can’t clearly articulate who they’re for. 

“Small businesses” isn’t good enough. If you can’t tell me the age, gender, geography, income level, habits, and places these people hang out (both digital and IRL), you will get nowhere. 

3. They can’t articulate why someone would pick them instead of someone else.

Most founders are either not different enough or they are building something that if it works will get copied in a nanosecond (I’m guilty here too). Few seek difficult-to-build opportunities or businesses with true network effects.

4. They are trying to do growth hacking way too early.

This is the most common problem I see. “Adam, can I talk to your cold email guy?” or “Can you connect me with your paid ads agency?” from people with less than $1m ARR. You're not there yet.

5. They’re trying to do too many things for too many people. 

Unless your name is Parker Conrad, niching down is the only way to get something from $0-$1m. Be like Nathan Barry and create an Email Newsletter App for Food Bloggers to start. Then slowly expand wider and wider.

TAKEAWAY:

Product-market fit is very difficult to achieve. 

Most startup founders will never get there. 

But here’s the crazy thing… 

The reason most founders won’t get there isn’t because: 

- They aren’t smart enough
- They don’t have a good enough team
- They don’t know enough about sales and marketing

Most founders won’t get to $1m ARR because they aren’t doing the horribly manual customer discovery process that going $0-$1m requires. 

I want to help.

We built a new private community for founders around these very simple ideas. 

We’re helping founders save months (if not years) on their journey to PMF by helping them refine their messaging and enter a true customer discovery loop.

In 2024, I grew RB2B from $0-$4M in 40 weeks. Here are the 7 biggest mistakes I made along the way (and the ARR ranges I made them):

1. I created a $0 and $495 plan, got 3,000 signups, and 13 paying customers

Revenue Level: $0-$75k

I had the genius idea to give infinite leads and the Slack app away for free, but charge for other integrations. People parsed the Slack app, sent the data wherever they wanted, and laughed at me. We should have done credit-based pricing from the start.

2. I thought running the leads through Clay would work for everybody

Revenue Level: $0-$1.5m ARR

Clay has been an incredible partner and when you have enough traffic and the right agency partner, it really works. I didn’t realize that all of that needed to be true for people to be successful.

3. I sold web visitors as leads, and “success” as booked demos.

Revenue Level: $0-$3m ARR

I didn’t realize that a site visitor wasn’t actually a lead, it was a signal, and that a signal can be very useful even if it doesn’t lead to a booked demo (what if the visitor ALREADY had a demo?). Web visit + other signals and criteria make a visitor worth contacting.

4. I thought people would know what to do with the data.

Revenue Level: $0-$2m ARR

I was surprised when “what now” came back as churn reason #1. We've finally solved this problem and made these signals actionable.

5. I didn’t invest in filtering and routing through the CRM until three weeks ago

Revenue Level: $0-$4m ARR

We tried to build an ICP filter, but couldn’t nail it. Clay does a decent job, but most people don’t want to add Clay just to use this. Running the signals through the CRM for filtering and routing is a relatively easy solution that should have occurred to me sooner, and did not. Thank you Jeremy Horowitz'. Our new Hubspot integration fixes this.

6. I had no idea how many people would copy us.

Revenue Level: $2-$2m ARR

ZoomInfo now jumped on the bandwagon, as copycat number 37. Shame on me for not realizing that any SaaS that works will immediately be copied by 1,000 people in 1 week.

7. I had no idea how bad churn would be.

Revenue Level: $0-$4m ARR

I thought that we would be able to make B2B companies SUPER successful because of how well we do for our larger ecommerce companies. But, we sell a $149/mo plan that churns at 18%/mo. I did not see that coming. Maybe I should have?

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are hard.

RB2B was really hard, too.

I made some big mistakes…

Not the least of which was assuming a site visitor makes a lead.

I hope I don’t make these mistakes again.

What I do know is that I’ll continue to make mistakes.

Just new and different ones!

That's part of the game.

We keep building.

COO Friend: I’m going to build my own SaaS. Should I raise $2m and quit my job today, or should I work nights and weekends and try to bootstrap it?

Me: I’ll give you the same advice I give everybody who asks me this… DO NOT quit your job until you KNOW you have something worth quitting for.

COO: What do you mean?

Me: Most startups don’t work. If yours does, you’re lucky. I know you’re burned out working for the man, but taking the leap from a stable job when you have a wife and a kid is a very big deal.

COO: But isn’t that what the $2m is for?

Me: In theory, yes. In reality, you will end up burning through the $2m in 18mos. You’ll build too much product without NEARLY enough customer discovery, since neither you or your co-founder have ever taken a product from 0 to successful before.

COO: But I’ve talked to a handful of people in our industry, and they’re all excited about my idea.

Me: One of the BIGGEST reasons founders fail is because NOBODY will be honest about your idea when you present it. They will be nice. A false signal.

COO: How do I make sure the feedback is honest?

Me: I do it one of two ways. The first is not let on that you are building anything, and just try to understand your prospect’s day, their workflows, and how your solution would fit into them.

COO: What’s the second?

Me: I sometimes sell people things that I haven’t started building yet. I get them to put an actual CC into a Stripe form. Or sign a contract. I love this method because it’s the strongest signal… But it comes after discovery.

COO: Won’t people get pissed you bait-and-switched?

Me: My experience is that if you have solved a painful problem, when you say “I don’t have this yet, but when I do, you will be the first one to get it”, they will wait patiently.

COO: That seems like it would be helpful. But my CTO is ready to quit his job too, and he’s a successful AI engineer at well known SaaS. Doesn’t that mean anything?

Me: That means nothing. The dream of being a Founder is too seductive. People only see where I am, they have no idea how hard it has been to get here.

COO: Isn’t the fact I can raise money a good indicator?

Me: Nope. You are a successful, intelligent, articulate dude. Investors are buying that. And they have modeled in a 70% chance that you will fail. That is COMPLETELY unrelated to your prospects wanting your product.

COO: Well, shit. What should I do?

Me: You should have 100s of discovery calls with prospects to validate what you are providing is valuable. Meanwhile, if your CTO wants to start working, figure out one narrow workflow he can hack together that can provide value, and try to start getting feedback from a light version of the product before you do ANYTHING. Try to get people to pay you for something you don’t have yet. If you do all that, you’ll know it's worth quitting your job for.

COO: On nights and weekends?

Me: YES, ON NIGHTS AND WEEKENDS

Don’t quit your job.

Don’t raise $2m.

You’ll thank me in a few years.

You’ll never lose an employee again.

When scaling a startup, every CEO should focus on 3 things (and it's not revenue, churn, or hiring great talent):

BACKGROUND:

Over the past 10 years, I read "The Great CEO Within" by Matt Mochary 4 times.

Each time I was at a different part of the scaling journey, so each time something different resonated with me.

When I read it recently, one idea stood out WAY more than it had in the past …

The idea that the *emotional burden* of scaling a startup is substantial.

And it's not fair to put the weight of that burden on your family.

You need a support system to deal with it along the way.

That's why I think every CEO scaling a startup should do 3 things:

1. Get a therapist

I finally found a therapist and now we meet regularly. I have been seeing her regularly, and interestingly, my wife thinks I’m less of an as*hole now. Every week my therapist makes me “bring something in” to talk about, and that alone is making me more mindful of the little things on a day to day basis.

2. Get a mentor or coach

Santosh Sharan has served as my main mentor figure for the past 20 months. He was a huge help with some glaringly obvious shortcomings I had around instilling processes.

A while back, I was explaining to Brian Lee🏌🏻 that I was looking for a mentor or coach, and he connected me to Matt Blumberg, who found Jonathan Shapiro. Jon worked with 8 of our executives, and we've rolled out Entrepreneur Operating System. I’m VERY happy I pursued the mentorship path.

3. Get a network of peers.

I was really sold on the idea of meeting with a group of CEO peers regularly. One of my friends joined YPO and said the forum was excellent, so I applied, went through that brutal screening process, and didn’t get in!

I then decided to join Pavilion and Sam Jacobs' CEO group. It’s definitely doing what I was looking for - a group of people at a similar stage to me experiencing a similar pain in a slightly different way.

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are hard.

Maintaining good mental health throughout the journey is even harder.

It’s not fair for your significant other to bear the burden.

I found a therapist, a mentor, and a group of peers to help me along the way.

Being a CEO can be pretty lonely.

But it doesn’t have to be.

You’re not Sam Altman. You’re not Elon Musk. You’re not Steve Jobs. And that’s OK. Instead of wasting years chasing VC funding and "massive" exits, most founders should focus on one goal: bootstrap to $3M ARR. Here’s how I grew my first $3M ARR startup into a $25M ARR SaaS with $12M in profit (without giving up control):

Company 1: Robly Email Marketing

My first startup was a bootstrapped email newsletter app. We got it to $3m ARR by going after Constant Contact customers with a cheaper/better offer (for a $40/mo product!). 

That only got us about 1% of their revenue, but fortunately we kept the team tiny, and were left with positive cashflow to keep building.

Company 2: GetEmails (now Retention.com): 

Started as a feature in Robly. People were using the feature (called RoblyID), downloading the file, putting it in Klaviyo, and said it was awesome. 

We spun it out, funded it with the cash coming off Robly, and despite being stuck several times along the way, it’s now over $20m ARR… And we ended up selling Robly for $10m to private equity.

Company 3: RB2B 

RB2B was the result of Santosh pushing me to create a GetEmails for B2B. Before RB2B, company-level ID existed, but not person-level. Now, we have around 20 competitors, including ZoomInfo. 

We used the cashflow from Retention to get it off the ground, went $0-$5.7m ARR in 18 months, and it’s nicely positive cashflow (albeit a bit stuck).

When you stack RB2B on Retention it’s $25m ARR and $12m run-rate profit. 

Sounds like a dream business. 

TAKEAWAY:

I don’t know why more people don’t follow the path I took.

Start small and profitable, then take bigger and bigger swings.

You’ll learn valuable lessons and become incredibly skilled when the stakes are low, so that when the stakes are higher, you can swing that much harder.

Remember:

You're not Sam Altman.
You're not Elon Musk.
You're not Steve Jobs.

Neither am I.

That's OK.

Start small.

Then go bigger and BIGGER as the journey progresses.

I bootstrapped 3 startups over the last 10 years. Here's the 5 non-secret secrets to scaling revenue when you don't have big VC money:

1. Stop focusing on revenue

- Only companies who are financially free can go for total domination
- Always have a few experiments running that can be 1000x-ers
- You need to be working on your next “S” curve

2. Keep making your core product better

- You can always get faster, easier, quicker time-to-value
- Competitors are always nipping at your heels
- Your work is never done

3. Come up with even more ways to deliver perceived value

- Hit people over the head with the value you generate
- Make sure they are seeing at it the same way you are
- There are other ways to provide value than $$$
- Can you educate them? Entertain them? Make something beautiful?

4. Be the leanest possible version of your current stage

- More people doesn’t mean faster - it usually means slower
- Lean has SO many benefits, culturally, financially, otherwise
- I don’t know how many times it will take me to learn this lesson

5. Invest in RevOps early

- You need to understand your metrics as you scale
- Where you deploy capital will soon become the most important thing
- I got this one completely wrong

You don't need to raise a billion dollars to build a great company.

In fact, that often makes it much harder.

Ignore the pomp and circumstance.

Commit to the basics and then execute.

Every single day.

$10M ARR is the FU MONEY of SaaS.

Here’s the breakdown:

I think $10m ARR bootstrapped is the new unicorn.

Why?

Because if you can bootstrap $10m ARR in a lean way, all your wildest dreams will come true.

You will be able to do whatever you want with your life.

(I know because I’ve done it)

Not only that, I think bootstrapping $10m ARR is actually way easier than creating a unicorn.

And WAY less risky, with a FAR higher probability-weighted financial (and happiness) outcome.

Here’s 6 reasons why all founders should commit to bootstrapping $10m ARR:

1. You and your co-founder will be making over $1m/yr in salary and dividends.

This is simple math (another benefit of a small, efficient team). You and your co-founder can easily clear $1M each at $10M ARR, and probably more. With VC money, you have to be much, MUCH larger before you can take home that kind of money. It will be years later, if it ever happens.

2. You can sell your business in ONE SECOND for $30-$40m (or more)

I’m sure you’ve all seen the math. Dilute yourself down to 5% on a 15 year run to $1B, and if you didn’t pull out HUGE secondary checks, you actually come out behind. Not only that - there are only a handful of buyers at $1b. There are hundreds - maybe thousands - of EBITDA buyers at $30-$40m.

3. You can hire a CEO to run your company, work 1 hour per week, and clip the coupon

4. You can work 100 hours per week and run yourself into the ground (if that’s your thing)

5. You can go raise $50m and build a unicorn

Your product and GTM will be so tight that if you want to hit a home run at this point, you can absolutely do it. And as a profitable company, you will have leverage to get good terms from growth equity funds. Many will put the money straight in your pocket.

6. You can keep running it lean, get to $25m ARR with 25 people and pay yourself $10-$15m per year.

This is a possibility that literally no one talks about. And again, I think it’s actually much easier and higher probability than creating a VC-backed unicorn. Exit or not, if you get here, game over. You get a decent exit every year!

TAKEAWAY:

If you can bootstrap $10m ARR, the options available to you are SO GOOD.

The harsh reality is that most companies never get there.

Why?

Because you get traction and VCs show up at your door.

They gas you up with hopes and dreams about how your SaaS will be a decacorn

They give you money that you don’t need, which you promptly turn around and spend.

All the while, it’s actually INTERFERING with the one thing that will make you great, capital or not.

Product-market fit.

If you can find PMF, bootstrapped, then use money from your customers to get to $10m…

You can do anything you want with your life.

Ross Andrew Paquette, who grew Maropost $0-$25M ARR profitably in 3 years, is the PERFECT example of this.

Two weeks ago we had our first MASSIVE f*ck up at RB2B. It caused 50% of active users to churn and caused lots of brand-damaging blowback. Here’s what happened (and how we fixed it):

To set the stage: 

- We launched RB2B (our Person-Level Identity tool) on March 1
- My plan was to give away the leads and push to Slack for free
- Then get people to pay $495 for integrations
- But people could parse the Slack block with Zapier
- And do whatever they want w/ the leads without paying
- There was too much value in the free plan, not enough in paid
- Nobody was converting

So a month ago we realized that despite having INCREDIBLE top-of-funnel and mostly positive feedback, with our current pricing, we didn’t have a business.

1. People could easily “steal” the paid plan
2. $495 was too high for small biz, pricing was broken
3. Mid-market needed a filter and Hubspot or SF integration to pay
4. Pricing was fundamentally broken

My original plan was instead of pulling value back from the free plan - which has had viral expansion - we would add value to paid, and eventually get people to give us $495.

Also I really liked the idea of giving the leads away and charging for a workflow, because selling leads and intent data as a SaaS is a high-churn category.

The more people we spoke to the more we realized that wasn’t the best plan.

Peoples’ willingness to pay was HIGH *before* they got a taste of the free plan.

Once they saw the insane value of free, willingness went to zero.

(We have an added internal issue where we are still creating our fixed-price data asset and at the moment we’re paying a high per-unit cost for data for the free users… Many of whom we believe may not be looking at the data regularly)

How did we solve these problems?

1. In mid-may, we created a “free trial” for pro, which would run out mid-June
2. People could continue with the free plan, but had to log in and click “free”
3. The free plan did not include killer features like the HubSpot integration, Hot Pages, ICP filter

This broke our internet and ruined Robb Clarke’s weekend.

Here are some stats:

1. Support requests for the week shot up from 1,571 to 2,319
2. “Script Churn” went from 7.6% to 52.4%
3. We were hurled hundreds insults over chat, email, and in LinkedIn comments

BUT…

We did manage to stop buying records for users that signed up, installed the script, and WEREN’T actively looking at them.

If you really cared about our data, you either figured out how to get it back on, or you talked to us.

And many people decided they actually wanted the paid features when the trial ran out.

TAKEAWAY

Startups are hard.

Epic fails are unavoidable, especially this early in the journey.

I hate the brand damage that comes from making a sudden change like this.

But the reality is that we don’t really have the time to roll things out properly.

And I’ve found that if your product is great, when you’re a young startup, most are forgiving.

Thank you for your patience! 🙏

In less than 10 years, I’ve taken startups $0-$10M ARR twice as the ONLY salesperson. And I’m doing it for a third time with RB2B.  Here are the 8 biggest pieces of advice I’d give to ANYBODY in startup sales:

1. Set Weekly Targets (not Monthly or Quarterly)

Weekly targets will drive the right sales activities and behaviors from Monday-Friday.  You need to create urgency for yourself to get that ONE EXTRA meeting in or push that ONE EXTRA deal to close by Friday at 5pm.  

2. Put in the Manual Work YOURSELF

You will learn a lot by hunting for your own leads on Linkedin and learning the landscape of your market. Book calls with others in the industry to learn, send the messages yourself to see responses, and ask for feedback when someone tells you no. DO NOT outsource this early stage work (to other humans or AI). It’s the foundation of your future growth.  

3. Hire a sales assistant before another sales person

In addition to the above point, you must truly maximize the amount of work YOU can do prior to hiring more sales talent.  You need to continue to see the full picture and minimize hand offs. A sales assistant will handle the admin work so you can sell more.

4. Sales is a process- stick to it

There will be ups and downs, good days and bad.  You will get the odd email of someone telling you to F OFF.  Stick to the process and you will never have 3 bad days in a row.

5. Track your success

Create a dashboard that you and EVERYONE else at the company can check on at any time.  Hold yourself accountable and let others hold you accountable as well.

6. Less Talk / More Action

Stop talking about the pitch and start doing it.  The real feedback will be in performance.  If you want to try a new position or pricing, don’t overthink it and just start pitching it and see if it lands.

7. Be Curious 

Every prospect, touchpoint and call is a learning opportunity and people like helping people.  Ask questions about your prospect’s  business and prepare questions for feedback on how they plan to utilize your product.  There is ALWAYS more to learn.

8. Figure out your Why

What is it that YOU are building for? You need to have a WHY in sales as there will be a lot of hard days. For me, it was my kids. I had just gotten pregnant when we started Retention.com. For you, it could be money. A new house. To become the best version of yourself. But you need to find your WHY.

Have any questions about startup sales?

AMA anything in the comments 👇

Going viral on Linkedin can be worth millions. Most people think it's luck. But in B2B, the best startups are engineering it. I’ve done it 50 times in the past year. Here’s the 5-step system I use to go viral on Linkedin every week—and turn attention into ARR:

1. Build in Public

But not just any build in public. Share things like full P&L, problems in your business, emotional agony, cease and desist letters… Things you would only share with your spouse behind closed doors. It will crush.

2. Credibility Posting

"I bootstrapped my startup from $1-$10m ARR in 14mo with 6 people…” Have you done something virtually no one else has? Post about it. Tell people up front why they should listen to you.

3. Failure Posting

Very few are willing to post about mistakes they’ve made on LinkedIn - they’re trying to look smart and successful. What they don’t understand is vulnerability builds more trust. Lean in to your shit and it will cut through.

4. Hot Takes

What strong, contrarian opinion do you have that is authentic to you but will FOR SURE piss off 25-50% of the people who read it? Write about it. If it goes viral, make it a content pillar.

5. Shitpost

This is my LEAST favorite but can be a valuable weapon when the time is right. Go STRAIGHT AT a larger competitor, and don’t stop until LinkedIn stops rewarding you for it. Fortune favors the bold with this one. It can also backfire, so pick your shots.

TAKEAWAY:

Going viral on LinkedIn - ESPECIALLY within your ICP - can be worth millions.

Just look at RB2B… 

We went $0-$5m ARR in 12mo with 6 people. 

But here’s the thing… 

Breaking through the noise, even once, is not easy. 

CONSISTENTLY going viral is even harder.

But if you can do it… 

You will possess the greatest power in the world today.

Attention on-demand.

I have 2.4 stars on Glassdoor. But over the last year, we've had near-zero voluntary employee attrition. Here's how I retain top talent:

1.  Focus on providing intellectual, interpersonal, and financial capital.

Forget the fancy office, the free lunches, and unlimited PTO. None of that matters. What matters is whether your people are doing the highest-level work possible, alongside the highest-level talent you can attract. And whether they're getting paid well enough to never entertain a recruiter's DM. Amazon can attract great talent without paying well. You can't.
 
2. Get an exec coach to teach you how to communicate clearly.

Two years ago I knew I was a horrible manager. I just didn't know the main skill I lacked was the ability to clearly define expectations and deliverables. Sounds simple. But if you spent 43 years not doing it properly, it's a hard habit to break. Jonathan Shapiro gets the credit for two years of hard work with our exec team, shaping us all into much better managers. Best money I've ever spent.
 
3.  Don’t squirrel.
 
Like any excitable founder, I used to get ideas and start working on them immediately. That works when you are 3 people, but not when you’re 30.  Teams get frustrated when they're told to work on one thing Monday and something completely different by Thursday.

We rolled out EOS (Entrepreneurial Operating System), and the single greatest benefit has been defining the work during quarterly planning sessions and refusing to deviate until the next quarter. 
 
4.  Give excessive recognition when good work is done.

Praising people for good work in a public setting is one of the most rewarding things you can do for your team members. Any time a shout-out is given in a smaller setting, make sure the exec team hears it, and shout out as many people as you can during all hands meetings. 

5. Every once in a while, do something fun.

I haven't done this, but if you asked each of our 35 remote team members what their favorite work moment of the last 12 months was, my guess is over half would say it was either our Cancun or New York offsites. Our global team gets together in person twice per year, stays in nice places, does fun stuff, and eats great food.  Yes, we're bootstrapped. Yes, it's expensive. But I know this small thing is a big reason people stick around.

TAKEAWAY

Finding and keeping a talented employees is like finding and keeping a spouse.

If you want to find a good spouse, you have to first live a life that is worthy of a good spouse.

If you want to find and keep good talent, your company has to be worthy of good talent.

What did I miss?

Two weeks ago Sam Jacobs said that “growth is worth 3x profit”. Here are 6 reasons why I think that’s the wrong way for early-stage startup founders to look at it:

1. Monetizing that growth number is difficult and low probability

I understand these numbers are market rates, but I speak for the founders here. It’s incredibly difficult (and low probability) for a founder to achieve a meaningful liquidity event. Market rates are true for investors, but they don’t handicap this dynamic for founders.

2. Monetizing profit is an absolute certainty

There is no market rate way to represent the value of an ongoing substantial cash flow and the effect that can have on a founder’s life over time.

3. Smaller, profitable companies are easier to sell.

If you generate lots of cash, you will not only bank money with absolute certainty, if you decide you want to sell, there are 100x more buyers who will buy something at $50m that is very cash positive than a unicorn, where there is either the IPO option or a handful of buyers.

4. You’ll own all of the equity of a smaller, profitable company

Some people manage to have massive exits and still have massive equity when that exit happens. We hear about them, and celebrate them. Most who go down that road DON'T. If they are lucky enough to have the billion dollar exit, they are usually diluted to a point where the cash to them at exit might end up being the range of the high-probability mid-8-figure exit of the profitable bootstrapper.

5. Most VCs don’t love the idea of large secondaries

Founders assign too high of a probability to selling huge amounts of secondary. Some investors will let you, especially if you have a 0.01% incredible startup, but most end up letting you take $1-2 million to help pay for food, schools, etc.

Do you know what type of investor WILL give you a large secondary?

A growth equity investor who invests in profitable founder-led companies who doesn’t want to put incremental capital into the business.

6. Valuation is temporary, control is forever

You also have control, and as Nathan Latka says, valuation is temporary, control is forever. Don’t underestimate the benefit that true freedom has on your wellbeing.

TAKEAWAY:

I get fired up about this topic because it’s a weapon that gets used against us.

Growth definitely IS worth more than profit…

On paper.

And, to investors.

Also to companies who are already public, or headed there with a high degree of certainty.

Here’s the problem.

If you’ve got meaningful traction as an early-stage founder, it’s SO hard to rise above the excitement and appreciate how valuable profitability - and control - actually are.

Because for the Founder, growth’s “worth” can only get monetized one way - with some type of low-probability exit.

As a founder, profitability gets monetized every single day.

With absolute certainty.

AND you completely control your own destiny.

What’s that worth?

Most marketers would say I’m an idiot, but I don't believe in attribution. It forces you to focus on the WRONG things. Here's 5 reasons why I don’t measure any marketing activity I spend time on:

1. The most important things in business can’t be measured

The two things that come to mind when I say this are “brand” and “demand creation”.

I can’t measure the direct effect that ANYTHING I spend 80% of my time on has on RB2B. I have no idea how many signups came from this post, and I don’t know what the 3 guest slots I did today produced.

Yet, I know it’s working better than anything I’ve done before, but if I were optimizing for things I could see with my own eyes (beyond MRR), my days would look totally different.

2. The least important parts of business are what you CAN measure

You can only measure demand CAPTURE - when someone actually clicked on an ad, booked a demo, hit your site from google, or responded to a cold email or LinkedIn DM.

3. Once you can measure something, you start optimizing for it and scaling it

How do we respond to #2? More paid ads, SEO, cold email, and LinkedIn messages, which are only CAPTURING demand, but not creating it.

Executive teams don’t have the patience to scale demand creation because 6 months in the CEO asks how many leads we got from the podcast (or organic social). When the response is “I don’t know”, the budget goes to paid search.

4. Tech platforms take credit for things that were going to happen anyway

This bothers me more than anything else. So many of our customers have made up their minds to buy before they were shown a retargeting ad.

But, Linkedin still claims the retargeting conversion, but the buyer came from listening to me on someone’s podcast, or from reading my posts.

Am I supposed to believe that our ROAS is positive? I’m really not sure.

5. Measuring leads to models in a spreadsheet that almost never happen

“If we hire X people in Y department, we’ll grow by Z.”

I've made this rookie mistake and I think most CEOs are right there with me.

I believe it never works because we don’t appreciate how important the unmeasurable, TRUE components of business growth like Brand and Demand Creation activities are. They don’t fit anywhere on that spreadsheet.

TAKEAWAY:

It’s 2024.

As outbound continues to die, the unmeasurable becomes ever more important.

The quickest way to grow a SaaS is by building a brand.

The best way to scale a brand is by building a personal (not company) profile.

Demand today is actually created through human-to-human connection.

Social media platforms facilitate this connection at a massive scale.

I’m creating human-to-human connection by:

1. Spending tons of time pouring my thoughts (and heart) out on Linkedin
2. Doing as many podcast guest slots as I possibly can 
3. Responding to every SINGLE comment someone leaves me

But I can’t measure what any of it is doing to our business.

Except for the most important measure of all…

ARR…

Up-and-to-the-right!

Last week Eli Rubel asked if Founder Brand will go the way of Outbound Sales (and podcasts). In short, will it lose effectiveness as more do it? Here’s why I think the best content will become MORE effective as more do it: 

1. Bad content will push the best content to the top.

Social media algorithms disproportionately reward the best content. More eyeballs come first, then more founder brand success stories, then more people trying. Platforms will serve MORE eyeballs the best stuff, everything else won’t get organic reach. We’re seeing this to some extent with LLM’s and AI. The best art is still created by people.

2. It’s really hard to create great content. 

Eli's comment came on a post where I pointed out why people are afraid to post on LinkedIn. It’s hard to be authentic, play the long game, have people hate you, and commit long enough to find your voice. 0.1% of people will actually do what it takes.

3. Millions of podcasts didn’t stop the good ones from growing.

Joe Rogan has more followers than ever… Eli talks about a distaste for the format, which I don't think happened. Yes, you probably can’t use a podcast to facilitate sales in the same way you might have been able to in the past, but for those doing it well, it is a highly strategic and valuable asset.

4. Unlike Outbound Sales, the delta between the top 1% and the bottom 50% is MASSIVE.

In Outbound Sales, there’s a playbook that performed for many years for mostly every company. The difference between an average organization and a great organization is maybe 2x. A great Founder Brand can get 20,000,000 impressions, while a good one might get 20,000. That’s 1000x.

TAKEAWAY:

The idea that people would get sick of the best Founder Brand content is flawed.

The best (think: Chris Walker, Sam Jacobs, Dave Gerhardt) are the best because: 

1. They know how to consistently cut through the noise
2. They are in tune with the changing tastes of their audience
3. They are truly gifted storytellers

The Founder Brand explosion we are about to see is not unlike the explosion of creativity and culture we have seen in every other art form.

To stand out you have to keep putting out new, better, and different stuff.

Snoop Dogg describes the job better than anybody else:

“But I … somehow, some way 
Keep comin’ up with funky-a$$ $hit like every single day …”

And that - in any art form - is what makes the best the best.

P.S.

Eli knows this. That's what makes him and his design agency NoBoringDesign so good. They are giving us a WILD brand identity. More to come. Definitely check them out.

Everybody thinks Clay raised at a $3.1B valuation because they grew 300% in 6 months. They’re wrong. They raised at $3.1b because they built a culture of Customer Discovery and Product Iteration. Here’s what NOBODY knows about Clay: 

Varun Anand joined Clay in late 2021 as a GTM co-founder.

At the time, Clay had less than 20 customers paying $100-$200.

I have spoken to 100's of early-stage Founders over the past two years, and messaged with at least 1,000 more.

If they were in Varun’s position, 99% of them would have ran this playbook:

1. Made a list of people they thought was ICP
2. Created hundreds of throw-away domains 
3. Run an instantly or smartlead cold email campaign 
4. Run some LinkedIn ads, and 
5. PROFIT (somehow)

Varun did the exact opposite. 

Here's what he did:

1. For 12 months he sat on calls from 10am-5pm.

2. He did a “reverse demo”… Instructed a customer how to solve a problem with Clay.

3. He got incredible product feedback and brought it back to Eric Engoron, where they constantly improved the product

4. He lived in communities like Jesse Ouellette's SaaS Yacht Club where their ICP (LeadGen Agencies) hung out all day looking for people with problems Clay could solve (which was the source of the calls).

No cold email. No paid ads.

Just manual, brutal sourcing of prospects and one-to-one conversations.

For 12 whole months!!!

I asked Varun why he thinks their valuation more-than-double from $1.25b to $3.1b.

What did he say? 

“It’s because we have a culture that is still doing EXACTLY what I did for that entire first year. We are all constantly talking to customers and using that feedback to improve our product, every single day.” 

TAKEAWAY:

Clay is the hottest company in B2B right now. 

They have INCREDIBLY strong product-market fit. 

Not only do I think it’s because they actually DID an insane amount of customer discovery to get there… 

But they built that process into their culture and are STILL doing it today.

Want to raise at $3.1b someday? 

You MUST start where Varun started. 

Because unicorns are born slowly… 

One discovery call at a time.

In 19 days, our entire $5.7M ARR company disappears for a week. AI agents will run everything - sales, support, development. Zero human intervention. This has never been done before at our scale.

THE CHALLENGE + JULY UPDATE:

We’ve been training our AI agents to handle a week with ZERO human intervention. 

We’ve been reading EVERY SINGLE RESPONSE our AI agents give, correcting to the best possible answer, trying to identify “lose-their-mind” type situations, coming up with solutions… rinse and repeat.

Robb Clarke and I have been doing this over and over again all month, and we think we’re in a pretty good spot.

———

What’s an example of a “lose-their-mind” type situation? 

RB2B sends a magic link to our users for login. 

Once or twice per week, somebody doesn’t get the email. 

They tend to get very worked up about it. I don’t blame them. 

The issue?

Sendgrid runs a tight “bounce protection” process, and the user’s email is usually on our “bounce protection” list within our sendgrid account.

We’ve been able to solve every magic link email problem after looking at sendgrid and either: 

1. Taking the email off bounce protection and telling them to resend the login email

2. Or identifying that it was an actual hard bounce, and the email was typo’d in the first place

We were freaked out because we KNEW this would happen a couple times while we were gone, and it’s not something that can wait a week. 

So - Robb started thinking about he could build an AI agent to solve the problem. 

———

24 hours later: 

1. Fin sends the email address to n8n

2. n8n checks Sendgrid’s API to see if the users email is on our “bounce protection” list 

3. If so, it removes the email from bounce protection, emails the user to try again

4. If not, it checks to see if it’s a hard bounce, if it is, emails the user that it’s a typo

This AI agent has worked 100% of the time the last 14 days. 

It’s agents like these that are going to save our lives when we disappear! 

———

July was a crazy month in the “signal/outreach” space we’re in.

- One competitor shut down
- Another doing the exact same thing raised $40m at $260m
- Another competitor (VC backed with 65 FTE) did a mass layoff

All that grabs headlines … but we’re slowly but steadily showing founders what’s possible. 

While competitors raise $40M and do mass layoffs, we’re proving you can hit $10M ARR with 3 people…

AND that you can disappear for a week and let your whole $5.7m ARR business run itself with AI.

Most founders will call this reckless.

The smart ones will ask: “How can I do this too?” 

Follow along - on September 3 you’ll find out whose right.

———

P.S. If you want early access to our full AI Agent Playbook, comment "AI" below and I'll send it once complete (make sure we're connected).

Business is the most extreme sport in the world. Every day, entrepreneurs and executives show up to make high-stakes decisions, facing brutal competition and enduring existential crises that rival any athletic endeavor. 

Just like athletes, business leaders combine strategy, agility, and teamwork to achieve success. 

However, there are some key differences between business and sports... 

There are no off-seasons or timeouts in the business world. 

There are no constants or rules in business. 

In sports, the rules of the game are always the same.

In business, there are no such rules.

You have to constantly innovate just to survive.

Extreme business can also be a spiritual quest

By pushing boundaries, you learn more about yourself

Through managing others, you learn to manage yourself

Bringing change in your business will often change you

When you become one with your action and commit everything you got towards  achieving your goals, in that very moment - you will find inner peace and begin to connect with your true self

For everyone playing the game, I salute you.

I hope you find what you are seeking. 

Just keep going and Keep enduring.

Linkedin’s user experience is rapidly deteriorating. Ironically, it’s their success that's killing them. Here’s why Linkedin may successfully cannibalize the very opportunity it created for itself:

I see a lot of parallels between email outreach and Linkedin’s business.

My Inbox is a war zone with individuals fighting for my attention. But so is my Linkedin feed and messages.

I have 100’s of unread emails and 100’s of Linkedin InMails that I don’t read.

Linkedin feeds and email Inboxes will only get noisier in the coming years. 

I am finding myself having to sift through way more ads and irrelevant content to find something useful on Linkedin.

That's not what I want.

I want to read posts from folks that I respect in my industry.

I don't want suggested "viral" content about Life Coaching.

I don't want to see another ad for Amazon.

Unfortunately, Linkedin does not have any feature that allows me to score, prioritize or filter posts out based on topics of interest or interesting individuals

While LinkedIn’s business model relies on impressions and ad revenue, it MUST find a balance to prevent the feed from getting overwhelmed with irrelevant content and spam.

Linkedin WILL have to come up with a different way to grow their ad revenues that is not lazy and far more relevant for the users

As it stands today, there's an inherent misalignment in Linkedin impression based ad-revenue business model and user's desire for relevant content. This misalignment is bound to lead to disenchantment for the users in the long run.

This also means Linkedin will never automate the feed or make it easy for us to see only the most important posts as such a feature has the potential to cannibalize their ad revenues. 

Supermarkets want their customers to walk around the store in the hope they pick up additional products, similarly Linkedin wants us to shift through many posts to find the one that we find valuable in hope of capturing additional impressions to drive ad revenues and engagement.  

If somebody developed a paid Linkedin agent (Chrome Plugin?) that crawls my post and provides a summary of the most important content based on the engagement from folks in my network that I respect most - then I would promptly switch to such an interface.

It's unlikely Linkedin would cooperate with such an initiative, but even if it lasts a few years, many stand to benefit from reduced noise and increased productivity on Linkedin. 

Competition is healthy for any ecosystem.

Linkedin currently has none.

On my run this morning, I was listening to "How to Make a Few Billion Dollars" by Brad Jacobs (founder of 7x billion-dollar businesses). He had an incredible take on hiring A Players vs B Players vs C Players:

The old adage is that A Players hire B Players.

And B Players hire C Players.

So never let B Players hire.

But Brad's take on it was simpler...

No C Players at all.

Have a short leash with B Players.

And give your A Players everything. 

---

The real question is:

How do you recognize A vs B vs C Players? 

The way he defined it is perfect...

When an A Player walks into your office to quit, you're reaction is: 

No. This business doesn't run without you. What do you need? What can I give you? It's literally debilitating for them to quit. 

When a B Player walks into your office to quit, your reaction is:

Ouch, this hurts. Definitely inconvenient. But I can probably find somebody to fill the role, maybe somebody who's even a little better than you.

When a C Player walks into your office to quit, your reaction is:

We were probably gonna let you go anyway.

---

The goal according to him is simple:

Don't have C Players at all. 

If you think that way about anybody... 

The time to have that conversation is now.

Anybody out there operating this way?

It's very, very hard.

In late 2023, my CFO grilled me about my Founder Brand investment. She said I was wasting time, being an ego maniac, and lighting $20k/month on fire to film a docu-series about myself. And she was right.

My first year of content creation was going terribly.

My CFO questioned everything:

– None of my social accounts had any followers
– None of my posts were getting any engagement
– I was spending insane money making a docuseries
– We couldn’t track any of it back to a single demo

I hadn’t seen the line-by-line breakdown of the costs.

I hadn't see the lack of results laid out like this.

She said, "We’re telling people to cut costs and you’re spending $50k/m on THIS."

I almost gave in.

I almost said, “Fine, I’ll stop. I’ll focus on improving the product.”

Instead, I said, "Give me 12 months to figure this out."

Because I saw something...

The real effects were coming to life for the first time on LinkedIn and Twitter. 

I showed her the inbound I was getting from recruits, partners, investors.

But I was sure I was going to be at war with her on this. 

A constant struggle to get invoices approved, always brought up in meetings…

Then the next morning, I got a Slack message.

With a note: "Thanks for explaining all of that yesterday. I still think this is ridiculously expensive, but I can see the upside. You have my blessing."

18 months later, I was at 135,000 followers on LinkedIn, had started a BRAND NEW company and RB2B was at $5.5m ARR… 100% from the founder brand.

What's my point?

Your team isn't there to be yes-people. 

They're there to make you think harder, defend better, and execute smarter. 

When my CFO challenged me, she wasn't being difficult.

She was being a fiduciary. She was doing her job.

But it's YOUR JOB as a founder to have a vision and understand your best investments can often look like terrible decisions at first. They require you to see around corners that others can't.

That $20k/month "ego project" became the foundation of a $5.5M ARR business. The "waste of money" became our most profitable channel.

Trust your gut. Defend your vision. But most importantly?

Give it the runway it deserves to take off.

If your GTM feels stuck, run this experiment.

It will take you 30 days:

1. Pick ONE growth goal.
Pipeline, activation, or expansion. Not all three.

2. Pick ONE audience.
Not "SMB + mid-market + enterprise." One.

3. Pick ONE offer.
This is what we do. Not five packages.

4. Pick ONE channel to win.
Support others lightly. Dominate one.

5. Define "enough reps".
3 posts/week. 5 sequences/week. 40 calls/day.

That's it.

Pete Crowley has spent the last 12 months talking to 200+ B2B founders as he's prepared to launch his new marketing consultancy, MarketWork. He can now tell in 5 minutes why a B2B company's GTM isn't working.

The pattern is always the same.

They're running growth like a buffet. A little SEO. A little paid. A little LinkedIn. A little "should we try TikTok?"

When you spread that thin, nothing gets enough reps to compound. Your message never sharpens. Your creative never improves. Your targeting stays a mess.

Focus means making a few choices so aggressive that everything else becomes obvious.

One channel. Your creative gets better faster.

One audience. Your messaging sounds like you're reading their mind.

One offer. Your sales team stops freelancing.

Tomorrow at 3pm EST on Unf*ck My Startup LIVE, my co-host Pete Crowley will be the guest and he'll show you exactly how to plan, build and run a 30-Day GTM Reset. If you feel stuck, if growth has flatlined, you don't want to miss this.

It's 2025. If you're a SaaS founder, you're probably screwed. Anything you do that works gets copied, CAC is up, LTV is down. Here are the 7 things I see that ARE working - in a world where most things are NOT:

1. Creating a TRULY AI-first startup

I'm not talking about slapping some LLMs on top of your old-school workflows and calling yourself "AI-native." I mean creating products on top of LLMs that increase productivity by 10x or more. Companies like Cursor, Windsurf, Icon, and Fyxer aren't using AI as a feature - they're using it as their foundation.

2. Word-of-mouth

This has always been true, but it's more critical than ever. With word-of-mouth, anything works. Without it, nothing does. In 2025, costs are up, attention is fragmented, and buyers distrust everything. The startups that are growing have products so good that users can't stop talking about them.

3. Personal brand

The ability to create organic content that your target market has demand for - completely independent of what you're selling - is the most efficient GTM motion that has ever existed. It's an automated trust-building machine, and trust = brand. In 2025, brand is built one post at a time.

4. Cold email ... in specific contexts

Enterprise buyers? Jesse Oulette says they're blocking it completely. But SMB and VC-backed startups? Blast away, but do it correctly. Most founders sending to an audience where it WOULD work can’t get it to work because of bad messaging.

5. Thought leadership ads

If you know how to create bangers on LinkedIn, pick the best ones and put some $$$ behind them. Promoting a post you know LinkedIn already loves is one of the cheapest sources of eyeballs you can get.

6. Cold calls

We had Kevin Dorsey on UnF*ck My Startup this week and he told us the EXACT cold call script that was generating a 12%-13% rate of accepting the pitch on 200 dials/day/rep that is booking him 20-25 meetings/week per rep. Today. In 2025. Calling works.

7. Staying ridiculously lean

I’m seeing startups winning that are running with tiny teams, staying profitable, and controlling their own destiny. Getting to $10M ARR with 10 people is now the gold standard… Not raising a $100M round at a unicorn valuation.

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are hard. They always have been. 

But in 2025, everything seems so much harder.

Most SaaS founders are going to fail this year because they're running playbooks that worked in 2020.

But if you focus on these seven things, you might have a shot.

I just have one question for YOU LinkedIn… 

Did I miss anything?

In June, we downsized from 5 to 3 FTE (40%), replaced 2 FTEs with a $99/mo AI clone, and grew 4.9% to $5.5m ARR. AI agents are now handling 90+% of sales AND support at RB2B. Here’s the good, the bad, and the ugly from June:

THE GOOD:

- Our monthly churn rate is around 7%. That sounds horrific to some of you, but it’s down from 15% at Thanksgiving
- Our Fin customer support agent is resolving 66% of all chat requests with no human interaction, up from 49% in May
- Our “Adam Clone” handled 1,700 inbound requests over the past two weeks - demos, SOC2 docs, pricing, product tours, GDPR, etc
- We’ve been reading and improving the responses - it’s getting good!
- We’ve solved a ton of product issues that have led to better experience

THE BAD:

- I haven’t talked to customers in 15mo because I was too busy building my brand and chasing dopamine hits from LinkedIn
- I became everything I used to hate about “influencers”, I lost touch and our product suffered badly
- To rectify this, I created a sequence that gets me on calls every Wednesday with 12 tier 1 customers
- I’m going through all resolved support and sales AI chats to make sure our AIs gave the best possible response… which gets me closer to customers
- I’ve kicked off a churn research project with the help of Jonathon S.
- While the product has improved, we need a transformation, which is coming
- I fear our 7% churn rate isn’t “real”… it’s seasonality and will go back up to 10%

THE UGLY: 

- Downsizing is terrible, if anybody is looking for AE or fractional growth, DM me
- It’s somewhat jarring how effective the AI is in handling inbound sales, in a “what does this mean for all of us” kind of way

TAKEAWAY:

Q3 and Q4 will be transformational for us. 

1. AI agents are now successfully handling 90%+ of our sales and support

2. Soon AI agents will be solving the core filtering, routing, and outreach issues inside our product

3. I’m in direct contact with dozens and indirect contact with 100s of customers every week

4. We’re picking cold email, ads, and SEO back up in Q3 and Q4

I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again…

$10m ARR is the FU money of SaaS. 

If Tate, Robb, and I can just maintain this 5% growth rate for the next 12mo, we’ll hit it by July 15 of next year.

Now I admit: 

- That’s not as exciting as selling for $80m after 6mo (Base 44)
- It’s not as exciting as adding $1m ARR per month (Fyxer/HeyReach)
- It’s not as exciting as being worth $9b (Cursor)

But here’s the hard truth:

While other founders are raising Series A to hit $10m ARR with 60+ employees, we’re doing it with three humans and a bunch of AI agents.

In front of you, with wild transparency, right here on LinkedIn.

Most of you reading this are building SaaS the wrong way in 2025.

You’re over-hiring, over-complicating, over-raising.

Prove me wrong.

P.S.

Want to see the UNCENSORED internal revenue dashboards of a $5M ARR SaaS? Comment “metrics” and I’ll send you access to our full metrics dashboard.
