3 weeks ago I posted that RB2B’s churn hit 17%/mo at $2.9m ARR. Since then we’ve lowered churn to 10.9% and grown to $3.5m ARR (+20%). Here’s what we learned, what we did, and what we plan to do:


WHAT WE LEARNED

1. Our product is unusable for our ICP (growth stage SaaS w/ sales teams)
 
If you're tiny and get 3 leads a day, it’s great. If you’re an Enterprise with a growth team and know exactly what to do with our feed, RB2B is great.

For growth stage startups with sales teams, filtering and routing is currently impossible without Clay. We are in the process of fixing this in several ways.

2. Our product exposes our customers’ traffic problems

Some people don’t realize how low a % of ICP visitors hit homepages in general. When our product highlights it, the product gets blamed, and in some cases, willingness to pay goes down ("Why should I pay for junk leads?").

3. We have broken LinkedIn links

We are in the middle of a huge database update. This problem will resolve itself in the coming quarter. We've had one public accuracy test done with Clearbit - we were far more accurate - and are having 11 more done now.

4. These aren’t actually leads

I’ve come to the realization that a site visitor isn’t a lead, it’s a signal.

We shouldn’t be selling demos, we should be selling alerts (and how to action them) to sellers that help them move prospects down the funnel.

Booking a demo is only one use case and it’s lower value than ongoing signals to salespeople from accounts they are monitoring and prospecting.


WHAT WE'VE DONE

- Added Hot Leads
- Added URL restrictions
- Changed weekly stats email to be more informative
- Added Zapier (usage is 4x what it was 2 weeks ago)
- Added “the most successful RB2B accounts do these 3 things” email


WHAT WE ARE GOING TO DO

1. Tell Hubspot CRM users EXACTLY how to filter and route in HS

We are going to create a feature that ONLY sends contacts at accounts that are already in Hubspot TO Hubspot, grab the account owner, then send it BACK to Slack with the rep tagged. We believe this will make our product usable for growth stage SaaS on HS.

2. We’re messing around with other delivery methods

We think reps might want this signal delivered to their Gmail (or Outlook) inboxes. If this works, it will eliminate the friction of marketers having to set up a HS workflow.

3. We think the “what now” problem is really a prioritization problem

A rep who carries a quota and/or manages a team has so much going on that they don’t want to take 5 mins to come up with what to write. We think we can use AI to tell the rep what they should say and why they should say it - and cut that to 15 secs.


TAKEAWAY

10.9% churn is absolutely god-awful.

While it’s better than 17%, we need to chop it in half.

My hope is if we keep listening and trying to eliminate churn reasons.

And we can come up with a product that growth stage sales teams LOVE.

THAT might get us to $50m ARR.

And I’d take $50m ARR.

So I’ll keep building.

Last week I walked into the woods of Colorado with just a backpack. No cellphone. No GPS. No plan except to avoid seeing another human for 6 days. Here’s why everyone needs to try “social starvation”:

1. It gives you time to think deeply about who you really want to be.

- Who do you want to be 10 years from now? 
- When you are 80 and look back on your life, what do you want to see?
- What do you want your children to believe?

2. You are able to think clearly about priorities and boundaries you want to set for yourself

- Am I doing too much travel for work? Is it worth what it’s costing me at home?
- Can I pull off a one-month personal trip with my family each year for the next five years?
- Can I spend Wednesday mornings with my daughter and make up for the time at some other point in the week?

3. I’ve done this three times now, and every time I’ve felt an overwhelming sense of gratitude for everything I have.

- My wonderful wife, beautiful daughter, and fiercely loyal 6lb chiweenie
- My incredible team, many of whom I’ve had the pleasure of working with 5 years or longer
- My wonderful community here in Austin, and the ways we get to spend our free time here

4. You can really reflect on business, the recent past, and the road ahead.

- So much has changed since one year ago when I did this.
- I’m imagining what my world will look when I do this again.
- I came up with a crystal-clear vision for what I think we should accomplish during the back half of the year.

When I was sitting there contemplating everything, the phrase “what got you here won’t get you there” kept running through my mind, over and over again.

Here are the top 7 reasons why you’re AFRAID to start posting on LinkedIn: 

1. You can’t be authentic.

You’re worried about what your investors/employees/prospects will think if you share what’s actually happening inside your company - which, let’s be honest, is not always good.

2. You can’t play the long game.

You know that 60 days in if you aren’t getting 1,000 likes per post you’re going to lose focus and squirrel to something else, so you already know it won’t work.

3. You’re afraid of the people who will hate you.

If you create content the right way - as the most unapologetically authentic version of yourself - you will get people who hate you. You may not be okay with that. But you have to be.

4. You’re in denial about outbound. 

You think that the reason you can’t build pipeline is because you have the wrong leaders or reps or the wrong tech or strategy, and you have yet to internalize that organic social is the only way to grow.

5. You’re afraid of how hard it is to be great.

This is legitimate, because it is hard to be great at literally anything in life. What makes it hard to internalize with social is the best gets SOOOO much more visibility than the 2nd best. And 3rd. Etc.

6. You’re afraid of the time commitment. 

You look at posts that I make about spending 25+ hours on Founder Brand content and podcast guest slots and think that you don’t have the time. You may be right - but soon, someone you are competing with WILL make the time.

7. You feel like you’re too far behind. 

The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago. The second best time is today. I was behind when I started 18 months ago - I never posted on LinkedIn before - and now I’m ahead. You could be too.

TAKEAWAY:

It’s okay to be afraid of posting on LinkedIn.

But here’s my question … 

As outbound continues to be ruined by:

- Automation/Increased volumes
- Spam Filters
- Recession

How long are you going to let your fear of LinkedIn destroy your business? 

The clock is ticking.

A CEO friend of mine raised $40M at $400M valuation. Two years later? The money’s gone and his ARR is flat. If you asked him the biggest mistake he made he would tell you: hiring salespeople. Here's why:

To be clear, it wasn’t JUST hiring salespeople… It was HOW he hired them.

Another founder buddy of mine recently did a Private Equity (PE) round.

His investors were pushing him to grow his team of reps from 5 to 20. 

Fortunately, my PE backed friend talked to my CEO friend first.

Here's how that conversation went:

PE Backed Friend (PBF): We just raised $25m and they want us to hire a bunch of salespeople.

CEO: Of course they do. But don’t do it yet. That pressure is EXACTLY what smoked me, wasted 2 years and $40m, and very likely shaved 10 years off my life.

PBF: Ok… well… what do I do? 

CEO: Are all of your reps at 100%? 

PBF: Not really. One might be, the rest aren’t. 

CEO: Do not hire ONE MORE REP until ALL of your reps are at 100% capacity. If you build a machine that has slack in it already, you will experience all sorts of cultural and motivational problems. The same amount of demos your marketing machine is creating and reps are capturing will go to even MORE people. Your team will miss numbers week in and week out. You will attempt to solve that problem by demanding reps you hired to be AE’s do more and more outbound. That will not work. Your sales leader will probably either quit or be fired, because you’ll have the exact same productivity on 4x the team size.

PBF: That’s terrifying. Especially now that we’re PE backed.

CEO: Tell me about it.

PBF: What do I do instead? 

CEO: Before you hire a SINGLE REP, make sure all of your reps are at 100% capacity. Make sure your marketing machine can actually produce more pipeline. If and when you can actually flood your reps with activity and the entire team is at 100%… 

PBF: Then I hire reps? 

CEO: NO!!!! Absolutely not. You work on raising the 100% higher. Figure out how you increase the capacity of the existing team to handle the increased pipeline generation. Can you create AI agents that save account research and follow up time? Can you hire sales assistants to do some of the unavoidable repetitive work? ANYTHING to get your already 100% capacity reps more productive. THEN… AND ONLY THEN… Do you start slowly adding reps onto the team.

PBF: I am so glad I spoke to you before I did anything.

CEO: Me too. 

TAKEAWAY

Institutional capital still wants to push founders into rapidly hiring reps to accelerate growth.

While that sometimes works, it’s VERY easy to do it the wrong way.

What’s the RIGHT way? 

1. Make sure your marketing machine can grow
2. Get all your reps to 100% capacity
3. Raise that capacity as much as possible
4. Slowly add reps to THAT machine

Build your team that way and you can’t lose.

FOUNDERS: WHAT KIND OF FUCKING MORON SIGNS UP FOR THIS?!?

VC was already a horrible deal for the Founder. If this is how the game has changed, I am even further emboldened that the bootstrapped path is the best path for MOST people in this game.

Unless what you do is highly capital-intensive, you should avoid this “changed game” like it’s the plague. The VC game was already bad: a 90% chance you'd kiss a decade of your life goodbye and walk away with nothing but an education. This new game is meaningfully worse in terms of probability-weighted financial success for YOU, the Founder.

I post here because I want people to realize that what I do is an option. I didn't know it was possible until I found a podcast episode in 2017 with Ross Andrew Paquette from Maropost, who dropped enough info for me to back into the fact that he had a $30m ARR biz dropping $20m to the bottom line, and he owned all the equity.

I had two epiphanies that day: 1/ that seemed like a better life for the founder than any other SaaS I had heard of, and 2/ it seemed much more attainable than hundreds of millions of ARR. So I became obsessed with Ross, tried to figure out how he did it, copied what made sense for my business, and fast forward 10 years and we're not quite there ($32m ARR, $15m run-rate profit), but we're close, and I'm more optimistic than ever about growing our profitability.

People always ask me what mistake I see young Founders make the most. It’s raising money, and it’s in two different situations.

Situation 1: they're at $1m ARR, growing 2-3% per month, and think money will speed that up. It won’t. ZERO percent chance. The only thing that speeds up a startup at that stage is more disruptive product + more disruptive marketing. Neither has anything to do with money. Yet they raise from people who think or say they are VCs, and enter the world of pain of the treadmill of capital without growth.

Situation 2: getting to $10m ARR quickly and raising, thinking your TAM is bigger than it is. I made this mistake, but thank GOD we were so profitable that I didn’t actually raise, I just grew my team from 13 to 60 in 60 days, burned through the TAM in 9mo, hit a wall at 100mph, and for the second time in my career fired everybody I hired in that delusional frenzy. When you take money at that point, you don’t have that option. You are forced to try to widen the TAM, you build a bunch of shit no one wants, and you enter the world of pain of the treadmill of capital without growth.

I want to be your Ross Paquette. This game isn’t easy. VC or not, you have to create disruptive products with disruptive marketing to win. That’s the only way you’ll grow. So, WHY NOT do it without selling your soul to a game you only have a 10% chance of winning? I PROMISE grinding your profitability higher from $15m 12 years into the game is amazing, and you have a WAY higher chance of getting there than going $0-$100m in 9mo.

Fuck Lovable. Stay small.

And keep building.

Me: I’m killing all our paid spend. Cold email, ads, UGC, SEO, everything.

CFO: WTF. What??? That doesn’t make sense. Didn’t cold emails and Linkedin ads acquire a ton of customers last year? 

Me: Our reporting said it did. And it may have helped… a little. But look at what happened as the year went on. The more we pushed - on ads, email, etc - the more money we spent and we got back less for every dollar. Diminishing returns. It’s not sustainable.

CFO: But if we turn paid off, won’t our growth hit a wall?

Me: In the short term, maybe. But maybe not. Nobody in B2B has the answer because everybody is terrified of turning anything off that “says” it’s working. Personally, I want to find out. And, I also want to spend ALL my marketing time and money creating a deep emotional connection in the mind of the market with the people who AREN’T in the market to buy right now.

CFO: That sounds great in theory, but how will you know it’s working? 

Me: Day to day we won’t. But here’s the thing - at any given time only 20% of our prospects are in market. If our stuff is good enough, it will constantly be in front of the 80% that aren’t ready to buy. We’ll know it’s working in a year or two… If we’re still growing faster than everybody else in our space with a fraction of the team size and zero paid spend (while they’ve ALL burned $10’s of millions of VC).

CFO: So your plan is to create organic social content for the 80% who AREN’T going to buy? 

Me: Exactly. The downside is we don’t have last-click or multi-touch attribution to tell us it’s “working”, but all that is BS anyway. Just because you can measure a click doesn’t mean that was why someone booked a demo. Most of the time it’s just tech getting in the way of something that was going to happen anyway, with vendors claiming credit to justify high pricing.

CFO: I still don’t understand why we wouldn’t focus on people who are ready to buy. 

Me: When people are in market, they are rationally shopping vendors for features and pricing. When they’re not, our organic content becomes an automated trust-building machine. When it comes time to buy, we’ll be who they think of when they are ready to add Person-Level Website Visitor Identity to their stack. Most of the time they’ll come straight to us, at the very least we’ll be in the deal.

CFO: So it becomes a type of moat...

Me: I watched 37 vendors whip up a similar product to ours in the 12 months since we launched last year. With AI, things are only going to move faster. In the future, brand will be this type of trust, built up over months if not years, one post at a time.

CFO: Alright, I’m starting to see where you’re coming from. 

Me: I forgot one more thing... If it all works out, RB2B will be WILDLY profitable. 

CFO: You know I love that. Spoken like a true bootstrapper!

18 months ago, I attended a birthday party for a founder who just raised $185M (at a $2B valuation) on the rooftop of the Four Seasons and was absolutely HUMILIATED by his incredibly attractive 28-year old blonde girlfriend:

Me: Hey, what’s going on?

Her: Thanks for coming. What do you do?

Me: I have this startup. What about you?

Her: I’m in marketing at UpWork

Me: I LOVE Upwork. We use them all the time.

Her: Cool. How big is your team?

Me: 6 people

Her: Oh... so you’re just getting started

*my internal monologue*

“Wtf… actually we are at $12m ARR, grew 200% this year, and me and my co-founders are making money hand-over-fist… we’ll have more revenue than your boyfriend in 6mo and we’ve PAID ourselves $5m getting here.”

…But I didn’t say that. 

My face turned bright red, but I just swallowed my pride, made my best attempt at smiling, said “yep, just getting started,” and walked away.

Why did this bother me so much?

Why did this feel so humiliating?

Because everywhere you go as a SaaS founder, the first (and ONLY) thing anyone asks you is how big your team is. 

They size you up.

When you say “six people”, you can see it in their eyes. 

It’s an “oh, that’s cute” kind of look.

Or they feel sorry for you. 

They definitely don’t take you seriously.

Most of time they start wanting to give you advice.

They don’t realize that your team of 6 gets more done - and has more ARR - than their team of 60.

Nobody cares that you have $2m ARR per employee. 

Nobody cares that you can do literally whatever you want.

Nobody cares that your stress level is close to zero.

They care about are the headlines about people raising $50m pre-launch.

They want to read press releases about acquisitions, IPOs, and big teams. 

This is the pressure that’s on the bootstrapped founder, every single day, from every angle, the entire journey.

It makes us feel little. 

But it shouldn’t. 

We have beautiful businesses that most VC-backed execs would kill for. 

It’s hard to remember that when your head is about to explode because someone says “you’re just starting out”. 

But you must remember, so you remain unbroken. 

Stay small.

Below is THE BEST breakdown of running ABM in 2026 I've seen. No $100k/yr 6Sense contract required. With AI + new tech, every company can now run ABM at scale. Here's how it works 👇

Traditionally, ABM was reserved for 6-figure deals and got a bad rep from players like 6Sense.

Now, it's accessible to more teams with less headcount.

But it’s only possible if you set up the right ABM infrastructure.

Here’s the breakdown in 4 stages:


Stage 1: TAM Mapping

• Analyze Closed Won: audit CRM, analyze LTV and NPS
• ICP Model: use firmographic, technographic & account-fit data
• Account Sourcing: databases, scraping, deduplication 
• Account Tiering: three tiers, focus ad spend on Tier 1
• AI Account Research: use Clay and ChatGPT to automate this.
• Contact Sourcing: decision makers, champions, influencers, org charts in CRM 


Stage 2: Signal Tracking

Track signals for every contact and company.

3 categories:
- 1st-Party Signals: Data you own.
- 2nd-Party Signals: Data given exclusively to you.
- 3rd-Party Signals: Public data.

From there:
• Aggregate signals in Clay 
• Sync them to CRM as custom events (HS) or objects (SF)
• Route signals to reps based on territory
• Create CRM tasks + Slack notifications


Stage 3: Awareness Scoring

Unlike other RevOps systems, reps LOVE this.

5 stages that auto-update with workflows:

• Identified
• Aware
• Interested
• Considering
• Selecting

First and last stage are simple:
- Identified = your target account list, no engagement yet
- Selecting = open deal

The middle 3 stages depend on your business.

Some of the variables you might wanna take into consideration include:
outbound email opens, multiple LinkedIn ad clicks, website visits (deanonymized), demo requests, etc


Stage 4: Demand generation

Use tiering + awareness for account planning.

1:1 Plays:
- Warm intros
- Personalized microsites
- Event invites
- Manual outreach

1:Many Plays:
- Automated emails
- Parallel dialing
- Retargeting ads
- Webinars
- Social content
- On-site content
- Video outreach
- Connection requests/DMs

Output: GTM Flywheel

___

Every marketer wants to know:
• Who knows they have a problem?
• Who already knows our company?
• Who's actively considering buying?

ABM infrastructure + signal stacking is the closest thing you have to actually answering them.

You just have to build it right.

If this feels overwhelming, don't worry. I got you covered.

In 9 years, Alina Vandenberghe grew Chili Piper to over $30m ARR. Here’s her 5-step “IRL Influencer” sales playbook for finding your startups first customers (and why it still works for them today):

1. Go to EVERY industry event

Alina’s co-founder (and husband) Nicolas went to every single B2B event they could find in the NYC area.

Pro Tip: After a certain amount of times that someone sees your face, people will feel like they know you. So just keep going to events in your industry.

2. Target influencers in advance

If you can get a list of attendees, figure out who has large, engaged followings, and make sure you speak to them before you leave the event. 

3. Identify influencers at the event. 

Observe the event attendees. Find the people who always seem to have people around them, no matter where they move in the room. Is someone hugging people more often than anyone else? Go talk to them. They are a hyper-connector.

4. Show them your doodle and ask for feedback. 

Before they had ANYTHING Nicolas was holding up a notepad with a drawing of what Chili Piper was planning to build, and asking if the influencer would buy it, and most importantly, if they wouldn’t, why not. 

Pro Tip: Alina said she asks as many questions as humanly possible, which informs what they are doing, or plan to do.

5. Once you have a product, get the influencer to use it. 

It is far better to get them to buy it, but if they won’t, free is better than nothing. Your product HAS to be valuable and different, but if it is, and it works, these people will talk about it, which is the entire strategy. 

BONUS: People lie on Zoom calls, so you need in-person meetups.

Alina prefers this in-person strategy because she believes that because of the camera or recording, people are unwilling to deliver the brutal truth necessary to create great products. 

Yes, it takes time to go to events, but it saves SO MUCH TIME getting to the core of what you need to be building.

________

Here's a real-world example of how this worked:

Kevin "KD" Dorsey was one of the early influencers that used Chili Piper, he saw immediate value, and talked about it to everybody he knew just because he thought it was awesome. Since then, more influencers in the ecosystem have adopted Chili Piper, and this strategy continues to drive their acquisition engine.

________

I'm sure many of you are thinking... 

“I could NEVER walk up to someone like that at an event”. 

I know how you feel. 

I felt the same way.

I used to go to events and be TERRIFIED of speaking to people.

Alina said she felt the same until she read a book called "Non-Violent Communication", which flipped her from an introvert to an extrovert. 

After I heard her that, I immediately went out and bought the book.

Because I think we all need to be implementing her playbook.

It's timeless and will work forever (no matter your product).

Cold emails and social media will only get you so far.

Build relationships IRL.

The accuracy of our de-anonymization ABSOLUTELY CRUSHED Clearbit. 

RB2B - 84% accurate
Clearbit - 59% accurate

You might be asking yourself:

The answer: 

They used the % of records that matched their form fill data.

So, we’re way more accurate than Clearbit, and probably 6Sense, Demandbase, and ZoomInfo, since they all do a similar reverse IP technology to resolve companies.

Period.

_______

THE GOOD #2: 

The overlap of audiences between the two solutions was TINY. 

ONLY 4% OVERLAP in the audiences between Clearbit and RB2B. 

We found the same to be true with 6Sense’s tool when we bought it.

If you are using Clearbit, 6Sense, or Demandbase, you need to USE US TOO.

But, we’ve been growing like crazy…

So that tells you who we’ve been selling to (SMB).

Here are the top 7 reasons why you’re AFRAID to start posting on LinkedIn: 

1. You can’t be authentic.

You’re worried about what your investors/employees/prospects will think if you share what’s actually happening inside your company - which, let’s be honest, is not always good.

2. You can’t play the long game.

You know that 60 days in if you aren’t getting 1,000 likes per post you’re going to lose focus and squirrel to something else, so you already know it won’t work.

3. You’re afraid of the people who will hate you.

If you create content the right way - as the most unapologetically authentic version of yourself - you will get people who hate you. You may not be okay with that. But you have to be.

4. You’re in denial about outbound. 

You think that the reason you can’t build pipeline is because you have the wrong leaders or reps or the wrong tech or strategy, and you have yet to internalize that organic social is the only way to grow.

5. You’re afraid of how hard it is to be great.

This is legitimate, because it is hard to be great at literally anything in life. What makes it hard to internalize with social is the best gets SOOOO much more visibility than the 2nd best. And 3rd. Etc.

6. You’re afraid of the time commitment. 

You look at posts that I make about spending 20+ hours on Founder Brand content and podcast guest slots and think that you don’t have the time. You may be right - but soon, someone you are competing with WILL make the time.

7. You feel like you’re too far behind. 

The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago. The second best time is today. I was behind when I started 18 months ago - I never posted on LinkedIn before - and now I’m ahead. You could be too.

TAKEAWAY:

It’s okay to be afraid of posting on LinkedIn.

But here’s my question … 

As outbound continues to be ruined by:

- Automation/Increased volumes
- Spam Filters
- Recession

How long are you going to let your fear of LinkedIn destroy your business? 

The clock is ticking.

I think HubSpot made a HUGE mistake. They never should have backpedalled on their decision to create the greatest data co-op in the world. 

Here is the simple reality. People would have whined about it on LinkedIn for two weeks, a handful of customers would have left, then everybody would have moved on to the next thing, and HubSpot would have been left with the single greatest data co-op that has ever been created. 

This would have been INCREDIBLE for every HubSpot user. What do I mean? Guess who knows the best contact information for every single business contact in the world??? The 1.4m active HubSpot CRM users, plus a handful of data scientists. 

This could have been an EPIC UNLOCK for HubSpots customers … and now it’s … GONE … and HubSpot is stuck trying to figure out how to keep the data fresh they got in the Clearbit acquisition, when the best source of data they could EVER IMAGINE is … you guessed it … right in front of their nose.

I think they just executed this poorly. Having people opt-in to a co-op has worked REALLY well in the past, even with enterprise companies (Abacus was an enterprise catalog purchaser data co-op that Double Click bought for $1b in 1999, as one example). In the US, if results are demonstrably better from giving up data, and the only way they can get those results is from joining a co-op, people will join co-ops. 

My good buddy Nick Weldon at 5x5 made a killer data co-op against all odds, and the largest publicly traded company in the data space is their largest customer.

I recognize that I am not HubSpot, my market cap is 1/100th of theirs, and I pride myself on taking an aggressive stance on issues like this. But I do believe that A) it was stupid to pull this back, because B) nobody would have cared after a couple weeks, and C) it would have REALLY helped their customers.

It’s a sad day for the small founder. We need all the help we can get.

Bring back the co-op, HubSpot, but make it opt-in.

It will crush.

Koala - DEAD. Warmly - DEAD. Common Room - DEAD. Pocus - DEAD. Unify - PIVOTED. Vector - PIVOTED. “Signal Orchestration” was supposed to be the future of outbound… But the space ended in an acqui-hire frenzy when nobody could raise their next round.

Here are my observations from this decidedly sad state of affairs:

1. MARTECH SUCKS

If you aren’t a CRM, you are high churn. Martech gets tried and ripped out, most of the time it’s not mission-critical. RB2B is the worst of it - leads/intent data sold as a SaaS to a high-churn buyer persona. Couple that with people raising money before the churn kicks in, and you get a bunch of companies that couldn’t raise the next round and were forced to puke to make payroll. 

This paradigm also applies to the zombies of the COVID era (6Sense, Salesloft, Clari), who thought they had large, sticky customers but ultimately did not. If I were in martech (which I am) and were dependent on a capital transaction to realize business value (which I am not), I would be… sad.

2. VC RUINS GOOD BUSINESSES 

A few of these businesses would have been nice bootstrapped, “lifestyle” businesses where the founders could have built cool stuff, had a happy team, and made millions of dollars per year on their own terms… had they set out to do that. Some combination of pre-churn euphoria and easy money, led to an entire space falling. Investors needed the companies to be bigger than they were meant to be, and the founders with either a little or a lot of convincing, agreed with them.

3. LACK OF TRANSPARENCY IS A PROBLEM 

Every “acquisition” gets framed as some positive thing, even though no price is mentioned, which is misleading to other Founders. An acqui-hire and earn-out is not what any of us are doing this for. Yet these are the headlines we see, and we send congratulatory text messages and DM’s. The problem is that this is a bad outcome, and most VC-backed companies either experience something like this or worse. 

What I want to see is a table of who sold for what and what the Founders walked away with. Then compare it to a table of bootstrappers. But we will we never see it, so the show will go on.

4. WHAT ARE YOU DOING THIS FOR???

It’s very easy to get incredibly ambitious with YC, SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI buzzing all around you. Investors all want those outcomes, so they all push you to believe it’s possible. For some people, it might be. But in most cases there is a huge amount of luck (along with skill) in becoming one of the 10% (or less) of people that succeeds after taking VC money. 

I have friends who just couldn’t be happy unless their business became enormous. Yes, you need VC for that. But most people who took money did so because it looked like it made sense at the time, and they were selling a small stake in their business so they didn’t think it was a big deal. But it is. It always is.

***CONCLUSION in the comments 👇

Employees join startups excited for stock options, but it's a total black box. Options are risky, unclear, and often worthless until an exit (if it ever happens). But there is a SOLUTION and I think Carta should build it:

BACKGROUND

When you get stock options from a startup it is only “rights” to buy equity “when” you vest. 

There are a lot of details that can alter the money you eventually make: 

- Exercise window
- Capital gains tax
- Exercise price
- AMT tax

The system is designed to be complex, and in most cases, employees never exercise their stock options. 

Even when they do, few see positive returns because investors prioritize preferred shares over common employee shares. 

It’s a BROKEN MODEL that leaves early employees with little reward despite their hard work and discounted salaries.

Here's the SOLUTION:

Issue Equity Tokens instead of Stock Options:

What if early-stage startups tokenized their equity and distributed equity tokens to employees via a decentralized blockchain platform? These crypto tokens could represent shares in the company, functioning just like traditional equity but stored securely in digital wallets. 

Who will build this:

I believe Carta could innovate by building such a system, streamlining crypto equity management and creating new possibilities for startups and employees alike. Imagine a platform where stock option agreements are transparent and startup equity is liquid.  

Liquidity: 

Tokenization enhances the liquidity potential of otherwise illiquid assets (stock options). The whole idea of equity tokens traded on a blockchain based trading platform is to allow increased liquidity. Owners should be able to sell their vested tokens without the approval of the board or exchange their tokens with that from other startups to reduce their risk.      

Fundraise: 

Tokenization of equity has already emerged as a powerful way of raising capital where startups issue tokens in exchange of capital thereby raising the value of their tokens. Early stage VCs may love this approach as it provides a lot more liquidity to the investments. 

Transparency: 

Blockchain technology ensures transparency in the transaction. In some cases the payment distribution is also encoded into the transaction itself enhancing trust. 

Voting Rights: 

Equity tokens can be handled like equity. They can offer dividends, voting rights and participation in the company’s governance.  

Innovation: 

Equity tokens can be a significant innovation in venture development, startups investing, VC/LP investments and asset ownership. 

All you seed stage and series A companies: 

What is stopping you from tokenizing your stock options and making it far more transparent, liquid and attractive than your competitors? 

Do you know of a tech startup that has tokenized their equity?

In the past 6 months I’ve spoken to over 50 founders doing $1m-$10m ARR. 99% of them feel STUCK. Here are the 6 biggest mistakes they’re making that prevent them from unlocking growth to $10m ARR: 

1. They’re trying to be the same but better. 

It’s easy to get early traction when you’re a little bit better than the incumbent. To reach scale, you need to be 10x better than what people are already using to get them to switch.

2. Their messaging isn’t clear enough.

Crystal clear messaging helps everything. Unclear messaging hurts everything. A decent product with subpar messaging can get to a few million ARR. You have to tighten it up to get to $10. 

3. They don’t know who their ideal customer actually is.

Taking money from anyone and everyone is often what you have to do in the beginning. Honing in on an ideal customer and building for them will often get you unstuck.

4. They don’t understand their unit economics.

If you don’t know what’s working and what’s not, you don’t know what to scale and what to pull back on. Many startups do everything in the beginning and stall out because they have no idea what was actually working and what wasn’t.

5. They don’t have word-of-mouth.

If you have word-of-mouth, everything you do will work. If you don’t have word-of-mouth, nothing you do will work. Some startups capture initial excitement but fail to deliver on promises made, and lose this critical tailwind.

6. Their churn is abysmal because the product isn’t there yet.

RB2B is guilty as charged. We’re working every day on a total reinvention, and if you also have abysmal churn at mid-single-digit ARR, you should tirelessly improve your product too.

TAKEAWAY

Startups are hard.

My life for the last 12 years has been getting stuck, then unstuck again.

In fact, I’m stuck right now!

The good news is that no matter how stuck you feel:

A. There are thousands of founders who are stuck right there with you
B. No matter how stuck you are, you can get unstuck, it’s in your hands

I’m here to tell you don't get defeated.

The rewards for blowing past $10m ARR are unimaginable.

Keep building.

I just hit 100,000 followers on Linkedin. It took 500+ posts and 40M+ impressions, but it transformed my life and business. Here are the 9 biggest lessons I learned after 24 months of posting on LinkedIn:

1. It’s a “long term game” and it’s going to start off slowly

- It’s probably not going to “click” for at least a year
- The harsh truth... you can use a ghostwriter to help get you started, but eventually you'll need to own it. It's YOUR thoughts, expertise and experience that matters. Own your brand.

2. It will open doors you didn’t know existed

- You’ll walk around trade shows and people will think they know you
- You can create a pull mechanism for investors, rather than a push
- It will raise your status in the ecosystem

3. Meme-type content builds the wrong audience

- Early on, I got really excited when I’d get 1,000s of likes from a meme
- But the engagers weren’t buyers or even potential buyers
- Our product only works for the USA and much of the audience was overseas
- Design your content strategy for impact, not likes

4. The right template can make a good post FLY

- I can’t emphasize this point enough: use templates!
- This doesn't mean copy other creators, it means don't reinvent the wheel
- Look at this post... the "hook" is full of #'s and social proof, there's an enticing cliffhanger, and then an easy-to-read list of learnings (look at my last 10 posts and you'll see a pattern)

5. Transparency and “working in public” content has killed it for me

- I share full financials, which is unheard of for a $23m ARR SaaS
- Doing something no one else is doing is the most effective way to cut through
- People LOVE to know how much money you are making (or losing)

6. Stirring it up in the comments early helps your posts

- I try to reply to every comment within 2 hours
- I then set a cadence of every 12 hours after that
- I have noticed that it boosts performance by ~33%
- It also gives you a pulse on the market (guides you what to write next)

7. Engage with other influencers who are in your ecosystem

- You’ll pick up audience from whoever you’re engaging with over time
- Want an audience of VP of Sales? Go find them and engage

8. If you’re not pissing anybody off, you aren’t going hard enough

- Getting told I’m an idiot and have no idea what I’m doing was hard (once)
- I got over it quickly when I realized the people saying it are just assholes
- Assholes help your posts, so be thankful they are there

9. Video is a superpower

- The power of a Talking Head style video is unmatched
- Let people see your face, how you talk, your mannerisms
- This is the quickest way to get people to know you and build trust

TAKEAWAY:

Yes, every CEO/Founder should post on LinkedIn.

But they also need to invest the time to learn how it works.

Unless you're willing to study the platform, measure your results, and adjust...

You'll end up getting frustrated (or posting memes like I did).

And you'll never truly experience the power of LinkedIn.

What actually IS an autonomous business?

I started noticing the term “autonomous business” when Amos Bar-Joseph entered RB2B’s space and made a splash with an incredibly compelling narrative about AI and building the startup of the future.

I remember reading posts from 2 years ago like it was yesterday…

He had this exciting way of positioning himself as a true AI expert, creating a totally new type of startup. 

“Just three guys and an army of 30 AI agents”, “scaling to $30m ARR” (my favorite credibility line ever). 

I - along with thousands of others - read these posts and WANTED all of these agents. 

But I also had this feeling that the way they were going about it, Swan AI wasn’t ever going to be truly autonomous … Nor was that the goal. 

These guys were actually working around the clock with these agents, and planned to continue to do so indefinitely. 

And by the way - there is nothing wrong with that. 

In fact, I’d go as far as to say if you are NOT committed to working around the clock indefinitely, you will almost certainly NOT be successful. 

But back to my original question … 

Is 3 guys working around the clock ACTUALLY an autonomous business? 

My answer would be “no”. 

I have a fairly un-evolved definition of an “autonomous business” … 

My definition is “a business that runs itself without any humans.” 

Ironically, when we started RB2B, that was the ultimate goal, but never became part of the story. We designed the entire machine to be simple enough to where all customer interaction could be handled by AI, and our cheap acquisition channel (my thought leadership) helped us price so low that people didn’t expect more than that from us. 

Fast forward 2 years...

We refuse to add anything beyond a pixel and a push, AI handles over 99% of our total customer tickets, and our CSAT is in the high 90’s. 

What’s even crazier is that we stopped working on RB2B six weeks ago to pursue MoltSets. 

What do I mean by that? 

- Tate has not touched the code in six weeks (true story)
- Robb spends under 15min/day answering AI-escalated tickets
- I post 3x/week on LinkedIn, ironically NOT about RB2B

… And we’re currently growing at over 7%/mo, will cross $10m ARR soon, and it’s taking under 90min of human time per week.

Based on my primitive definition - a business that runs itself w/o humans - RB2B is the closest thing to “autonomous” that I’ve ever heard of. 

How would you define an autonomous business? 
What are other examples?

I just bootstrapped RB2B to $5m ARR in 13mo with 5 people. I also bootstrapped Retention.com to $13m ARR with 6 people. My secret? What I do is repeatable. Here’s my 7-step playbook to 7-fig ARR with tiny teams:

1. Validate demand before building ANYTHING

- Retention started as a feature in my first startup, Robly. People loved the identity feature but hated Robly, so we knew the demand was there
- RB2B is a B2B version of Retention. We did 300 discovery calls with marketing leaders to validate the market wanted person-level ID for ABM

2. Create a DIFFERENTIATED (albeit terrible) v1 of your product that people will talk about

- Retention was originally a batch spreadsheet of site visitors. Pretty terrible user experience, but it was so different that it got tons of traction
- RB2B is riddled with horrible problems to this day – but 1 year ago we were the only vendor who resolved site visitors to the person-level

3. Create MASSIVE AWARENESS… Through your HUMANITY

- The best way to accelerate word-of-mouth is through social. I did a crazy FB ads campaign for 6mo when we launched Retention. It stopped working, but EVERYBODY in our TAM saw them… That + word-of-mouth + cold email
- For RB2B I was able to create viral LinkedIn thought leadership to our addressable market for the 6mo prior to launch. We had a 3000 person wait list

4. Eliminate sales and onboarding friction

- At Retention, we gave our customers 25 free emails, then forced them to a call with Diana. She did thousands of 5min presentations that answered key questions and got people to do a 2mo paid trail, then upgrade (or drop)
- At RB2B, we did a freemium product to a PLG with a sales rep answering questions and helping with tactical onboarding for high-value users

5. Wait an unreasonably long time to hire ANYBODY

- At Retention, we had the same 6 people at $13m ARR as we did at launch
- At RB2B, Robb has managed to create an AI that supports 40k free users

6. Spend time and money on very few wildly positive ROI things

- At Retention, we had so few people that we had to focus on what mattered. Product, onboarding, cold email, demos, and “wow-ing” our customers
- At RB2B, we cut all paid marketing spend ($100k/mo) and our growth sped up

7. Keep doing steps 1-6 until you hit $10m ARR

- At Retention, not only did we not burn any money, we actually distributed $5m of cash to the co-founders on our journey to $10m ARR
- At RB2B, 12mo in and we are already profitable, with no plans to grow staff or spend on anything until $10m ARR

TAKEAWAY

Getting to profitability is the promised land for early-stage startups.

Yet VCs want Founders to raise money, usually to crash and burn.

I think more people should start startups my way.

If you can bootstrap $10m ARR, you can do ANYTHING you want with your life.

You will be making millions of dollars and playing by your own rules while enjoying total freedom.

I know because I’ve done it. That IS my life.

You can do it, too.

Last week I saw several Linkedin posts recommending SDRs do 10,000 units of outbound/month and maximize sales channel activity. This is bad advice. The brute force approach is short sighted and will kill your credibility and annoy your buyers. 

There’s a reason why those are upper limits. 

We don’t need to hit them every week. 

I don’t understand why Sales leaders constantly suggest hitting those limits to meet goals. That’s such an old-school approach. It may have worked when the market was not saturated. 

But not anymore...

Here’s the Model they're recommending:

Model 1: Maximize Channel Activity

- Maximize Linkedin connects (200/week)
- Maximize dials (500/week)
- Maximize emails/account (1000/week)

This may have been OK when you didn’t have to create demand. 

When demand already existed and you could capture it through rapid conversations. 

Increasingly, this transactional approach has only suited high-velocity, low ACV SaaS products with short sales cycle and quick onboarding. 

But with sustained use, you risk losing trust and credibility with your buyers in the long run.

Here’s the model you should instead opt for:

Model 2: Maximizing Trust

- Research and Understand Pain Points
- Present yourself as a resource to the buyer
- Build relationship
- Solve relevant and targeted problems
- Don’t maximize outbound

This approach can be slower and more expensive. 

While we historically saw this approach followed by ABM marketers for large ACV, high margin products - now it is increasingly relevant to all solutions. 

This leads to more strategic conversations and allows an AE to create an environment where demand creation or demand inception can happen.  

TAKEAWAY:

Don’t maximize your channel outputs with relentless Calls, Inmails or Emails. 

Do your research. 

Use Signals. 

Use Inbound-Led Outbound or slightly warm outbound. 

What’s good for the industry and buyers is also good for you. 

We are all in this together. 

Everybody wins or Everybody loses together.

This weekend I was speaking to the CEO of a $100M apparel brand who hit a wall in Q2. His CAC was performing 15-20% worse, he revised his 2023 forecast down $20,000,000.

He’s all Meta and Google. 

He’s been growing at 100% per year, and over time, repeat customers have become more and more of his business. 

Things were fine when they reached 40% of his ad spend. 

As they got to 50% and 60%, things started slowing, and the ads performed worse.

TAKEAWAY

Sometimes a simple change can have a massive impact. 

Never stop throwing spaghetti against the wall.

Building Products in 2012 vs Building Products in 2023:
 
Building Products in 2012:

- Let’s save money and get v1 built overseas
- Let’s just copy [insert market leader]’s UI/UX
- Let’s build it first and once it’s almost done let’s find our customers
- We should build a market-leader’s feature set before we launch
- Doing the same thing as the market leader for a cheaper price will work
- Let’s try to under-cut a $30/mo SaaS by 50%
- Let’s go into a super-mature, super-commoditized market
- Let’s have 25 salespeople and 1 engineer and zero product people
- Let’s build a small lifestyle business

Total minimum viable product build time = 18 months
 
Building Products in 2023:

- Only entertain ideas that are “money for a discount” and show quick ROI
- Stay away from any idea that is less than $1,000/mo SaaS
- When you come across an idea, talk to 100 people in the ICP about it
- Watch their facial expressions, see micro-reactions to judge how good it is
- Make sure 80% of people have “holy shit, how do I get that right now” face
- If so, figure out if MVP is possible with zero engineering resources expended
- It’s ok to do everything manually with VA’s until 10-20 cases are proven
- If dev work is required, do as much as possible outside of core team
- Create so few features that the experience is “borderline unbearable”
- Gather feedback for 60-90 days of the initial cohort of users
- See if they still consider your "unbearable" experience a high NPS product
- If so, team up with product, figure out how to make the experience delightful
- Once UX is done, cut the line in the dev queue and insert yourself at the front
- Do whatever intricate go-to-market motion makes sense for the product

Total minimum viable product build time = less than 8 weeks

Every single thing that I did when I built my first SaaS product I now think is wrong. 

In fact, I’m proud of myself for how far I’ve come.

Not just as an entrepreneur, but how careful I am with engineering time.

I messed up everything I could the first time around. 

Don’t make the same mistakes I did.

#startups

rows.content:
Last week Sam Jacobs said "The Golden Age of SaaS is over". 

This means The Golden Age of B2B Sales is dead too.

Golden Age of B2B Sales (2007-2023):

- Most Markets were still unsaturated
- There were plenty of net new customer acquisition opportunities
- Several large markets opened up in horizontal SaaS
- Cheap capital and low interest rates led to conversion and expanding ACVs
- SDRs could still book meetings
- Decreasing CAC, ever increasing LTV
- Cold outreach (email and phone) worked and accelerated growth
- Rapid business growth led to rapid career growth and promotions
- Sales led buying process meant sales had a chance to influence decision
- Discovery could start early as early as 10% of the buying process

The New World of B2B Sales (2023 -????)

- Most SaaS markets are now saturated 
- No net new opportunities left, all opportunities are competitive displacements
- A lot of the future opportunities are in niche vertical markets (much smaller)
- Capital is expensive (5%+) leading to longer sales cycles and shrinking ACVs
- SDRs are having a hard time booking meetings and will continue to do so
- CAC is increasing, LTV is decreasing
- Cold bulk outreach (email and phone) will increasingly not be effective
- Slower business growth will also result in slower career growth
- With Buyer led sales and PLG - sales has less opportunity to influence
- Discovery is starting late as late as 80% of the buying process

Here's the silver lining:

No matter what changes in sales...

Relationship, trust and credibility still matters.

In fact, maybe now more than ever.

The key for sellers will be developing and sharing unique insights:

- on products
- on competitors
- on customers

Because activity alone isn't going to get you there anymore.

B2B Sales is about to get tough.

Successful reps will "coach buyers on how to buy" and will go out of their way to "provide value" in making the buyer successful.

This will involve shifting the focus from mindless activities to quality conversations and trusting relationships.

Evolve or die.

Last week I spoke with an enterprise AE at F100 company who closed over $5M in 2023 (3x his quota). The surprising part? He generated 90% from Linkedin. Here’s what the enterprise social selling playbook looks like:

1. Community:

Successful sales reps are constantly enhancing their community on Linkedin. They invite key prospects, customers and other stakeholders to their network. As an AE or Exec, it helps to stay in the same domain over time so you can engage with the same community but across different employers. The compounding effect of your network is exponential.

2. Content:

Engage frequently with your community. Stay ahead of the curve and ensure your content reflects that. Not all content has to be original and unique. Most Linkedin users are looking to consume content that will help them be better at their job today. Share best practices, success stories and recommendations. If you stay in the same domain, the quality of your content will grow as you build trust within your community.

3. Signals:

Get a good understanding of the triggers and signals that impact demand in your target segment. Use these signals to focus your attention on select individuals as they become active. 

4. Offer Help:

Be mindful of any request for assistance within your community. If you are going to stay in the same domain for long, expect your community to do the same. Offer to assist even if it does not directly help your business. Chances are these interactions will lead to deep relationships in the long run. 

5. LinkedinOps:

This is often an ignored part of social selling. For the same reason that Inbound leads perform so well (because they are warm), somebody that visited your profile also has a relatively high probability to respond in the first 24hr. It’s the job of LinkedinOps to run all active engagers through an ICP filter and then follow up on good fit candidates. 

6. Outreach:

I have seen some successful reps use personalization tools to find the right messaging or conversation opener for Linkedin outreach. It makes sense to do an outreach with the good-fit engaged audience within 24-48 hrs of the engagement. Don’t hesitate to ask for referrals. 

7. Tracking: 

Track engagements and metrics. Score and rank your audience every week for good fit top engagers. Your top engagers are the ones who will likely take your call. Your LinkedinOps can help you with analytics.

8. Convert:

Know when and how to move your conversation outside Linkedin. Linkedin is great for capturing demand signals or for generating trust. Look for the right moment to share a calendar link or an email to move the conversation to a different platform.

TAKEAWAY:

Your buyers are already on Linkedin. 

With a little discipline and LinkedinOps, you can close revenues while enhancing your brand and handling objections at scale. 

I've been helping GTM teams for 15+ years.

Never before have they had access to such a powerful platform.

Take advantage.

rows.content:
When writing copy — it’s very easy to come off as desperate.

Instead: write like you’re writing to someone you’ve known for years.

It’ll put you in the mind frame of being comfortable with the way you write, which signals status and makes people respect you and trust you.

For example, I ‘could’ say:

“Hey there,
I’m Adam, the founder, and CEO of Robly!
Thanks for sending your first email with us. Myself and my team are happy to have you on board with us!
You are now a member of our family!
Don’t hesitate to ask me any questions and we’ll get back to you within 24 hours.
Yours truly,
Adam Robinson”

This is a “take me out of your system, I’m switching to Sendlane as we speak” email.

It’s trying too hard.

And it’s SO obvious that the purpose of this message is to be a little bit ‘too nice.’

It just feels like I’m about to ask for your credit card information. Yuck.

Write like you’re writing to a peer, and the person will feel like you’re a peer.

It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Don’t be needy.
Don’t say too much.
And of course, have a little bit of fun with it.

That’s how you write high-converting copy.

The last few months have been ROUGH for Retention.com

Here are the dirty details - broken down by MRR:

February: $1,333,331 (10.2% growth)
March: $1,441,924 (8.1% growth)
April: $1,509,890 (4.7% growth)
May: $1,566,145 (3.7% growth)

That is not the direction we want to be headed.

Or the news I want to be sharing.

But here’s the thing…

Building in public means sharing the good, the bad and the ugly.

And we’re 100% committed to transparency.

But May was emotionally grueling.

And confusing…

THE ANALYSIS:

In early 2023, we experienced a surge of demand and insane sales metrics with new and untrained employees that led us to BELIEVE we should keep growing headcount as fast as possible and go for the land grab.

But once we got fully staffed up, everything just stopped…

And it’s NOT totally clear why.

We think we can fix a lot of the problem and get moving again (maybe slower, but still moving) with sharper focus on doing things that matter and more careful spending.

However, some of it seems to be market-related.

Anecdotally, I have been speaking with revenue leaders from other SaaS vendors who sell into the Shopify ecosystem and they had terrible months in April and May as well.

The interesting thing is that we're not hearing that the merchants are hurting.

The hope is that they are just waiting to see if there is a huge dip before the holiday season, and if there isn't, they start gearing up again.

Our product is very Black Friday friendly. And I bet we see a tailwind.

THE TAKEAWAY:

Will we hit $4m MRR by year-end?!?!?!

It's not impossible. But after these past few months, it's become a truly epic challenge.

As I have reminded myself, when your team has bootstrapped $1.55M MRR and a surprisingly soft month is growing that MRR by 3.7%, I have nothing to complain about.

This would have been my dream only months ago.

$2.5m MRR would be 100% YoY growth for us.

Will we get there?

I think so.

But the BHAG goal is $4m and that’s still what we’re aiming for.

There will be ups and downs, but I’ll be sharing every step along the way.

Updates daily!

Last November we bought 6sense for $18,000 so we could compare it to Clearbit and our Person-Level Identity tool. Last week our rep told us renewal will cost $55,000!  Here are my 6 theories why they are 3X-ing our pricing and don't want us using their tool:

1. 6Sense knows their data is terrible

Let’s be honest with ourselves. 

Company/Account level site visitor identity isn’t nearly as valuable as Person-Level ID, and the more we compare results of our data vs theirs, the higher likelihood we are to have a case study reporting how many more demos we booked using our tech (which is free) than theirs. The good news for 6Sense is that our sales team thinks it’s so bad they won't use it!

2. 6Sense is worried what we’ll find when we compare it to Clearbit and our product. 

We actually DID this, and the results were very interesting. 

There was single-digit overlap between the three - Clearbit, 6Sense, and RB2B. 
What this tells me is that if you can make one of them work, you should use them all. If you can’t make any of them work, you should only use the free one.

3. 6Sense is actually worried about the VIRAL expansion of our free tool.

We don’t have tech we could sell to a mid-market 6Sense customer yet, but we will. In the meantime, we’ve had 4,780 people sign up with an 80% self-serve script install rate. 

Are they seeing people churn off an $18-100k solution to use a free one? 

If that is actually happening, that would worry me too.

4. 6Sense knows that their 3rd party intent signal isn’t a buying signal. 

Content consumption doesn’t equal purchase intent. 

Genius marketing makes you believe that it does.

The market COULD BE starting to understand that most of the value of 6Sense is in different methods of retargeting website visitors, in which case, our Person-Level Website Visitor Identity tool is in direct competition with the most valuable use case at 6Sense. So, they are figuring out the nicest possible way to say “F OFF”.

5. 6Sense's pricing is just wrong, and they are scared of the future.

I heard that they will GUESS the contacts on your site for another $30k/year, on top of the tens of thousands that you’re already paying for an inferior product to what we’re giving away for free.

6. 6Sense wanted me to post about it.

If THIS was the goal, mission accomplished. 

You got the eyeballs of my LinkedIn audience!

TAKEAWAY:

6Sense doesn’t want us to use their product. 

I can understand why. 

It’s so bad that our sales team won’t even use it... 

Even though we paid $18,000 for it!

Surely they must be hearing the noise of what RB2B is up to, and the positive response we’re getting.

Here’s my biggest question...

Should we just pay the $55,000 to piss them off and make them ask... 

“Well, what do we do now?!?!?!"

In 3 years, Retention.com went from an unknown startup struggling to close our first deal to a $20M ARR company serving the world’s top Shopify stores.

Here's our 5-step playbook for bootstrapping your startup:

1. Decide in your mind that you're going to GO FOR IT

- This may sound silly, but this change in mindset is hugely important
- It changes how you look at investments related to brand, events and visibility
- It needs to be the right time, but if it is, there’s nothing like being all-in

2. Start creating “Founder Brand” content on Linkedin and Twitter

- This raised the visibility of our brand more than anything else we have done. 
- I have been crazy about building in public, sharing financials, and using video.
- Be 100% transparent, share wins and losses. Don't hide anything.

3. Buddy up with all of the influencers in your space and start doing events

- Small, cool private events did well for us
- We found people with networks of brands and partnered with them
- DTC Surf Club in Austin, Post Malone booth in Toronto, Pizza Tour in NYC

4. Get on stage at a bunch of different venues (big, small, doesn't matter)

- GROW LA/NYC were my favorites … Get on stage with your best customers
- We sponsored tons of other events, but none have been as good as Grow
- Shout out to Greg Ashton for putting on a great event

5. Hire an incredible partnerships team

- In our business, the ecosystem is super important
- We have been able to get in front of every major agency
- It's a long-term game, but the potential reach is far & wide

This is what worked for us.

Will it work for you?

Maybe!

There's no one-size-fits-all approach.

You have to constantly experiment.

Test and see what gets you traction.

Then double down.

That's the key.

You got this!

Lacework (valued at $8B) announced yesterday that they are in talks to sell the business for $150-300M. Needless to say at this price, the employees will make absolutely no money. I am afraid, this is the beginning of a long trend. 

Here are 4 key lessons for employees and job seekers in VC backed companies:

1. Don’t take equity compensation seriously

With high interest rates, large IPOs or big acquisitions are behind us. 

In 2024, the probability of a windfall from acquisition dropped significantly. A lot of the companies with inflated valuations will end up accepting deals like Lacework that result in common shares going underwater and no employees making money. 

If you're considering a job in one of these companies, look at equity objectively. When leaving, don't use your retirement to exercise. 

2. Startup game is rigged against employees

As an employee, you will own common shares, stock options or RSUs, whereas Institutional investors have preferred shares and liquidity preferences. 

In terms of payout, the investors have far less risk than the employees. Investors are also investing their firm’s money whereas you're likely borrowing from your retirement or savings to exercise and pay AMT (taxes). 

3. Even during success, there's a chance you may never excercise

Let’s say you join a company at a discounted salary and get $100k worth of stocks that vest over 4 years (300K stocks at an exercise price of $0.33 each). 

You worked hard for 4 years and helped the company grow. 

During this time the company raised a lot of capital.

All this success increases the 409A valuation and common stock price to $5 per share. So on paper your $100K stocks is worth $1.5M.

Once you vest all the shares, you decide to leave for another job.    

You resign and now have 90 days to exercise. 

Only then do you realize that in addition to the exercise price of $100K, you owe taxes that can run into hundreds of thousands of dollars. 

4. Manage your taxes

The only way to maximize your earnings is to manage your taxes. If you fail to exercise early, you end up paying income tax vs long term capital gains tax. On a large sum of money, this can add up. 

The best strategy is to get your employer to pay a sign in bonus that enables you to exercise on the first day you join the company. This minimizes your AMT taxes and hopefully provides you with the capital gains benefit. 

_

Now, back to Lacework...

If I am to guess, all the common shares will go under water in this transaction. 

While the company is selling for $200M, the investors are distributing $800M of the remaining cash amongst themselves. 

It would be nice if the Lacework investors put aside a small amount of the proceeds to share it with the common shares. 

In addition to being a good gesture, if this became a common practice - it reduces the risk of working for a VC backed company and provide some downward protection to everyone that took a risk on the company and not just the investors.

Over the past 12 months I spoke to 50+ top-tier VC firms about investing in my bootstrapped (profitable) $22m ARR SaaS. Here are 7 reasons why I walked away and decided NEVER to take VC money:

1. Dividends are good

If you create a successful early-stage startup, you should be rewarded by getting paid millions of dollars every year… Not just some *potentially* astronomical number at some point MAYBE in the future.

2. The investor value prop is weak (if you don’t need capital)

I listened to pitch after pitch of investors saying their “go-to-market advisory would be game-changing” for us. This pitch was weak and designed to get founders like me dreaming big dreams that if they panned out would largely be my team’s doing.

3. A new seat at the table is a net negative. Period

At best, investors will slow you down. At worst, they will ruin your life AND destroy your common equity if your business slows down for macro reasons outside of your control.

4. Investors are in the portfolio game. You’re not

Situations can emerge - FREQUENTLY - where what is best for your life and company can be usurped by a group of investors wanting a quick 2x. Even if they have a minority position, there are SO many ways they can exert influence and drive the outcome that is best for the fund.

5. I want to do things investors would not tolerate

My strategy for 2024 is to give away a super-valuable product to millions of people using viral distribution strategies and do a lightning-fast PLG. I want to do it with a team that is unreasonably lean. I want to continue to add value to the free offering. I want to give away 6 Teslas (more on that coming soon). THE SECOND any of this plan went sour, I would be told to stop, and if I didn’t, I’d be fired.

6. I don’t believe in measuring things or spreadsheets

This is going to be highly controversial. I think almost all measurement (aside from top-line ARR) is complete garbage and leads to bad long-term decision making in favor of optimizing in the short term for whatever metric you’re going for.

7. Large carrots dangled in front of us make us make bad decisions

An investor’s job is to try to figure out what number will motivate the founder to transact, and once identified, get them to attach their identity to that number. We love validation that our beautiful business IS worth $100m, even if it actually lowers the probability-weighted financial outcome for the founder.

TAKEAWAY:

Last year I was seduced by the idea that I could take millions off the table and move even faster.

After speaking to an investor a week for all of 2023, I realized that those millions would likely change many of the things about my life that I value the most.

I’d sacrifice independence, freedom of choice and it would slow us down. 

That's why I'm a bootstrapper at heart. 

And I always will be.

Last week I spoke to the CRO of a $50M ARR SaaS who just KILLED a six-figure ABM campaign because after 8 months they only booked 3 meetings. Here's what went wrong and why (broken down by the #'s):

BACKGROUND:

The ABM campaign ran to 1,600 target accounts from January to August across digital ads and email marketing. 

Here's the numbers breakdown:

- 1,632 target companies
- 13,000 contacts
- 231 people engaged with the ads (1.7%)
- 66 visited the website (0.05%)
- 3 demos booked

Here's the vendors they used: 

- Terminus was used for ads
- Hubspot was used for email
- Salesforce was used for reporting

Here’s how my conversation with the CRO went: 

CRO: Adam, it was a very horrible outcome.

Me: If you could do it over again, what would you change?

CRO: Well, this campaign started before I arrived, and we didn’t have a tight definition of our ICP, relevant content, and personas.

Me: Sure, that'll lead to abysmal results in any campaign. What else did you think was the problem?

CRO: Well, we sell to 500+ person companies, and we only had company-level website visitor resolution. We knew that 66 companies hit the site from the campaign, which is low, but honestly I was fine with it… But our BDRs had to try to figure out which of 20+ people at the company it might have been! It was a huge undertaking that yielded very few results.

Me: What if I could tell you the exact people at those companies who were on your website? 

CRO: My BDRs would be all over it. We might still be running that campaign!

TAKEAWAY:

ABM is expensive and hard.
 
What makes it even harder is that once you actually drive the right person back to the site, vendors like 6Sense, DemandBase, and Terminus only tell you the company they work for and the geolocation.

If you’re selling to enterprise, this information is not very helpful.

That's why we need a new “Identity Layer” as the last step in the loop.

Meaning...

An *exact match* to the individual that hit your site, rather than only the company name.

99% of SaaS revenue leaders aren’t aware this is even an option. 

But it is!

And it's going to change the trajectory of ABM in 2024.

P.S.

DM me if you want to know how to add person-level identity as the last step of your ABM campaign.

Here's 6 reason why SDR response rates have plummeted in the last 12 months (and what you can do about it):

1. Inboxes are ruined

We have all responded to lower conversion rates by adding domains and inboxes (and sending far more volume). Any attempt you have made at low-volume personalization is drowned out by everyone else’s high-volume spamming.

2. LinkedIn is even worse

Between automation tools, outbound services attempting to execute “push” plays, and InMail, every prospecting LinkedIn message looks identical to the last.

3. Phones only work for certain TAMs

More people are working from home than ever. Carrier blocks on cell phones and certain TAMs that just don’t answer at all make cold calling 100x harder than 15 years ago.

4. Money isn’t free anymore

Every day that goes by where you can get 5%+ on your cash in a checking account makes the entire world increasingly question the need to purchase anything, software included.

5. Fundraising has effectively ground to a halt

Klaviyo IPO’d and there have been a handful of SaaS deals, but growth capital into companies scaling out teams and buying more software is nothing like it was 24 months ago.

6. The (now busted) Salesforce playbook hasn’t changed in over 10 years

100,000 SaaS companies are still trying to build an assembly line lead generation process when it’s not what the buyer wants and #1-5 render it completely useless.

So...

What can you do about it?

🎥 On today's episode of our docuseries BILLION DOLLAR CHALLENGE, I get into why we've leaned so heavily into LinkedIn content creation, the new tech we're quietly rolling out for B2B sales teams and the positive changes taking place in our core Shopify business.

Because here's the truth:

Response rates aren’t bouncing back anytime soon.

We need to build a new B2B sales model.

This is what I think it looks like:

- Tiny SDR teams with messages triggered on signal like social engagement, job change, website visits, tech deployment/removal, progression in partners’ CRMs, etc

- Partner and ecosystem plays drive indirect high-intent leads to your sales team

- Demand created over months (if not years) through founder-led and edutainment content that cuts through 

- High-Intent demand captured through an ultra-lean, super-experienced sales team

- Conversion rates > 60%, sales cycles cut by ⅔ 

- Your sales team only spends time talking to people who want to buy

The classic Salesforce playbook doesn't work anymore.

It's bad for business and it's bad for salespeople.

We need to design sales teams in a new way.

That's what we're doing at Retention.com

The product adoption lifecycle curve is dead. Here's what the current slump in Electric Car Sales teaches us about the future of SaaS sales:

For over 6 years now, I've been driving an electric car.

I LOVE that I don’t have to go to a gas station for refills. 

Recently, the electric car market exploded with all the majors manufacturers launching their own version.

But with all the increased choices and an expanded changing network, the actual demand for electric car sales has been decreasing instead of expanding. 

Why is that?

What *really* changed?

This question bugged me so I went searching for answers...

I ran into several reasons, but none convincing.

Then I thought about my tech sales background. 

Could the sales for electric vehicles be down because the early adopter market is saturated and demand from other demographics is much slower? 

Most of us view the world as Gaussian and think that most things are evenly distributed in a bell curve and follow the Pareto law. 

If we follow the product adoption cycle from Geoffery Moore then perhaps with EV sales, we have simply hit the chasm (see picture) from early adoption and there may be a slowdown before hitting mainstream adoption of EV vehicles.  

That's why I think the Curve Adoption Cycle is Dead: 

In the past, products have traditionally followed the bell curve adoption lifecycle, however It will be fair to say that the Bell Curve Product Adoption life cycle is dead specially in tech.  

With increased information symmetry amongst the buyers and social media, we are seeing a very different kind of product adoption lifecycle. 

Where disruptive products get instant adoption leading to an overnight success. 

OpenAI is a great example of an overnight success. 

They did not follow the traditional Gaussian curve of adoption. 

Disruptive products sometimes age unevenly leading to a period of rapid decline giving way to an entirely new market innovation or substitute. 

With the increased pace of innovation, even successful products have to be careful not to lose market share to new innovations and substitutes. 

Because the decline can be as rapid as the adoption.   

P.S.

Few questions I could use your help with...

What do you think of my hypothesis? 

Will EV Car sales rise again? If so, when?

Is the Product Adoption Lifecycle Curve *truly* dead?

9 things that will kill you as a first time startup founder:

1. You can’t convince a real CTO to work for you (you don’t even know how to find one)

2. You don’t pair up with the right sales and marketing co-founder

3. You build way too much product as your MVP. This is almost everybody

4. You raise too much money too early at too high of a valuation

5. You try to do too many things because everything seems so exciting

6. You copy the industry leaders’ feature set and attempt to compete on price

7. You don’t realize that you should spend as little money as humanly possible

8. You try to solve a less painful problem for a lot of people, rather than a very, very painful problem for a much smaller group of people

I share an office with a billionaire — and it changed my life.

Here’s the fascinating story:

When I started GetEmails, I was burned out from my prior startup, and the plan the whole time was to sell after 18 months

GetEmails turned out to grow way faster than we had hoped, the market was hot, so we were able to get a smoking offer for it at the end of last year

I was at the 1-yard line of getting this off my hands, and I had someone coming in the next day to sign an Asset Purchase Agreement

The buyer bailed. At the last minute. Ugh.

This sudden loss of a life-changing amount of money threw me into an emotional tailspin for 24 hours

I had completely internalized the identity of a semi-retired dude who was going to spend time learning about crypto and doing the minimum possible to hit earn-out targets

I went into the office to talk to Dave Rogenmoser (CEO of JasperAI), I told him what happened, and he went on a rant for almost an hour that I wish I’d recorded

It would’ve been an audio recording worth a billion dollars

He told me about every single thing they were doing, and how they were aiming for the moon

He told me they hired Shane Orlick, the former Chief Revenue Officer of WalkMe, how big Shane thought, and how he attracted some of the best talent in the world to work with Jasper

He told me how they were now on the IPO track, and gunning for that within a handful of years

He told me they were on an absolute rocketship, and he told me I was thinking WAY too small

I realized my product was equally as good as theirs was

My feedback from customers and my numbers (kind of) reflected that

The difference?

They were spending over $1M+ a month on sales & marketing, at $50M ARR

I was spending $30K a month on sales & marketing (all of that was sales), at $8M ARR

Lightbulb goes off

Where would I be if I was in a position to spend $1M on salespeople (and/or marketing) for my operation?

I’d be at LEAST at $50M ARR

I decided that I had no choice but to think as big as Dave and the Jasper team were. I was playing way too small

Now, because of that conversation, I’ve done everything I can to be in the same place as Jasper is this year, by this time next year

There’s no way we’re not at $50M ARR by this time next year

If you’re curious where Jasper is now…

They just raised $125M at a $1.5B valuation in 18 months — after contemplating quitting the game and starting a restaurant 18 months prior

If you asked me in January 2021 if I believed that was possible for them, I would’ve cried laughing

It just wasn’t in the cards. I literally would have said “impossible”

But they proved to me and everyone else that it’s possible, and I’ve never been more motivated in my entire life

Hopefully this is a signal to you, too, that a failing business does not spell “The End”

Business and entrepreneurship are unpredictable. Every situation is different. But we can all think bigger, and execute on a much larger vision

Jasper proved it.
