In 2023, I spent $10,785 on PR Newswire to push press releases out about scaling Retention.com. It was a mistake. Here’s the unfortunate truth about bootstrapped startups and PR:

It doesn’t work!

The traditional top-of-funnel PR machine is expensive, inefficient, un-engaging, and for a startup, it’s very, very hard to see ROI. 

BACKGROUND:

Last year we pushed a handful of articles to PR newswire.

We didn’t have much to say, so we announced things like: 

- big hires
- a rebrand
- a docuseries

But these articles were just SOO boring. 

It was a perfect example of a big trap startup founders fall into:

Doing things that you THINK you need to be doing but you’re not sure why.

Most of the time it’s driven by watching what others are doing and copying them - without understanding why they are doing it (or if it's even working).

I have 3 key issues with strategies like this:

1. Pushing something out that you know sucks over a channel that you know won’t do anything for you because you feel like you have to is very “old way”

2. It’s a very NOT-human way to (attempt to) build brand 

3. You aren’t fostering any type of two-way engagement or community building 

I think traditional PR as a brand building strategy is completely dead, and the world is set up for startups to build FAR MORE trust in a much faster, capital efficient way. 

How? 

By becoming an “influencer” and crushing the organic social media game. 

Here’s why organic social absolutely crushes PR: 

- People are on social media all day every day (more than any one publication)
- People are on social media to connect with other people
- You can form ACTUAL RELATIONSHIPS through creating great content
- You can widen the attack surface by building up several internal influencers
- You build HIGHLY VALUABLE community through dialogue in the comments
- You have a GREAT feedback loop - you can see what hits and iterate on it

The future of B2B sales is Human-to-Human. 

Traditional “push” PR efforts like PR Newswire and paying $2k to be a Forbes contributor are losing ground to the far more engaging world of storytelling on organic social media. 

Your prospects want a relationship with YOU.

Not your company.

Not your 22-year-old SDR.

You can build that relationship by making yourself an “influencer”, drawing people in with your content, and engaging with them in the comments section. 

It’s a push vs pull model for PR and brand building. 

In 2024, pull wins

Bootstrapping vs. VC

A debate that continues to rage on in my comments that isn’t really a debate at all…

Look. I’m not saying VC-backed companies can’t be successful. I’m just saying the safety net provides a false sense of security. 

Bootstrapping puts the emphasis on spending less and generating more, while a pile of money to sit on usually leads to a lack of urgency (and a lack of profit). 

Retention.com went from 0 to profitable in 12 weeks. We had no choice.

Yes. I’ve been around the block more than once but bootstrapping with focus on velocity made this company explode.

I wouldn’t change a thing.

I’ve had 18,402,926 views on my Linkedin posts over the past 365 days, and I plan to double that in 2024. Here’s my 5-step content plan for next year (and how it’s changed from 2023):

BACKGROUND: 

1. I have a $22m ARR bootstrapped SaaS, selling into ecommerce
2. We are launching a person-level identity product to the B2B SaaS space
3. I am now spending 90% of my time building (and creating content for) the new product

Doubling impressions from such a high number is going to be hard. 

And it’s going to require being DIFFERENT.

We have to give people something new. 

Something they’ve never seen before. 

So what are we going to do? 

Here’s the five-step Retention.com content playbook for 2024:

1. Daily high-quality posts, coming from 3 different execs at our company

- Santosh, Diana, and I will all post regularly to expand the attack surface
- We will continue to use our favorite templates/formats (that crush) 
- Our hook and “takeaway” game will get even better 

2. Build-in-Public, taken to the EXTREME 

- This year we gave monthly updates w/ MRR and shared quarterly financials
- In 2024, we want to do DAILY updates with a new reality show called "$0-$10m" which documents every step and details of us building and selling our new B2B product
- We want it to be an immersive, reality-show type experience
- We are going to host it all in a community space, where we’ll be constantly publishing GTM/outbound experiments we’re doing and sharing what’s working and not

3. Bi-Weekly “AMA”-type Virtual Events w/ me & Santosh

- We want to give more time and direct access to our audience
- This is also a great source of content (ask Linkedin OG Chris Walker)

4. Get on as many B2B sales/marketing podcasts as possible

- Demand is created when you get in front of new audiences
- NOT by BDRs, they capture demand created elsewhere
- I’m going to take these video recordings and the AMA and make them our podcast, as well as distribute weekly on LinkedIn as 1-5 minute video clips (with text) optimized for in-feed consumption

5. OVER-use Video 

- I think video is more powerful than anyone realizes
- I want to do talking heads, shorts, reality show episodes
- Video accelerates the automated trust-building machine
- Text only is great for reach, but connection is built with your face!

TAKEAWAY:

Creating great content is HARD, especially on LinkedIn.

It takes time, energy, and persistence.

But every CEO (especially in B2B) should be doing it.

In fact, your executive and front line team should be doing it too!

Don't just reshare company blogs and boring ghost written content.

Invest the time to learn how it works.

Create a unique voice and develop a POV that's different.

Then study the platform, measure your results, and adjust...

That's the only way to harness the power of Linkedin.

And in 2024, organic content will be king!

Between 2015 and 2018, Drift raised $107M and built one of the best brands in B2B SaaS. In 2021, they found an acquirer at a $1B valuation. Now, I'm trying to do the same with R!B2B with $0 raised. Here's my brand playbook:

The “Drift Way”: 

- Build the affinity around the company itself
- A steady stream of books, podcasts, blog posts, and shareable PDFs that made you feel like you really needed it and gave you EXTREME FOMO
- They had a lightning bolt on their website and they had a lightning emoji everywhere (you couldn't escape it)
- Have a sexy, cutting-edge website that changes almost weekly
- Have a super-expensive physical presence - lots of people, offices, etc
- Pay for it all with over $100m of VC $$$

The “R!B2B Way”: 

- Build affinity around individual social profiles of individual thought leadership (not the company)
- Create a type of trust in top execs that can only be achieved human-to-human
- Build the business and offering to compliment and amplify this megaphone
- Use influencer and UGC marketing to build a different type of trust
- Have the top executives be the face of the brand, make their faces synonymous with the product category
- Do not worry about what the website looks like (use a template, get it up)
- Do not hire people, use chatbots instead, don’t have offices
- Pay for it with free cash from another business unit

TAKEAWAY:

I was intoxicated by the brand David Cancel & Dave Gerhardt created at Drift.

It attracted the best employees, customers, investors, and acquirers.

However, it required a ton of capital, both human and financial. 

We’re trying to use LinkedIn to create the same brand (without the capital).

I’m watching it happen in real-time.

We booked 300+ calls with ICP execs, driven thousands of waitlist signups, and over 1,500 free signups for our tool without spending $1 on ads.

How?

People know and trust Santosh Sharan and I because of our content.

I think the next generation of unicorns gets built like we’re building R!B2B. 

Light, fast, hyper-capital efficient.

But here's the thing...

It all starts with building a brand.

The one true moat left in SaaS.

You can't hire a fancy PR firm or marketing agency to do it for you. 

You (as founders and execs) have to invest the time to build it yourself.

That's the “new way”.

Why Salesloft’s acquisition of Drift signals the beginning of a nightmare-era for SaaS startups. Here's my analysis: 

I see a lot of comments congratulating Salesloft and Drift on this brilliant merger. I have friends in both these companies and I have resisted congratulating them. To me, this is a merger that marks the beginning of many such mergers across all VC and PE portfolios that will play out in the next 1-2 years.

Let’s look at the two companies: 

During the good times, Vista paid a high multiple for both these businesses. 

Revenue multiple Vista paid for Salesloft (2022): 23x 
Revenue multiple Vista paid for Drift (2021) : 17x [estimated]

Now, when the hard times hit - we know the company valuations have dramatically decreased, churn and downgrades have increased and the market has changed in a way that there’s no coming back from.

It’s no surprise that both Salesloft and Drift had layoffs in 2023. 

The competitive landscape for both these companies don’t look great either. 

Salesloft is in the Sales Engagement segment and Drift in Conversational Intelligence/ Chatbot segment. While both the companies are market leaders in their category, they face stiff competition as product differentiation rapidly wanes. 

On G2, there are 163 companies listed in sales engagement category and 169 companies listed in conversational intelligence. Both these categories are heavily commoditized. 

I don’t think Salesloft or Drift are particularly faring well as competition continues to chew up their bottom end. 

It made sense for Vista to combine the two businesses and cut their losses, this will decrease some costs and potentially leverage new synergies, particularly around buyer-led growth. Individually, both of these businesses would have a hard time maintaining their leadership, however they have a better chance to justify the high multiples together. This also signal’s Vista’s lack of confidence in the businesses to fare well on their own. 

Here’s why I worry:

There were a large number of PE deals done at astronomical valuations in the last few years. A lot of them are likely under water now. We will see several mergers like what Vista just orchestrated. This is a sign that the powers to be have given up on their ability to run these companies independently to justify the high multiples. Things can get much worse from here.

Buckle up.

We're in for a bumpy few years.

Last year I spent $100,000 on Data Privacy lawyers. Today I want to clarify my thoughts on Data Privacy for the angry CISOs and B2B Marketers who keep showing up in my LinkedIn comments:

1. A consensus view does not exist (despite what the loudest activists think)

There is a group of cybersecurity professionals who believe that there is a consensus that Data Privacy is unambiguous and clearly expressed in the GDPR. If you suggest that there are people in the world who believe differently, they say you are a dumb SaaS Bro and a sociopath (!).

2. There is no moral obligation for an American company to adhere to GDPR

I live in the US, vote in the US, and pay US taxes. I comply with US law, so do my customers. Many CISOs believe that I should follow regulation by other countries, instead of regulation in the country I live in. I disagree.

3. People (incorrectly) think the US is headed towards GDPR

State-level regulation is fast-moving and confusing. There is no question that regulation is tightening in the US, as it should. What I advocate for (and what is playing out in California) is disclosure, consent (through cookie banners with conspicuous statements), and opt-out. That’s very different from GDPR, which is a 1st party opt-in for data collection. The US is not currently headed in that direction.

4. Cookie banners are our friends

All anybody is asking for is disclosure, consent capture, and opt-out. The cookie banner, if the right language is used, can achieve all three. That will all but eliminate legal risk not only for our tech, but all types of pixel retargeting. US regulators aren’t trying to stop these practices - they are trying to make the consumer aware and give them an opt-out.

5. A website visit isn’t that special. 

If I have BuiltWith alert me when a competitor script goes on my site (behavior) and look in Apollo for the CMO’s contact info (PII) then connect with them on LinkedIn and send them an email (action), I don’t see the major difference between a website visit (behavior) and us providing the website owner the CMO’s contact info from Apollo’s API (PII), then the site owner connecting on LinkedIn and sending an email (action). 

If anything, we enable more targeted outreach than today’s accepted standard.

TAKEAWAY:

Some think every word of the GDPR is a human right. 

Other's believe the natural outcome of digital life is being tracked.

There’s one thing I know for sure. 

If you’re a company in the US, if you simply:

- Implement a cookie banner
- Have the proper language
- Provide a conspicuous opt-out

You lower your legal risk of using our tech (and others) to damn near zero. 

But don’t say that on LinkedIn… 

You might just get your teeth knocked out!

P.S.

*I am not a lawyer. This is not legal advice.

Last week I moderated a roundtable with Devin Reed - the mastermind behind Gong’s game-changing LinkedIn strategy - about growing your personal brand. Here are his 8 secrets to LinkedIn success:

1. Be inappropriate.

LinkedIn is the “safest” social network out there. People behave like they would at work. If you can be bold, offensive, or even the slightest bit inappropriate, your content will stand out. For example, at Gong they put out content saying to swear in the subject lines of emails.

2. Start small, very niche.

I’m the CEO of a bootstrapped SaaS. My content about struggling to grow my bootstrapped SaaS will resonate more (and lead to a deeper connection) with founders struggling to grow their bootstrapped SaaS rather than if I were to write about entrepreneurship broadly.

3. Post every day until you find content/market fit.

Content-market fit is when you know exactly what your readers want and you have a growing audience with increasing engagement. This took me 12 months to achieve. I’ve heard similar timelines from other people. Once you find content-market fit, you can scale back.

4. Recycle and repost your old stuff.

Devin downloads all of his Linkedin content once every six months, goes through his posts that killed, and either copy-pastes them and schedules for later, or if he thinks he can write it better now, he improves it.

5. Build growth loops.

Devin uses his LinkedIn for discovery, and drives readers to his Newsletter. He can then use his Newsletter to drive traffic back to LinkedIn posts that he wants to see more engagement.

6. Small posts can have a BIG effect.

Broad, viral posts may get lots of likes, and grow your follower count. But often the posts that lead to the deepest connection and real business are niche posts about a specific topic that not very many people are interested in. Devin said that Dave Gerhardt reached out to have him on his podcast from a post he would have otherwise deemed totally unsuccessful.

7. The algorithm isn’t THAT consistent.

But it is SORT OF consistent. Meaning, on average a great post will do better than a bad post, but day-to-day, you never know. Just because a post didn’t get the attention you thought it would, doesn’t mean that it won’t if you modify it slightly and repost 8 weeks later.

8. Hardly ANYONE will see your post.

Even your huge posts are seen by a tiny audience relative to the size of LinkedIn. Peter Conforti did an analysis of my audience and 85% of my engagement is unique post-to-post. Don’t be afraid to repost, and don’t be afraid to put your best content out over email. It WON’T hit the same people.

TAKEAWAY:

Crushing LinkedIn in HARD.

It takes long-game dedication that most people can’t handle.

But if you commit, it unlocks a marketing channel unavailable to most people.

Not only that - if you do it right, it’s the single most efficient trust building machine on the planet.

And trust = brand.

In 2024, brand is built one post at a time.

Revenue leaders are getting the Outreach/Google announcement wrong. It doesn't mean the death of cold email. In fact, cold email is about to become even MORE POWERFUL, but the playbook looks very different... 👇

Here's the breakdown:


The Old “Predictable Revenue” Cold Email Playbook (2011-2023): 

- Download a target list of accounts and contacts from ZoomInfo/Apollo based on firmographic data, title, and relevant tech

- Have young, untrained, North American BDRs stick them into Outreach, which will send a generic, un-personalized flow, and have zero regard for negative engagement metrics (like the 3/1000 SPAM limit that Gmail will start imposing soon)

- Send a daily Salesforce report of engagers to your BDRs so that your reps can attack people who made the mistake of opening or clicking an email

- Get frustrated when none of this works because inboxes are ruined

- Yell at your team that they aren’t working hard enough, keep increasing activity metrics

- Either you let go of the BDR leader or they quit, hire a new leader, only to repeat the exact same process, step-by-step, oblivious to the fact that 2023 broke this busted playbook…


The New “Inbound-Led-Outbound” Cold Email Playbook (2023-????):

- Build an audience before you even have a product with Linkedin, Podcasts, Virtual/Live events, etc

- Invest in community WAY TOO EARLY, by answering every comment on Linkedin, leading weekly work-in-public workshops, and cultivating a group of brand ambassadors

- Download that same target list of accounts from ZoomInfo/Apollo, but cross-reference it with your community of engagers on social media and events, and start there

- Create 20 inboxes in Outlook (not Gmail) across 10 “look-alike” domains and make sure the DNS, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and redirects are all set up correctly. Use Instantly to warm up the inboxes.

- Systematically send friendly, open-ended messages through Instantly to PEOPLE WHO ALREADY KNOW YOU through your content, and land in the primary folder because of how diligent you were setting up the infrastructure

- Get absurdly high reply rates because of the relationship you have previously established with these prospects, the fact that you aren’t a BDR half their age who understands nothing about them, and your email is a friendly, inviting, non-sale.

- Use a Person-Level website identity tool to see who has hit your website, and based on the users pageviews, do ever-more targeted outreach, automated and manual, nudging them down the funnel.

- Watch yourself close MORE deals FASTER with ABSURD efficiency because your trust-building and education process has taken place over months if not years of steady content creation.

- Stay bootstrapped longer than anyone previously thought possible because you are trading a small amount of predictability for a HUGE amount of capital efficiency

It’s a Push vs. Pull model. 

In 2024, Pull wins.

The other week I got some blowback from my 6sense post. A few of the sales influencers we lined up for a RB2B marketing campaign dropped out. Here's my question for LinkedIn:

If you got messages like this (see image) EVERY DAY, wouldn't you feel obligated to say something??

This is just ONE seller at a big tech company:

“My company bought 6Sense thinking it was the greatest thing since sliced bread. We’re getting less than 10% of numbers correct and my entire leadership has been sacked. I only wish they’d been able to see the tool for what it is - snake oil. Thank you for calling out these rats.”

But I get DMs like this one… LITERALLY… every day.

From VPs of Marketing, CMOs, CEOs and AEs.

From the whole GTM community.

If you need more examples, just read through the comments on any of my 6Sense posts.

There are so many people who feel they were sold expensive tech that doesn't work.

People who feel they were taken for a ride.

People who lost their jobs.

Some said my last 6Sense post was thirsty.

Other's have said it's time to move on.

But of the 1000+ comments I've gotten.

NOBODY said I was wrong.

So my question for you is this...

Should I move on?

If you got sent stuff like this, would you move on?

If in private you were bombarded by 6Sense hate…

But in public all you saw was 6Sense envy, with their glowing G2 reviews and Gartner rankings.

Or would you dig a little deeper to figure out why there's such a disconnect?

I’d love to know…

What would you do if you were me?

It’s 2023 and we’re *still* setting up young salespeople to fail.

99% of companies assume their BDR teams create demand (they're wrong).

This idea is leading to TERRIBLE outcomes for both companies and sellers: 👇

It looks like this...

- The “Predictable Revenue“ model  (or what I call the Old Way) requires us to create a revenue goal based upon an arbitrary growth rate

- We then look at the BDR team’s productivity and fail to realize 90% of the demand they captured would have found its way to you through another channel (Yes, it’s really 90%)

- We then take the number of reps divided by the number of demos they booked per month and assumed that if we hire 4x more reps we'll have 400% more demos

- We then grow our BDR team by 4x with young reps, don’t train them how to sell, and teach them a playbook that literally does not work anymore

- We then layer on managers to help with the new headcount, add expensive tech, the whole nine yards

- Then nothing appears to be happen… but that’s okay, you just need to give it 6 more months (maybe more!) to actually start working

- Then 6-12-18 months goes by and EVERY WEEK the manager of the 400% bigger BDR team is asked by the executive team why they're missing their targets by 75% 

- Finally, either the manager quits or is let go, the BDR team shrinks to the size it used to be or smaller, pipeline remains unchanged, and you feel guilt/shame for having put everyone through it all 

Trust me, I know.

I just went through this at Retention.com

Here's the takeaway:

The Predictable Revenue model is broken.

If you're going to work for a company that still runs that playbook, be careful.

It fails to acknowledge:

- Cold outreach doesn’t work in 2023 like it use to
- BDRs in 2023 are capturing (not creating) demand 
- Growing teams won’t actually grow demand

And it puts salespeople and their managers in an impossible position.

Our young sellers deserve better than that.

Train them right.

Flood them with demos. 

Be content-led.

Capture demand through traffic to the website (both identified and anonymous) 

Use partnerships, influencers, and other ecosystem plays. 

And let sellers sell. 

Stop trying to replicate the Salesforce playbook.

It's not 2010 anymore.

Your salespeople (and your bottom line) will thank you for it.

Last year I was in Aspen with a startup CFO friend who ended up selling her fintech company for $250M after 7 years of hard work.

As part of the deal, she got a cushy desk job with 3x the salary she had before and a guaranteed 3 year deal with rolling equity.

She had made enough money to retire. 

More than most will ever see.

She was *literally* set for life.

When she told me all this I was expecting her to be ecstatic.

Being THAT cash rich is what we all strive for, right?

Wrong.

Turns out, the exact opposite was true. 

She was bored, burned out and in a post-exit depression that I often hear about.

What are the lessons here?

I’m not sure I have all the answers. 

But it does confirm a feeling I’ve had for a while...

That if I sold Retention.com tomorrow for $1 Billion… 

I'd probably end up deeply depressed.

Because startups aren't just about BIG exits.

Building a startup is about the journey.	

And the struggles that come along with it.

It gives life purpose.

So don't forget...

No matter how rough it gets out there.

Enjoy the ride while it lasts.

Last week I walked into the woods of Colorado with just a backpack. No cellphone. No GPS. No plan except to avoid seeing another human being for 7 days. It was incredibly therapeutic. Here’s 4 reasons why I think every founder needs to try “social starvation”:

1. It gives you time to think deeply about who you really want to be.

- Who do you want to be 10 years from now? 
- When you are 80 and look back on your life, what do you want to see?
- What do you want your children to believe?

2. You are able to think clearly about priorities and boundaries you want to set for yourself.

- Am I doing too much travel for work? Is it really worth what it’s costing me at home?
- Can I pull off a one-month personal trip with my family each year for the next five years?
- Can I spend Wednesday mornings with my daughter and make up for the time at some other point in the week?

3. I’ve done this twice, and both times I’ve felt an overwhelming sense of gratitude for everything I have.

- My wonderful wife, beautiful daughter, and fiercely loyal 6lb chiweenie
- My incredible team, many of whom I’ve had the pleasure of working with 5 years or longer
- My wonderful community here in Austin, and the ways we get to spend our free time here

4. You can really reflect on business, the recent past, and the road ahead.

- So much has changed since two years ago when I did this.
- I’m imagining what my world will look like in two years when I do this again.
- I came up with a crystal-clear vision for what I think we should accomplish during the back half of the year.

When I was sitting there contemplating everything, the phrase “what got you here won’t get you there” kept running through my mind, over and over again. 

I realized that the future of our company is a product that we have in beta right now, that not only helps people with their email, but also helps people with their ads, by extending the life of the cookie. 

We're nearing $20M ARR.

Our goal is to build a unicorn.

What got us here won’t get us there.

Just 24 hours after changing RB2B's entire pricing model (and adding $150k ARR in a day!) we are changing it AGAIN. Here’s how we screwed up, and how we plan to fix it:

BACKGROUND:

- We “accidentally” launched our person-level identity product Mar 1
- We gave the leads and a push to Slack away for free
- We charged $495 for integrations, but you can parse the Slack block
- Our free-to-paid conversion rate was only 1.3%

That pricing was broken because: 

- Smaller co’s couldn’t pay $495
- Higher traffic sites needed an ICP filter
- Nobody knew what to do with the leads

So, two days ago we pushed out pricing that looked like this on the site: 

Credits: 

200: $119/mo
300: $179
500: $299
700: $419
1000: $599
1000+: Talk to us

Then our “enterprise” pricing was: 

2,000: $1,139 
3,000: $1,164
5,000: $2,466
10,000: $4,140

What happened when we pushed it out? 

PROBLEM #1: 

People who were over 1,000 credits per month were scared of pricing they would see once they talked to a rep. 

I know because a few people messaged me their concerns.

PROBLEM #2: 

We found ourselves in the middle of a bunch of conversations of 2-5k contacts of people that were like...

“What happened to the $495/mo unlimited?”

 I get that.

They felt bait-and-switched.

PROBLEM #3: 

Leadfeeder is part of the (inferior) company-level identity market, and they publish pricing. 

If I look at their pricing, the price-per-lead drops DRAMATICALLY at 1,000 leads/mo. 

400: $358
700: $499
1,000: $549
2,000: $649
3,000: $699
…etc

What’s a possible explanation for this? 

I’ve noticed that the lower a customers’ traffic volume is, the higher % of ICP visitors they have.

Why? 

I think it’s because marketing campaigns that drive traffic to your site raise overall traffic but lower traffic quality. 

Under 1,000 leads/mo is probably before people run campaigns. 

So smaller traffic companies can actually AFFORD to pay MORE PER LEAD than larger co’s. 

Because the quality of their traffic is higher. 

WHATS OUR SOLUTION?

We lowered the high end of our pricing, and undercut Leadfeeder. 

So, better product AND lower price.

This is one of my favorite value frameworks: 

“Great taste. Less filling.”

Our new pricing: 

Contacts: Was / Is: 

2,000: $1,139    /   $599
3,000: $1,164    /   $649
5,000: $2,466    /   $799
10,000: $4,140  /   $1,149

EVERY mid-market SaaS will be paying us $1,149 or under, monthly. 

With a 17% discount if you want to pay annually. 

TAKEAWAY:

Santosh and I declared that we would optimize RB2B for: 

1. User Growth 
2. Low time-to-value
3. Eliminating friction

Our “Day 1” pricing change was the opposite of #1 and #3. 

I think we’ve fixed the problem with our new pricing. 

And I think we’re giving Mid-Market SaaS what they want. 

Nobody wants long-term, slow-to-negotiate, over-priced contracts in 2024. 

They want it now, want it for free, and if you prove value, you earn your dollar.

And at RB2B, we want to earn every dollar we collect.

In 44 months, I grew my startup from $0-$20m ARR. Here are the 8 biggest mistakes I made along the way (and the revenue levels where I made them):

1. We sold to anyone who showed up at our doorstep

Revenue Level: 0-$12M ARR

Not focusing on an ICP and running a self-serve app was the story of our first 2.5 years. I didn’t realize how wrong this was until later. Now I know we would have gone *farther, faster* if we sold only to big Shopify stores.

2. We wasted 6 months and $300k working towards a sale that didn’t happen

Revenue Level: $5-$8M ARR

We attempted to sell the entire business in late 2021. Such a waste of time and money. Thankfully we didn’t sell. We’re much more valuable now.

3. I got major FOMO
	
Revenue Level: $14-$17m ARR

I felt like if we didn’t go as fast as humanly possible we were going to miss the opportunity. This led to panicked hiring, a horrible corporate spending culture, and a bunch of wasted time and money trying to “be everywhere”.

4. I thought our sales and onboarding was easier and less complex than it was

Revenue Level: $12-$18m ARR

We thought we could have inexperienced AEs closing 5 deals per day with a 7 day sales cycle and rush people through onboarding. As you can imagine, that wasn't true! We needed alignment on expectations and what success looks like.

5. I set a FY23 revenue target that was 50% too high
	
Revenue Level: $13-$18m ARR

My idea of “We have to get to $50m” led to over-hiring before we truly had a repeatable sales model. Empty AE calendars led to turning everyone to hunters, which didn't work (because most demand is created elsewhere in 2023). Then our VP sales resigned and we shrunk from 15 to 4 reps.

6. I assumed other vendors’ playbooks would work for us

Revenue Level: $12-$18m ARR

Because Klaviyo and Yotpo had a large agency partnership sales motion, I thought we needed one too. We have a great opportunity in the partnerships space, but it doesn’t look like either of their motions. We had to figure out what works for us.

7. We created a $5k/mo unlimited pricing tier
	
Revenue Level: $12-$19m ARR

This just didn’t work to capture mid-mkt market share. Pricing is relatively less important to those companies. What it did create was existing customers contracting down to 5k, capped our upside, made overage impossible to capture, and upgrading non-existent.

8. We oversold people and didn’t realize it for 5 months

Revenue Level: $12-16m ARR

This was my fault for not seeing it coming. The consequences were horrible. It created a euphoria about the opportunity that led to over-hiring and overspending, then on the back-end led to a massive wave of dissatisfaction, contraction, and opt-outs at 60 days. We're doing the opposite now.

TAKEAWAY:

Growing a startup is hard.

I hope I don’t make these mistakes again. 

What I do know is that I’ll continue to make mistakes...

Just new and different ones!

Here's the trick:

Make sure you’re doing 9 things right for every 8 you do wrong.

Over the past 60 days, my COO and I have spoken to 80 founders, marketers, and sales leaders about 6Sense and DemandBase. Not a SINGLE PERSON said it was a “slam dunk”, despite spending $50-100k/yr or more. Why?

To set the stage:

- We have been doing market research for our person-level identity product
- We’ve been speaking to customers of 6Sense, Demandbase, Clearbit
- All vendors stop resolving anonymous visitors at the company/account level
- We’ve been trying to figure out why nobody has closed the loop on ABM

There seem to be six MAJOR problems with the existing ABM technology.

1. The 3rd party intent signals provided were never actually “intent”

6Sense and Demandbase build audiences based on CONTENT CONSUMPTION, rather than actual intent to buy. Genius marketing, pioneered by the concept of the Dark Funnel, combined with teaching marketers how to show claimed revenue reporting to execs, fueled exponential growth of the two companies over the past 5 years.

2. Most of the value of the products comes from retargeting website visitors

There was consensus that the intent-based audiences were somewhat “meh” and most of the conversions came from retargeting of people who hit the site. Retargeting tech in general introduces the problem of whether or not the tech actually created a NEW conversion, or just got in the way of something that was going to happen anyways, and claimed the $.

3. False positives can be a MAJOR problem for high-ACV SaaS companies.

There wasn’t a single person we spoke to who had a high level of confidence in the accuracy of the website visitor reporting below true enterprise (which isn’t valuable anyway - who cares if someone from Microsoft in Atlanta is on your site).

4. It’s hard to use, and time consuming to onboard.

I saw a few actual DemandBase instances and they made me want to vomit. Apparently 6Sense is moving towards an easier-to-use platform built for sales, but I’ve heard it can currently take up to 90 days for a larger org to onboard.

5. It’s expensive.

I spoke to people paying $50-250k/year for the tech, I’m sure at larger companies the bill is even higher. Part of the reason the sentiment was so “meh” is because there were few (if any) cases where tremendous ROI was obvious.

6. Their website visitor resolution stops at the account/company.

I'm beating a dead horse here, but people actually want to know the individual who was on the site, not the company.

TAKEAWAY:

I have a deep respect for 6Sense and DemandBase.

Especially the go-to-market efforts.

But I think there’s room for something new and wildly different.

People want to close the loop on ABM.

They want to figure out the PERSON who hits their site.

That's why we’re launching a person-level ID tech that you can use alongside 6Sense, DemandBase, and ClearBit, where we push the LinkedIn profiles of your website visitors to a Slack channel in real-time.

It’s 100% free.

Sign up for early access here: https://rb.gy/8jioxt

In 2012, when I joined ZoomInfo as the VP Product, Growth & Strategy, they were stuck at $9M ARR. When I left 5 years later, we were at over $80M ARR.

Here’s the 5-step GTM playbook we used to get unstuck and build the foundation to scale:

Step 1: Develop contrarian products that satisfy unmet demand

- Most companies can't convince themselves to radically innovate
- In 2012, data companies were selling CSVs, no one was investing in product
- We took massive risk and doubled down on building products to streamline data delivery
- We started to "look different" from the space
- Sometimes it's better to "look different" than "be better"

Step 2: Focus on SMB or lower end of the market

- Market disruption always happens at the low end
- As a small company, it’s difficult to compete for your competitor’s best customers
- Instead aim your efforts at the customers your competitors would give up without a fight
- We focused on the SMB and lower mid market with a self-serve product at a low price
- Everyone else was fighting for the more lucrative enterprise customers

Step 3: Increase Prices, Decrease Churn, Add Features Rapidly

- We rapidly developed features that gave GTM teams ammo for upgrades
- With new products, we could add a new line item in the invoice and post growth with relative ease
- New features also gave us the reason to reach out to customers to talk about upsell
- All this was predicated on our ability to develop a sustained product roadmap with a strong understanding of the impact on GTM and our ability to attach growth initiatives to every small feature release

Step 4: Intentionally Design Market Expansion for Virality

- Nonlinear growth comes from getting the inbound engine started early
- At first, we went after the spray and pray approach with some automation, which worked well
- However, our revenues exploded when we started getting strategic with TAM and went after market niches, especially the ones that were ignored by other B2B data vendors
- This allowed us to dominate multiple small verticals and as we got popular within those verticals it resulted in word of mouth - virality, inbound inquiries and increased retention contributing to the non linear growth

Step 5: Cultivate a Leader's Mindset

- Startups are often fighting just to stay afloat - this creates chaos, panic & unrest in organizations
- By switching the mental model from a survival mindset to a leader's mindset, you can switch from a perpetual struggle for revenue growth to attempting to decimate competitors
- You switch from being a price follower to becoming a price setter in the long run
- This mindset provides a purpose, a better decision making framework, and results in a much healthier business and work culture

TAKEAWAY:

Markets are always evolving, and every market can be disrupted.

Any business can get unstuck.

The specific plays required to disrupt the B2B data market would be different today, but the ZoomInfo playbook's principles are timeless.

99% of startup founders THINK they know what their business is going to be when they start. They're almost always wrong. Why? Because human intuition is a terrible indicator of market viability. Here are 3 examples from my life:

1. Robly Email Marketing in 2014

What we thought it would be when it started: 

- Merchant-side customer review platform with email newsletter app for VSMB
- Inbound marketing strategy led by direct mail (this was completely insane)
- Value prop was strong enough to gain quick and large market share, 9 fig sale

What it ended up being: 

- Email Newsletter app ONLY (turned off the reviews app after 6mo)
- Stuck at $3m ARR for 3+ years
- Great lifestyle business, sold for $10m

2. GetEmails (now Retention.com) in 2019

What we thought it would be when we started:

- Thought large affiliate senders (credit card, solar, finance) would be market
- Thought 3rd party cookies were ending in 18 months, tech would die too
- Thought it would be a way to make a quick few million bucks and move on

What it ended up being: 

- Bootstrapped $22m ARR/$6-8m profit 4 years in
- Tech no longer uses 3rd party cookies (we help extend 1st party cookies)
- Have a killer team of 55 who is working on continuing to grow this fabulous business

3. RB2B in August 2023

What we thought it would be when we started:

- Person-Level Website Visitor Identity for mid-market B2B rev teams
- $30-50k ACV deals, entirely sales-led
- Goal was (relatively) low-churn, quick ARR

Where it is today: 

- Massive freemium offer (unlimited LI profiles to slack/teams $0)
- Underpriced, self-serve PLG ($495/mo, one plan, for all features/integrations)
- Goal is a massive user base, global domination play

TAKEAWAY:

In the startup game, you rarely end where you thought you would.

Why?

Because our gut instinct about products is (most of the time) pretty bad. 

Luckily there’s a proven and fairly simple way to build great products. 

1. Talk to prospects before you start building, make sure they want it
2. Build the smallest product that meets their needs to see if they use it
3. Keep talking and iterating until they have something they are raving about

In 2024, once you have word of mouth... 

Everything else becomes 10x easier.

For 7 months, my Glassdoor approval rating has been under 40%. Our company is rated 2.3 out of 5 stars. So last week I finally sat down and read them. Against advice of counsel, I recorded the painful experience. Here's why:

To set the stage: 

1. In the summer of 2022, we had six employees and zero Glassdoor presence
2. We hired over 50 people in 60 days
3. It was a complete disaster, which culminated in our VP sales quitting
4. We downsized our sales org from 15 to 4
5. Our understandably upset former employees let us have it on Glassdoor
6. Those were our first reviews, with no positive reviews to offset them

CURRENT STATE:

My goal on LinkedIn is to show the emotional journey of being a founder.

Nobody has ever done it with the level of transparency I aim for:

Real financials, big wins, big losses, embarrassing moments, and set backs.

And this is my most transparent moment yet....

Despite some laughter out of disbelief, it was an incredibly painful experience. 

You might be asking yourself:

"Hey Adam, why I haven’t you read your Glassdoor reviews?"

The answer is simple:

I hate Glassdoor. 

We scaled up our sales org too fast, had to do a layoff, and we got blasted.

My People Ops team thinks managing your Glassdoor presence is inauthentic.

So we have refused to use the strategy most companies use which is "highly suggesting" their team and new employees leave glowing reviews. 

Would this balance out the bad ones and give a more representative picture of what it’s like to work at Retention.com?

Sure, but I don't want to play that game.

My team told me the substance of the reviews when they were posted.

Much of it we deserved, and what we deserved, we’ve taken action on.

Scaling a startup is hard.

Making the tough decisions required to run a great business, and knowing that you can’t please everybody, is one of the hardest parts.

Letting people go is always terrible.

It's difficult to make decisions that impact people's lives.

But as CEO, that's your job.

And when you make those decisions quickly you end up with an efficient, productive team… 

Which is what you need to survive in 2024.

Unfortunately, Glassdoor may destroy you for it.

I actually say that Retention.com is spliced into two different eras.

Before October 24th, 2022, and AFTER October 24th, 2022.

We went from struggling to close deals, having too many options, having some tough clients, struggling to retain customers…

To having a machine that delivers insane results for high-quality clients and generates good revenue for us at the same time.

On October 4th, we switched to annual pricing. And it changed everything.

Let’s talk about why we did it, and why you should probably do it too.

When we had monthly pricing, it was really confusing.

It was based on how many unique US visitors a brand was bringing in.

That changes all the time, which means that customers would come in and downgrade when their traffic went down.

My partner and I both had a limiting belief that we weren’t going to be able to sell an annual plan.

It’s very expensive for the leads we were getting. We imagined that if people were churning from the monthly because it was too costly, the annual plan DEFINITELY wouldn’t make sense.

We began testing a product that was more specific. Instead of just capturing web visitors, we were capturing abandoned cart data.

But because this product was so stable, we knew that no one would cancel it. It was too good.

We changed our offer:

An annual deal with a 60-day trial period, using the more specific product as the flagship (because it has a 5x ROI), and then throw in everything else that we offer “for free”.

With the combination of moving upmarket in terms of our demographic (Shopify Plus only), and this new offer, this was one of the best things we’ve ever done.

The first day we tried this new offer, my partner closed 3 out of 3 deals that were on the calendar that day. October 4th.

We knew we were going to move toward a higher-revenue, lower-churn machine that was going to completely take over the Shopify Plus ecosphere.

Here are some key takeaways:

1. The velocity is insane.

We’ve had AEs with no prior sales experience close 5 for 5 in their first 3 weeks.

If you know anything about enterprise software sales, this is crazy.

It’s just such an easy offer to sell.

2. We closed 81 deals in December.

That’s $3M ARR.

3. We closed 92 deals between January 1-20th.

That’s around $3.3M ARR. Average contract value of $30,000.

This has been a huge success.

The lesson here is this:

As a founder, you probably have a ton of limiting beliefs around what people will be willing to buy/spend money on.

Diana and I certainly felt the same way.

If people don’t like our monthly plan, how could they possibly opt for our annual plan?

It goes to show that 1+1 does not always equal 2.

Hope this story helps.

Do not spend a single dollar before you have SOME indication that someone will actually buy your product.

Ads are expensive. Product development is expensive. Scaling a business is expensive.

Get an indication that your intuition is correct before you light your money on fire.

Don’t ignore this step.

Last week I spoke to the CRO of a $50M ARR SaaS who just KILLED a six-figure ABM campaign because after 8 months they only booked 3 meetings. Here's what went wrong and why (broken down by the #'s):

BACKGROUND:

The ABM campaign ran to 1,600 target accounts from January to August across digital ads and email marketing.

Here's the numbers breakdown:

- 1,632 target companies
- 13,000 contacts
- 231 people engaged with the ads (1.7%)
- 66 visited the website (0.05%)
- 3 demos booked

Here's the vendors they used:

- Terminus was used for ads
- Hubspot was used for email
- Salesforce was used for reporting

Here’s how my conversation with the CRO went:

CRO: Adam, it was a very horrible outcome.

Me: If you could do it over again, what would you change?

CRO: Well, this campaign started before I arrived, and we didn’t have a tight definition of our ICP, relevant content, and personas.

Me: Sure, that'll lead to abysmal results in any campaign. What else did you think was the problem?

CRO: Well, we sell to 500+ person companies, and we only had company-level website visitor resolution. We knew that 66 companies hit the site from the campaign, which is low, but honestly I was fine with it… But our BDRs had to try to figure out which of 20+ people at the company it might have been! It was a huge undertaking that yielded very few results.

Me: What if I could tell you the exact people at those companies who were on your website?

CRO: My BDRs would be all over it. We might still be running that campaign!

TAKEAWAY:

ABM is expensive and hard.

What makes it even harder is that once you actually drive the right person back to the site, vendors like 6Sense, DemandBase, and Terminus only tell you the company they work for and the geolocation.

If you’re selling to enterprise, this information is not very helpful.

That's why we need a new “Identity Layer” as the last step in the loop.

Meaning...

An *exact match* to the individual that hit your site, rather than only the company name.

99% of SaaS revenue leaders aren’t aware this is even an option.

But it is!

And it's going to change the trajectory of ABM in 2024.

P.S.

If you want to to add person-level identity as the last step of your ABM campaign, go here to install RB2B (100% free): https://www.rb2b.com/

Within the next 24 months, 2 out of 3 current SaaS startups will likely be forced to shutdown. That sounds terrifying, but it's not all bad news for founders. Why? Because we're on the verge of a new 30-year market cycle:

Last week I was on G2 and pulled the total number of companies in select sales/marketing categories.

It was a shocking reminder of how bloated SaaS has become:

- Conversational Intelligence : 156 companies
- Email Marketing Software : 561 companies
- Marketing Automation : 390 companies
- Sales Intelligence : 246 companies
- Auto Dialer : 147 companies
- CRM : 290 companies

This is just the tip of the iceberg.

In the US alone there are 15,000+ SaaS companies.

And many of these are very, VERY similar in capabilities.

Of course, there's nothing wrong with having 500+ marketing automation tools, but you have to be profitable...

How many of these SaaS companies do we think are profitable?

Realistically:

- Only 32% of current SaaS vendors are "somewhat" profitable
- Only 20% of all SaaS companies survive the first 5 years
- Only 16% sustain the classic VC Rule of 40. 

With high interest rates here to stay and raising CAC, most of these companies will not make the cut for further financing.

Is this the end of entrepreneurship as we know it?

Of course not.

It only signals that we are switching from one cycle into another. 

The next batch of startups will focus on AI and related tech (ex: smart workflows, enhanced compute, AI dev tools).

It will be a whole new game for entrepreneurs and investors.

New market cycles are a reminder that growth and transformation cannot come without pain

The rules of the game are shifting.

Early adopters will have the advantage.

New GTM playbooks will need to be written.

New AI friendly business models will need to evolve.

If you're a founder or work in tech I only have one piece of advice:

Embrace the change. Be ready to pivot.

Don’t get left behind defending the status quo.

The next cycle starts now.

***

They’re just not dumb enough to post about it on Linkedin.

That's the tradeoff with building in public.

100% transparency or bust.

Here’s what went down at Retention.com in October 2023: 

What I’m Proud Of: 

- We crossed the $21m ARR mark in and generated around $325k cash flow
- We continued to make progress in tightening up the delicate dance between sales and CS to create a positive customer experience
- We released our new dashboard to give customers a better understanding of our impact on their business
- We dipped our toes into our new DTC media brand centered around micro-interviews with interesting people at in-person events

Things I’m not so proud of:

- I’m annoyed we can’t get our growth to 5%/mo

Our biggest opportunities:

- We’ll see how this 100ish person event in LA goes … If we can get the right people there, it could be a major unlock for us
- A continued drift upmarket will put wind in our sails

TAKEAWAY:

Things have been really hard since Q2. 

It doesn’t seem to be getting any easier. 

The good news is that we’re still a profitable, growing SaaS company … 

Even if it’s not growing as fast as I’d like it to.

Profitable will never go out of style.

Against the advice of counsel, I'm posting Retention.com's Q2 P&L.

Here's my analysis on the current state of our business: 👇 

Q1 was peak euphoria, mid-Q2 was peak disillusionment. 

It seems like most (or all) of the vendors selling into our ecosystem had a hard time this quarter.

Pipeline growth basically stopped, and to make the problem worse, we switched prospecting strategies from a "spray-and-pray" to a personalized approach... 

Meaning we went from "stopped" to "really stopped". 

We ended up fixing the problem and finished with a very strong June. Just for context, we do a 12mo deal w/ 60 day opt-out. Here are 12mo deals initiated, by month, in ARR:

Jan: $1.75m
Feb: $2.3m
Mar: $3.0m
Apr: $2.0m
May: $1.68m
Jun: $2.2m

Let's get into the BIG PICTURE details...

What we did well:

- Successfully switched our sales culture to a team of "hunters"
- Started paying attention to spending (we're back to running a tight ship)
- Have less than 10% of our current revenue in month-to-month deals
- Experimented with a new product that expands TAM
- Grew our engineering team from one to 6
- Nailed down our partnership motion 
- Made A TON of RevOps progress. 
- Brought our flagship product (Reclaim) into 100% Klaviyo AUP compliance - without sacrificing customer ROI 

What we could have done better:

- We should have moved slower. Knowing what I now know, and knowing a macro slowdown was looming, I would have. 
- We ended up overselling a chunk of deals in Q1, which has led to contraction at the 60-day period. It was a headwind for growth in Q2. We see the problem as solvable, and if we can nail it, we believe we will be back to 10% growth months.
- I could have been a better forecaster. Because of all of the above, I was off by a mile. I'm off my $50m end-of-year ARR target. We are aiming for $25-30m, highly profitable, and believe that is firmly rooted in reality.

What we are focusing on the rest of the year:

- Spending less and making more every month.
- Focusing on the customer lifecycle to minimize contraction
- RevOps/Reporting. Lots more wood to chop! 
- Bringing the new product to market.

BONUS INSIGHT:

We believe there is a large B2B opportunity within our product suite and will start experimenting this quarter. If you want to know what visitors are on your pricing page and want to be a beta tester, DM me.

Keep following along to watch us build a unicorn in public.

I’ve been selling software for a little while now.

I’ve sold $15 software, and I’ve sold $30,000 software.

For a myriad of reasons (some more obvious than others), I enjoy selling the $30,000 software much more than the former.

In the early days of Robly, we ran an experiment.

We had one price for the premium version of our email marketing software: $15 a month.

Most people will know how impossible it is to be profitable on $15 conversions.

Instead, we decided to have 3 price options instead of just one.

A $15 plan, a $22 plan, and a $60 plan.

We said that the $15 plan had limitations, the $22 plan was unlimited, and the $60 plan was white glove.

We also highlighted the $22 plan and said it was the “most popular” plan.

There were hardly any limitations with the $15 plan, and the $60 plan took hardly any time to quickly onboard people and provide some extra assistance.

Guess what happened?

Our conversion rate stayed the same…

65% picked the $22 plan…
20% picked the $15 plan…
And 15% picked the $60 plan.

We did nothing different other than make our current plan look cheap and less useful than two other plans that we pulled out of nowhere.

It took our average price per customer from $15 to $27. Up 75%.

This can be a bit trickier if you’re selling a DTC product — but if you’re in the B2B world, it’s probably a sign to raise your prices 😉

99% of startups think they need to maximize predictable revenue. They're wrong. The next crop of $1B unicorn startups will solve for sales velocity above all else. Here's 9 reasons why velocity will define the new world:

1. Revenue was never actually predictable

Everybody underestimated their revenue in 2021-2022 and overestimated their revenue in 2023... all while making staffing decisions that were backed into from year-end growth targets.

2. Prospects do their own research

The best GTM motions touch the prospects early and often in the research process with timely and relevant content that helps them on their buying journey. Making it easy for prospects who aren’t ready to buy to access and consume your content to wins deals down the road.

3. Outbound channels are maxed out

Automation overwhelm has led to response rates being cut in half over the last 24 months. Inboxes are ruined, LinkedIn is worse, and AI tools will increase problem 100x. Most sales teams are reacting by increasing activity!

4. The world is set up for a new GTM model

As cold outreach becomes more difficult, the model of the future will be one that warms prospects up through founder brand, innovative marketing strategies, UGC-generating machines, small events, indirect channels like partner and affiliate, and captures demand VERY low in the funnel. Close rates are 2-3x, sales cycles are 60% less and sales teams will be smaller.

5. “Influencers” will become more powerful

As the era of AI content unfolds, the best, most authentic content coming from the most trusted voices will become even more powerful. Social continues to become the primary method to create awareness, even for software platforms. 

6. High-Velocity environments attract the best talent

The best people want to be on teams that prioritize moving FAST. The antithesis of this is a bloated GTM org that values head count above all.

7. You can be profitable (at the expense of being predictable)

Running a lean team that captures demand at the bottom of the funnel (and most importantly resists the temptation to layer on outbound reps who will simply capture the demand that you are creating elsewhere) will increase focus on capital-efficiency, reduce system-wide dependence on external funding and create a less volatile ecosystem in the long-term. 

8. Massive user acquisition sets you up for global domination

Santosh always says that 100,000 users is the equivalent of a $1B/yr marketing budget. I have yet to successfully execute this pay, but we’re going to try to with our B2B person-level identity product. 

TAKEAWAY:

It’s almost 2024.

The Predictable Revenue model is dead.

The next great startups will sacrifice predictability for velocity (and profitability).

Not only is it what our buyers want from us, but...  

It will create healthier companies with happier employees.

Everything is setting up for this to be the next great go-to-market motion…

I'm calling it “Inbound-Led Outbound”.

Only 10 weeks after launch, RB2B has officially hit $500k ARR. Here are the 4 biggest mistakes I've made so far, why only 1.3% of users have converted to paid, and how we're going to fix it:

1. I got our pricing model totally wrong.

My thought was that if we gave the leads away and pushed to Slack for free, people who found them valuable would self-serve their way to $495 for integrations and the business would be low-churn. 

It turns out that: 

- You can parse the Slack block with Zapier
- There was too much value in FREE, not enough in PAID
- $495 is too much for the little guy 
- The big guy needs an ICP filter (coming)

We’re going to push out lower pricing next week that caps the free plan so that the top 15-20% of people are forced to pay. 

Thank you LinkedIn for all of your wisdom and comments on this subject.

2. I thought we could run a PLG with no sales.

We can help anyone who already knows how to book an outbound demo if we quickly explain best practices and connect with the rep who will be working the leads. Best practices aren’t intuitive and people don’t want to read documentation. 

Answer: lightning-fast, two-touch sales motion.

3. We’re not getting anything back from our free users.

My good friend Stuart Chaney has told me over and over again “every user is some type of currency, either money, or something else”. We believe our users can help us with reviews, UGC, and referrals, but as of right now on 6,300+ users we have only 52 G2 reviews, under 10 pieces of UGC, and we don’t have a referral program. Improving this activation is a top priority.

4. We didn’t start a LIVE Weekly Event event until two weeks ago

Thanks to Chris Walker for encouraging me to start a weekly live event. We call it the *Inbound-Led Outbound Workshop*, there’s new content every week, and it’s Tuesdays at 3pm EST/12pm PST on LinkedIn Live and Zoom. We value seeing you and hearing your questions, and wish we had started sooner.

TAKEAWAY:

This is my third time launching a startup from zero.

The model already looks totally different than what I thought. 

And it’s only been 10 weeks!

One thing I keep learning is that no matter how much experience I get…

Most of my basic assumptions continue to be completely wrong. 

I think I pivot quicker now than I used to, but I also have a new secret weapon... 

My amazing LinkedIn community tells me in real-time when I’m messing up, and even how to fix it!

Just letting you know that I’m going to keep it coming…

Because this is the single most valuable conversation I’ve ever had. 

Thank you, LinkedIn community.

Keep building.

After four DOWN months in a row, I’m happy to report Retention.com ARR was up 1.6% in April. RB2B is up to $242,400 ARR (from $61k). Here’s what went well in April, what didn’t and why we’re not out of the woods quite yet: 

WHAT WENT WELL: 

Retention.com

- Up month (whoop! Go team!)
- I have successfully handed off day-to-day operations to Diana Ross
- We’re continuing the EOS build across all of our business lines
- We’re learning the meaning of “putting process in place” 
- We have a new deep understanding of the competitive space we find ourselves operating in (which is VERY different from 18 months ago)

RB2B: 

- One word: VIRALITY
- 5,043 companies signed up in 60 days, 78% have collected >1 contact
- We're at $242k ARR and don’t have any of the features we plan to charge for
- We pushed Hubspot integration yesterday, ICP filters and “credit system” next
- We think we’ve figured out a no-brainer offer for LeadGen agencies
- Support still greater than 90% non-human, cheers Robb Clarke

WHAT DIDN’T GO SO WELL: 

- We only generated $300k of cash in April. 
- I was expecting $500k. If April had 31 days, we would have generated $425k. 
- We make performance bonus payments quarterly, which weighed down April.
- Apparently we had a few chunky invoices, and it’s trade show season in DTC
- We have made several hires related to the Enterprise Data Sales business Santosh is building - positive for the long run, but negative for April’s cash
- Did I mention we're building an Enterprise Data business as a 3rd startup??? 
- Revenue growth of RB2B has been slower than expected as my initial PLG thesis was dead-wrong and we’ve had to figure out a new hypothesis

WHY WE’RE NOT OUT OF THE WOODS YET

Retention's market has become highly competitive.  

Determining a growth strategy in that environment is difficult on its own, but we’ve put it on the back burner to implement EOS so that no matter what happens we’ll run like a real company in the future. 

While all of that has been going on, we have been investing heavily in what Santosh has always said the larger opportunity was for us in the first place…

Taking our existing tech to the B2B space. 

I believe we are currently in the middle of our darkest moment. 

At Retention, we’re being forced to adjust to a new reality which is worse than we thought it would be a year ago. 

Meanwhile, we are investing in new businesses that aren’t going to meaningfully contribute to growth until later this year. 

But, if I close my eyes and imagine what this will all look like in 12-18 months:

1. EOS is fully rolled out, R! is running smoothly
2. We have come up with a credible growth strategy 
3. RB2B is humming, in the high single-digit ARR with 5 employees
4. Data Sales is contributing low single-digits  

There’s a chance we’re at 30m ARR with the crew we have right now, growing at a very healthy clip. 

That … for me … is the Promised Land.

Just keep building.

In 10 years, I’ve bootstrapped $0-$1M ARR twice. And I’m about to do it a third time with rb2b.com. Here are the 6 biggest pieces of advice I’d give to ANYBODY bootstrapping their startup:

1. Spend as little money as humanly possible.

This is the single most important thing to do. I wasted so much money on so many things my first time around. I bought a phone system (WHY). I got an office (SO DUMB). I stayed in an expensive apartment in Manhattan. I bought two expensive cameras to film content (USED ONCE). 

Money is your lifeblood. Be as frugal, because things are going to get unimaginably tight before you reach the other side.

2. Product-Market Fit is EVERYTHING.

If you achieve true PMF, everything will be amazing for you, and everything will seem easy. If you do not, everything will be a grind. And nothing will work like it needs to. I’ve spent many years on both sides. Until you have a product that is growing on its own by word-of-mouth, don’t do anything other than trying to make it better.

3. Learn as much as you can about marketing.

Once you have a great product, I believe the best way to grow a SaaS today is by creating a high-velocity inbound engine. The art and science of marketing is the way you make that happen. Learn offers, funnels, conversion, paid ads, organic social, being different, channels, content, and pricing. 

Developing a deep understanding and intuition about marketing will serve you much better than trusting someone else to make fundamental decisions about your business.

4. Hire unreasonably slow, fire unreasonably fast.

My biggest piece of advice is don’t hire your first employee until it’s killing you. Then, wait until you are all in pain again until you hire the next one. 

It’s really hard to fire people when you start out. But eventually you’ll be like the rest of us vets and the SECOND you see there isn’t a fit you will make the cut, knowing that all parties are better for it. A wise man once said, “I never regretted letting someone go, I’ve just regretted not doing it sooner.”

5. There’s no shame in starting small. 

It’s tempting to be incredibly ambitious. That isn’t a problem in itself, but typically bringing substantially larger ideas to life are more complex than smaller ones and have a much higher degree of difficulty. I personally started small, and each venture has been orders of magnitude larger than the last. 

6. Surround yourself with people that you trust and respect.

The reality of the game we’re playing is the odds are stacked against us. There’s a very tiny chance we’ll create huge companies, a decent chance we’ll create a “meh” company, and a really good chance that what we’re working on goes bust. 

Any of those scenarios are tolerable if you are spending your days with great people. All are unbearable - even great success - if the opposite is true.

Have any questions about bootstrapping?

AMA anything in the comments 👇

This will not be a popular thing to say on LinkedIn, but my bootstrapped $20M ARR SaaS just shrunk our sales team from 15 to 4 reps and growth SPED UP (!).

The days of massive sales teams for early stage startups are numbered. The next crop of tech unicorns will have BDR orgs that look VERY DIFFERENT than Salesforce. Here's the breakdown: 👇

The Old “Predictable Revenue” Push Way:

- You choose a revenue goal at the beginning of the year that is based on a “predictable” growth rate

- You see what current reps were producing the year prior and hire X more of them based on assumption of linear productivity

- You see “proof” early on that assumptions were accurate from the first round of hires. Exciting!

- You decide that “it’s working” so you should “really go for it”

- You accelerate the pace of hiring reps and layer on managers and tech

- You don't provide proper training because how could we when you have to move this fast!

- The whole thing breaks when you hit a (very mild) macro slowdown and buyers stop mindlessly buying anything and everything

- As the BDR team stops producing, you make your AEs prospect because their calendars are 20% of what they need to be

- Of course, your AEs aren’t booking demos either because they too are using the same busted outbound playbook

-  You are looking at the whole massive org and how much time talented (and expensive!) reps are sitting in front of screens putting so much in and getting little back

- You give all of your best leads to your top 3 sellers, which makes the other 12 miserable (can’t blame them), and has severe negative cultural consequences

- You’re sitting there, trapped, wondering how the f*ck you ended up here


The New “Ultra-Lean, High Velocity” Pull Way

- Very small team of reps (we have 4 and are at $20m ARR), literally flooded with demand of high-intent, low-in-the-funnel prospects who close at above 60% in 25% of the time

- Demand is created over months if not years through content that cuts through

- High-intent, low-in-the-funnel demand is captured through indirect, high-velocity external channels (partners, small events, influencer/affiliate), fully-automated, high-volume, low conversion email (AKA spray-and-pray)

- Your 1 BDR is focused on missed demos, closed lost, referrals, inbound from founder brand and podcast, changed jobs, and high-value intent data… Your org NEVER touches a cold lead

- Your buyers have a relationship with YOU (the Founder) through your content, and haven’t been qualified/sold by someone half their age with 1/100 of the knowledge and experience

- You actually close MORE ARR and grow FASTER because your reps are senior, can handle more, been around a long time, and make fewer mistakes

- Your company culture improves dramatically because hyper-efficient companies are fun to work at and you don’t have a single person who isn’t crushing it

It's a Push model vs a Pull a model.

And in 2024, Pull wins.

The current DemandGen model is broken. Business has become complex. Buyers need their business problems solved. Yet Sellers are not incentivized to solve Buyer’s problems. Here's a few examples:

BACKGROUND

Today's seller simply wants to sell their point solution.  

Best of Breed (SaaS) strategy have created tech stack chaos for buyers

But buyer problems are often complex and require multiple sellers to collaborate to come up with an ideal solution. 

Here's an example:

Imagine a Buyer’s problem is “Outbound no longer works for us, what do we do?” 

A ZoomInfo seller will try to sell accurate data as a solution to low outbound response rates

A Hubspot seller may peddle their personalized email capability to solve the outbound problem. 

A Bombora seller may argue that Intent data is the reason why their outbound does not work. 

A Gong seller may insist that switching to Gong and related insights will solve the outbound problems

And so on… 

Ironically, the ideal solution may even involve all of them (and more). 

It will require a deeper understanding of where the buyer is failing and an unbiased mind to make recommendations.

Sellers are biased and not structured to get that level of understanding especially if the solution requires recommending other vendors - sometimes even their competitors 

Sellers are speaking a language that buyers no longer understand

Hence Buyers are not interested in talking to the sales reps until after 75% of the buying process is done in isolation

How do you recommend this gap be bridged, so sellers can be engaged in a higher level conversations and get a chance to share best practices ? 

I have come up with a solution that I will share in the next post but am curious to hear how Marketers are currently bridging this communication gap. 

Please share your thoughts below!

Hey B2B Marketers, today I want to introduce a new concept in DemandGen that I call “Demand Inception”. It precedes Demand Creation and Demand Capture. Here's how it works: 

BACKGROUND

Upon encountering their ICP, most marketers immediately pull out their Demand Creation or Demand Capture playbooks.

However, it's a mistake to assume that your buyers are interested in your product segment or prepared to give you their attention.

Buyers require priming.

That means creating the appropriate environment before an offer is presented. 

That's why I think a more effective DemandGen cadence may be: 

Demand Inception → Demand Creation → Demand Capture

Buyers are focused on their own issues, which may not align with any specific vendor solutions. Sellers need to establish empathy, trust and credibility with the buyer to earn the privilege of presenting their message. 

👉 How to Start Demand Inception:

A strategy session can be an effective tool for Demand Inception. Remember, the goal of this session is to simply foster trust, empathy, credibility and create an environment where DemandGen playbooks can be executed. 

Such a session should be led by the marketing team rather than sales with the objective to intimately understand the challenges of the buyer. 

The outcome can be a carefully crafted proposal outlining industry best practices to address the buyer’s issue. If the buyer perceives this gesture to be beneficial, then it's only natural for them to consider including your solution among several others that address their problem.

A social media post (particularly on LinkedIn) addressing a buyer's problem can serve as a powerful tool for Demand Inception, provided it reaches the right audience and drives engagement. 

👉 When to Use Demand Inception: 

Utilize this approach only when selling high-value, high-margin products requiring complex sales processes and multiple touchpoints for closure. Employ it when you're committed to investing in a strategic, long-term relationship. Once a trusted environment has been established, the Demand Capture playbook will prove more effective.

👉 When to Avoid Demand Inception: 

Demand Inception is a resource-intensive process and may slow you down. Avoid using this strategy if there's no need to generate demand for your product; if demand already exists, opt for a quick conversation to capture it. Disregard this approach for transactional sales that have low ACV, short sales cycles and quick onboarding.

Many account-based marketing (ABM) teams may already be employing Demand Inception without explicitly labeling it as such. By introducing this new terminology, I aim to garner greater attention from enterprise marketers toward this aspect of demand generation.

Can you relate to the concept of Demand Inception? 

What other methods would you employ to foster an environment that will lead to more effective Demand Creation or Capture ?

Please share your thoughts below.

Last week on Jason Bay’s webinar Mark Kosoglow called BS on my idea of Inbound-Led Outbound. He said, “Adam, do you REALLY think anything you are doing is new?” It was a fair question. Here's my response:

What do I think?

- Each individual thing I am doing is not novel in itself
- The combination of all of it together is not only unique, it’s tough to replicate

Here’s the breakdown of my Inbound-Led Outbound plan, point-by-point, and how it’s new and different:

1. Be the #1 Founder Brand on LinkedIn.

Mark said, “Everybody is saying I need to do what Adam’s doing, so it’s going to stop working like anything else.” 

Frankly, I don't think “everybody” can do what I do. 

Here’s why:

- Few have the patience to learn the craft. It took 12 months of zero results
- Few are comfortable sharing what I share. They have investors, etc
- Few have the capacity to dedicate their life to it. They're CEOs of scaling co’s.
- Few can spend the money on the team and production with ZERO connection to business results.

Founder brand is not new. 

I believe the way that I am approaching it is.

2. Have a crazy freemium offer that drives insane word-of-mouth.

My obsession with Mailchimp is ultimately responsible for our insane pricing. 

Having a free offer is nothing new. 

I believe that the REASON I’m doing it…

Designing a business model that THRIVES when outbound response rates literally go to zero… 

ESPECIALLY in the product category that we’re in…

Makes this unique and different.

3. Get a guest slot on EVERY podcast in the B2B space.

The idea of a Podcast Tour is also not new.

The issue is that no one wants you until you have a large audience!

What’s new is that all of a sudden I can actually get ON all the podcasts.

4. Drive visitors to the site. If they don’t sign up, personalize automated outreach.

Retargeting is not new. 

Person-Level Website Visitor Identity with RB2B IS new.

Running visitors through Clay to determine ICP and send a message written by chatGPT IS new (and it converts at 11%!).

TAKEAWAY:

Mark is right.

There is nothing new about any individual thing that I’m doing. 

I know to some, it just looks like marketing.

But I believe that the combination of it all… 

And the WAY we are doing it… 

Everything together IS new and different.

Everything together is Inbound-Led Outbound.

It’s not every day that you hear about a guy in his 50s who consistently goes viral on TikTok and has a massive audience of people who actually want to hear from him.

I recently just did a podcast with Moises Sanchez, one of the most interesting people I’ve ever spoken to…

He came to America from Mexico illegally as a 12-year-old, has been to prison, and now in his 50s, owns a $50M a year roofing company.

And I’m not the only one who thinks he’s extremely interesting.

There are half a million people on TikTok who think that this guy is awesome.

I got to ask him about 3 of his best tips for going viral on TikTok (or any social platform)

Tip #1: Make 100 videos a day.

It sounds crazy, I know.

But we’re talking about brute forcing your way to virality. THIS is force.

These aren’t complicated videos. Each video is 15 seconds long, and you break it up into 5 blocks.

20 videos in each block, 5 times a day. It takes hours, but it’s worth it if you’re trying to grow.

Moises’ videos are all lifestyle content. If you have a cool lifestyle, all you need to do is showcase your surroundings.

If your videos are about excel tips, do a bunch of tiny tips at once. And then every day, post the same tips, but repositioned.

Tip #2: Stick to a micro-niche.

This is super important when you’re just starting out.

TikTok wants to see you reaching a higher percentage of a particular audience, not 0.00001% of the entire platform.

Moises’ micro-niche ended up being his ability to show off a closet full of designer clothes and his supercars in the driveway as a hispanic man in his 50s.

This will help your account.

Tip #3: Shock people.

We all know how social media works at this point.

The more shocking you can be, the better.

This is a growth-hacky way to go viral, but views are views. Followers are followers.

Shocking people is the easy part. Your job is to capitalize on the eyeballs once they’re on you.

You do this with pattern breakers – if someone’s expecting one thing and they receive another, that’s how you hold people’s attention.

Or, if you just so happen to be an unusual person with unusual hobbies or belongings (like Moises), then shocking people will be easy.

It’s a matter of creating enough content to see what hits, and then going even harder so you can keep those people in love with you.

I highly recommend that you check out this episode of the podcast so you can hear this guy’s story. It’s a great one.

I’ll drop it in the comments below.
