In less than 8 years, the best salesperson I ever met went from an intern at Xerox, to closing $1M enterprise deals to becoming the co-founder and CRO of a Unciorn-bound tech startup.

Here are the 9 things that made her a top 0.1% seller:

1. She truly believes what she sells is best for the customer

Call it drinking the KoolAid. The best salespeople are the best because they believe their customers will be far worse off without the solution.

2. She hits her activity goals every day (no matter what else is going on)

Traveling to NYC for meetings? Wake up early and prospect to hit your activity goals. Have a company-wide offsite all week? Stay up late and hit activity goals. Have to work the booth at a trade show? You get the point.

3. She generates her own leads, even when it’s "not her job"

She was always a “full-stack AE”. Even when her job involved a large amount of inbound, she took it upon herself to build systems that were automating outbound for her. 

4. She intimately understands what customers care about

She doesn’t just talk, she listens. Over time she develops a deep understanding of who the customer is, what matters to them and what doesn’t. She’s able to cater the pitch to who she’s talking to, and has a deep intuition for personas.

5. She understands the product better than anyone

She developed a unique understanding of what her product does, relative value of its component, and what features should be built. This allows her to emphasize and de-emphasize certain parts of the product depending on the situation.

6. She has a Kobe Bryant-like commitment to excellence

She doesn’t understand when people don’t do things completely and correctly, because that’s what she would do if she were doing it. She expects the same out of the people who work for her.

7. She knows where to spend her time and the company’s money

You only get to #1 if you figure out how to get the maximum amount of revenue from the minimum amount of money and energy spent. Then do it all over again as fast as you can, every single day.

8. She is extremely focused on her craft

Her whole life is family and work. This type of focus is necessary to be successful in anything you do. This may sound depressing to some, but it’s the reality of what it takes to be #1 in anything year in and year out. You need to decide if that’s actually what you want.

9. She’s never complained about anything, ever

This quality is present in truly elite sellers that often goes unmentioned. Great sellers don’t have time to complain. They are too busy making sh*t happen.

...

So who is this Hall of Fame seller?

Her name is Diana Ross.

My good friend and CRO at Retention.com.

Remember, the playbook for sales success isn’t complicated. 

It just requires a level of dedication that few people are capable of.

If you follow Diana’s lead, you can be #1 too.

P.S.

What do you think makes top 0.1% sellers?

Share in the comments👇

Last week I had a 5 minute conversation with the Head of Ops at Clay that changed the trajectory of our startup. Here are the 3 questions I asked him, his answers, and why founders must seek OUTSIDE perspective:

BACKGROUND:

I'm currently in a state of confusion and emotional pain.

Two common feelings for founders.

What about?

Our free-to-paid trial conversion rate SUCKS.

We somehow managed to get 1,000 free signups our first week, but only 7 converted to paid.

This is my first time ever building a PLG motion.

So I have a ton of questions, all anxiety inducing:

- Are people not getting value from the tool?
- Is this because we don’t have key integrations?
- Is it because we lack features?
- Is this because we don’t have in-app messaging?
- Is it because I don’t have a lower pricing tier?
- Is this normal for your first week???

If you’ve never done PLG before, the above is enough to drive you nuts.

So I reached out to Varun Anand (Head of Ops at Clay) to bounce some of these questions off him. They've been on the PLG journey for years.

Here's what I asked him:

Question (1):

“I have a free plan, which pushes LinkedIn profiles of website visitors to Slack. Then I have a $495 plan, which is to push data everywhere else. Is that just WRONG?”

Varun said that he actually thought it was a decent idea, it would:

- Give us a chance to focus on our highest-value prospects
- Allow us to figure out what exactly they would pay us for
- Give us time to see if we could keep them happy once paying

He thought that once we figured out our “free-to-paid” motion, we could add a lower tier.

Question (2):

"I want to invest massively in a content-driven community related to signal-based selling. What are your thoughts about that?"

Clay has a vibrant community in Slack, but it’s because that’s where people go to get product support. He said that he thought I was already doing a great job at building community on LinkedIn and that I should focus there until we’re farther along.

Question (3):

I wanted to ask Varun about the Clay Creators effort they are making, because I was planning to do a bunch of “influencer” marketing very early.

Varun pointed out that if we’re picking up 1,000 free signups in a week without even trying, acquisition is NOT our problem. Our problem is free-to-paid conversion. Once we had that dialed in, speeding it up would be a problem, but until then... it’s not.

TAKEAWAY:

This call was 5 minutes but it was powerful enough to make me rethink everything.

I killed two massive initiatives so that my team can focus on what matters.

Focus on LinkedIn.

Focus on free-to-paid conversion.

Drop everything else.

Outside perspectives can be incredibly valuable.

You just have to be willing to listen.

In 4 months, I generated 2.5M views on LinkedIn, grew my following 400% and booked 100 meetings. As a GTM executive, I've fallen in love with the platform. But LinkedIn is missing a HUGE opportunity. Here are 6 features if Linkedin develops, it can unlock billions of dollars in new revenue:

BACKGROUND:

Forget SLG (Sales Led Growth) or PLG (Product Led Growth), the future belongs to LLG (Linkedin Led Growth). 

Linkedin is where the funnel collapses and one-to-many demand is created.

If Linkedin pays attention, it can transform itself into an end to end GTM platform that not only generates demand but also tracks, prioritizes and converts this demand into revenue.

Old GTM:

- No Audience
- SDRs <> Decision Maker
- Qualify -> Outreach -> Convert
- Slow conversion funnel

New GTM:

- Engaged audience on Linkedin
- Decision Maker <> Decision Maker
- Engage -> Qualify -> Outreach
- Collapsed conversion funnel

At Retention.com we are generating 100's of qualified leads/mo, without investing in expensive outside tools or teams - all while enhancing brand recognition. It's hard to replicate this success with traditional GTM processes. 

HOWEVER...

We are putting in a lot of manual effort to make this work. The product team at Linkedin should consider adding a few features and turning Linkedin into a full blown GTM platform to deliver on LLG.

Here are my 6 recommendations:

1. Score my post or my company's best engagers. Use this score when showing contacts in my connections. I want to see my audience sorted by engagement score and ICP match

2. Allow companies or individuals to define ICP and upload target account list to improve their engagement score. Use this ICP to drive targeted content engagement

3. Sync best engagers with my CRM: allow me to push my best engagers to CRM of choice

4. Allow best engagers to schedule meeting on my calendar: consider providing a native scheduling app or integrating with popular calendar apps

5. Develop a better way to natively use Linkedin forms (like leadgen) to create signup list or micro surveys from this engaged audience

6. Dashboard to show targeted audience expansion, best posts, engagement metrics, conversion metrics, pipeline metrics, meetings booked and revenues generated from Linkedin Led Growth

I would be willing to pay big money for a unified view of my audience, demand creation, demand capture and fulfillment; all in the same platform. 

Linkedin has so much untapped value that it boggles my mind.

As traditional demand creation strategies becomes ineffective and the world shifts towards community and first party data; Linkedin has the opportunity to unsettle large GTM vendors like Salesforce or Hubspot as the most dominant GTM platform. 

P.S.

What features do you think LinkedIn should add?

Do you think Linkedin should play an important role in the next evolution of GTM by automating and enabling key workflows?

Retention.com has driven over $350M in Klaviyo revenue for Shopify stores this year (up from $150M last year).

Here is the 8-step process we use to clog leaky funnels for DTC brands and make them traffic re-capturing machines in just 60 days:

Step 1: Audit Klaviyo Account (Day 1)

- See how many of the 5 Fundamental Flows the brand has set up
- Observe email newsletter size and send cadence
- Evaluate SMS flows

Step 2: Install Retention Scripts (Day 1)

- Install Grow Pixel
- Install Reclaim product, cart, and checkout abandonment pixels
- Instal suppression scripts on email signup forms and checkout 
- Install revenue tracking script

Step 3: Integration with Klaviyo (Day 1)

- Set up our OAuth integration
- We hash subscribers currently in Klaviyo account
- Import hashed list as a suppression list

Step 4: Set up Klaviyo Flows (Day 1-5)

- Create new flows for cart, product, and checkout abandonment
- If product flow doesn’t exist, create two versions of it - Klaviyo version and Retention version
- Set up “Bruce Bolt” implementation for Grow

Step 5: GO LIVE (Day 7)

- Brand signs off on flows
- Our CS team flips on all of the scripts
- The leaky funnel starts getting clogged

Step 6: 15-Day Checkup (Day 15):

- Make sure all of the scripts are firing appropriately
- Check that all of the flows are working properly and showing ROAS
- Make sure email list rules are set up properly, and unengaged users are being removed quickly

Step 7: 30-Day Checkup & Optimization (Day 30):

- Make sure ROAS is on track to exceed expectations
- Suggest tips and tricks to improve flow performance
- High ROAS = everything is great. Low ROAS = creative and flow optimization

Step 8: Analyze Performance (Day 60):

- Look at ROAS across our two products (almost always stellar)
- Predict 12mo CLTV for Grow and Reclaim given time of year and seasonality of business
- The trial period is over, and the Brand becomes a lifelong customer

And that’s that.

TL;DR:

Step 1: Audit Klaviyo Account
Step 2: Instal Retention.com Scripts
Step 3: Integration with Klaviyo
Step 4: Set up Klaviyo Flows
Step 5: GO LIVE
Step 6: 15-Day Checkup
Step 7: 30-Day Checkup & Optimization
Step 8: Analyze Performance

From 2016-2020, my email marketing startup was stuck at $3M ARR. Literally *nothing* I did moved the needle. I was completely demoralized. 

Here's the story of how we hit $20M ARR (and my message to founders who feel like quitting):

BACKSTORY

In 2016, I hit $3M ARR in the highly competitive Email Marketing SaaS space.

To do this, we used a creative data mining/cold calling strategy.

It seemed like leads would flow forever.

Until they didn't...

Things got so bad I was forced to scale back the team. 

It was the hardest day of my life.

I tried to remain optimistic.

But I had no idea what to do.

No move I made worked.

As I scrambled, two unfortunate patterns emerged:

1. I would meet someone who did X and they would convince me that X was my problem and the reason I was stuck. So, I would spend thousands of $ on FB ads or a new website or SEO or a partner program, which never worked.

2. I would meet someone I saw as an expert and they would tell me to sell the company

The problem was no matter who I met, I took their advice WAY too seriously. 

That's how desperate I was.

I had constant anxiety.

I wanted to quit.

My dream-life was collapsing before my eyes.

Then one day I learned something new...

I heard you could resolve anonymous website visitors to an email address. 

This was mind blowing.

Our current customers biggest problem was shrinking email lists. 

"Damn," I thought.

If I can turn anonymous web traffic into emails, I can sell it to anyone. 

It took us 18 months to figure out how to do it. 

I thought it would be a cool feature inside our app.

But then we noticed something...

People were signing up for our app, using the new anonymous ID feature, downloading the data, and using it in another email app and saying it was amazing. 

I read once that if someone is willing to endure a brutal user experience and still give you a high NPS score, that’s an early sign of product/market fit.

So we made a major pivot.

We spun out the anonymous ID feature as its own product.

I got the UI and front-end of v1 done on Upwork. 

Then I ran a $5,000 Facebook ad campaign to promote it.

And something amazing happened...

We got $10,000 back in MRR!

That was the moment Retention.com was born.

Since then, we’ve had plenty of bumps in the road.

But it’s been mainly up-and-to-the-right.

Why am I sharing this?

Because when I was stuck, I would have done ANYTHING to hear from a founder who was going through the same.

To read their words, what they were trying, what was working and not. 

I would have done ANYTHING to learn how to get unstuck.

That's why I create all of this content on Linkedin about my business.

That's why I share about the journey.

I’m doing it for the founders who are stuck

I'm doing it for a younger version of myself.

If you're out there and you're stuck... 

Know this:

The breakthrough is around the corner.

It may not feel like it.

You may want to quit.

But just keep building.

I meet with 100’s of executives and aspiring founders every year. They often ask for advice on how to bootstrap their own startup. Here’s what I tell them:

1. Keep throwing spaghetti against the wall:

- You need to find an “S” curve… a 1,000x
- The only way to find it is to run a bunch of wild experiments
- 9/10 of them will be total failures

2. Maintain your financial freedom.

- The only way to run crazy experiments is if you have free cash
- Investors would never let you behave in the way necessary to create an “s” curve
- If your growth slows down, that can’t lead to killing the crazy experiments

3. Try to be the 800lb gorilla in your space.

- Winner-take-all economics exist in tech 
- Compete in a way where you are impossible to compete with
- Try to compete for market share rather than growing revenues

4. Be obsessed with delivering value to your Ideal Customer Profile.

- If it doesn’t drive immediate revenue for merchants, don’t build it 
- Focus relentlessly on minimizing time-to-value
- Figure out how to show incremental revenue as clearly as possible

5. Stay lean, but when the time is right, go as fast as possible. 

- We bootstrapped $14m ARR with six people
- We figured out that large Shopify stores were our ICP
- We grew to a team of 50 in 60 days

TL;DR

1. Keep throwing spaghetti against the wall. 
2. Maintain your financial freedom.
3. Try to be the 800lb gorilla in your space.
4. Be obsessed with delivering value to your Ideal Customer Profile.
5. Stay lean, but when the time is right, go as fast as possible.

#startups

Two weeks ago we (accidentally) launched R!B2B. We got 2,122 free signups and 1,083 script installs, but only 14 paying customers. Am I worried? Nope. In fact, here's a 20-page guide explaining EXACTLY how to never pay us:

To set the stage: 

- We launched our Person-Level Website Visitor Identity tool March 1
- It’s for Slack, but we are trying to charge $495/mo to push data elsewhere 
- 19 days in we have a 0.7% conversion rate to paid, and it’s getting worse
- One (of many) reasons is you can parse the Slack block w/ Zapier and send it wherever for FREE!

As you can imagine, when I learned this for the first time, my reaction was... 

“Well, shit!”

We had spent weeks building integrations to Instantly, Apollo, and Smartlead, thinking that many of our “little guy” customers would use Slack like a dating app and pay $495 to push a contact that looked good into a sequence in one of these enablement apps. 

It turns out, zero people have wanted to pay $495/mo for that use case. 

*Sigh*

My emotional state went from disillusionment to despair as I realized that the main thing we were hoping to charge for… filtering and a push to Hubspot or Salesforce CRM… could be done with a workaround using Zapier. 

I'm realizing that the fundamental problem is that people are getting an UNBELIEVABLE amount of value from our free tool, and very little INCREMENTAL value from paid. 

Especially because you can do what you need to do with Zapier.

So, what do we do???

- Do we gate the Slack app like everybody is telling me to do? 50% resolution free, 100% paid?

- Do we bag the forever free offer entirely and do a 14-day free trial? 

- Do we try to somehow scramble up the Slack blocks and make it so Zapier can’t parse the LinkedIn URL and send it elsewhere?

- Do we stop going for market share and focus on a mid-market sales-led motion (like I planned originally)? 

None of these sound like great options. 

Especially given the insane positive feedback we’re getting from our free users. 

Instead, I decided to make a 20 page step-by-step google doc explaining EXACTLY how you can avoid paying us FOREVER using Zapier.

Why?

1. I included reasons why you would actually pay us in the doc
2. I want as many people to book demos with R!B2B as possible
3. I want the challenge of adding value to our paid plan BEYOND the integrations, rather than pulling back value from the free plan

The best companies have something so good people can’t stop themselves from talking about it. 

I’m trying to do everything I can to speed that process up. 

Enjoy the guide!

Nobody realizes that Apollo and ZoomInfo were both stuck at single-digit ARR for YEARS. When they finally got unstuck, unlocked rapid growth, and hit billion dollar valuations, both companies had ONE THING in common:

They hired Santosh Sharan.

Here are the 7 things that makes Santosh a top 0.1% unicorn builder:

1. He understands the mechanics of exponential growth

Santosh believes that sustained growth is about “Stacking S-Curves”. Meaning, you bang your head against the wall for years, then something hits, explosively. During that explosion you're working on your next S-curve. Steady exponential growth is about stacking these curve.

He also appreciates initiatives that have the potential to unlock non-linear growth (such as LinkedIn for RB2B), and the drivers of growth you can’t measure.

2. He doesn’t play to win; he plays to destroy all competitors

Santosh’s instinct is to design businesses and GTM strategies that are impossible to compete with, which usually means forgoing near-term revenue in favor of virally expanding user bases. When you become the 800lb gorilla and synonymous with the category you can charge premium prices and see exponential revenue growth.

3. He deeply understands all of the key departments of a startup

Santosh started as an engineer, moved into Product and Growth, and then moved on to running Sales and Marketing teams. He approaches all teams with an engineer’s mindset. He sees his role as removing blockers in one department and moving to the next.

4. He knows what the building blocks of massive future success look like

Santosh has been a part of the largest data companies when they were fledgling startups. He has seen, over and over again, what a unicorn looks like as it’s being born, and knows the opportunities worth pursuing.

5. He is empathetic towards employees and customers

No matter the problem, Santosh has seen it. He understands the immense pain that we go through as we grow. He also believes in creating businesses that treat customers well and make the world a better place.

6. He knows how to put together a killer data asset

Few people in the world could put together a fixed-price data asset that would allow us to make the free offer we have at RB2B. Santosh is one of them. 

7. He understands fundraising and M&A

Santosh has run many transactions as the buyer and seller, and has done countless VC and Growth Equity rounds. He understands what investors and acquirers look for in companies, which informs growth and product strategy.

Every serious entrepreneur needs to study this person.

I’ve recently become a fan of MrBeast — and I’ve got 4 lessons for you that I’ve learned from him that you should take with you and implement in everything you do, starting right now:

1) Success is not random or accidental 

When talking about virality, everyone always puts the blame on the algorithm. “The algorithm made you famous”, etc.

Virality is not an accident. Success is not an accident.

MrBeast is proof that you can go viral again and again and again — if you have the right formula.

He’s spent over a decade developing an SOP for exactly how to get hundreds of millions of views and get the world to talk about you.

2) Choose your friends wisely

If you’re playing a big game and you don’t have friends that don’t point out your weaknesses, you’re never going to be as big as you’d like.

MrBeast had a posse of ragtag YouTubers who would review each others’ content and give brutally honest feedback about what could be better.

You need to have friends like that who will call you out on when you’re not at the top of your game, whatever that game is.

I share an office with the Jasper.ai guys for a reason. We all give each other feedback and help each other grow.

Neither one of our companies would be this big if we didn’t get involved in each others’ stuff.

3) Your content sucks. Sorry.

If you watch one of MrBeast’s videos, you immediately should feel humbled.

It’s like watching LeBron play basketball. There isn’t a person in the world who can make content the way he makes content — the way he engages an audience for as long as he does.

It makes you want to be better at both short and long form video.

4) There is great joy in the pursuit of excellence

I listened to him on Joe Rogan, and he goes on for hours about how much he loves the idea of being the best.

He commits every hour he has and every dollar he earns into making better and better videos for his audience. It’s all he cares about.

He doesn’t want to be a billionaire like some of us do.

He doesn’t care about a 50,000 square foot mansion and a 300 foot yacht.

If he wanted to be worth $5 billion, he could make two phone calls, sell his empire, and he’d have everything he wants.

But that’s not his pursuit.

His goal is to be the absolute best in the game of content, and I believe he’s already there.

That’s all I’ve got for you today.

In the past 90 days, using LinkedIn we generated 2,500+ signups and booked 328 meetings with VP and C-level marketers for our new Person-Level ID tool. Here’s our Inbound-Led Outbound playbook:

1. Create the BEST content. Full stop

You need killer headlines. Each line has to be so good it makes you want to read the next. You have to wrap it up with something coy and create a dopamine hit. Not only that, you have to have unique takes that provide a POV. It helps if you provide a level of transparency and authenticity no one else will. 

It took me a year to crack it and it’s STILL a ton of work. But, these posts drive insane engagement. They are automated trust-building machines, and when we put a call to action in them, it drives demand.

2. “DM me if you’re interested in…“

My LinkedIn consultants also do inbox management, because Santosh and I get 100s of inbounds a month. Depending on what we’re trying to accomplish, they either set calls or put them on a waitlist. 

We have far more demand than we can handle. Right now Santosh is taking 5 calls per day and Pete is taking 8. We aren’t selling, we are using these for discovery and relationship building, so we can find product market fit.

3. Spend WAY too much time in the comments

The comments section of LinkedIn posts is where B2B companies should build their initial community. You form real relationships with people. This is how your brand gets built, one comment at a time. Once your community is vibrant enough, you can take it off-platform. Until then, spend more time in the comments.

4. Share successes (and failures) by working in public

We’re all in this grind together. Everybody wants to know what everybody else is doing, what’s working and what’s NOT working. If you have traction and you share things about your business that others wouldn’t, ESPECIALLY your failures, you will build an audience.

5. Get other people posting

I had been the only person at my company posting until Labor Day. Something clicked right around then, and we wanted to get Santosh involved to try to improve the attack surface. I’m now posting 3 times per week, Santosh is up to 2, and Pete is going to start posting soon.

6. Connect with your site visitors over LinkedIn and Email

This is shamelessly self-promotional, but we’re booking several demos per day with the strategy. Using our Person-Level Website Visitor Identity tool, we connect with ICP visitors on LinkedIn, send them a thoughtful email, send a LI message +24h, send a 2nd email +24h.

7. Use Video

I don’t think we understand how powerful a talking head video is. The actual face, mannerisms, etc. I know that if people feel like they know me and trust me, they will try my product… And video is the quickest way to get there.

TAKEAWAY:

I’m dumbfounded by the power of our Inbound-Led Outbound model.

I’m trying to figure out ways to go even deeper.

We’re seeing a massive shift from push to pull models for SaaS GTM.

Nothing pulls quite like LinkedIn.

Retention.com posted a PAINFUL down 1.4% for January, only our 4th down month in 51 months of existence (Jan ’21, Jan ’22 and Apr ’22). Notice a pattern? Here's why January sucks and what it says about our business:

The nature of our product lends itself to be bought BEFORE the holidays by brands looking for a boost.

Unfortunately the opposite is also true… it gets cancelled after the holidays.

Why didn’t January last year suck?

In late 2022 we honed in on ICP and grew our staff.

We sponsored everything in the ecosystem.

Long story short, we created a sh*t storm.

As a result, we had a MASSIVE January in 2023 (+10%).

The unfortunate reality of that 10% was we were overselling.

This lead to the most painful period of my career.

Our VP sales quitting, shrinking our sales org by 2/3, and lowering my topline  growth targets from $50m ARR (+350%) to $22m ARR (+60%).

What’s in store for '24?

I overestimated the effect on GRR that honing in on our ICP would have.

I thought our churn would go from awful to acceptable.

While churn improved a ton, it's still not great.

From my 50+ conversations with investors, I’ve come to accept that we're simply a high-churn product category (intent data) selling to a high-churn buyer persona (SMB ecom).

The fundamental problem is that in MarTech, being a system of record is the base-case for low churn.

Klaviyo and Hubspot are systems of record.

There’s only one reason you quit Klaviyo – to switch to Sendlane.

Sadly, there are 8 different reasons you stop buying us.

Accepting this and its implications on future growth was the worst part of 2023.

Yes, we can make it better.

Yes, we have the entire org focused on things within our control.

Please don’t DM me telling me you can help.

We know what we need to do, I promise.

As an aside, competitors will say this is an indication of the quality of the product. The truth is they're either lying about their own situation, overstating the revenue they drive for you (I can show you how), or are too early to see the problem.

Enough of the sob story...

Now for the wins.

We’re bootstrapped, generated $500k in profit in January, and the feedback on our new B2B tool is like nothing I’ve ever seen.

PROUD OF:

- We hired Eddie as our VP Rev Ops, it’s life changing
- We are executing a focused upmarket effort
- We sped up time-to-value and grew audience size
- We have 100+ beta users for our B2B product
- The free forever Slack app is dope, we’re booking a demo/day w/ it
- We hired Pete to build out chat bots to run the B2B sales/CS org

NOT PROUD OF:

- See above about churn

BIGGEST OPPS:

- Focus on key accounts on the Ecom biz
- Soft launch Feb 15 on B2B

TAKEAWAY:

Writing updates like this one SUCKS.

But I’m committed to doing it.

Why?

Because we need to tell the real story of what it’s like out there.

I’m sharing all of this so that you know you’re not alone.

2023 and early 2024 sucked for all of us.

Keep your head up, and keep building.

We used to spend $875,000 every year on our BDR team. Here's the uncomfortable truth about that rate of spend:

BDR teams have stopped working.

Our outbound sales performance plummeted over the last 12 months.

Just like everyone else’s.

Why?

Because buyers’ inboxes are ruined

99% of tech companies:

- Use the same automation tools 
- Send the same email cadences
- Contract the same data vendors 
- Message the same prospects

Which is bad, but...

Then AI tools came and made it 100x worse.

Here's the “old way” of running a sales organization:

- Pick a revenue target for the end of the year
- Model out how much manpower it’s going to take to get you there
- Hire, hire, hire, and then... hire some more

Retention.com was guilty of this.

Then our VP of Sales resigned. 

Of course, it was a surprise at first.

But it caused me to rethink how we run our business. 

I had read a few posts from Sam Jacobs about the “new way” of running sales.

Where $30M ARR companies were doing MORE sales with 2 reps than 25.

I spoke to founder friends and investors who were seeing the same.

So we shrunk our sales team from 14 to 4, eliminated the entire BDR team, had our CRO become VP of Sales, and decided we were going to create one of these “new way” super-light, super-lean sales machines.

What’s shocking about it is that we’re better on every metric than we were before we made the move.

Here’s what we did after we downsized to generate pipeline:

1. We DRAMATICALLY stepped up the Founder Brand content

- I used a ghostwriter which was building an audience, but not generating leads
- I now use a consultant, which is more work, but building the right audience
- I use some templates, but lots of vulnerable stories and personal experience
- We did a targeted connection request campaign to get the audience going

2. Grew an overseas team doing “spray and pray” cold email

- We build lists using tech lists on BuiltWith and have the team find the email
- We have the team manually send emails from multiple inboxes on our Gmail
- I don’t even think about this as direct-response… It’s more just branding, like an “ad unit” in inbox

3. Created more content and hosting events that cuts through.

- We’re making a super-high-quality docuseries called “Billion Dollar Challenge”
- We’re recording podcasts to write Linkedin posts that we know do well
- We’re targeting guests who are big names for our target audience
- We're hosting large and small events for our ICP and influencers

This isn’t predictable, but it’s creating 3x the pipeline with 20% of the sales org we had 120 days ago.

Will this work for everyone?

Probably not.

But the next generation of unicorns will look more like us than Salesforce.

Running as lean as possible. 

And leading with great content.

Hey CEOs: if you disappeared into the woods for 7 days, would your company run smoothly without you? This is the ultimate test of your delegation skills. 
 
I tried it. Here's what I learned: 

–

The CEO is the Chief Emergency Officer.

Anytime there's a fire, the default is for the employees to bring it to the CEO to solve

You need to switch this default option.

Instead of coming to you for a solution, empower your employees to solve huge problems on their own 

–

CEO involvement kills scale.

If the CEO has to be involved in every decision, the company will never grow past the CEO's personal capacity.

Delegate as much decision-making power as possible. 

–

The CEO's job is NOT to run the company.

The CEO's main job is recruiting A+ talent.

I worked my ass off to recruit great people.

Now I can sit back and allow them to work their magic. 

– 

My company does $20 million in annual revenue

The larger we get, the less important I should become 

When we had 5 employees, I was 20% of the team

But when we have 1,000 employees, I'll be just 0.1% 

– 

A lot of these are counter-intuitive, but your job as CEO should be easier as you scale

The playbook you created is playing itself out.

You *should* be less involved in the day-to-day.

Think big picture and trust the process.

2. It’s not nice.

3. It’s not good for 6Sense’s brand. 

Suing the little guy is already bad enough for your brand. Suing the little guy for something you’re doing back at him is appalling.

Look at the comments on any post I’ve written about anything to do with 6Sense and ABM. Almost nobody makes money from the tool, despite the FOMO-driven sales motion that pulled everyone in.

6Sense - I completely understand your desire to eliminate RB2B in its early days by suing us into oblivion.

Yesterday Salesforce shares dropped 21% after reporting missed earnings for the first time since 2006. I am afraid this is only the beginning of a long trend. Many enterprise SaaS companies are set to miss their forecasts. Here’s why (and how GTM teams should react):

BACKGROUND

Salesforce enjoyed at least 18 straight years of perpetual growth. 

During this low interest rate period, Salesforce GTM teams 

- saturated the CRM market 
- maximized account penetration 
- increased sales quota and hired large GTM teams 

Now with high interest rates, Salesforce customers are beginning to realize:

- that a significant number of salesforce licenses are barely or never used
- that teams can be as productive without having salesforce licenses 
- that they need to question all large spends 

It’s becoming commonplace for CFOs to show up on renewal discussions, asking for significant discounts. 

Research says 33% of all SaaS spend is wastage. 

I expect this will be corrected in the next 4 quarters. 

Here are 6 things enterprise GTM teams can do to react:

1. Lower Price: 

SaaS prices have been going up 18% YOY. For the last two decades, most enterprises focused on going upstream and took pride in large deals. The pressure to lower prices will be the highest at the top of the market. Proactively lowering prices will help retain some of these accounts. 

2. Expand into the low end of the market: 

With significant brand equity, enterprise SaaS brands can comfortably take out smaller vendors and consolidate the low end of the market.

3. Lower Sales Quota: 

We have ended up with unreasonable sales quotas, most of which are not going to be achieved. It’s time to get realistic about sales efficiency and quotas. 

4. Reduce or Optimize expenses: 

GTM teams and GTM processes have grown significantly. Now is the time for companies to optimize expenses and focus on profitability.

5. Seek growth in APAC:  

While US and EMEA markets may be saturated for some, APAC can prove to be a high growth market given the lag in software adoption. For Salesforce, APAC will contribute 24%, EMEA 9% and Americas 11% of next quarter’s growth. 

6. Consumption based pricing: 

SaaS vendors that provide consumption or usage based pricing before their competitors do will gain an advantage and exhibit stronger growth.

TAKEAWAY:

The economic pressures are going to be more severe at the top of the market.

The winners of the next economic cycle will figure out how to provide value to users at a much lower unit price than their competitors.

The natural tendency for the enterprise GTM teams will be to ignore all the recommendations above until things get MUCH worse.

Don't.

This discussion needs to happen NOW.

With high interest rates, the world has changed. 

We can no longer expect the same results as before. 

It is time to evolve and align with the macro changes. 

We can't bury our heads in the sand anymore.

Most B2B companies suck at building communities. Why? Because they think it means firing up a Slack channel, inviting customers and then watching as $$$ rolls in. Here's the difference between a Bad and Good B2B community:

Bad B2B Community: 

- Vendor says “Let’s start a community on Slack”
- Vendor has no social presence, so no idea what to talk about to draw people in
- Goal is to drive sales
- Vendor only invites customers
- Convo is about features/product 
- Turns into forum for complaining about product
- Moderated by an intern with zero expertise
- Seen as a cost center by execs at the vendor
- When inevitably it doesn’t “work”, it gets dialed back

Good B2B Community: 

- Goal ISN’T to drive sales, does not roll up into a revenue team
- Goal is to GIVE - educate, connect people, make people better at their jobs
- Current customers AND non-customers are welcome
- Built around deep subject matter expertise in a given topic/topics
- Topics are known because vendor has already built community on social
- Conversation is about these topics, not about vendors product/features
- Moderated by someone WITH the actual subject-matter expertise
- Effortlessly flows from digital to physical events and spaces
- Gets more investment with zero attributable revs b/c vendor gets it
- Gives access to individuals that the community cares about
- Creates one of the only two moats in SaaS (brand is the other)

TAKEAWAY:

It’s easy for founders to think that starting a community is as easy as:

1. Firing up a slack channel 
2. Inviting your customers
3. Waiting for the $$$ to roll in

That’s NOT what makes a great community. 

Community is about giving and expecting nothing in return.

What’s Retention.com's plan for 2024?

1. We’re going to record and publicize our weekly strategy calls & my meetings, so people can see what it actually takes to build a business.

2. We’ll have a bi-weekly ask-me-anything with me and Santosh Sharan, to talk about your startup. 

3. We'll provide updated playbooks on signals-based selling, outbound and PLG motions we're using to grow Retention's new B2B product.

4. We’ll have monthly “LinkedIn Influencer” planning sessions and content teardowns w/ me and Alec Paul (my coach) for our top-tier members, so you can master LinkedIn.

Plus, Santosh and I are going to moderate the community ourselves!

Not some underpaid Community Manager.

That’s our starting point, but I know it won’t be where we’ll end.

In 6 months, I grew my startup from $0-$1M ARR with six people and zero funding. I’m about to launch a new startup and plan to hit $1M ARR in 50% of the time (with even fewer people). Here’s my 6-step playbook for building a lean, mean, high-velocity growth machine:

To set the stage:

- Our current startup is $22m ARR, bootstrapped, we sell to ecommerce
- We are launching a NEW product for B2B that identifies your anonymous web traffic, then sends their LinkedIn profiles to a Slack channel, in real-time
- I’m totally addicted to watching these leads roll in.

Now, to the 6-step playbook to get from $0-$1M in 90 days: 

Step 1) Have insane product-market fit.

- If you don’t have strong word-of-mouth, nothing else will work
- If you do, you can accelerate things in so many different ways
- We have a product that when I show people what it does, their jaws drop 

Step 2) Make it free, unlimited use

- It’s 2024. Buyers don’t want to talk to salespeople
- They want FREE, with MASSIVE value. Don’t hold back
- Figure out how to get on millions of sites, then gate features later somehow

Step 3) Create virality through all available channels

- Social is everything. Influencers are everything. Founders are the best.
- Build systems that create user-generated content - reviews, social posts, etc
- Create viral loops that turn 1 free user into 2 more

Step 4) Start investing in community Day 1

- Community will be your biggest driver of user-generated content
- Community is your only true moat. Anyone can copy software and GTM
- Deliver content that builds community around expertise, persona-by-persona

Step 5) Build in Public. Be ridiculously transparent

- This just works. Trust me. I've been doing it for over a year. Look at my posts
- Share as much as you can. The more naked you get, the more eyeballs
- If you can, make it a reality show. I literally did that last year. It’s on my profile

Step 6) Charge a throw-away price to larger businesses

- To start, sales velocity and market share are more important than revenue
- Gate things at low price points that are obvious value
- Take the pricing discussion off the table.

TAKEAWAY:

Every business is different. 

What I’m trying this time wouldn’t have worked for me last time. 

(It may not work this time… We’ll see!!!)

What’s the same is I’m starting with a product that makes people’s jaws drop.

But unlike last time, I’m making the product 100% free. 

Free is the global domination play. 

And, if it catches fire, it's the quickest way to $1m ARR. 

PS.

DM me if you want to: 

1. identify the anonymous people on your website, and 
2. Get their LinkedIn profiles sent to a Slack channel, in real-time

…It’s 100% free. 

No, I am not kidding.

Last week I had a viral Linkedin post on why if I founded a startup today, I would focus on GTM instead of technology innovation and forgo the $100M exit. Many people did not agree! Here are the 5 major objections (and my clarifications):  

BACKGROUND: 

You can read the original post here: https://lnkd.in/gEr_uc4A

Here are the objections I received on the above model. 

1. Not doing anything Novel is anti-innovation: 

I recommend staying away from doing anything novel on the technology front. Creating a moat with technology innovation is expensive and requires tech savvy entrepreneurs. It’s a MISTAKE to think that all innovation comes only from tech. Offering the product for a disruptively low price and yet staying very profitable requires a ton of innovation as well.

2. It is not possible to build a SaaS tool in six weeks without a large team:

I have an automation in mind that will allow one to build an entire SaaS tool in six week with 1 engineer. Allow me the indulgence for now, I will soon do a post detailing a blueprint on this topic and seek feedback. While I have seen this done before for simple tools, with AI, Automation and some human intervention, it will be possible to accelerate this even further. 

3. This is contrary to why founders start companies: 

Not entirely true, in some market segments we start with simplicity and go towards complexity (such as AI), but in other market segments, such as SaaS - we start with complexity and go towards simplicity (SAP -> Siebel -> Salesforce -> Hubspot -> Newco). 

I am suggesting that there’s value in taking this minimalist approach beyond just product and apply it to the entire organization. I am challenging founders to go back to the first principles and explore if you can run a $5M ARR company with 5 people and drive MINIMALISM beyond design or product to customer success, support, customer acquisition, marketing, sales strategy, outreach, etc.   

4. Isn’t copying unethical? 

Let me clarify here, I did not suggest copying the IP, javascript or source code from your competitor or doing anything illegal. Having said that, all companies take inspiration from each other’s publicly accessible content including product interfaces. 

As a GTM startup, intent in lowering the cost of technology development - its important to choose which 50% of the features are most important and while I recommend copying those features from the competitor - it’s always easy to apply a different skin or make 10% tweak or remove some complex workflows. Surveying competitor’s customers to understand what features they use is a great way to build this solution. 

POST CONTINUED IN COMMENTS 👇

If you're over 40 you might not recognize this guy, but every serious entrepreneur needs to study him.

Here's 4 lessons you can learn from a group of college-age friends who turned a video game YouTube channel into a $1 Billion brand listed on the NASDAQ.

Let’s take a look at the backstory...

In 2010, three gamer kids with the nicknames “CLipZ” (pictured), “Timid” and “Resistance” started a YouTube channel showcasing their Call of Duty skills.

They called themselves FaZe Clan.

Through a mix of engaging content and the force of their personality, they reached a million subscribers within 2 years.

After expanding into other games and winning tournaments under the FaZe brand, they attracted outside investors like Pitbull, Ben Simmons and Offset.

They acquired teams to participate in other competitions, increasing their brand recognition and presence across the Esports world.

In July 2022, FaZe Clan went public in a $725 million SPAC

Today, they have top level teams in ten of the hottest games on the market and continue to be leaders in the world of not just Esports, but youth culture. 

Here's the 4 lessons from their entrepreneurial journey:


1) Find your niche.

In 2010, the Esports streaming world was filled with players posting their winning shots. FaZe focused on trickshots that distinguished them from the bunch. Winning a tournament? Easy. "360 noscope headshot jumping off a ledge"? Unforgettable.


2) Expand on brand.

FaZe’s mission has always been to recruit talented and engaging personalities who build relationships with the audience. When adding teams for Counter-Strike, Fortnite, or FIFA, the goal remains the same. Expand vertically or horizontally, but always on brand.


3. Skate where the puck is headed.

When FaZe’s YouTube channel gained traction, the world of Esports was wide open. People were hungry for competitive video game content presented in a fun way by relatable creators. FaZe saw the opportunity ahead and invented the branded Esports team


4. Protect your brand.

In 2021, members of FaZe used their platform to push Save The Kids token, or $KIDS, a pump and dump cryptocurrency, to its audience under the guise of raising money for sick children. The offending members were immediately removed from FaZe and an apology was issued.


Today, FaZe Holdings is a publicly listed company on the NASDAQ and had $70M in revenue in 2022.

Not bad for three kids playing video games.

What do you think?

Confession: we got absolutely crushed in April.

I talk a lot about everything we do at Retention.com.

I talk about when we crush our goals and surprise ourselves, but I should probably talk more about things we’ve done that aren’t ideal.

It paints a more realistic picture of what growing a business looks like.

It’s not always sunshine and rainbows.

Before this past period, we were crushing.

A $1M ARR week, we were growing super fast, we hit all the targets, etc.

But that was short-lived.

We recently hit a wall.

We stalled completely.

We were hitting targets at 50% of what they should’ve been.

We tried a price experiment that took our average contract value from $30k to $12k…

Our top-of-funnel tracking got scrambled, so we have no idea what’s happening.

And lastly…

I got hit with a random tax bill for $300k while in a break-even period.

It would be easy for me to be down in the dumps. But I can’t do that.

We’ve got mouths to feed.

So here’s what I’m doing in light of this “L” to fix this mess and learn from my mistakes.

1. Roll back pricing.

The pricing experiment was a failure. We tried to raise prices because we felt like we were undercharging…

But you shouldn’t mess with what’s working.

We’re going to go back to what our prices originally were, because it’s just such a no-brainer for the customer.

Our most stacked plan is still cheaper than our main competitor’s entry-level plan.

The way we have it currently is way more approachable. We’re not gonna mess with it.

2. Add. More. Value.

We’re probably leaving 60% of the value on the table of what we can offer to merchants.

We need to do SMS.

We need to do back-in-stock flows and price-drop flows.

We’re building out integrations to other apps that will make the experience better for the customer.

It’ll just continue to add more buzz to what we’re doing and demonstrate just how much of a necessity our product is.

3. Collect more data.

For the points mentioned above, we want to get a ton of data about exactly how much value we can add with SMS, back-in-stock, and price-drop flows.

Get solid numbers on what our TAM is, and how much revenue we can drive for the companies we work with.

4. Be grateful.

I need to remind myself sometimes that the problems we experience as a company are good problems to have.

A year ago, I would’ve killed to be in this position.

Regardless, this is still a ride I wanna be on. It doesn’t matter what happens in the day-to-day, I’m so grateful to be working on this company with some wonderful and talented people.

I wouldn’t have it any other way.

As a CEO, your job is to solve problems quickly.

Unfortunately, you don’t have time to sit around and feel sorry for yourself.

Not if you have a team that’s relying on you, and a mission to conquer.

Nowhere to go but up.

In 3 months, you’ll forget all about these problems as long as you take action on them today.

Thanks for reading.

Since November, we've used LinkedIn to drive 600 calls, and I’ve answered 5,000 comments. When I told Chris Walker this was informing our entire pricing and GTM strategy he said, “You’re MISSING OUT on the most powerful channel by far."

The Weekly Live Event.

In Chris’ words, the fast feedback loop is EVERYTHING in the early days. 

I agree with that, which was what I was gloating about in the first place. 

The combination of the MASSIVE free offer we have, PLUS the feedback I get when I post - mostly about being wrong - about our GTM with RB2B is SOOO helpful. 

What do I mean? 

I had the initial hypothesis that in order to attempt to create a low churn business, we would:

1. Give the leads away for free, along with
2. A push to Slack

And charge for a TINY percentage of high-value users who wanted a Hubspot and SFDC integration $495/mo, and everybody else would enjoy the product for free.

As we all now know, I was very wrong about this. 

You can parse the Slack block with no code using Zapier and send the leads wherever you want.

I also heard “there was too much value in free, not enough in paid”, and realized a MASSIVE amount of our signups just couldn’t jump to $495/mo. 

So, we decided an appropriate strategy was sell credits, with 80% of our signups getting the product for free forever.

As one LinkedIn community member commented on one of my posts: 

“Well the good news is that you got a year’s worth of information in 6 weeks.” 

So, back to Chris...

He said his Weekly Live Event is an even BETTER feedback loop, from MORE people, FASTER than LinkedIn.

Chris gets 50-200 people to show up every week.

Then another 10,000 listen to it on the pod.

He starts off with a 10-30min monologue, then opens it up for questions.

Why is the live event so good for Chris’ business?

1. He gets REALLY fast feedback
2. He can figure out what people are struggling with
3. He can work on his messaging to the market

But my absolute FAVORITE part of Chris’ whole event motion…

Which I have seen NOBODY copy to date… 

Is that LITERALLY 100% of his LinkedIn posts come from the event.

1. Record live event
2. Team clips out short form video by topic
3. Wakes up in the morning, looks through the clips, picks one, writes post

Partnership is the future of Sales. Here’s how smaller SaaS startups can team up and fight back against billion dollar behemoths like ZoomInfo and Clari:

SaaS started as best of breed approach.

Not anymore.

Increasingly, SaaS companies aspire to become all-in-one platforms. 

Here why it makes sense for a SaaS endpoint vendors to become a multi-solution platform company:

- Reduces churn
- Increases market power
- Enables economies of scale
- Creates data contribution flywheels
- Reduces cost of customer acquisition 

However, to become a platform company (through either build or buy) requires MASSIVE investments with billions in valuations and hundreds of millions in fundraising - which most SaaS solutions providers cannot afford. 

Only through innovative partnerships, can they compete against the big guys. 

What if the following companies got together to create a stack that starts to compete with the likes of ZoomInfo or Clari ? 

Partnership Stack 1: 

Seamless (data) + Instantly (email engagement) + Nooks (automated dialer) + Fathom (Conversational Intelligence) + Intentsify (Intent) + Builtwith (Technographics data) + RB2B (Website Signal) 

Partnership Stack 2: 

Cognism (data) + SmartLead (email engagement) + Orum (automated dialer) + Jiminny (Conversational Intelligence) + Foundry (Intent) + HGInsights (Technographics Data) + RB2B (Website Signal)

(if you notice RB2B is a must have on all stacks:) 

What if they sell the above as pre-integrated solution stack for a single subscription price ? 

The future belongs to companies that can pull off these novel partnerships and integrate multiple end point solutions to create a single platform. 

This will subsidize CAC, enable startups to move upmarket and potentially offer cost reduction for enterprises and more functionality to buyers. 

P.S.

What's your dream GTM stack? Who should partner up to offer a single integrated platform? Tag them below!

We closed out February at $1.8M MRR (-0.2%), our 6th down month ever. We also (accidentally) launched R!B2B 5 days ago and have 10 paying customers and $4.2K MRR. Here’s what SUCKED and was AWESOME in February: 

First, what SUCKED:

At Retention.com, activity still feels slow from the holiday season, cancellations are high, and we saw an uptick in competition for parts of our core offering. 

That sounds terrible, and I’m sure if you’re rooting against us, you’ll enjoy the next several months as we figure out how to navigate through this operating environment which is decidedly more difficult than it was a year ago.

One thing I can see from looking at BuiltWith is that many of the rising stars in the Shopify ecosystem are experiencing a similar malaise - some severe.

I’m just the only idiot writing about it publicly!

While we’ve had trouble growing topline the last 60 days, we have continued to improve bottom line, and we’ll be in a position to resume growth in the Q2.

What was AWESOME:

We generated $624,132 of free cash in February, which was our 2nd highest month ever.

We also accidentally launched rb2b.com - our person-level website visitor ID product - a week ago and got 1,000 free signups without even intending to. But, we only have 10 paying customers. Not a great conversion rate.

There is a LONG road ahead of refining our PLG motion, which either currently doesn’t exist or is all wrong. 

My emotional experience has gone from euphoria to disillusionment as the excitement we built over the past six months was met with a product that lacks the key features and integrations we need for paying customers to find value.

On the bright side, our top-of-funnel has been excellent. 

Santosh and I have done great generating meetings and signups on LinkedIn, our cold email effort that Taylor is spearheading has had great results.

Also, our plan to have AI chatbots handle the bulk of support requests is working (here's a few staggering early numbers): 

In the past week, we had 1293 instances of users seeking support:

- 1230 (95.1%) were resolved by ‘self-serve support’
- 28 (2.2%) were resolved by a human straight out of the gate
- 35 (2.7%) started self-serve but needed human help

That's nuts!

We still have LOTS of work to do to help people along the activation journey, and some pricing changes and messaging to inform people of what they can pay for and why. Plus, building the features (mainly filtering for ICP contacts) and integrations (mainly Salesforce and Hubspot) that we’re missing, but...

We'll get there.

_

Success doesn’t happen in a straight line, as you’re witnessing now.

However, if we keep our heads down and keep pursuing excellence we’ll get through this uncomfortable period. 

I’m sure some of you are absolutely crushing it out there, and to you, I tip my hat. 

For the rest of you, I just want you to know that you’re not alone. 

What we do is freaking hard. 

Keep your head up. 

And keep building.

Daniel Murray has built The Marketing Millennials audience of over 600,000 people.

And he let me in on a secret to making LinkedIn content go more viral:

Dumb it down.

Let’s take email marketing for example.

Explaining something about email marketing to an audience of agency owners will look a lot different than explaining that same thing to an audience of people like your mother.

See, you have a bias that makes you think you need to sound smarter than everyone else.

You believe that the best way to get ahead is to be so much wiser and more profound that everyone will trust you more. That may be true for some audiences.

But you need to understand that the world we exist in is only a tiny fraction of the population. 

Less than 0.1%.

If you want to make content for as many people as possible (and there’s nothing wrong with that), you absolutely *cannot* go ultra-meta and talk about niche things that only a handful of people understand.

You need to take more cues from someone like MrBeast.

I talk about MrBeast in this newsletter all the time, because I think he is one of the best examples of what “greatness” looks like.

MrBeast makes content for everyone.

He gets billions of views because his videos are about something everyone understands and loves: handing out money to strangers.

There’s not a whole lot of talking. It’s very visual. It’s like a kids’ show for adults.

Couple this with the fact that he has dozens of other channels for different languages, and you suddenly have an asset that most of the world can enjoy.

How does this apply to you?

Dumb. It. Down.

Make content for more and more people.

That’s how you grow your audience, and become a thought leader for people who are outside of your bubble.

I wanted to share something that I used to be deeply ashamed of.

Truly one of the worst things I’ve done as a founder, and I hope that no one has to go through the same thing…

In my early days as a founder of another startup, I’d gotten my hands on a list of leads from a data mining company. A *lot* of leads.

We knew the quality would be pretty close to 100% trash, but we didn’t know how close to 100% trash they were.

In order to figure it out, we had 3 of our best sales guys go through some of these leads and see if they were workable.

After a brief testing period, it seemed like they were qualified enough that we could scale this thing as fast as possible.

We were foaming at the mouth to get a ton of sales talent on these leads.

So we hired a head hunter to get us a bunch of top salespeople, trained the heck out of them, and put them on the new lead list.

Very quickly, we realized that these leads were 99.99% trash. As close as you can get to what we hoped would *not* be the case.

Crickets.

Not only were these leads not converting… they weren’t even answering the phone when one of my 25 new salespeople would call them.

It wasn’t a problem with our scripts, our product, or our talent. 

It was a lead problem.

I’d made a massive mistake.

I’d just incurred the expense of bringing on some expensive salespeople, and they suddenly had *nothing* to do all day. We were burning daylight trying to get this lead list to work.

The day we realized this, it was a nightmare.

I’d spoken to some of my mentors at the time, and they all told me what I already knew.

The next day, I took 25 of my 32 employees into a room, and I said:

“If you’re in this room, you no longer have a job with us.”

I had wasted the salespeople’s time, the recruiter’s time, the people that trained them, etc.

I felt horrible. Leading on 25 people who thought they had an opportunity, and I blew it.

Firing ONE person is hard.

Firing 25 is a tragedy.

Hopefully sharing this helps you learn from my mistakes, so you don’t have to go through the pain that this hard decision caused.

Out of all Ronak Shah’s accomplishments (including having built a DTC brand to $40M in revenue in 3 years), the thing I was most impressed with was his insane network.

After chatting with him for an hour, I gathered 5 traits that he excels in — and if you’re trying to build a powerful network, you need to do these too:

1. Work. In. Public.

It’s the title of one of my YouTube series for a reason.

Working in public is a selfless way to teach people about what you’re working on, so that others can use it to help themselves.

Tweets, blogs, LinkedIn posts, or YouTube videos will document what you’re doing while you’re doing it.

It inspires, and it teaches.

People need to know that you’re working on something in order for them to pay attention and be interested in you. Which leads us to #2…

2. Post regularly.

If you’re gonna work in public, be consistent about it.

Ron posts multiple times a day about the things that are working for Obvi, and he only tweets things that he believes will teach people something.

Even just 3 posts a day (which can be repurposed across every platform) is sufficient to leave an impression.

3. Dedicate time to jamming freely with people.

This is one thing that I have a specific block on my calendar for.

I absolutely love talking to entrepreneurs who own businesses similar to mine so we can swap stories and tactics on growth.

Always be open to connect and speak freely about things you’re both passionate about.

4. Send opportunities to others (for free).

When you get to a certain level in an industry, you have people asking you for recommendations on agencies, freelancers, experts in XYZ field, etc.

Just because you can ask for a commission/referral fee doesn’t mean that you should.

Having people owe you a favor down the road is much more powerful than a few hundred dollars that you’d get for an intro email.

5. Collect connectors.

I’ve met people who aren’t rich, famous, or particularly talented at something, but they’re one of the most valuable people to have around because of who they know.

Connectors are people that you can go to and they have a guy or gal for everything.

Get in touch with 2-3 people who have a black book worth billions, and make sure you provide them with as much value as you possibly can.

The saying is cliche, but it’s true — your network is your net worth. And I hope these 5 tips help you build yours. Share this with a founder who might need it.

I had a very interesting conversation with Erik Huberman, the founder of Hawke Media, a $150M e-commerce marketing behemoth. 

If you have visibility into thousands of businesses ranging in size from $1M a year to $1B a year, you’re going to have some extremely valuable data that no one else has.

I was curious enough to ask him about some of the best tools that every e-commerce brand needs to be utilizing right now, and how they should be doing it.

These are the 3 that he absolutely insisted on:

1. Postscript

It may come as a shock to you, but I’ve noticed that 20-30% of brands I speak to are still not sold on SMS.

They think it’s expensive, invasive, and they want to be respectful to their customer by not annoying them with text messages.

SMS is opt-in.

If they give you their number, it’s fair game.

If they don’t want to hear from you, they’ll unsubscribe.

So many brands leave money on the table by not doing SMS because they’re afraid to annoy people.

You won’t. It’s industry standard now.

If you write fun copy that makes people laugh, that’s even better.

At LEAST set up an Abandoned Cart flow. Bare minimum.

2. Hawke AI

Yes, Hawke as in Hawke Media. An incredible agency play is to take what you’ve learned through working with clients, and package that into some sort of info tool to lift all ships.

Hawke AI is a collection of data across 8000+ brands, which allows marketers to look at this data and identify weak points for your own brand.

You can analyze how you stack up against everyone else in terms of performance across channels, where you’re overspending, etc.

You can’t rely on just your own data to make decisions for the future of your brand.

Having access to other brands’ data is what’ll help you grow sustainably.

3. Retention.com

Listen, I know what this looks like. But I did not pay Eric to say this. He said this of his own accord. And I’m just paraphrasing it.

He said this:

“Retention.com is just capturing so much more data and so much more audience, you just need to do it. There’s no question here. You’re trying to build a business? You should check these boxes. Retention.com is one of those boxes.”

In terms of ROI alone, this makes sense for virtually any DTC brand over $5M in annual revenue.

Like I said…not to toot my own horn…but check this out if you trust the good word of Eric Huberman…the founder of a $150M agency…

Also. I’m curious. What tools would you add to the list?

Ekster spent $500 in total on their launch and made $350k back.
$350,000 on launch, from scratch. How?

It wasn’t some super sneaky, scrappy early-stage founder strategy.
They used Kickstarter.

Olivier and his co-founder had studied Kickstarter for years beforehand.

The science behind the biggest launches, how they went viral, and all of the ingredients that went into a ton of eyeballs for little-to-no money.

The $500 was spent on a video, shot and edited by Olivier’s sister.

To turn that into $350k in sales, the key is to get to the “Taking Off” section of Kickstarter.

These are the 5 things they did to get there.
1. Nail PR.

Reach out to journalists who can cover what you’re building in advance of the launch.

Do a social media campaign to collect emails of people who are interested in the product or the brand.

Kickstarter launches don’t operate in a vacuum. Just because you’re on Kickstarter does not mean that you’re going to make guaranteed money.

You still need to build an audience and a reputation beforehand.

2. Get as many pledges as possible.

A pledge on Kickstarter is a way of demonstrating support with a quantifiable number.

Every project creator sets their project's funding goal and deadline.
If people like the project, they can pledge money to make it happen.

If the project succeeds in reaching its funding goal, all backers' credit cards are charged when time expires.

Make sure that you have a low pledge AOV so that more people will be able to participate.

3. Engage with the people commenting.

This is where you start to get a little scrappy.

One of my favorite startup motifs is “do things that don’t scale” from Paul Graham.

As the founder, make sure that you interact and engage with every single person who comments on your video so that you can build that authenticity with your audience.

These people will be crucial to the success of your business down the road.

Your first 1000 customers are the most valuable thing to a launch like this. Make sure they know that.

4. Update your audience regularly.

Once you have someone’s email, or their phone number, or they follow you on social media, etc, update them as frequently as possible.

Brands often fizzle out when they have a great launch and forget to keep their leads excited in the time it takes to create and ship the product.

Communication is key.

As long as you’re in contact with them and letting them know where you’re at in production, no timeline is too long.

5. The first 24 hours can make or break you.

A while back, I wrote about BarkBox and how successful they were when they launched.

The founder of BarkBox literally went up to strangers in a dog park and sold them on preorders for dog toys.

His first 24 hours were indicative of how well the company would do years later, and now they’re worth $1.6B.

If you can nail the first 24 hours, you’ll be golden.

And if you have a product like Ekster, maybe you’ll get to $50M a year like they did, too.

90% of PLG (Product Led Growth) companies are overlooking 2 growth strategies that have the potential to unlock billions of $$$ in new revenues from *existing traffic*. Here's how it works:

Below are two key questions PLG companies face and how to answer them:

1. "Should we allow users to sign up with a business or personal email?"

With business email there’s a direct path to prospecting and revenues, but insisting on business emails reduces signups. On the other hand, while personal emails drive higher signup metrics, now you don't know where your customers work and have a harder time converting individual sales into an enterprise MSA.

It is a tough call to make between revenues and signup metrics.

What if I said... you could have both? 

Here's how to Maximize Sign-ups while Targeting Prospects:

i) Maximizing PLG Signups: Allow users to sign up using personal emails to maximize signup metrics

ii) Identify if any from your ICP signed up: Using Retention.com’s new person-level identity solution, identify if any of the PLG signups match with your key account list and ICP. Provide a differentiated service to select users if they are in your key account list.

iii) Target with Precision: Once an individual user has had a positive experience with your solution or has provided a positive NPS, request an introduction into other team members

2. "How do we deal with password sharing?"

A few months ago, Netflix said they were losing $6B+ in unrealized revenues due to password sharing. I suspect this number for B2B must be in 10’s of billions of dollars.

Most PLG companies either ignore password sharing or deploy access denial strategies to log out the first logged in user once the third user logs in resulting in a bad user experience. 

But there’s a much smarter approach to this challenge:

i) Treat each individual using a shared password as a net new revenue opportunity and a free lead

ii) Using Retention's person-level ID solution, identify these individuals and have the marketing team tailor their outreach accordingly

iii) Some strategies that I have seen work are offering discounts and promotions so they can create a new account or extend free licenses to their individual email addresses to foster user engagement and loyalty

Have questions about PLG growth? 

AMA anything in the comments. 👇

I'll be around for the next 45 minutes.

P.S.

If you're PLG company and want to test this playbook to drive additional revenue from existing traffic, DM me and we'll help you build it.

In 2023, I spent $350,000 producing a reality TV show about building Retention.com. This year I plan to spend DOUBLE that on video. Here's why video is the biggest bet I'm making (and the 6 areas we're investing):

BACKGROUND:

Why is video the biggest bet I’m making this year? 

1. None of us realize how powerful the unmeasurable combo of video/ story is
2. I realized making compelling video is a superpower we have as an org
3. The future of B2B marketing is content that competes w/ TikTok not ebooks
4. I believe making key team members influencers leads to really low CAC
5. We’re not in B2B sales, we’re in human-to-human (H2H) sales.

And there’s only one way to scale H2H sales...

Through really, really good video. 

Here are the 6 BIG (and not so big) bets I’m making with video: 

1. “Events that Don’t Suck” Episodic Series (Ecomm)

We spent stupid amounts of $$ on big trade shows last year, then realized that small-to-medium-sized events (where we control the list) were the only for-sure wins for us. We did a 100 person wellness-event in LA that had a 10X ROI. So we're doubling down and creating a media brand following Kyle Standaert as he builds out this motion.

2. “Art of Excellence” Episodic Series (Ecomm)

We are creating a mini-series where we tell the incredible stories of our most successful customers. Nothing to do with our product whatsoever, just their stories, aligning their excellence with our brand. 

3. B2B Work-In-Public (B2B)

I’m recording and publicizing our weekly team meetings along with my meeting notes so that you can watch our company grow from $1.2k MRR (and 3 paying customers) to wherever we get by the end of the year. You will be able to look back on the entire year week by week to see where we were at, key metrics what we were trying, what worked, what didn’t. All hosted in our video-based B2B community.

4. Ask-Me-Anything with Adam and Santosh (B2B)

This is another community feature. You get access to myself and Santosh to discuss why we’re doing what we’re doing, and how that applies to your startup, go-to-market, or product.

5. Monthly LinkedIn Teardowns (B2B)

This is reserved for our Elite community members. We will let you in on our monthly LinkedIn strategy sessions, then you can submit posts for us to critique and we will show you how to master LinkedIn.

6. More talking head videos on LinkedIn (B2B)

Interestingly, when I post an episode of our reality TV show, I’ll be lucky if it gets watched for 6k minutes, despite the huge effort and high production value. If I post a talking head of me riffing about VC vs. Bootstrap in my office, it gets watched for 40k min.

TAKEAWAY:

 I am investing what some consider to be WAY too much in video. 

There is no way we will be able to measure what came from it.

Why is this my bet for 2024?

Because I believe there are two moats left in SaaS: 

1. Brand
2. Community

Great video does both of these things. 

Better than *literally* anything else.

I bootstrapped my startup to $12M ARR with only 6 people. Now I’m launching a brand new product called RB2B and plan to get it to $6M ARR by the end of 2024 with no more than 5 people. 

Here's my 6-step playbook for launching 7-figure products with tiny teams:

Step 1: Test a valuable, differentiated product

- We are testing an individual-level website identity product for B2B
- All of the other products in the space are IP > company name
- We will deliver LinkedIn URL and business email to a Slack channel, for free
- We have our early UX and building out integrations

Step 2: Create an inbound sales engine

- We will use two main channels: cold email and founder brand
- We are validating demand before we even start building the actual product
- Taylor is crushing it with our Inbound-Led Outbound Playbook
- Founder Brand is LinkedIn content (text posts and add a video element)
- I amplify everything by “working in public” and sharing financials as we go

Step 3: Develop the product

- With feedback from early users, we are developing the right feature set
- We’ll build as light of a version as possible as quickly as we can
- Tate, our CTO, is the master at this lightning-speed building
- Build/improve sales channels BEFORE the product is done

Step 4: Create a viral (and free) core offer

- I believe that word-of-mouth is the most important thing in a startup
- We’re trying to make our core offer so absurd that people HAVE to talk about it
- We’re going to attempt to nail down distribution before monetization this time
- I am obsessed with watching the rise of Mailchimp from the sidelines in my former life

Step 5: Automate 97% of customer support

- Onboarding is simple - it will be mostly self-serve
- With our current company, we got to $12m ARR with just Clint (rockstar)
- With RB2B, we hired Robb and Pete to automate it 
- So far we’ve been able to handle 93% of CS request with chatbots and support docs

Step 6: Make everything go faster with a few marketing campaigns.

- We’ll team up with sales, marketing, and SaaS influencers and drum up a buzz
- I’ll want to go on a podcast tour, and give keynotes where I can
- It will be interesting to see if there is a strong affiliate/reseller channel for this product

From here, we just keep trying to find ways to go even faster.

I think we can get to $6M ARR by the end of 2024.

That is 1,010 people paying us $495/month.

My first SaaS had 5,000 customers in 36 months.

We onboarded 1,500 customers over the last 12mo at a much higher price to a much more price-sensitive DTC Shopify store audience at Retention.com.

I’m feeling really good about the playbook.

Remember:

You don't need a BIG team to make BIG money.

Stay lean and thrive.

P.S.

Want the LinkedIn profiles of your anonymous website visitors sent to Slack in real-time? It's 100% free (seriously). We got 3,000 users the first month. Sign up here: https://www.rb2b.com/

Proud of: 

- Increased growth AND profitability. Incredible financial positioning for 2024.
- We pulled off our first successful medium-sized event in LA.
- We got over 50+ leads for the B2B product from a single LinkedIn post!
- We think we’ll have a B2B product by late next week. WHAT?!?!?!
- We started the process to onboard and support platforms beyond Shopify
- We added Abandoned Checkout flows to our product suite
- We released features to accelerate our SOC2 compliance process
- We built processes around supporting complex customer tech stacks
- Sharon is back from maternity leave and taking over leadership of CS
- Making progress to between CS and sales to very clearly define ICP, which is the single most important factor to reduce churn

Not So Proud of: 

- We’re struggling to get on the same page & operationalize it (i.e. OKRs)
- We don’t really have the ability to predict what’s going to happen in the future - I wouldn’t have said we were going to hit 4% this month … I wonder if anyone does these days.
- It was brought to my attention during a meeting with a recent hire that our Glassdoor presence is absolutely terrible (1.5 stars) because of the layoff we did when our VP sales resigned and the fact that we had 6 employees until Oct of last year. Not sure what to do about it.

Biggest Opportunities: 

- The B2B product. I can’t wait to get this thing off the ground and grow it. 
- The interest from Linkedin has been so crazy that Warmly (a competitor) has been cold emailing people who engaged with our posts...  and we don’t even have a product yet!!!
- We are creating a series of features for mid-market omnichannel retailers using CDPs that will expand our TAM and (hopefully) lead to larger, lower churn deals for us.
- Continuing to hone in on our ICP, not selling to people we know will not be successful (therefore lowering churn)

And the biggest opportunity...

50% growth rate and 50% run-rate EBITDA margin by the end of 2024. 

Anybody think that’s possible?

It seems crazy to say it. 

I’d settle for 25% and 25%.

But when I look at our current growth rate, the state of our Ecommerce business, and the response to these LinkedIn posts… 

I think we might just be able to do it. 

And that would be a MONSTER 2024 for Retention.com.

The good news is that you’ll be able to follow it all, the W’s and L’s, the misery and euphoria, right here on LinkedIn.
