We scaled to our SaaS to $12M ARR in 2 years with a team of 6 highly-efficient people.

But, we ran into a big problem.

The main roadblock was that my co-founder Diana Ross was in charge of all things related to sales.

She is insanely talented and was able to close at a high % 

But she was really the only person who had any real information on how to make decisions that everything had to go through her.

Everything.

This slowed us down a ton.

The solution?

Hire more A+ players. Build systems to empower them to make decisions and move with speed. And get out of their way.

This also freed Diana up to work on other, higher-leverage tasks in the business.

The lesson? Delegate. Delegate. And delegate some more.

PS - follow me Adam Robinson for more insights as we scale Retention.com to $50M ARR.

Last week our VP of Sales resigned. 

Instead of replacing him, we made the difficult decision to scale back our sales team from 14 to 5. 

As a commitment to building in public, I'm going to tell you why:


Back in December, we decided to ramp up our sales team and “go for it”.

My vision was to have 3-4 AE’s that were flooded with demos.

But that's not how it played out...


PROBLEM #1: I got the TAM totally wrong. 

We were overselling in Dec-Mar.

And we had no visibility into our product’s performance.

We didn’t find out until months later we were hitting the wrong target.

I thought we could sell a $30k deal to a universe of 50k customers.

And because of that belief, I had the absurd goal of trying to get to $50m ARR by year-end (from $7m). 

I was way off on all of these assumptions, and it caused us to over-hire. 

This was totally my fault.


PROBLEM #2: On April 1, the music stopped.

We had just got done celebrating a $1m ARR week. 

The next week we closed virtually zero business. 

Meanwhile, we kept hiring AE’s and BDR’s, thinking it was temporary.

That adding sellers and making them "hunters" would get us to $50m ARR.

This was also wrong.


Our VP of Sales resignation was a huge blow.

It forced me to ask some tough questions:

"What type of organization am I running?"

"Why would someone so important just up and quit?"

"Is it me? Is it my exec team? Is there a long line of others waiting to quit?"

I came to the conclusion that the thing we needed to change most in our sales org was empty calendars.

Just not nearly enough demos were being set.

This wasn't why the VP sales quit, but it is, at this point, the quickest way to right the ship.

This was a real wake-up call for us. 

If your VP of Sales quits, what you're doing isn’t working. 

So, I made the case to the exec team that we should pursue our original vision. 

Build a sales team that is completely inundated with demand. 

Lean, mean, and high-velocity.

This meant we had to do the hard thing, and scale back the team from 14 to 5.  

I’m sure competitors are going to start talking about how the walls are on fire Retention.com.

They’re not. 

We're going to be an unbelievable financial position in a few months.

But startups are hard, and this is the hardest part. 

Letting go of incredible team members.

It's hard sharing this failure publicly. 

"What will this make future candidates, prospects, investors think?!?!?"

But I’m going to keep building in public. 

I’m going to share my biggest L’s, in addition to my biggest W’s. 

Sharing that video about how we hit $1m ARR in a week felt so good. 

Sharing this feels terrible. 

But, it’s the journey we're on.

Back when I worked for Lehman Brothers, I believed that the only reason why people worked was to make as much money as possible.

Since then, I’ve had a change of heart.

I’ve seen how much pride and satisfaction our team is getting from working for this company. Employee satisfaction is just as important, if not more, than making huge profits.

How do you improve it?

Simple. Here are 5 ways to 10x employee satisfaction in your company:

✅ Make sure that your mission and vision is clear so that new recruits have a full understanding of what it will be like to work for you and your company.
✅ Put your employees first. If your employees feel that they’re valued and appreciated, they will take care of your customers.
✅ Optimize for velocity and reduce friction.
✅ Goal Setting. Make huge goals and show your employees why they’re achievable.
✅ The best leaders harness positive energy and transfer it to their leadership teams so that it trickles down to their teams, the customers, and partners.

Save these for when you're building out your team.

Over the last two weeks I’ve spoken with 25+ founders, marketers and sales leaders about 6Sense and Demandbase. Why?

Because Retention.com is about to launch a new product into the ultra-competitive and noisy $500M+ intent data market. Here's what I learned (and why founders must do their own research):

To set the stage:

- We are creating a “person-level identity” product for B2B SaaS companies
- Rather than account/company level ID, which is standard today
- We are using the same core identity tech we sell to ecomm
- We are going to build the entire business in public

Here are the 6 biggest things I learned from my deep-dive:

1. People actually DO want to know the individual website visitor (rather than the company)

- 6Sense and Demandbase give you a company and geolocation, then guess
- This isn’t actually that valuable, especially when selling to enterprise

2. 6Sense is pivoting towards pushing an easier-to-use tool for sales teams, Demandbase is staying true to their original tool

3. I never heard that the ABM/advertising part of the platform was a resounding “slam dunk”

- This could have been adverse selection… 
- Maybe I just got people who wanted to vent?

4. The value of 3rd party intent data varies wildly by use case.

- Is someone reading an article that mentions Apollo.io really in market for a sales intelligence tool?

5. False positives from intent data can be a major problem for high-ACV SaaS companies.

- If you’re playing a low-volume, high-ACV game, you can burn accounts by putting them into an ABM campaign based on a website visit that didn’t happen

6. There is demand from salespeople/growth hackers at smaller companies (sub-50 employees) and marketers/rev ops at larger ones (250-750 employees).

- I also heard many times that marketing will have the budget for this, even if sales has to implement it

TAKEAWAY:

Launching a new product into a new market the RIGHT way is a ton of work.

My calendar is so full when I look at it I want to vomit. 🤮

What I thought our MVP (minimum viable product) was has changed once a week for the last two months.

Who I think our ICP is -- meaning what size company and what department we’re going to try to sell into -- has changed three times in the last two weeks.

The thing that keeps me going is this: 

1. My current business is $21M ARR after 4 years
2. It didn’t have 1/10 of what this had going for it when we started
3. Our team has learned so much building that business
4. I am so much better as an entrepreneur
5. I think this product has the potential to be so, so, so much bigger

And of course, for those who follow me...

I’m going to be building the entire thing in public.

With radical transparency, right here on LinkedIn.

Stay tuned.

P.S.

If you're a revenue leader, tell me...

If you could get the Linkedin URLs of 30% of your anonymous website visitors (and what pages they viewed), would that be valuable?

We're looking for some beta testers.

DM me if you want to try it.

Earlier this year, I was in Aspen with a friend who had been building a fintech startup for 7 years as the COO/CFO.

They sold for $275M 🤯

And she now has a cushy job where her salary is 3x what it was before…

She has a three-year deal where she's rolling equity…

And she made enough money on the sale to retire.

I was expecting to show up and have her glowing because cruising and being cash rich is what we all strive for. The crazy part?

I saw the exact opposite.

She was so bored, burned out, and in a post-liquidity even malaise that I hear about more and more. What are the lessons here?

I’m not sure I have all the answers. But it does confirm the feeling I’ve had that if I were to sell Retention.com today for $1B … I’d deeply miss the thrill of building this company.

2023 was a PAINFUL year for Retention.com. We made 3 HUGE mistakes - overselling, overspending and overhiring. And yet we ended 2023 growing ARR 59% YoY and generated $1.35m free cash in Q4 alone.

Not only that… We’re about to launch a B2B product that seems like it’s a BIGGER opportunity than the ecomm business.

Here’s what I’m proud of (and not so proud of) that happened in 2023:

Proud of: 

- We assembled a team of absolute rock stars. 
- We ended the year with >25% EBITDA margins after being break-even for the first 9 months of the year
- We went from single digit employee count and zero processes to (almost) operating like a “normal” 60 person company
- We built a trusted brand in the Shopify ecosystem
- We built an amazing product and engineering team
- Our CS team became a well oiled machin
- We figured out who our TRUE ideal customer profile is
- I grew my Linkedin following from 10k to 60k and built an amazing community
- We are in beta with a B2B person-level ID product that I've been using since  November and now think is mind-blowing

Not so proud of: 

- I was delusional about our growth prospects. I thought we were going to hit $50m ARR in January (look at the slope of the line in Jan/Feb), but I was wrong by over ½. 
- We were overselling and didn’t realize it for the first 5 months of the year
- Our VP sales quit, which led us to downsize our sales org. It was the correct decision, but terrible
- We had 10 “key hires” (VP and director level) start on Feb 1, only 4 remain. BUT, our employee attrition was only 2.1% in total in Q4, so we have ended in a place of stability.
- I created a horrible spending culture that put us in a very uncomfortable cash situation. We're now acting like bootstrappers again, which I love
- We onboarded a BUNCH of customers earl in the year who we now realize weren’t going to have success, which led to churn and brand damage

Biggest Opportunities: 

- Santosh and I are spending all of our time on our B2B product. Our enthusiasm, along with our beta testers, continues to grow
- We decided to offer the b2b person-level identity product 100% FREE with unlimited use (you read that correctly). If you need to push data elsewhere, you pay in a PLG motion
- We're going to create the most immersive build-in-public that has ever been created, documenting the launch of the B2B product, warts and all.
- We will improve our DTC product to serve mid-market use cases, which will hopefully raise ACV & lower churn

There's much more, but that's all I could fit in a single post!

Bottom line:

Startups are hard. 

Building in public is harder. 

2023 felt like it was both the worst and best year of my career.

I’m so grateful for my team and to be in this situation...

A rock-solid, profitable, scaling core business, and a totally new, unknown project where we’re playing for global domination. 

What could possibly go wrong??? 

Hah!

Stay tuned. 

I’ll be reporting it all, the W’s and the L’s, right here on LinkedIn.

After a VERY hard Q2, things are feeling better at Retention.com. We grew ~9% this quarter (slower than I would have liked) and had big operational wins that are setting us up for a strong 2024. Here’s what I’m proud of (and not so proud of) that happened in Q3:

Proud of:

- We crossed the $20m ARR marker and we’re back to profitability (thank God)
- Santosh joined us full time on Sep 1. Big win!
- We identified a major problem in Q2 (overselling) that was leading to terrible downstream consequences (60-day contraction/opt-out, bad customer experience, etc). We fully reversed this problem through underselling, managing expectations, and creating alignment on what success looks like. 
- We made incredible progress on our B2B product. We should start charging our first customers in the next few weeks. Our resolution rate is fantastic (~40% of US visitors to a LinkedIn URL). If you want to know more, DM me! 📪
- We slightly increased our growth rate while downsizing our sales force
- We made a major tech improvement to one of our core products, Reclaim, that boosted performance by 15%, cut sends by 65%, and made the product 100% first-party opt-in.
- Our product and engineering teams are functioning extremely well, led by Anne Vickman and Michael Cottenden.
- We onboarded 4 engineers who are already making meaningful contributions to our product, added a product marketer and senior product designer, redesigned and launched our customer-facing dashboard, completed integrations with Attentive, Yotpo SMS Bump, and Listrak, and pushed around 60 other product improvements. GO TEAM!   

Not so proud of:

- We still don’t know some key business stats, but we have done our first round of tagging of active accounts for our analytics dashboard, so it’s not far away.
- An operational issue caused us to miss around *274 demos* over the last few months of people that were qualified when they filled out the form, and we routed them incorrectly. This is bad for our revenue and for the brand.
- We gave up on the $50m ARR by the end-of-year target that I was yelling about and held onto for WAY too long. It led to a lot of bad decisions and wasted money. We should end the year at $22-23m ARR, generating $500k/mo free cash, growing around 60% YoY. I’m not complaining, just not proud of that whole exercise.

Biggest Opportunities:

- I’m so excited about launching our B2B product I can barely sleep 
- We’re launching a free Shopify app that’s a “lite” version of our core product
- I think we can do some pretty amazing DemandGen for the B2B product using LinkedIn. My B2B posts have been doing well, Santosh opened up with a big one, Diana starts this week (go follow her)
- We’re re-working our entire outbound strategy for the DTC side
- We know exactly what we need to do for the next 12-18 months

Q2 was brutal. We bottomed out in Q3. 

I can’t wait for what’s to come in Q4 and 2024.

Scaling a startup isn’t easy. 

Doing it in public makes it even harder.

Today’s podcast episode is a WILD ‘rags to riches’ story.

This might be one of the most insane “American Dream” success stories I’ve ever heard. Don’t say I didn’t warn you!

Moises Sanchez’s path to success certainly wasn’t easy. After leaving Mexico with a 6th-grade education, his family moved to the US (illegally) with no money and not a word of English.

He became a guerrilla marketing phenom in real estate by the age of 18 and eventually worked his way to a successful multi-million dollar roofing business that brought in $50M last year.

But there’s so much more to his story than that. While in the US, enjoying tremendous success in real estate — he started going down the wrong path.

With outstanding warrants in the US, his parents forced him to leave the US and move back to Mexico.

This is where it starts to get crazy. Moises moved back to Mexico with $350K, met his wife and bought a pig farm. Life was great until he eventually woke up to gunfire from Narcos in Mexico.

After nearly losing his life, he left Mexico to return to the US, but was arrested by the FBI and ended up in jail. Moises did his time, got released, and started a new life with a roofing business. 

And the rest, as they say, is history.

Today’s episode is a powerful story of inspiration, how true success is often found by overcoming many impossible obstacles, and how the American dream is possible if you hustle and never give up.

If Moises can do it, then nobody has an excuse.

Last week I spoke privately with a BDR working at a $6B unicorn startup and what he told me about life as a seller was shocking. Here's how our conversation went:

BDR: By Friday every week I feel like my soul has been destroyed.

Me: Why? 

BDR: The repetition is completely unbearable. 

Me: Geez. What do you mean? What did you actually do today? 

BDR: I looked at the report of my accounts in Salesforce. Found the ones who have opened my emails (I have 60 of them) and sent them Amazon gift cards because it’s Prime Day. 

Me: Why on earth would you have US-based reps doing that? How the other BDRs feel?

BDR: Let me hit a couple on Slack. 

(a few minutes pass… )

BDR: Okay - I got 3 responses:

“it feels like there's so much pressure on us that trickles down from the top because if we’re not successful everybody suffers.” 

 “the constant changes make it feel like you're behind, no matter what type of preparation you do.” 

 “We don’t get recognized as much for all the work we do. It’s a constant struggle mentally, physically, emotionally … I sometimes can’t keep up.”

Me: That's rough. What’s your guys ACV? 

BDR: $25k and $50k annual plans. 

Me: So your managers are telling you to book 3 demos per week, and you’re booking one. 

BDR: Yep. Me and basically the whole team. Over half of us, at least.

Me: And every week they ask you what you are going to do to hit your target next week… to which you respond…

BDR: MORE ACTIVITY!!! 

Me: Right. 

BDR: The worst part is that they are threatening to take away our personalized flows in SalesLoft. If they do, I’m quitting. They just want more, more, more. And it's not working. 

TAKEAWAY:

We're witnessing a mega-trend. 

It’s been happening for a while, but 2023 accelerated it.

It's no longer possible to ignore.  

BDRs teams are failing.

Why?

Because:

- Your buyers don’t want to talk to salespeople
- Inboxes are ruined, so personalization doesn’t work, which...
- Leads to EVEN MORE SPAMMING using the same busted playbook

Look, you need outbound sales.

I get comments all the time saying I'm "anti-outbound".

Wrong. I've built two startups on the back of outbound.

But we need to do it smarter now.

Using fewer people, using signals and automation and data to cast a massive net that your buyers will swim into when they’re ready.

It’s 2023. 

Telling BDRs they just need "More activity" isn't going to cut it.

60 days ago, we bought 6Sense and Clearbit’s company-level Visitor ID to compare them to each other AND our new Person-Level Visitor ID. The results were SHOCKING. Here's what it means for YOUR ABM strategy:

First, what was so shocking?

The overlap of common identities between the three products was VIRTUALLY ZERO.

Here's what that means for your ABM strategy:

1. One company-level provider either isn’t enough, or is too much. 

If you CAN make the company-level signal work, then buy them both. If you CAN’T, stop spending money on it in the first place, and use our free person-level solution.

2. Person-Level Identity is far more useful. 

We’ve been able to connect to the people we identify in our ICP on LinkedIn, email them within minutes, send a LI message 24 hours later, and send a follow up email and book a TON of demos. 

You simply can’t do that with a company-level signal.

3. Everybody’s ID process is totally different. 

6Sense and Clearbit are both using a reverse-IP lookup method, whereas we are using a publisher network to ID the individual. 

I’m shocked that the seemingly same method - reverse IP lookup - produced such different results for 6Sense and Clearbit. 

4. You have to use 6Sense and Clearbit for visitors outside the US. 

Unfortunately due to compliance reasons, we can’t ID people who are outside the US. 

GDPR doesn’t apply to our tech because it’s US only (there is no European jurisdiction over tech that is deployed in the US), but still, you need the other tech for your overseas ABM.

5. The free option makes sense no matter what.

You can either get the company-level ID going, or you can’t, and if you can, it comes down to what you’re paying 6Sense (a lot) and Clearbit (less, but still a bunch) to keep sending you leads. 

Our person-level ID product pushes Linkedin profiles to slack 100% free… You have to at least try it no matter what you are doing with the other two. 

TAKEAWAY

ABM vendors have been black boxes for over a decade.

My goal is to demystify the space by being as transparent as possible. 

Want us to help you close the loop on your ABM? 

Sign up for R!B2B if you want us to:

1. Identify the anonymous visitors on your website, and 
2. Send their Linkedin profiles to Slack, in real time. 

It’s 100% free. Not kidding.

Get it here: https://www.rb2b.com/

‘Slow and steady’ business growth is a bit overrated.

Instead, I prefer to look at one metric (the most important business metric out there in my opinion):

VELOCITY.

Let me explain a bit more…

✅ Grow with velocity.

In 13 weeks, we grew RB2B from $0-$806k ARR with 4 people and zero funding. But we have a *broken* PLG model with a 1.3% conversion rate. Next month, we’re rolling out a two-touch sales motion that may (or may not) work.

Here’s a breakdown of the “Old Way (PLG)” vs “New Way (Sales-Assisted PLG)” GTM: 

OLD WAY (broken PLG) - March 1 - June 30 2024:

Model: 

- Free/unlimited push to Slack
- People will pay for integrations 
- Pricing is $495/mo no matter who you are
- I will wake up every day to hundreds of $495 upgrade button clicks

Problems:

- Too much value in FREE, not enough in PAID
- $495 too expensive for little guys 
- Not enough features (yet) for big guys (need ICP filtering & Hubspot)
- You can parse the Slack block with Zapier and send the leads anywhere

NEW WAY (Sales-Assisted PLG) - July 1 2024 - ???

- 90% of users will always be free, but cap free plan at 200-250 LI profiles/mo
- Tiered pricing starting at $99/mo, volume-based up to $750/mo
- Enterprise deals for $100m SaaS and above, super high traffic
- Of the 10% we try to charge, find out if they have a sales org when they join
- If they know how to book demos already, get them on phone
- If they can’t book demos, put them in the “toy funnel” (don’t try to convert) 
- For high value, set up ICP filter, have their best rep do 1-to-1 outreach
- Find out what a demo is worth during the initial setup call
- Our rep stays on top of customers’ rep until demo is booked
- When demo is booked, close monthly, make a compelling annual offer

Problems: 

- Don’t know yet, but there will be many I am sure!

TAKEAWAY:

I’ve never done a PLG, but I HAVE created a high-velocity inbound sales model. 

It was called GetEmails (now Retention.com), and I grew it to $12m ARR in 2.5 years with 6 people. 

I have a very strong feeling that with how RB2B is going that it will be bigger, faster. 

But here's my biggest challenge...

I’m not a salesperson, so I have no idea if this PITCH DECK I made is any good.

LinkedIn community - any feedback on the sales deck?

Rip it apart!

I need your feedback :)

Sales KILLED sales. Don't take my word for it. That's what Kevin "KD" Dorsey told me the other week. The way we do outbound makes it 10x harder on all of us to do outbound. Here are real #'s KD saw on the frontlines: 

Connect Rates: 

2020: 12-17%
2023: 3-4% 

Open Rates: 

2020: 50-60%
2023: 25-30% 

Response Rates to a sequence (emails 1-4):

2020: 10% -> 8% -> 6% -> 4%
2023: 5% -> 4% -> 3% -> 1% 

I'm sure you're thinking:

"Adam, of course outbound is harder now. There is SO MUCH more of it."

True, but...

The more we do the worse we also seem to get at it!

That's not how it should work.

Personalized emails objectively perform better.

Yet 93% of emails sent today are automated.

Why?

Because companies are addicted to speed and scale. 

They've forgotten what “good” looks like.

Here's how we fight back:

We have to create messaging that is so good that it survives in a low engagement environment.

What does that mean?

We need to start building our outbound machines based on inbound signals. 

Here's a few suggestions from KD:

1. Huddle with marketing.

- What are our highest performing headlines? >> make subject lines of emails
- What are our best performing content pieces? >> lead with value
- What are our best short/long tail keywords?  >> speak to problems 

2. Start with email

- Start with your highest ACV/lowest churn/stickiest buyer persona
- Create persona and industry-specific messaging
- Make the messaging problem-based
- Drive inbound w/ outbound activity

3. Stack calls on top of email engagement.

- Every vertical has a different pickup rate w/ calls.
- Use what you learned in email to formulate the call scripts.
- If your email inboxed, the iPhone MIGHT add your name to callerID (big win)

4. Iterate

- Forever
- Never stop
- Keep testing

TAKEAWAY:

If you’re selling on the frontlines (or running a team of sellers), you know outbound is harder than it used to be.

That doesn’t mean it’s not the SINGLE BEST WAY to scale your startup.

But the engagement rates from 2015-2021 aren't coming back.

We must fight back against endless sequences and mindless automation.

We have to create better, personalized messaging.

We have build a better, more efficient, signal-based machine.

It’s time to sell better.

P.S.

2024 is fast approaching. 

How are you going to do outbound better next year?

Share your thoughts in the comments 👇

Let's learn together.

A few weeks ago I had a viral post about 6sense and Demandbase.

Awesome, right?

But then the next day I was forwarded some *surprising* emails.

Friends were getting cold emails from a competitor using a screenshot of my LinkedIn post and Retention.com as the subject line.

At first, honestly, I was annoyed…

"This is MY audience!"

"This is MY content!"

"This is MY face!"

Of course, I was wrong.

As more people forwarded me the email, I felt validated and encouraged:

- This is positioning us as the market leader (even though our product isn't out)
- If I email these same folks, the odds are the response rate will be 10x higher
- It’s elevating my status as a thought leader in the space

Finally, I had a moment of clarity.

This is EXACTLY what I've been saying BDR teams should be doing!

This is the “new way” of doing outbound.

This is signal-based selling.

This is inbound-led outbound.

This is the playbook.

My takeaway:

There are downsides to building an audience in advance of launching a product.

But the trust you build and community you foster far outweighs any negative.

And I have to give them credit...

It was a clever and well written cold email.

A solid play to add to the the inbound-led outbound playbook.

👏👏👏

In 2023, we spent $750,000 on 3 large trade shows trying to generate leads. Here's the harsh truth I learned about trade shows at that rate of spend (and how it's driving our entire event playbook for 2024):

The truth is... 

I wish we hadn’t spent $1 on trade shows!

The ROI was minimal and the time-suck was huge. 

Why? 

Because trade shows (at least for us) don't work. 

There are TOO MANY people and the environment is awful:

- Bad coffee
- Loud music
- Bright lights
- Crappy food
- Air conditioning
- People droning on onstage
- Overloaded with pushy vendors

It’s such a nightmare that some brands walk around with their badges turned around so they don’t get attacked by vendors.

What we learned from this is simple:

We do FAR better on small to medium-sized events (where WE control the list).

That's the GTM event playbook our team has been perfecting this year:

Our journey started with a few small dinners with other vendors where we both brought customers and prospects, and split the bill. 

It then progressed to an “NYC Pizza Tour” where we got prospects and customers together and took them around to all of the best pizza spots in NYC.

Then we decided that we wanted to try something BIGGER.

An event that fixed all of the problems we have with traditional trade shows. 

Trade shows wear you down.

You come home exhausted and hungover (physically and emotionally).

What we wanted to do is create an event that did the EXACT opposite. 

So last month the Retention.com team rented a mansion in the Hollywood Hills, packed the rooms with different wellness experiences (breath work, cold plunge, iv and b12 injections, yoga, sound healing) and a steady flow of fireside chats from known DTC operators.

It was an invite-only experience. 

Big enough to not feel cramped, small enough where you could speak to everybody.

And as a bonus, we hosted a sushi dinner and a crazy DJ party.

It was an incredible success (see video below).

Here are the results:

- 200+ founders & brands in attendance (35 from our Top Accounts List)
- $2.2B in combined annual revenue in attendance
- 64 Agency Partners & Sponsors
- 20+ Investors & Influencers
- 15.8% Engagement Rate (300%+ increase)

We’re betting BIG on these type of events in 2024.

This is exactly what our GTM event playbook will look like.

Not just for DTC, but for B2B too.

Why?

Because true connection & community is formed outside the convention center.

In 2023, if you followed the classic B2B sales playbook (like I did), it either broke you or left you licking your wounds. That's why the next B2B tech unicorns will be built like DTC companies. Here's a $50M example:

Enter: Ryan Babenzien and his company Jolie.

In 18 months, he bootstrapped his DTC beauty brand from $0-$50M.

And with a team of only 3 people!

His main product?

A shower head.

Here's his playbook and how I think B2B companies will steal it:

1. The Jolie Water Report

DTC Play:

While Ryan was building the product, he created a lead magnet called The Jolie Water Report, which allowed users to see what chemicals were in their local water supply. It made the market problem aware (i.e. "oh sh*t our water is full of toxins!") and generated THOUSANDS of leads.

B2B Equivalent:

Build a massive, thirsty audience, pre-launch. I’m doing it by writing on LinkedIn about the problem we're going to solve MONTHS before the product comes to market.

2. The Massive UGC Machine

DTC Play:

In 2023, Jolie generated 10k pieces of UGC, which was one of the secrets of their explosive growth. They hand-picked medium-sized influencers, sent them a shower head, and said if they liked it, review it. 

B2B Equivalent: 

I’m currently trying to accomplish something similar, using a combination of influencer outreach and incentives in our PLG motion. This is a TOP priority of mine, because I believe the world is set up in a way to absorb this UGC, much better than any other type of marketing you could do.

3. Non-Traditional Advertising

DTC Play:

Ryan does things like wrap trucks with things like “your water is dirtier than this truck”, and puts stickers on the subway that say “your shower water is dirtier than the handle you are about to touch”.

B2B Equivalent:

I’m trying to advertise our company in a way that no one else is, mainly using video. We’re creating two episodic shows this year, along with three other video content lines, including me publishing weekly team calls as we grow our startup from 3 customers and $1,250 MRR to ??? at year-end.

4. Tiny, highly-capable Internal Team

DTC Play:

This is my favorite. This team outperformed every other DTC brand with three people and zero funding. 

B2B Equivalent:

My goal is to keep our core team to five, using “consultants” from our DTC operation to execute on things that are not full-time roles. A key requirement is to make support 100% handled by chatbots. Not just a first line of defense. 

TAKEAWAY:

For the future of B2B go-to-market, look to the top-performing DTC companies. 

The $1B enterprises of tomorrow will have lightweight, fast GTM motions with tiny, highly-efficient teams.

In 2024, the idea that more salespeople equals more revenue is dead.

We can no longer afford to run that outdated playbook.

It's time to get creative.

2 years ago, GetEmails was stuck at $8M ARR and I was burnt out.

But now, we’re at $20M, on the path to $50M ARR.

Here’s *exactly* what I did to turn things around:

First, I hired Santosh Sharan.

He came on after having built multiple HUGE data companies.

He was the catalyst.

Within 2 months, we were selling all annual deals at high velocity.

Here's a few of the changes we made:

- We rebranded to Retention.com (this was BIG)
- We built out an influencer/affiliate channel
- We build out an agency partnership team
- We built a more robust product suite
- We built out an events channel
- We built out a BDR function
- We only did demos for ICP

Need I go on?

“What got you here, won’t get you there.”

That's one of my favorite quotes.

$50M ARR is solid goal, but...

In order to hit it, we need to have our sights on $250M.

Here are 3 tangible lessons for startup founders from our journey so far:


Lesson 1: What got you here, won’t get you there

I mentioned that already, but it's worth repeating

Newer entrepreneurs don’t believe this. 

They think that this only applies to *some* companies.

I am telling you: it applies to everyone.

Certain channels will only work up to a certain threshold.

Same with talent. Same with products.

You need to keep iterating if you want to grow.


Lesson 2: Think WAY ahead.

I’m talking years down the line.

Not just about how to solve problems that’ll arise a week or a month from now.

You ever wonder why people describe entrepreneurs as having “great vision”?

It doesn’t mean that they’re visionaries, even though some are.

It means they can literally see into the future.

To see what’ll work and what’ll be relevant.

Do your best to think about what you need to do way down the line.

Prepare past the next two quarters.


Lesson 3:  Stack S-curves.

An S curve is exactly what it looks like.

You bang your head against the wall for months and months, and then you hit a curve. You grow like crazy for a few months, and then you stagnate.

Newer entrepreneurs think that when this crazy growth happens, it’ll keep going forever.

And then it throws you into a depressive episode when you stagnate.

Guys like Santosh have seen this time and time again, and he knows that every growth spike is temporary.

You need to be working on your NEXT S-curve while you’re in the growth phase of your current S-curve so that the stagnation is temporary.

Stacking S-curves means you’re having a crazy growth event more frequently than if you just had one.

By the time the first S-curve flattens out, the next S-curve will be doing its thing and keeping you growing.

That makes a hockey stick.

Vertical growth.

For us to achieve this, there are 2 options:

We can either add more features for the same users…

Or keep the same features for new users and a different audience. 

This usually means going up-market.

P.S.

We're quietly rolling out a product for B2B sales team. 

If you want to try the beta, DM me.

In 2023, I had to spend $100,000 on speaking engagements to get in front of my target market. In 2024, I’ll spend $0 to speak in front of 10x as many people. Here's what changed:

I achieved what I call “influencer/market fit”. 

BACKSTORY:

In September of 2022, with $12m ARR and 6 FTE, we decided to hone in on our ICP of large Shopify stores.

At the time, we believed we had single digit penetration into the Shopify Plus ecosystem, and a product that crushed for all of them. 

I viewed this as an awareness problem. 

A friend recommended I read "Founder Brand" by Dave Gerhardt.

I loved what he said, but since I’d never posted on social, I was scared to start with ZERO idea of how the game was played. 

I was stuck. 

Shortly thereafter I met Tommy Clark.

He thought I should start posting and that LinkedIn was the place to start.

Most importantly, he said he could write for me.

So began my journey as a CEO making content.

This was October 2022.

We got some pretty early traction. 

I wanted to use video and ended up putting out one per day for 8 months.

People were starting to recognize me at trade shows…

Saying that they watched all of my videos every day.

This was very cool, but there was a fundamental problem:

I didn’t have much to say to ecommerce operators!

I wasn’t one of them.

I didn’t know what to talk about other than my own business, and when aimed at ecom founders, it resulted in “meh” engagement.

—

In mid-August, we started beta testing a B2B SaaS tool that identified website visitors at the PERSON-level, which was novel, as vendors like 6Sense, Clearbit, and Demandbase weren’t doing it.

Around Labor Day, with encouragement from Alec Paul, I decided to start writing entirely to B2B SaaS revenue leaders instead of ecomm founders. 

But there was a catch...

I had to write myself.

What happened next? 

I dropped 4x posts in a row that had 50x the engagement from the prior six months.

The rest is history...

Why was it such a dramatic change?

Because I was speaking to an audience I was a part of:

- My perspective became more relevant and valuable
- The pain I was articulating was IDENTICAL to the pain they were experiencing
- As a $22m bootstrapped SaaS founder, I had a level of success other SaaS founders hoped to achieve

Last but not least, SaaS founders and revenue leaders LIVE on LinkedIn, unlike the ecomm ecosystem (who live on X/Twitter)

All of the above is why I believe that “influencer/market fit” is a massive moat. 

My content works because of who I am and where I’m coming from.

I know because it DIDN’T work nearly as well when I was writing to ecomm.

This is why I’m now getting invited to speak at conferences that I would have had to pay BIG $$$ for before.

I'll be keynoting the next @SaaSOpen in NYC Sept 5th. 

See you there: https://lnkd.in/gTA45pXh

I ran several businesses before starting Retention.com.

There are a few areas you absolutely need to nail when starting a business.

1) Great product
2) Understanding your customer
3) Repeatable sales process

Everyone knows this.

But they're much more complicated than people think.

While building my first few businesses, I was sharpening my skills.

Knowing your customer takes a lot of nuanced knowledge.

It sounds simple, but it takes years to master the in's and out's of your target audience

New founders always look for the hacks and shortcuts.

But experienced founders know that they have to just start with an educated guess, and then whittle down to the 'right' answer.

It takes months, if not years, to nail down your product. Let alone selling it.

How can you repeat what I've done?

By starting with your best guess, and then adjusting after you learn what your customers want.

My greatest successes took thousands of iterations before I nailed it.

Your first guess will be wrong.

But your 1,000th educated guess might be genius.

I just got off the phone with the CEO of a $125 million DTC appliance brand. His CAC is up by 32% since iOS14, and it’s up another 15% since mid-April. He’s spending $3M/mo on ads and wants to 5x his adspend, but he can’t do it at these CPA’s. 

“Do you know what happened on April 23?” I asked him.

“No… what happened?” 

“On April 23, Apple made it so that Meta and Klaviyo can’t track a user longer than 7 days."

His jaw dropped.

He couldn't believe it.
 
–

BACKGROUND:

In layman terms, here's what happened on April 23rd:

There is a set of pipes that connects your Shopify site to Meta and Klaviyo. 
 
Those pipes used to last for many months. 

Now, Apple breaks those pipes after 7 DAYS. 

Meaning, historically if a visitor clicked on a Meta ad, browsed around, and came back to the site a month later, Meta could serve them a retargeting ad. 

That worked beautifully, and the ability to track that returning visitor’s behavior was a big part of the magic behind Meta's infamous targeting machine.

Now, if someone clicks on a Meta ad and comes back just 8 days later, Meta doesn’t know who they are, and can’t show them an ad.

–

Back to the executive...

“That sucks!" he said, "What am I supposed to do about it?"

I let him know that he doesn’t have to sit there and keep taking licks.

Retention.com has a secret project in the works that solves this.

It’s literally magic. 

We figured out how to extend the tracking time in Klayvio and Meta from 7 days to 180 days. 

And that, so far, we're seeing CPA’s drop by 20-30% over several weeks. 

Want to know how it works?

Like this post and comment APRIL 23 below and I'll send you the details.

The Great SaaS Pipeline Crisis of 2023-2024 (explained in 60 seconds):

- Cold outreach is a fraction as effective as it was last year
- 10/8/6/4/2% response rates are now 5/4/3/2/1%
- Sales leaders are responding with higher activity targets
- AI copywriting and sending tools are increasing volume even further
- Cheap domains and tools like instantly make more volume even easier
- Higher volume drowns out any attempt at great personalization
- LinkedIn inboxes are even worse (mine is like nothing I have ever seen before)
- Fed at 5%+ interest rates has every company (and person) spending less $
- Follow-on rounds are questionable at best
- “Buy less SaaS” is the world-wide directive

TAKEAWAY:

The Predictable Revenue model (born in 2012) died in 2023. 

Anything your reps did to create pipeline 24mos ago produces 50% the result.

Luckily, certain pipeline-generating tactics are working better than ever. 

There’s a NEW MODEL centered around C-level executives creating content that cuts through, which builds trust over months (if not years) directly with the market. 

Signal-based selling allows you to nudge prospects down the funnel, capturing them when they’re ready to buy. 

You close MORE ARR and grow FASTER, because your reps are senior, can handle more, been around a long time, and make fewer mistakes.

Plus, sales cycles are 2/3 shorter because your reps aren’t spending any time with people who aren’t ready to buy.

Your company culture improves dramatically because hyper-efficient companies are fun to work in, and you don’t have a single person who isn’t crushing it. 

It’s a Push Model vs. a Pull Model. 

One side of that equation ISN’T feeling the Pipeline Crisis.

In 2024, pull wins.

1. Somehow retool your product/brand so that you can serve a broad, untargeted ad that converts. (HARD)

2. Hit retail harder and faster than you ever would have before. (ALSO HARD)

3. Use a combination of all of the best identity technology available to run your own private customer graph to maximize signal to the ad platforms. (SURPRISINGLY EASY)

Number 3 seems like the no brainer.

Ad platforms need the ability to track users over time. 

So brands must be feeding events back into them with identifiers attached. 

Meta’s equation for determining the winner of an auction is: 

Cash Bid x Estimated Action x Ad Quality = Total Value

If you tell Meta who is looking at products and abandoning carts, that will help your Estimated Action score because Meta will know who are the most likely to convert. 

Result? 

- Same cash bid 
- Higher total value
- More auctions won with the same cash
- Lower CAC
- Higher growth with the same capital

Don’t sleep on the importance of Onsite Visitor Identity. 

It’s becoming a more important pillar in the DTC tech stack every day.

My 6 predictions about AI over the next 12-24 months: 

1. AI becomes the new leveler 

Several opportunities in AI will be capital intensive and favor large companies, however a ton of applications will need to be rebuilt and AI startups are set to mushroom in the next 24 months. We will see massive wealth transfer from large tech companies to smaller counterparts as AI becomes the new differentiator and established companies struggle to catch up. 

2. Sustained high interest rates and rise of efficient ventures:

As capital continues to stay expensive, demand for operationally efficient AI ventures will rise. Small but efficient teams will scale large companies with a handful of FTEs and plenty of contractors and agencies.

3. Corporate Venture Investments will boom: 

There will likely be far less large tech IPOs. Big enterprises will want to catch up on AI providing increased investment and liquidity opportunities to startups via strategic investments and M&A.

4. Massive Opportunity for Data and Analytics:

Several billion $ opportunities will emerge around AI Models on enterprise data to push data analytics and insights to the next level. Existing data companies are well suited to exploit this opportunity, however I expect most to miss the bus given radically different business models. 

5. New Opportunities:

Here are the themes that stand out for me:

- IT infrastructure and developer platforms that enable the rise of AI apps and small purpose built AI models

- Next generation RPA and intelligent workflow. The way we engage with every application is up for disruption. With multi-modal Gen AI we may be able to interact with applications using a combination of text, speech, gestures leading to a more organic and human experience.

- Enterprise decision making tools will further democratize access to data and analytics making decision making more aligned and automated. This will lead to large gains in efficiencies. 

- GTM will be a large recipient of “AI assisted Data Analytics” best practices. We will see use of AI to make micro recommendations to push deals across the pipeline, score outcomes and recommend strategies.

- Opportunities for System of Record companies: Any GTM vendor that is sitting on significant customer data can generate incremental revenues by passing this data through generative AI models to identify new opportunities and influence business decisions. 

6. Talent Wars:

AI tech expertise will become a scarce resource. Companies will source AI talent from across the world. Competition around AI will turn into a battle for recruiting AI talent. Recruiters specializing in AI talent will prosper. Both companies and employees will prefer 1099's over W2s.

In the long run AI will likely cause massive displacement in employment. I will write a separate post about it, however in the short run this is once in a lifetime gold rush that everybody should take advantage of if they can. 

These are exciting times to be in tech.

B2B buyers hate talking to salespeople. Gartner shows this trend getting worse every year. The solution? Companies need to invest in creating a new Buyer Enablement Playbook (here's what it could look like):

BACKGROUND:

Buyers engage with sales ONLY after 80% of buying process is over. 

By the time they talk to a rep, it is too late to influence them.

Instead, buyers are speaking with 2-3 vendors up front, and leaving the 20+ other vendors out of the process entirely.

The only way for companies to stay in the game is to influence the buying process, which is not *traditionally* the job of sales. 

Here are 5 ways this change in buyer behavior needs to cause a reset in GTM teams and Buyer Led Sales tool stacks:

1. Are GTM Teams Missing a Buyer Enablement Playbook?

At any given point, only a handful of buyers in your TAM are looking for new vendors. Through intent data and website visitor ID tools, we can identify who’s in market. However, instead of handing these over to sales - companies could set up a buyer analyst team that assists buyers identify the vendor with best fit (even if it meant directing them to competitors). The top 1% sales reps already do this.
 
2. Where are the Buyer Enablement Teams ? : 

We already have plenty of teams that help sales sell better (AEs, Sales Ops, Sales Enablement). Where are the teams that intercept the buying process to enable the buyers to "buy" better - Buyer Ops, Buyer Enablement? 

Here is a quick search for US titles :

- Sales Enablement : 10,000
- Buyer Enablement : 50

- Sales Ops : 53,000
- Buyer Ops : 800

We are missing buyer enablement teams. 

3. Which team should Buyer Enablement report into?

Buyer enablement teams could report into Product Marketing or marketing but ideally not Sales. BE teams can consist of in-house analysts available as a resource to enterprise buyers on demand. They can offer content or advisory with topics such as “industry & vendor landscape”. Think of a buyer analyst as a customer success rep but for top of the funnel and with great understanding of the industry landscape. 

4. Exec presence : VP of Buyer Enablement:

We need a VP of Buyer Enablement reporting to the C-suite to give the buyers a voice in the exec team, to ensure that some GTM resources go into enabling buyers to buy better and not just to enable sales to sell better.

5. We need more Buyer Ops Tool Stack:

As buyers continue to change the way they buy, valuations of peer review sites such as G2 or Trustradius have steadily risen. Gartner has acquired several assets in this space (Peer Insights, Capterra). We need a lot more buyer enablement tool stacks to identify and assist buyers with their research. Several new billion $ companies will emerge in this space to assist the buying process beyond just reviews. 

What do you think?

Will we see more Buyer Enablement teams in 2024? 

It's time for the sales process catch up with the buying process.

Every CEO should post on LinkedIn. In the last 28 days, I've had 3,801,489 views on my LinkedIn posts and it transformed my business. Here are the 8 biggest lessons I learned after 12 months of posting on LinkedIn:

1.  It’s a “long term game” and it’s going to start off slowly

- It’s probably not going to “click” for at least a year
- The harsh truth... you can use a ghostwriter to help get you started, but eventually you'll need to own it. It's YOUR thoughts, expertise and experience that matters. Own your brand.

2. It will open doors you didn’t know existed

- You’ll walk around trade shows and people will think they know you
- You can create a pull mechanism for investors, rather than a push
- It will raise your status in the ecosystem

3. Memes build the wrong audience

- Early on, I got really excited when I’d get 1,000s of likes from a meme
- But the engagers weren’t buyers or even potential buyers
- Our product only works for the USA and much of the audience was overseas
- Design your content strategy for impact, not likes

4. The right template can make a good post FLY

- I can’t emphasize this point enough: use templates!
- This doesn't mean copy other creators, it means don't reinvent the wheel
- Look at this post... the "hook" is full of #'s and social proof, there's an enticing cliffhanger, and then an easy-to-read list of learnings (look at my last 10 posts and you'll see the pattern)

5. Transparency and “working in public” content has killed it for me

- I share full financials quarterly, which is unheard of for a $20m ARR SaaS
- Doing something no one else is doing is the most effective way to cut through
- People LOVE to know how much money you are making (or losing)

6. Stirring it up in the comments early helps your posts

- I try to reply to every comment within 2 hours
- I then set a cadence of every 12 hours after that
- I have noticed that it boosts performance by 33% or so
- It also gives you a pulse on the market (guides you what to write next)

7. Engage with other influencers who are in your ecosystem

- I haven’t been doing this because I was focusing on Twitter, but I’m going to
- You’ll pick up audience from whoever you’re engaging with over time
- Want an audience of VP of Sales? Go find them and engage

8. If you’re not pissing anybody off, you aren’t going hard enough

- Getting told I’m an idiot and have no idea what I’m doing was hard (once)
- I got over it quickly when I realized the people saying it are just assholes
- Assholes help your posts, so be thankful they are there

TAKEAWAY:

Yes, every CEO should post on LinkedIn.

But they also need to invest the time to learn how it works.

Unless you're willing to study the platform, measure your results, and adjust...

You'll end up getting frustrated (or posting memes like I did).

And you'll never truly experience the power of LinkedIn.

Top SaaS salespeople are underpaid. The best reps should be making $3M+ a year. Here's why companies must run sales teams like a professional sports team and pay their top AEs like MVPs:

BACKGROUND:

In a recent report from Guy Rubin and Sam Jacobs , they found that in 2023 less than 20% of the reps pulled in 80% of the revenues.

Read that again:

Less than 20% of reps generate 80% of total revenues!

Whether we like it or not, we are entering the era of the Super-Rep.

And they need to be rewarded accordingly.

We love to say salespeople are the professional athletes of the business world, but we still don't pay them that way.

Why is that?

Let's look at professional sports for context:

- NBA: In 2023, Stephen Curry took home $52M as the highest paid player while the average player made $9.7M (Ratio of 5:1). 

- NFL: The highest paid QB’s took home $55M while the the average QB made $10M for 2023 (Ratio of 5.5:1).

The current ratio for tech sales talent compensation is half of that.

Why shouldn't we normalize this for B2B sales as well? 

After all, like in sports, in sales it's easy to spot the best from the average. 

Why not reward the best players disproportionately? 

If you are a coach for the Lakers, do you spend your energy turning all your players into performing at the same level as Lebron James or instead you focus on ensuring that Lebron gets the best ball in the game to ensure chances of team’s success? 

Somewhere we went wrong with the B2B sales.

Over the last decade, we've attempt to make everybody a superstar via coaching or education.

Companies strive for a salary range and aim at making everybody in the team a superstar instead of letting few make disproportionate salaries compared to the average.

I think that's wrong.

While inequality and uneven distribution of wealth and resources causes social tension, it does act as a motivator for all of us to perform better. 

For profit companies can learn from the sports team. 

By rewarding their best players disproportionately, they are also providing a motivation for their average players to improve their game and become the best version of themselves. 

Isn’t that our goal after all?

I’ve been in the world of entrepreneurship for over a decade

It has been the craziest roller coaster I’ve ever been on. Both emotionally and financially…

After this amount of time doing various projects, making money, losing money, meeting people, and learning from all of it, I’ve grown a lot.

And now, at age 43, only NOW do I feel like I’ve finally gotten to a place where I’m genuinely excited about the future.

This is all congruent with a quote attributed to Tom Clancy that I absolutely love:

“An overnight success is 10 years in the making.”

It resonates because it’s true.

It’s the reason I decided to call my podcast ’10 Years in the Making.’

We think of success as a thing that happens to us — not a thing that we do to ourselves.

We make it sound like a completely random event that appears on our doorstep at a certain point in time when we’re deemed lucky enough.

A major fault in this line of thinking is that we refer to success in “outputs” instead of “inputs”.

When I had my friend Chase Dimond on my podcast, it just solidified this idea for me

Chase is one of the top experts in eCommerce, email marketing, and DTC copywriting

He has 100K followers on Twitter, over 150K followers on LinkedIn, and he has over 50K subscribers on his personal newsletter

He owns an 8 figure digital marketing agency, working with some of the biggest names in DTC, and consults for public companies on a monthly basis

For someone with this much success, you’d be surprised to know that he’s only been “famous” in the industry for 2 years

And you’d be even more surprised to know that he was almost COMPLETELY unknown for 5 years before that

Tweeting and posting to an audience of 5, and 4 of which were related to him

An overnight success, though, right?

Chase was not successful because he had a viral moment and rode the wave for as long as he could. That’s “output” success

He was successful because he posts multiple pieces of content per day that are valuable to hundreds of thousands of people. And he never took a break. That’s “input” success.

The inputs were very calculated and measurable.

In the short term, you are guaranteeing “input” success by contributing a penny every day to the platforms you want to grow on.

In the long term, you are guaranteeing “output” success, because the rest of the formula is already complete. Good content + posting consistently + time = output success.

This is true in Chase’s case, and it’s just finally become true in my case.

I have spent the last 10 years fighting for “output” success, frustrated because I thought all of the inputs were there.

It was only when I began putting 110% of my time into Retention.com that I realized that I actually had a shot at output success.

The lesson here is that success is an equation.

And we almost always forget time.

Time allows us to compound knowledge, experience, and reach.

And it’s the only true way to become an overnight success.

🤝

rows.content:
Building in "stealth mode" is the DUMBEST thing a startup founder can do. Here are the top 6 reasons why building in stealth mode is a rookie mistake (and why I won't sign your NDA):

1. No one is going to steal your idea.

Anybody who is capable of executing your idea is already busy doing something else that they believe is more valuable than whatever you share with them. Don’t make people sign NDA’s to talk to you. It makes it clear that you don’t know what you’re doing.

2. You NEED feedback.

People farther along in their journey can often help you avoid mistakes that all entrepreneurs make (and you will make, too!). More importantly, you need to be speaking to your ideal customer profile to figure out if your product is even valuable.

3. Ideas are like assh*les. 

Everybody’s got one. Furthermore, this is hard to believe, but someone is definitely working on whatever your idea is already (if it’s even a halfway-decent idea). That’s just the world we live in.

4. Ideas are just multipliers of execution.

Jeff Bezos and Elon Musk created trillion dollar companies through being the best at execution. Many others had the ideas of online bookstores, electric cars, and rich guys have been trying to go to space (unsuccessfully) forever. A great idea makes great execution go even faster, but is worth nothing on its own.

5. Building in stealth increases the risk of your startup to a point where you will almost certainly fail.

Please read “Four Steps to the Epiphany” by Steve Blank. The ONLY shot a startup founder has is to follow the method in this book. You must be developing the customers for your product simultaneously with the product itself. If no one will buy what you are building, you must stop and start over. The sooner you find out the better. There’s no way to find that out in “stealth mode”.

6. Our intuition is a terrible indicator of market viability.

You simply have no idea what the market is going to want, with the one exception of you building something to solve your own problem. However, that is still a market of one, and you need to go out and validate that others have the same problem to even have a SHOT at succeeding. 

TAKEAWAY:

Don’t build in stealth mode. 

Go get feedback from your ideal prospects.

Talk to founders who are more experienced than you.

Build up your customer base before you start building your product. 

Read “Four Steps to the Epiphany”, and treat it as Gospel. 

But please, pretty please, above ALL ELSE…

Don’t ask me to sign an NDA to hear about your “idea”.

In 27 months, I grew my SaaS startup from $1M-$10M ARR in with only 1 salesperson doing 100% OUTBOUND SALES. Here’s my 7-step playbook for building a lean, high-velocity cold email machine:

Step 1) Make sure you have product-market fit

- My thesis for 2023 and beyond is without word-of-mouth, nothing will work
- But if you have strong word-of-mouth (from PMF), many things can help speed you up, including high-volume, low conversion outbound - which we ran

Step 2) Identify your target audience

- We used BuiltWith to ID domains who used complimentary tech
- We then ran the site traffic with SimilarWeb
- For us the winning combination was Shopify + Klaviyo above 10k/mo uniques

Step 3) Get creative about getting email addresses

- The *lazy* thing to do is pull directly from the data vendors
- We find the contacts on Linkedin, then use Skrapp and Hunter to find emails
- We would include up to 5 potentially relevant people and copy them all
- We sell to the high end of SMB (so we always include CEO as well)

Step 4) Create short email sequences

- We have used a very similar 3-part sequences for the last 3.5 years
- Email 1: Present the main idea. For us, “We can get you email addresses of your anonymous web traffic, even if they don’t fill out a form”
- Email 2: Social proof from brands they truly admire (hard in the beginning)
- Email 3: A super-simple use case email explaining the actual workflow

Step 5) Write clear and simple copy.

- Each email should be no longer than a few sentences
- Make each sentence its own paragraph 
- Have no more than one idea per email
- Keep it conversational
- CTA is a Calendly link in both the body and signature of the email

Step 6) Manually send the emails, rather than using automation tools.

- We have a team of VA’s in the Philippines manually sending from Gmail
- Any response gets routed back to a BDR/AE in the USA
- The team in the Philippines also does the lead gen, very manually
- Cold email gurus will say this is stupid and sucks, but … scoreboard!

Step 7) A/B test the sh*t out of it. 

- Change something, pick a winner
- Try to hone in on things to optimize
- You’re building a machine that improves itself

It may not work for everybody, but it worked for us.

Happy to answer questions in the comments! 👇

TL;DR

Step 1) Have Product-Market Fit
Step 2) Identify Target Audience
Step 3) Get Email Addresses
Step 4) Create Short Sequences
Step 5) Write Clear/Simple Copy
Step 6) Send Manually
Step 7) A/B Test

I bootstrapped my startup to $12M ARR with only 6 people. Now I’m launching a brand new product and plan to get it to $10M ARR by the end of 2024 with no more than 5 people. 

Here's my 7-step playbook for launching 8-figure products with tiny teams: 

Step 1: Beta test a valuable, differentiated product

- We are beta testing an individual-level website identity product for B2B
- All of the other products in the space are IP > company name
- We will deliver LinkedIn URL, email, phone, and page view history
- We are doing everything manually, delivering files daily to beta testers

Step 2: Create an inbound sales engine

- We will use two main channels: cold email and founder brand
- We are validating demand before we even start building the actual product
- Cold email is a team in the Philippines - low conversion, high volume
- Founder Brand is LinkedIn content (text posts and add a video element)
- I amplify everything by “working in public” and sharing financials as we go

Step 3: Build the product

- Once we have decided the exact feature set we want, we’ll start building
- Well build as light of a version as possible as quickly as we can
- Tate, our CTO, is the master at this lightning-speed building
- Build/improve sales channels BEFORE the product is done

Step 4: Hire one SUPER HUNGRY AE

- The idea is the sale is a 15min close, this AE does 8 demos per day
- The goal is to have this person completely flooded with activity
- This person likely needs a sales assistant to help with follow-up and admin

Step 5: Hire one onboarding/CS rep

- Onboarding is simple - it will be mostly self-serve
- With our current company, we got to 12m ARR with just Clint (rockstar)
- The job is answering questions, making sure value is understood
- Need the kind of person that literally CAN’T leave things undone

Step 6: Figure out how we’re going to create self-serve customer support documentation

- Anne is the best in the game at this, but she is now our VP product
- This is a critically important piece of this that I don’t have a solution for yet

Step 7: Make everything go faster with a few marketing campaigns. 

- We’ll team up with sales influencers and SaaS influencers and drum up a buzz
- I’ll want to go on a podcast tour, and get key people on mine
- It will be interesting to see if there is a strong affiliate channel for this product

From here, we just keep trying to find ways to go even faster. 

I think we can get to $10M ARR by the end of 2024. 

That is 1,667 people paying us $17/day (or $500/mo). 

My first SaaS had 5,000 customers in 36mo.

We onboarded 1,500 customers over the last 12mo at a much higher price to a much more price-sensitive DTC Shopify store audience at Retention.com. 

I’m feeling really good about the playbook. 

Remember:

You don't need a BIG team to make BIG money.

Stay lean and thrive.

P.S. 

As we push to $10m ARR, I'll report it all on Linkedin. The good, the bad and the ugly. Follow along for the ride.

Entrepreneurship is art.

It’s a creative pursuit.

But where does creativity come from? And where does it NOT come from?

Legendary music producer, Rick Rubin, wrote a book, titled The Creative Act: A Way of Being, which teaches readers that creativity and being an artist isn’t about your specific output, it’s about your relationship to the world.

While this isn’t a book about business, it’s the best book I’ve ever read on how I approach my craft as an entrepreneur.

In business, there are intangible factors that have a major impact on the success of your company.

For instance…

How does someone FEEL when they use your product or service?

Does your brand provide so much value that people just can’t help but talk about it?

Until I read this book, I never really knew how to communicate these unmeasurable forces in business.

These forces are very much a part of the entrepreneurial journey—which is something that my advisor, Santosh Sharan, and I, both agree on.

After reading the book, Santosh felt like we could write a book that focuses on everything Rick Rubin is saying about art, as it pertains to the world of business and entrepreneurship.

Last week the CEO of Cognism ($87M Series C) posted about how from 2018-2022 they grew their SDR team from 5 to 95 reps and hit $45M ARR.

That's insanely impressive. BUT... if I was an early-stage founder reading that post my question would be, "What's going to work the NEXT four years?" 👇

Why?

Because the Golden Age of SaaS (2007-2023) is over.

The ability of founders to raise HUGE stacks of cash and hire HUGE teams is not coming back.

That model (aka Predictable Revenue) assumed response rates that were 2x what they are now.

That model assumed you could fundraise your way to your next level of growth.

Here's the truth about SDR teams and startups today:

1. Their response rates are 1/2 of what they were 12 months ago
2. They only playbook they know is based on MORE (activity, people, etc)
3. Which will DEFINITELY make the whole picture worse over the NEXT 12mo
4. So most leaders are scratching their heads, looking for a plan that makes more sense

And here’s the reality of raising money for those same startups…

1. They will not be able to raise the funding they need to bankroll headcount
2. They can no longer invest in growth (and software), neither can most customers
3. As a result, CAC/LTV keeps inching higher every year WHILE the need to be profitable becomes even more urgent

Of course, I have huge respect for James Isilay - and leaders like him - who have been massively successful in building top-notch people machines.

People (and your ability to hire those people) are necessary to build huge companies.

Personally, my people process sucks! 

I’m sure I have a lot to learn from James on that.

But if you’re a startup doing $5M ARR, know you're not alone.

I’m talking to dozens of early stage founders who are disenchanted by the current SDR model.

Because sales is math.

And the SDR math isn’t working like it used to.

45 days ago, we launched our new startup RB2B. We have driven 4,757 signups with an ~80% install rate, but only have 13 paying customers! Here are the 3 most embarrassing pricing mistakes I've made (and how to fix it):

To set the stage: 

- We launched our Person-Level Website Visitor Identity solution on March 1
- It’s a free/unlimited push to Slack… I wanted to charge for other integrations
- What I didn’t realize is you can parse the Slack block and push for free 
- Feedback is great, signups are great, installs are great
- We’re just not getting paid!

What are the three biggest mistakes I’ve made with pricing?

1. Our pricing is broken for smaller B2B companies

- Smaller, low-traffic B2B companies aren’t paying $495 for this no matter what
- Even if they would, the jump from zero just feels like too much

2. Our pricing is broken for larger B2B companies

- At 100+ leads a day there is too much noise, we need a filter (don’t have yet)
- Larger, higher-traffic B2B also want a Hubspot/SF integration (don’t have yet)

3. There’s too much value in the free plan, not enough in paid

- We’ve observed willingness to pay drop when people see what they’re getting
- People can also just take the data out of Slack and do what they want with it
- I suspect that even when we have filters/integration people still won’t pay

How do we plan to fix the problem? 

1. Gate the free plan for the top 20% of signups

- I didn’t want to do this, but I think we have to because of the Slack parse
- After X leads/mo, we’ll serve a headshot (will be totally free for 80% of users)
- We’ll still do a 30 day full-featured unlimited trial for everyone
- We’ll have a much lower-priced entry point than $495

2. We need to build three major features THIS QUARTER

- We’re starting with Hubspot integration and ICP filtering first, SF next. 

3. We're going to try adding one hyper-productive AE for a 2-touch sales cycle

- We want to segment our high value customers during onboarding and get them on the phone to make sure they are using the tool correctly
- We’ll then reach out at the end of their trial to see if they booked any demos

4. We’re focusing on our B2B Agency motion

- We’re getting lots of traction with B2B demand and lead gen agencies
- The HubSpot agency community is excited about what we’re doing too 
- We’re extending preferential pricing to agencies that is a win/win for both side 
- DM me if you want the details!

TAKEAWAY:

I was so confident at launch that we could PLG our way to the $495 plan. 

That has happened ZERO times in 45 days and almost 5,000 signups. 

I’m realizing that:

a) Our product isn’t good enough 
b) My LinkedIn community was right about pricing (THANK YOU!)

Too much value in the free plan, not enough in paid. 

The longer I do this, the more times I re-learn the universal truth of startups.

Things never look like you think they will when you start.

But that’s okay, if that’s what you expect. 

You just have to keep building.

rows.content:
Affiliates have absolutely crushed for Retention.com in the last few months as we’ve scaled to $20M in ARR.

It’s a great way to complement your other sales and marketing tactics — and I wanted to give you an inside look at how we run our program (steal it):

I will mention that this can work for everyone…

But it works even BETTER if you have a great business that people want to brag about (as do most GTM strategies).

We have that at Retention.com

So… we can pull up a simple spreadsheet and show our potential affiliates:

→ What type of revenue we drive for a company like BlendJet
→ How they’re getting a 100X ROI

And it gives our affiliates the true conviction they need to sell this stuff with confidence

Oh, and it also helps that they get 20% of the deal when we close (we make sure our people get paid).

So here’s the 3-part checklist of why our affiliate channel is working so well:

1) Product-market fit

We know we have product-market fit because every single person who hears about our product is blown away.

It’s unlike anything I’ve ever experienced before.

Product-market fit means it’s very easy to display what type of value our customers will get when they use us.

2) Above-market commissions

Again, we make sure our people get paid. And this includes affiliates.

We pay our affiliates very generously because we know how valuable they are to our company at this point.

Early companies will pay much higher commissions, but as they grow, those have to go down because shareholders will probably tell you to.

We don’t really have that problem — we’re bootstrapped 😉

3) Have multiple tiers in your program

In the Shopify Plus community, it seems like people are very well connected.

Finding people who will be an affiliate for your product is great…

But finding people who will introduce you to other people who will affiliate for your product is even better.

The well-connected person who helps find more affiliates for you should be compensated as well.

20% to the bottom tier, 5% to the second tier.

4) Show them the money

Show them what you’re going to do for your customers, and show them how they’ll be compensated.

I absolutely love breaking down the money math for our affiliates, because they see dollar signs for themselves and for their brand-owning friends.

Nobody wants to refer business to a company that sucks.

Make it look like a no-brainer for them to send you intro emails.

5) Send gifts

We just started doing this, but it’s been huge for us.

We send AirPod Max’s to anyone who sends us a deal and didn’t expect commissions.

It doesn’t have to be a pair of $600 headphones. It can be anything, really.

Just don’t do the money tree. Or the brick. That’s played out, lol.

Making someone feel special anytime they do something good for you is a good way to build goodwill.

I hope these 5 tips make you (and me) a lot of money.

PS — For more advice, follow Adam Robinson to see how I scale Retention.com from $20M to $50M ARR.

During my career I helped price 10+ SaaS products that have generated over $3B in revenues. Recently my CEO Adam Robinson and I discussed how to price our new B2B product. Here's a breakdown of our thinking:

BACKGROUND:

We are launching a new identity-resolution product that is arguably superior to other substitutes in the market. 

The market we operate in has organized itself into two tiers: 

High and lower priced solutions. 

Here’s a pricing wisdom that I have developed over time : 

1. If you want to increase revenue incrementally, increase price 
2. If you want to increase revenue exponentially, decrease price
3. If you want to dominate your space, give it away for free and charge later

When pricing, it’s important to understand your motivation:
 
- Are you trying to capture more revenues?
- Are you trying to compete more effectively?
- Do you want to switch market segment or increase TAM?
- Do you want to comfortably win or completely dominate the space?

Once there’s clarity, it becomes easy to use pricing as a lever to navigate the business towards the desired outcome.

We are fortunate to have a profitable business that’s generating $22M+ in ARR.

This allows us to go slow on monetization. 

From our initial discussions, it was clear we needed to optimize our pricing and GTM for rapid market adoption and not short term revenues. 

Largest growth always happens at the latter end of the curve, but for that we need to have a bulk of the market already using us.

We will try and get 250K+ domains (including free signups) in the next 2 years.  

Once we decided we wanted to go freemium, it made sense to double down on self serve motion. This also gave us some direction to the kind of GTM team we want to build. We also knew backend data costs had to be fixed with zero marginal cost to support freemium pricing. 

To increase our likelihood of capturing a significant TAM, it only makes sense to decrease all friction to adoption - including pricing.  

Most of the competitors are charging on traffic volume. To change the game, we took volume out of the picture. Given we can provide this solution at no marginal cost, we will resolve unlimited traffic (fair usage) for the same price. 

We are instead charging on integrations. The lowest priced plan requires users to work with excel files. Whereas the other more expensive solutions provide additional integrations. 

We think disruption happens at the low end of an established market. So we  have a laser sharp focus at the SMB/lower MM users to drive our signup numbers.

We ended up with:

Plan 1: Perpetually Free, but no download
Plan 2: $295/mo, csv download, slack integration
Plan 3: $495/mo, Sales Integrations
Plan 4: $995/mo, Sales + Marketing Integrations 

(no annual deals, only M2M) 

Remember:

Pricing is an iterative exercise.

We will watch the impact of our initial assumptions and recalibrate.

I’ve been unfortunate enough to have to let go of some very senior people in my last decade. There’s a right way and a wrong way to do it.

In my experience, I’ve learned a lot about it. So, God forbid you have to fire a senior employee, this is how you should go about it:

1. Be definitive.

When you decide to have that conversation, you need to be extremely precise with your wording.

It’s like a breakup.

If you plant a seed in someone’s head that there may be some opportunity down the line, it’s much worse than being upfront about what you mean.

There can be no door left open. Just be straight up and tell them what YOU would want to hear so that this senior leader can move on.

2. Be kind and empathetic.

Even if it’s clear that the employee and the company are not a good fit for one another, and you both *know that,* you still need to absolutely be kind to the person you’re letting go.

I’ve been fired from some high-paying jobs. It sucks, even though I didn’t like the job.

They’ll feel blindsided, but you need them to know that it’s not them, it’s you.

3. Be generous.

This is absolutely crucial if you value your reputation as a company.

Again, to go back to the breakup analogy, if you end things terribly with your partner…word will spread.

You’ll get bad reviews on Glassdoor (the group chat) and nobody else will want to work with (date) you.

It’ll cost you some time and money to be generous enough to give them some leeway, but it’s worth it.

For example, work out a deal where the senior employee can actively search for other positions while they’re working for you.

Or, you could say that they resigned instead of saying that you canned them. That’s nice.

And obviously, a severance package can be negotiated if you’re up for it.

Some companies have paid up to 24 months of compensation for employees that have spent more than 5 years working there.

That’s a little crazy, so hopefully, that doesn’t happen to you. But, it is what it is. Reputation is everything.

4. Help the person find another job.

I wouldn’t make this a LinkedIn post about this.

Maybe go direct to your network and see who’s hiring so you can make an intro.

That’s likely the best way to go about this to eliminate any sort of shame or embarrassment for the employee.

This will go a long way if you want to create a positive culture inside and outside of your company.

If you’re on either end of this exchange, I’m sorry.

And my DMs are open if you have questions.
