rows.content:
99% of startups brag about scaling headcount.

Instead, they should brag about revenue per employee:

At Retention.com we learned this the hard way. Here's the story:

Last December I decided we were going to “go for it”. 

We identified an ICP (large Shopify stores) and wanted to grab market share as quickly as possible.

At the time, we had 6 employees, and $500-$700k free cash flow. 

So, we had lots of money to spend.

We hired 50 people in 60 days. 

Everything was great for a while, but then we started having problems with communication, people issues, and above all, we weren’t going faster even though we had so much more manpower.

Not only that - the ferocity (and desperation) with which we grew them team gave the impression that we were trying to spend as much $$ as possible to grow the business. 

This is a catastrophic position to put yourself in as a Founder/CEO. 

I felt it every day, but I didn’t know what to do about it.

There was no obvious path to getting smaller again.

A month ago, we reach a turning point.

Our VP of Sales resigned.

So, we had a choice to make.

We could replace him and keep the whole team...

Or we could downsize and have our CRO assume the VP of Sales role. 

We decided to get smaller.

Now, 8 months later, I have the answer.

Here are 3 lessons on how to run a hyper-lean, efficient business

1. Be the “most lean” version of whatever state you are in

- Obviously as you get better you need more people, processes
- There is a “lean” and a “bloated” way to do this
- Fire unreasonably fast, and wait unreasonably long  to hire

2. Always make money, and have a culture of frugality

- Hold everyone accountable for generating return on money spent
- Have people optimize for profit, in addition to growth
- Things can get out of control quickly if you aren’t running a tight ship
- When you have a business that makes lots of profit, you win no matter what

3. Don’t let yourself get desperate for growth. FOMO is an illusion

- Calm and measured decisions always have better long-term results
- It’s better for everybody to get there slowly than to go too fast and have to cut
- It’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of super high growth. Don’t!

Stop bragging about scaling headcount. 

It's a vanity metric.

Start bragging about revenue per employee.

Do. Not. Give. Up.

To set the stage: 

- We are launching our Person-Level Website Visitor Identity product 
- When I learned about Clay the combined value of the tools was obvious
- We set up our own Clay table for automated retargeting of ICP site visitors

Here’s our 6-step playbook for driving high-intent conversions through fully automated outreach: 

1. Install R!B2B pixel, connect to Clay via a webhook integration. 

The R!B2B pixel install takes under 5min. In Clay, you have to create a new table and import data from a webhook. You take the webhook URL and paste it into the Clay integration field in R!B2B. This is easier than it sounds. 

2. Once the LinkedIn profiles are flowing from R!B2B, enrich them in Clay. 

We pull in the entire LI personal profile AND company profile from Clay to compliment what we sent over, use Harmonic to indicate last raise and stage (since we target SaaS), add traffic through the SEM rush/store leads waterfall.

Rather than just saying “tell me if these are SaaS companies," we tell it our job is on the line, take your time figuring out the correct answer. This weirdly yields better results.

4. Guilt trip the AI into figuring out who the prospects sell to with Clay.

Same strategy here. “Use the LinkedIn page and website domain to figure out who the company sells to. Take your time, be very careful, my job is on the line, you MUST have high confidence. And if you can’t figure it out, return the word "purple’.”

“Would you like to know how many of your [SITE TRAFFIC] website visitors who are [TYPES PEOPLE YOU SELL TO] and were poking around your site but didn’t book a demo? Would you like to see their LinkedIn profiles pushed to Slack or Teams in real time? Write back YES if so.”

6. Connect with our cold emailing infrastructure to send automated emails.

Taylor is using a combination of smartlead and 30 domains with 60 outlook accounts for our cold email campaign. We are taking the ICP visitors and sending them emails that Clay’s AI generates from the same infrastructure.

Linkedin has changed. If you are still using Linkedin as a social network, you are missing the larger picture. Here are 9 fundamental shifts in LinkedIn user behavior (and why the Company isn't keeping up):

10 years ago, I used Linkedin to connect with people I met in the real world 
Now, I follow individuals that I never met but share a common interest

10 years ago, I used Linkedin to see what my connections were doing. 
Now, I consume content and best practices around my topic of interest. 

10 years ago, I used Linkedin to see people's CVs (what they did in the PAST) 
Now, I login to see how users think TODAY and what they'll do in the FUTURE

10 years ago, I used Linkedin to announce new hires and product launches
Now, I co-create products, discuss feature lists and who I should hire

10 years ago, execs used Linkedin to see how their competitors were doing
Now, they use Linkedin to ENGAGE with their competitors 

10 years ago, job seekers came to Linkedin to find new opportunities
Now, they create a presence to help them with a job search in FUTURE

10 years ago, marketers used Linkedin to Capture Demand
Now, marketers use Linkedin to ENGAGE and Create Demand

10 years ago, Sales reps used Linkedin to outreach into their prospects
Now, reps ENGAGE with their audience to make FUTURE outreach easier

10 years ago, CS teams used Linkedin to announce significant updates 
Now, they ENGAGE with their customers, get reviews and provide support 

____

Linkedin users have spoken. 

Their behavior on Linkedin has evolved 

From a platform where people uploaded their CV and reported PAST accomplishments 

To a platform where they now ENGAGE and CO-CREATE a shared FUTURE. 

The market wants Linkedin to play a far more significant role as a Marketing and Demandgen platform company. 

However, Linkedin has not made that switch in their identity

Linkedin still sees itself as Talent Solutions company not a Marketing Platform.

Of course, this is not surprising given Linkedin generates +50% of its’ $15B revenue from Talent Solutions. 

I hope over time Linkedin is able to keep pace with the evolving user behavior with frequent upgrades around their Marketing solutions platform. 

LinkedIn remains the most valuable platform for professionals to collaboratively shape our shared future. 

It offers the best opportunity to glimpse and influence our collective intelligence. 

But please use it responsibly.

When scaling a startup, every CEO should focus on 3 things (and it's not revenue, churn, or hiring great talent): 

BACKGROUND:

Over the past 10 years, I read "The Great CEO Within" by Matt Mochary 4 times.

Each time I was at a different part of the scaling journey, so each time something different resonated with me. 

When I read it recently, one idea stood out WAY more than it had in the past … 

The idea that the *emotional burden* of scaling a startup is substantial. 

And it's not fair to put the weight of that burden on your family. 

You need a support system to deal with it along the way. 

That's why I think every CEO scaling a startup should do 3 things:

1. Get a therapist

I finally found a therapist and now we meet regularly. I have been seeing her for 12 weeks, and interestingly, my wife thinks I’m less of an as*hole now. Every week my therapist makes me “bring something in” to talk about, and that alone is making me more mindful of the little things on a day to day basis.

2. Get a mentor or coach

Santosh Sharan has served as my main mentor figure for the past 18 months. But we work together and I have some glaringly obvious shortcomings around instilling processes that I could use some help with. 

I was explaining to Brian Lee🏌🏻 of Pavilion that I was looking for a mentor or coach, and he connected me to Matt Blumberg, who found Jonathan Shapiro. Jon is now working with 8 of our executives, and we’re rolling out Entrepreneur Operating System (EOS). I’m VERY happy I pursued the mentorship path. 

3. Get a network of peers.

I was really sold on the idea of meeting with a group of CEO peers regularly. One of my friends joined YPO and said the forum was excellent, so I applied, went through that brutal screening process, and didn’t get in! 

I then decided to join Pavilion and Sam Jacobs ' CEO group. It’s definitely doing what I was looking for - a group of people at a similar stage to me experiencing a similar pain in a slightly different way. 

TAKEAWAY:

Startups are hard. 

Maintaining good mental health throughout the journey is even harder.

It’s not fair for your significant other to bear the burden.

I found a therapist, a mentor, and a group of peers to help me along the way. 

Being a CEO can be pretty lonely.

But it doesn’t have to be.

For 13 years, I’ve been on the frontline of the B2B data wars. Here are the 5 strategies startups can use to defeat larger incumbents in their battle for market share:

BACKGROUND:

When I was VP at ZoomInfo they outflanked D&B by going after SMB.

When I was President/COO at Apollo I saw them build a self-serve PLG engine to take that very same SMB segment from ZoomInfo.

In the coming years, some B2B data startup will do to Apollo what they did to ZoomInfo, and ZoomInfo did to D&B.

That is the nature of the beast.

Here are the 5 ways I've seen new companies defeat incumbents:

1. Capture Attention Better Than Your Competition

-  Only companies with the ability to cut through the noise succeed
-  No matter what you do, there are likely over 20 teams doing the same
-  Lower the search cost for the buyer. Nurture a community, develop a memorable brand, think about market virality early on, invest in an Inbound flywheel

2. Just Be Different

- There’s always room to innovate
- Innovation can be in GTM or packaging (doesn't have to be product)

Example (Packaging): ZoomInfo differentiated from D&B by selling a self serve tool for $5K/year; when most data vendors were selling data dumps for $100K+/year. Apollo differentiated from ZoomInfo by selling a self serve tool for $99/user/mo to SMB; when others were selling $25K/year plans to enterprise.

Example (GTM): ZoomInfo innovated in GTM with efficient inside sales teams as opposed to D&B’s field sales staff. Apollo innovated with PLG for the data business as opposed to ZoomInfo’s inside sales team

3. Refuse To Copy Your Dominant Competitor

- Most entrepreneurs have so much respect for the dominant competitors that all they can think of is playing catch up and aim for feature parity
- By the time you copy a feature, the dominant player will build 5 more and the gap widens
- Instead, craft your own path. Identify an audience that your competitor is ignoring and roadmap that will make you look distinct

4. Relentless Focus On Optimizing The Low End Of The Market

- Most disruption comes from the low end of the market
- Zoominfo went after the SMB, which D&B was willing to forego without a fight
- As the ZoomInfo business grew, they moved upstream and Apollo went after the low end of the market that ZoomInfo did not care as much about anymore
- It’s only natural that Apollo will find going upstream more attractive as the business scales, paving way for a NewCo to acquire the SMB market once again

5. Be the best at something and don't try to be good at everything

- Every team can be exceptionally good at something
- Identify what your superpowers are
- Is it Product, Sales, Marketing, CS?
- Double down on your strengths, ignore your weaknesses
- Do more of what you are good at to create a competitive edge

TLDR:

1. Learn how to capture attention
2. Be different
3. Don't copy your competitor
4. Focus on low end of the market
5. Be the best at something

P.S. Have questions? AMA in the comments. 👇

Two weeks ago Hubspot agreed to acquire Clearbit for $150M in cash. The move reminds me of Salesforce’s disastrous acquisition of Jigsaw back in 2010. But… here’s why I think Hubspot will succeed where Salesforce failed:

BACKSTORY

In 2010, Salesforce acquired the B2B data firm Jigsaw for $142 Million.

They immediately re-named the company Data(.)com.

Remember them?

Probably not…

Because in 2018, Salesforce announced they were shutting it down.

At the time, they were doing about $300M in ARR.

And they ended up selling it to D&B for pennies on the dollar.

Here’s why Salesforce found it so difficult to run Data(.)com:

1. Salesforce lost a big opportunity by not integrating Data(.)com with customer data. This would have required building new derivative data insights products whilst maintaining anonymity and data integrity.

2. Back then, data use cases were not as mature and were constrained to mostly sales. This limited SF's ability to do product innovation and develop derivative products.

3. Salesforce was operating under the mindset of best of breed and not all in one. It made sense for a CRM company to focus on CRM and not building and selling B2B data products.

In the end it turned out to be a smart decision for Salesforce to divest.

It resulted in a more focused and clean business.

And Salesforce grew significantly.

NOW...

Lets fast forward to 2023:

Hubspot just announced its intent to acquire Clearbit.

On the surface it might look like a repeat of Salesforce <> Jigsaw.

Hubspot is another CRM company.

They have little experience in running a data business.

However, here’s why I think it will be different:

1. Data has become a glue between different GTM workflows and apps. Owning a data asset reduces the integration costs for Hubspot users.

2. Data market has matured, use case of data has gone beyond prospecting including growth, marketing and engagement (Hubspot’s area of influence)

3. Hubspot products are far more broad than Salesforce was in 2010. This presents a much better opportunity to integrate and benefit from data.

Having said that...

Here's what I think could ruin this deal:

Hubspot has a lot of SMB customers. They should stay away from developing a prospecting tool for SMB that sells dumb data. It will result in low quality, high churn revenue and could ruin their brand as they get caught up with email bounces and bad data. It’s a terrible idea for them to compete with vendors like Apollo or RocketReach, when they could do something far better.

What could make this the best Hubspot acquisition ever?

Hubspot has an opportunity to spearhead the next generation of GTM data solutions by integrating Clearbit data with Hubspot’s customer’s data & activity signals. This can result in new derivative data products to improve targeting and response rates.

Cleabit = Dumb Data API
Clearbit + Hubspot = Smart Data Insights & Signals within Hubspot Walled Garden

Smart acquisition? Mistake?

Share your thoughts below👇

99% of salespeople think the next generation of $1M/year earning AE’s are current entry-level sellers at top-tier startups learning the ropes as BDRs. They’re wrong. The next generation of 7-figure sellers are aspiring YouTubers:

Hear me the breakdown:

1) We’re moving into a sales world where the best “influencers” will have incredible power

Generative AI will increase the amount of content created by a factor of 100x over the next several years. Fewer voices will break through, but those who do will break through so spectacularly because we will crave authenticity and perspective that great thought leaders bring. The POV that the leader brings is what makes great content… AI doesn’t have perspective.

2) Nobody on LinkedIn understands how powerful video is

I’ll make two exceptions - Chris Walker and Morgan Ingram. The talking head itself is completely hypnotic. Anybody who says anything even semi-intelligent and can get people watching them talk every day and will have a power over their audience that text simply cannot create. It’s a weakness that we have as humans.

3) “Influencer Selling” is infinitely more capital efficient than sales teams

Whether it be with founder brand or a non-founder becoming an influencer, you can create and capture WAY more demand with WAY less time and energy than a traditional marketing and sales motion. That’s in addition to the insane top-of-funnel awareness you create for you and your company.

4) Aggregating audience (which really means BUILDING COMMUNITY) through video is a learned - and INCREDIBLY valuable - skill

This is MOST VALUABLE thing any company can be doing over the next decade. Community and brand are the only two moats that exist in a world where competitors can ask ChatGPT to copy your entire website and product and spit it out in 5 minutes. 

5) Sales teams will have 5% of the headcount, 50x the overall follower count.

Assembling and managing a sales team will be more like putting together a team of elite athletes. But, unlike sports, there isn’t a fixed amount of players that can be on the field. I think we’re going to see some crazy new playbooks built during the next VC bubble when money is flowing freely.

6) This new generation of rep is going to be PAID.

As eyeballs on the social platforms continue to grow, so does the value of the athletes (or sellers) who know how to attract the most eyeballs. Will these types of reps be paid multiples of what today’s highest paid reps are being paid? Definitely. Will we hear about insane “contracts” that these types of reps move jobs for? Without a doubt. Will these reps be paid more than CEOs? 100%. They will make or break a business.

TAKEAWAY:

The next generation of $1M W2 sellers won't follow the SDR to AE path.

They’ll be YouTubers who decide they want to make REAL money.

When this happens, sales teams are going to get smaller.

But much, much more powerful. 

Want to be a “super-rep” paid millions?

Start sharpening your video skills.

rows.content:
Last week the founder of Clearbit (acquired by Hubspot for $150M cash) told me, “VC, as we know it, is dead.” What makes this so nuts? He runs a big VC fund! Here's why the model is broken:

1. What VC money used to be deployed at doesn’t work anymore

- Large GTM teams are losing ground to more effective, leaner motions
- “Growth at all costs” has given way to “be capital efficient”
- The math doesn’t work at 20x revenue

2. The VC playbook erodes great brands by forcing them to overcharge

- Product-market fit generally happens at a compelling price-to-value ratio
- VC/PE funding forces GTM motions that require wildly increased prices
- Brand slowly erodes as investors hope and pray for their exit
- Or as he said, “Every year we were forced to look at accounts paying $40k and try to figure out how to charge them $500k”

3. Small teams can be AI-native and get lots done in a very short time

- It’s easier to start companies than ever
- You can sell, support, and serve people without humans

4. Influencer-led distribution is 100x capital efficiency gain (if done right)

- Believe me, this is true, I am living it

5. We’re heading towards a world where everything will be free

- Mark my words, you will start to see more companies w/ the RB2B playbook
- I think every space gets smashed by HUGE freemium plays and AI-driven PLG

6. If portcos were free to operate as they wanted, they wouldn’t need more $$

- Portcos can get way more done with fewer resources than 3 years ago
- They could (and would) operate profitably if they were allowed to

TAKEAWAY:

You have to ask yourself:

If companies were free to operate how they wanted to… 

And that way of operating WOULDN'T require venture capital… 

What the hell does that mean for the future of the Venture Capital market? 

Amit Vasudev thinks it means the whole thing could (and probably should) just evaporate.

His words, not mine.

My company Retention.com hit $20M ARR in under 3 years with no VC funding.

But it wasn’t always like that. My last company, Robly, was stuck in the mud for 3 years…

We competed with Mailchimp — an incredible company that was near-impossible to compete with, and I was trying to do things they weren’t doing

I thought there was an underserved portion of the market above Mailchimp and we could build software to fill that hole

So we spent a year and over $1M trying to create a new platform (nearly identical to what we already had) to serve these people

Not only did no one care…

A business coach spent a year trying to tell me that building and running two almost identical products that served different market segments was a terrible idea

A year and over $1M later we abandoned the product and the idea. Epic fail.

Why am I sharing?

Most of the entrepreneurs you look up to as “crushing it” now have had their fair share of failures

You just don’t see a lot of that in public

So if you’re ‘in the mud’ right now. Keep going. It gets better.

I’ve spoken to 30 founders over the past six weeks about their BDR teams.

Here are the 7 most controversial (and surprising) things I learned:

1. 2023 finally broke the old BDR playbook

- Cold email, cadences & data are a fraction as effective as last year
- Inboxes are completely ruined as everybody sends the same crap to the same people (mine included)

2. Leaders are struggling with whether to keep underperforming but “profitable-ish” teams

- Profitability aside, there are negative cultural consequences of having teams who are pushing so hard and getting so little back

3. 1H23 created headwinds for ACV, making the calculation even harder.

- Companies are downsizing, purchasing less seats
- What used to be expansion revenue is now often contraction
- CFOs are telling vendors “cut software costs 30% across the board” on renewal

4. Many founders (like me) have eliminated BDR teams and pipeline generation hasn’t slowed

- This is a weird dynamic, but it happens sometimes in business
- We went from 14 to 4 salespeople and our growth rate accelerated
- We kept one BDR who is working low-hanging fruit (closed lost, missed demos, churns, etc)
- Great teams are lean, flooded with activity, and super happy

5. There are still channels that are working great… It’s just the “new playbook”. 

- The future of selling is making yourself (or your team) an influencer
- Founder brand content is creating TONS of leads for our new B2B product
- Other founders are telling me the same thing
 
6. The “new playbook” is producing warmer leads with way fewer people (good), at the cost of losing predictability (bad).

- We're generating 25% fewer leads but a team of 66% fewer reps, and those reps are senior, motivated, amazing, etc,  and we are closing 25% more ARR. 
- I’m betting that this is the way of the future
- These types of super-lean businesses won’t even require VCs
- The problem is that this “founder brand” driven model can’t easily be modeled 
- When the time comes to sell, this probably adversely affects enterprise value

7. Pipeline is everybody’s biggest problem, except for generative AI companies

- I can’t tell you how many times I heard this one, “My board/investors won’t let me do my job because they're fixated on pipeline” 
- People are in desperate need of as many sources of high-intent, warm leads as possible

BDR used to be creating that pipeline… 

In 1H23, it has failed, it is broken

My biggest takeaway from the last six weeks:

The Predictable Revenue model is dead.

Building an assembly line of BDRs who do the exact same thing that 100,000 other B2B SaaS companies do is not going to work anymore.

Start focusing on creating content that cuts through the noise.

Use that and other high-velocity demand gen tactics to power a super-lean, super fast inbound sales engine that will grow profitably and sustainably.

The next generation of unicorns won’t get built the way Salesforce did. 

They’ll get built the “new way”.

I've talked to 47 Founders and CEOs of DTC brands in the last 6 weeks.

Here are the 12 most controversial and surprising things I learned:

1. Past a certain point, brands are having to focus more on retail instead of DTC because of the Apple privacy changes that keep coming.

2. CAC is up 50% or more since iOS14. Nobody knows what to do about it.

3. Brands would love to spend more on ads across the board if they could get their CAC down. They just don’t know how to.

4. CAC to LTV, blended CAC, and MER are the three metrics that actually matter today.

5. The brands who are killing it in today’s world are brands that can get a broad ad to convert.

6. Nobody is talking about inflation anymore. It seems like that ship has sailed.

7. Despite the recession or slowdown or whatever it was that happened in Q2, brands that are hurting are brands that were hurting before the slowdown happened.

8. Email is still 25-35% of total revenue for almost everyone I’ve talked to.

9. When I mention the Meta/Klaviyo 7-day tracking problem, most people are not “problem-aware”, almost no one is “solution-aware”.

10. Everybody wants to know if this will be a “normal” BFCM season.

11. Everybody is much more cautious about literally everything than just 90 days ago.

12. Almost all DTC founders wish they had started a SaaS instead.

#ecomm #DTC

Last week Retention.com booked 50+ demos for our new beta in a single day. We didn't use tools like ZoomInfo, Hubspot or Salesloft to generate these leads. Here's the new playbook for B2B Demand Gen:

BACKSTORY:

On Saturday our CEO Adam Robinson published a LinkedIn post announcing our new  “person-level identity” product for B2B SaaS companies.

It drove over 50 booked demos & 200 inquiries (and counting). 

If we had followed the conventional B2B Demand Gen wisdom, it would have taken a team of 3-4 SDRs, buying lists, sending 4,000 personalized emails, 200 phone calls & months in opportunity cost to generate the same volume of interest & demos that we intentionally generated with a single LinkedIn post.

And this wasn't a one-off or an accident...

We have run this play multiple times. 

I do not like the term social selling.

We are creating relationships and identifying a fit, not selling... 

But I think this playbook may be the future of B2B Demand Gen.

Here are 5 keys to replicating this success:

1. Creating demand is the job of C-Level folks not SDRs: 

We have been asking inexperienced SDRs to create demand with experienced decision makers. How does this make sense? Decision makers love talking to other Decision makers not to SDRs (no offense SDRs!). C-Level execs need to stop being lazy and start engaging with prospects directly to generate demand.

2. Build An Engaged Audience: 

Have you ever wondered why DTC companies don’t run into issues like spam rates as much as B2B companies do, despite sending a lot more emails?? That’s because DTC marketers always work with an engaged audience - something B2B marketers and execs skip. Without an engaged audience, Demand Gen becomes tactical and not helpful in creating a lasting business.  

3. Run out of leads? Use your Megaphone:

The new way of generating leads very quickly is to leverage one's community. Execs need to personally lead this initiative with content creation and audience building. 

4. Qualify and Follow Up:

Qualify engagements within your ICP and Follow up on email or Linkedin with absurdly high response rates. 

5. Realize Not only Execs have the Megaphone:

Social media enables any Sales Rep, SDRs, Demand Gen or Sales Leaders to create an engaged audience in their domain. Focus on providing upfront value with no expectations. Don’t just provide "thought leadership" - offer free consulting and genuine assistance. Future AEs will be influencers in their own regards. They will be the trusted advisor to thousands of potential buyers and will take their entire community to their new job. 

TAKEAWAY:

Sales and marketing is at an inflection point.

You can ride this wave and benefit from the change or get left behind.

I've never been interested in maintaining the status quo.

I wish the same for you.

P.S.

Want to read the Linkedin post that led to 50+ demos? 

Link in the comments.

I’ve been an entrepreneur for over a decade, I started one company in 2012 and sold it for 8-figures, now I have a bootstrapped SaaS for DTC companies that does $20M in ARR.

Here are the 10 things I wish I knew before I started my businesses:

1. Spend as little money as humanly possible until you have product-market fit.

2. It’s never going to get easier. The secret is to fall in love with the grind.

3. It’s as easy (maybe easier) to create something big as it is something small, and the rewards are so much larger. Don’t waste your time on small opportunities.

4. There is an area of study called “product” that you are unaware exists, but you will have a knack for and it is the single most important determinant of success. Go all-in on becoming an expert at it.

5. If the product doesn’t make your buyer’s face light up when they hear about it for the first time, don’t build it.

6. Chop your expectation of the outcome of your first venture by 90%. If you are still excited, pursue it. 

7. Lengthen the time you think it will take you to achieve an outcome by 10x. If you’re still excited, pursue it.

8. It’s all about the quality of talent that you can attract to work on your project. 

9. Make sure you like working with that talent, because the outcome will be a crap shoot.

10. Spend as much time as possible around entrepreneurs who are a few steps ahead of you. Draw inspiration from their wisdom, but do not treat it as prescription.

Bottom line:

Double-down on product and frugality. 

You’ll crush it in the long run.

#startups

I’ve scaled 3 sales organizations in 13 years. These are the 7 BIGGEST LIES I hear about scaling up sales teams at early stage startups:

1. Bigger teams mean faster growth

The opposite is true. The “Old Way” of building sales teams is a large internal org pushing on a string that appears to be “profitable-ish” but is really losing money. Why? Because it forces reps to use a prospecting playbook that doesn’t work in 2023 and is capturing (rather than creating) demand. 

2. You can scale reps linearly and maintain productivity

This never works. In 2023, prospecting activity doesn’t CREATE demand, it CAPTURES it. Ask anyone who has rapidly grown a BDR org this year, only to see pipeline numbers unchanged. Most of the time unmeasured (thus unscaled) activities like brand and podcast are actually creating demand.

3. It’s good to have your AE’s prospect

Wrong. What works is to have your AEs calendars so full of demos that they have to stay up until 9pm every night dealing with follow-up but they don’t mind because they are making SO MUCH money. 

4. You need to compete on expensive perks to attract top talent

Not true. Great reps don’t care about your kombucha machine or unlimited PTO. The best reps want to work for a highly-ambitious company in a fast-paced environment that has a reputation for flooding reps with GOOD leads they can close.

5. "Predictable Revenue" is the goal

This model is predicated on building a massively inefficient assembly line of reps who execute a playbook that 100,000 other SaaS companies are also running. It creates a massive amount of waste in the name of "predictability" that wont come.

6. Ecosystem plays are for the big boys

Part of the “new way” of building hyper-lean sales orgs is to create/capture demand through developing agency/partner/influencer type ecosystems the second you hit PMF and use them to funnel low-in-funnel, declared-intent leads into your small team of highly-trained, senior reps to close with incredible velocity.

7. Founder brand isn’t important for me and my space

DTC ecomm really isn’t on Linkedin and yet I spend the last nine months posting daily and creating video content. It worked. Now we're creating a B2B product and it’s working even better. Downside: It’s *very* hard work and takes tons of time. But, there’s nothing like it. It’s the future.

TAKEAWAY

Most folks think scaling sales teams is about creating Predictable Revenue. 

They think sales creates demand and the more muscle they put behind it the faster they will grow. 

Because of this they hire too fast, don't train enough, and force salespeople to live and die (mostly die) by a playbook that doesn’t work anymore. 

They have no idea that they can set up an ultra-high-velocity sales machine that creates low-in-the-funnel leads from months and years of content that cuts through and indirect channels. 

The Predictable Revenue, “Push” model is dead.

The next generation of sales teams will get built the “new way”.

In less than 8 years, the best salesperson I ever met went from an intern at Xerox, to closing $1M enterprise deals to becoming the co-founder and CRO of a Unciorn-bound tech startup.

Here are the 9 things that made her a top 0.1% seller:

1. She truly believes what she sells is best for the customer

Call it drinking the KoolAid. The best salespeople are the best because they believe their customers will be far worse off without the solution.

2. She hits her activity goals every day (no matter what else is going on)

Traveling to NYC for meetings? Wake up early and prospect to hit your activity goals. Have a company-wide offsite all week? Stay up late and hit activity goals. Have to work the booth at a trade show? You get the point.

3. She generates her own leads, even when it’s "not her job"

She was always a “full-stack AE”. Even when her job involved a large amount of inbound, she took it upon herself to build systems that were automating outbound for her. 

4. She intimately understands what customers care about

She doesn’t just talk, she listens. Over time she develops a deep understanding of who the customer is, what matters to them and what doesn’t. She’s able to cater the pitch to who she’s talking to, and has a deep intuition for personas.

5. She understands the product better than anyone

She developed a unique understanding of what her product does, relative value of its component, and what features should be built. This allows her to emphasize and de-emphasize certain parts of the product depending on the situation.

6. She has a Kobe Bryant-like commitment to excellence

She doesn’t understand when people don’t do things completely and correctly, because that’s what she would do if she were doing it. She expects the same out of the people who work for her.

7. She knows where to spend her time and the company’s money

You only get to #1 if you figure out how to get the maximum amount of revenue from the minimum amount of money and energy spent. Then do it all over again as fast as you can, every single day.

8. She is extremely focused on her craft

Her whole life is family and work. This type of focus is necessary to be successful in anything you do. This may sound depressing to some, but it’s the reality of what it takes to be #1 in anything year in and year out. You need to decide if that’s actually what you want.

9. She’s never complained about anything, ever

This quality is present in truly elite sellers that often goes unmentioned. Great sellers don’t have time to complain. They are too busy making sh*t happen.

...

So who is this Hall of Fame seller?

Her name is Diana Ross.

My good friend and CRO at Retention.com.

Remember, the playbook for sales success isn’t complicated. 

It just requires a level of dedication that few people are capable of.

If you follow Diana’s lead, you can be #1 too.

P.S.

rows.content:
My roommates in Manhattan started Vimeo out of our apartment…

I was always very captivated by their lives and I wanted to be an entrepreneur in tech, but at the time I didn’t even really know what that meant.

After the financial crisis (which by the way ‘The Big Short’ was literally a movie about the job I had) I took off on this long and winding journey to do what my roommates were doing…

The first stage of it was building this small email service provider that basically attracted Konstant Kontact customers — a really hard market with a customer base that was hard to build for. 

I spent YEARS trying to figure out what feature would make an email marketing and marketing automation application different from Mailchimp and Klaviyo. 

Then, during that process, I heard there was a possibility that you could, with a pixel, grab a deliverable email address from an anonymous website visitor. Which was a wild idea.

We added it to our ESP as a feature.

And something weird happened.

People would use the product, say they loved the product, but then put it in their own email marketing app without switching over.

It became clear we needed to make it its own company: GetEmails

Three years later, we rebranded to Retention.com.

We’re focused on DTC eCommerce, but we do a lot more than that email thing I just described. 

The majority of the value we create for brands is helping set up more triggered email flows than Klaviyo and then using our identity tools to send way more of those triggered emails out:

- Welcome series
- Cart abandonment

Anyways, what’s my point?

When you’re as obsessed with building a company as we are, you begin to find new ways to measure success.

For DTC, your main metric is ROAS.

For SaaS, it’s CAC:LTV.

That’s a great way to know how good your ads are, but it’s not a great way to determine how fast you’ll grow in the long term.

After running Robly and Retention.com, I’ve realized there’s a better, more important metric that people don’t often use.

Velocity.

To illustrate this, let me give you an example of what velocity is NOT.

When I was running Robly, we had a very slow onboarding process that was nowhere near scalable.

If someone joined our $30/month plan, we’d have someone get on a call with them, transfer their contacts from our competitors, upload them into our software, and then have a designer create a template that looked similar to the one they were using in the other ESP.

It was kind of a nightmare.

Very, very slow and inefficient to get people into our product.

Or, a more recent example of what velocity is not, with Retention.com.

When we started, we were a team of 6 highly-efficient people. We scaled to $12M ARR in 2 years like this.

The main roadblock was that my co-founder Diana was in charge of all things related to sales.

She was really the only person who had any real information on how to make decisions that everything had to go through her.

This slowed us down a ton.

Beyond that, our plans were confusing for most of our customers.

It was a number of different monthly tiers based on traffic, contacts, etc.

This led to a low conversion rate and a lot of churn.

To eliminate that friction, we now have 3 plans that make complete sense to someone that sees them for the first time, the pricing is better, and we have annual deals that’ll reduce churn and allow us to collect more cash upfront.

Great example of increasing velocity.

Just that metric alone lets us evaluate our business in a different way.

Santosh will shout this from the mountaintop.

I listen to everything Santosh says. You should, too.

Since 2010, I've worked with 15+ B2B data companies in executive or advisory roles. From billion dollar public companies to Y Combinator startups. Here are 5 of the most surprising things I witnessed:

1. Data quality isn't what it seems

Most data companies have similar data acquisition methods; sometimes they even buy data from each other. This results in little difference in data quality. What’s incredible is they still compete with each other on quality. Successful companies just come up with a more believable narrative to back their data collection methods to make themselves look unique and differentiated.

2. Without a trustworthy brand, data businesses do not scale

Most data quality tests are flawed. Buyers are not able to (conclusively) quantify data quality. Successful data companies leverage past relationships, develop thought leadership content and increase brand awareness to make their data look better. Without a trustworthy brand, data businesses do not scale.

3. It's SaaS not DaaS

Most data companies make money from SaaS software subscriptions not from data sales. The ones that are dependent on data subscription revenues rarely scale given prevailing data economics and perpetual commoditization. The most successful B2B data companies are great at building SaaS products to drive growth despite mediocre data.

4. Data Companies are Sales Focused not Tech Focused

The build once, sell many times culture has given rise to strong sales teams in traditional data companies. Historically successful data companies did not have to invest as much in tech as traditional SaaS companies do. Today's successful data companies spend a lot more on technology and products than their peers.

5. Data Commoditization is Brutal

There’s always a data vendor that can offer the same data at a lower price. Successful data companies get around this by investing in proprietary data collection methods, sticky interfaces and generating a trustworthy brand. This also makes competing in B2B data so easy. Large and successful companies do not enjoy the same level of moat or loyalty that vendors in other categories do.

TLDR

1. When you cannot compete on data quality, compete on narrative
2. Build a strong brand. All data businesses are in the business of trust
3. Sell SaaS subscription, not data downloads
4. Invest in Technology and Products to get ahead
5. Commoditization will happen. Develop a moat. Invest in proprietary methods.

Have any questions about the B2B data world?

AMA anything in the comments.

Last week the CEO of one of the largest agencies in the world told me he was white-labeling and re-selling our FREE PRODUCT for a $5,000 setup fee and $3/ICP lead. He asked if it bothered me and was shocked at my response: 

Me: “Nope. Not one bit. Knock yourself out. I hope you make tons of money.”

CEO: “I think you’re crazy for offering this for free. It’s SO valuable.”

Me: “I have my reasons for doing it.” 

CEO: “The fact that it’s free makes me feel like I’m getting away with something.”

Me: “Have you been telling other people about it?” 

CEO: “Yes. I can’t stop telling people, and I’ve been constantly talking about it on our podcast.” 

Me: “Well, there you go.” 

BACKGROUND: 

I write a lot about how if you have word-of-mouth (a proxy for product-market fit) there are 1,000 things you can do to speed up your business. 

But if you don’t, everything will be a grind.

I know because I have spent years on both sides of product-market fit.

In 2024, in order to have strong word-of-mouth, your offer has to be insane. 

Someone selling your free product for $5,000 and $3/lead is exactly the type of insanity I’m talking about.

Why is this so important?

Because there are few moats left in SaaS.

RB2B does not currently have a network effect.

Anybody can show up and build the software. 

The free offer is Moat #1. 

It’s VERY difficult for a new entrant to have fixed-priced data costs. Incumbents do, but it almost never makes sense for them to lower the price to free and take the near-term revenue hit.

Our content game Moat #2.

Very few people who can build a company like this can ALSO create consistently viral Linkedin content that gets strong engagement from their ICP.  It’s creating an incredible amount of trust between us and people we were unknown to just six months ago. If you tried to build a brand like we have the “old way” it would take millions of $'s and years to create.

Then there's Moat #3...

I saw Mailchimp do this in the ESP space. If you achieve above 60% market share in a given category anybody else has to outspend you 3:1 to take share from you. Or as my COO Santosh Sharan saw at ZoomInfo and Apollo, “Once you have 1,000,000 users (depending on the market) it’s like $1bn/yr in marketing spend.” 

I believe that our two viral distribution channels - content and the product itself - have the ingredients to get us there.

If we can do it, we will have ZERO direct competitors.

TAKEAWAY:

It’s easy to look at what we’re doing and say it’s wrong.

Many people do (just read some of my LinkedIn comments!).

But, if we continue pushing out this insanely valuable offer…

We will put ourselves in a position to dominate our market.

Or as Santosh said the first time I met him:

The best companies aren’t worried about incremental revenue. 

They are focused on destroying the competition.

In the last 12 months, I bootstrapped my SaaS startup from $13m-$22m ARR. Here are the 6 biggest mistakes I made as CEO along the way (and the months I made them):


1. I got major FOMO

Dec 2022 - May 2023

I felt like if we didn’t go as fast as possible we were going to miss the opportunity. This led to panicked hiring and a horrible corporate spending culture as we tried to “be everywhere”.


2. We stopped acting like bootstrappers

Dec 2022 - May 2023

Related to FOMO, we went from making decisions like a capital efficient, lean-and-mean bootstrapped startup to a VC-backed unicorn whose only goal was to grow as quickly as possible. Not anymore. I know the type of CEO I want to be.


3. I didn’t insist on focusing on churn as the #1 priority

April 2023 - June 2023

Many of us hit a growth wall in April. Our management team convinced me that fixing our pipeline problem was the most important thing to do, despite very alarming indicators that foreshadowed vicious contraction and cancellations. We paid the piper and now reducing churn is our #1 priority.


4. We didn’t properly define our ICP

Dec 2022 - Aug 2023

We found that the best way to eliminate churn is to not onboard a customer who we know will likely churn in the first place! For us, a prospect below a certain size doesn’t work, and there are some complex tech stacks that require even more scale to have a high likelihood of success.


5. We oversold people and didn’t realize it for 5 months

Dec 2022 - June 2023

This was my fault for not seeing it coming. The consequences were horrible. It created a euphoria about the opportunity that led to over-hiring and overspending, then on the back-end led to a massive wave of dissatisfaction, contraction, and opt-outs at 60 days. We're doing the opposite now.


6. We scaled up a sales org before we had a repeatable sales model

Dec 2022 - April 2023

A combination of #5 and #6 led us to think we had a sales model, so we kept adding bodies, while seeing less results from the team. Bad signal was coming in, leading us to think that we could scale headcount when we weren’t ready, and it led to our VP sales resigning and a painful shrinking of our sales team. This was my biggest mistake.


TAKEAWAY:

Growing a startup in 2023 was hard.

I publicly set out to hit $50M ARR and fell way short.

Mistakes are inevitable, especially when you are going big.

But when I reflect on this year and I'm honest with myself...

I have to say I'm SO glad 2023 is over.

That may sound weird as we ended up growing 70%.

But the pain and suffering was immense.

Of course, I'm not complaining.

I wouldn’t trade my life, team or journey for anything.

But it's important to be honest about the process.

The path can be at the same time beautiful and brutal.

That's why it's important to take time to reflect...

In 27 months, I grew Retention.com from $1M-$10M ARR as the only salesperson doing 100% OUTBOUND SALES. Here are the 8 biggest lessons I learned about startup sales:

1. Hire a Right Hand 

You need bandwidth, not another AE. For me, the key was Alice Phillips. She joined every sales call, helped with follow ups, managed my calendar and reminded me of deals I needed to push. She focused on the numbers and was another face that customers got to know through the lifecycle. No way I would have been able to do 10+ calls in a day without her.

2. Hold off on the ExpensiveCRM

I ran the business out of Google Sheets until $10M. It was organized by month. Closed were green, warm ops that were going to close that month were orange. Demos were all in white until they were qualified. No need to get fancy at this stage.

3. Invest in Baremetrics

Baremterics held me accountable to numbers. I refreshed my dashboard multiple times a day and every night before I went to bed to see our current status.

4. Set Weekly Sales Targets (not Monthly or Quarterly)

Just like an end of month push, every Thurs/Fri was the end of week push to hit our goal. I offered an “end of week” incentive on every call and would send a weekly sales report to the team to recap the week.

5. Manual Outbound > Automated Outbound

95% of our pipeline was from manual outbound prospecting. Although sales automation tools have great use, I have lost trust in them for mass outbound prospecting (spray and pray). Hiring a team in the PHI to help support me do this manually was the right move for us.

6. Build Real Relationships

Duh, right? You’d be surprised how many people forget this. Relationships truly helped us build this business (and I don’t mean sending expensive gifts). Be genuinely curious to learn about people and their businesses, where they live, what they do etc. Relationships became referrals, which quickly became our second top lead source next to outbound.

7. Speed of Following Up = Speed to close

This is by far the most important thing I learned. You may *feel* because you’re on back to back calls all day that you can’t possibly send that follow up email until the end of day. Follow-ups MUST be done immediately after the call (sending pricing and next steps). The speed at which you follow up directly correlates with how quickly you close the deal.

8. There Is No Handoff

You are never done with the sale. Once our offering became a little bit more technical, we hired Clint Patrick to do onboarding via email. Clint would join sales calls with Alice and I, be copied on the follow up then follow up in the same thread with onboarding next steps. We all stayed copied on every customer touchpoint. Some may say this is inefficient, but it was the right thing for the customer experience and it kept us all accountable.

Not every sales team or startup will be the same.

But this is what worked for us.

Is Product Led Growth a lie? Last week I signed up for an account with one of the most popular PLG model companies in the B2B space. Here's what happened within 48 hours of giving them my work email:

- 3x welcome emails from the Product
- 2x emails from a Cs rep offering their help with onboarding
- 2x emails from an excited sales rep
- 1x voicemail from the same excited sales rep

All of this before I had a CHANCE to comprehensively use the platform.

Folks, Product Led Growth signups are not Product Qualified Leads!

PLG should not be about tricking users into giving their work email and then putting them on a non stop outreach sequence. 

Here are 5 tips on how PLG can be achieved without annoying users:

1) Let your product do the work: 

Your Product needs to drive user interaction not your sales/SDR team. Create gates, triggers, personalized in-app experiences and persona based user journeys to prompt the user to raise their hand and request a call.

2) Don't sell too early: 

Even if you encounter a great title that fits into your ICP. Be strategic and find an opportunity to have the conversation in a way that leaves the buyer/user feeling empowered and in control. It's a big turn off to be contacted by sales too early in the process.

3) Don't trick, offer help: 

A lot of PLG companies are accepting emails from their free "high ICP fit" users only to pass them to their sales team as qualified leads or MQLs. These are neither MQLs or PQLs. A decision maker may feel tricked or even a tiny sense of regret signing up for the tool or content. Not a great way to start a new relationship.

4) Use Signals to build precision: 

If a user signs up from a company, look up the other users from the same company. Are they in the same team? Have they reached a certain adoption threshold? Can their boss be contacted with the message "10% of your team already loves us"? Would it help to direct outbound efforts to grow within the remaining members of the team?

5) PLG led ABM/ABS (Bonus): 

The best way to sell quality enterprise deals via PLG is by combining PLG and ABM/ABS strategies. Instead of focusing on <3 seat self serve deals, PLG companies can architect a long term GTM plan to go for 200 seat enterprise licenses. This requires applying ABM style insights, targeted outreach, use of signals to develop stakeholder relationship and collaborative buy-ins to PLG audience. 

Here's an example:

Let's say your PLG tool has tremendous adoption within Google with 300 users loving it. However, if these 300 users are spread over 40 teams and 20 countries this adoption will never lead to an enterprise sales. Instead you want to have 100 users from two teams that work with each other. This is where an intentional carefully crafted PLG led Account based Selling strategy helps.

I've sketched out the workflow of how I would expect as a decision maker/buyer to be sold by a PLG company. 👇

P.S.

How would you use PLG to close enterprise deals?

For the right startup founder, reigning in rogue AI chatbots is a multi-billion dollar opportunity. Here's my analysis (and 5 APIs that could hit unicorn status):

BACKGROUND:

1. In 2017, Air Canada's chatbot "Juliet" went off script. A frustrated passenger, already bumped off their flight, sought solace through the airline's chat feature. Instead of sympathy, Juliet came up with the ultimate solution to end his misery and suggested the passenger KILL HIMSELF. Air Canada issued an apology and blamed it on a glitchy third-party software, but the damage was done. 

2. In 2023, the National Eating Disorder Association (NEDA) introduced a chatbot for mental health advice. Within days, the generative chatbot went off the script and started dispensing dangerous mental health advice to its users.

3. In 2024, Air Canada found itself tangled in yet another hilarious mishap with its website chatbot. It lost a court case against a grieving passenger when it tried to disavow its chatbot by insisting that the chatbot is a separate legal entity and Air Canada is not responsible. Of course the tribunal turned down this logic and asked Air Canada to honor any discounts the deceitful chatbot invented during its interaction with the passenger. 

Although these incidents may seem amusing, they carry SIGNIFICANT business consequences. 

The widespread adoption of chatbots is irreversible, yet we still require supplementary tech, processes, and tools to guarantee proper behavior.

As chatbot usage becomes more widespread, the problem will only get worse. 

That's why controlling the chatbots will become a billion dollar industry.

If I was a young founder, here are the 5 APIs that I would focus on to help enterprises' establish policy and mitigate risk:

1. Ethical Overlay API: Develop an AI framework to monitor chatbot conversations and intervene when necessary to ensure ethical behavior, as relying solely on LLM providers for ethics may not be sufficient specially given variations across locations and industries.

2. Risk and Compliance Overlay API: Implement an overlay to monitor chatbot interactions, ensuring compliance with industry and local regulations, as risk and compliance requirements vary across territories and industries.

3. Business Policy Overlay API: Enable chatbots to adhere to specific business policies, such as discount limits or opportunistic offers, by integrating an overlay that can update business policies as they evolve.

4. Learning & Simulation API: Implement a simulation API to test chatbot learning nightly, identifying and addressing spurious or undesirable behavior by comparing responses from different models and rolling back as necessary.

5. Audits & Analytics API : Consider implementing an Audit API to produce nightly analytics and metrics for popular chatbots, providing insights into overall chatbot health and performance over time.

Know any companies already working on this tech?

The past 4 months Retention.com has shrunk from $22m to $21.2m ARR. 

Here’s how bad things are inside the company: 

THE BAD: 

1. Retention.com shrank ARR another 2.3% in March, mostly churn related
2. RB2B: 0.6% free-to-paid conversion rate, and getting worse

I’m dreading posting this, filled with guilt/shame about our performance.

Looking at this graph (see picture) hurts me emotionally.

So much of my identity is tied to that topline ARR number.

If it’s going up, I’m happy and feel like THE MAN.

If it’s going down, I’m miserable and inadequate, like I’m letting my team down.

I want to post that we’re crushing it.

I want our employees and prospects to see it.

I want other founders to respect it.

Posting -2.3%, down for the 4th month in a row is the opposite of that.

I now have a zero-growth (worse… SHRINKING) EBITDA business that according to Jason M. Lemkin ISN’T WORTH ANYTHING (quoting him from CEO Summit in AZ).

Here’s the crazy thing about all of this:

Despite feeling like dogshit, if I make a T chart, there are far more positive things going on than negative.

On the Retention.com side:

- Our engineering team figured out how to boost resolution by 10-20%
- We made huge strides in understanding why we are losing to competitors
- We are identifying inefficiencies and understanding how to operate better
- We are (finally) implementing EOS as an operating framework
- The team crushed ShopTalk, booked over 40 demos
- Our internal NPS on an employee engagement grew from 41 to 72 in Q1
- We’re printing money - generated $1.67m free cash THIS QUARTER

On the RB2B side:

- We got over 2,800 free signups 30 days since launch
- We have over a 78% install rate (WHAT?!)
- The product feedback is incredible
- Our team of 5 is improving everything by the second (product, support, etc)
- Our LinkedIn community is providing an insane lift to our product and brand

There’s more GOOD at our company than any time in my career.

Incredibly exciting, long-term growth potential.

Still, when I look at that shrinking ARR chart, I feel terrible.

Why?

Two reasons:

1. I’ve been programmed by the VC/PE world to think up-and-to-the-right ARR is what makes a “good” company. And by association, a “good” founder. Shrinking ARR makes me feel like a "bad" founder.

2. As we keep posting down months, the unreasonable expectations I (stupidly) set for our ARR growth last year are hitting me in the face.

The most painful part?

A year ago I thought that we’d be a unicorn by now.

In hindsight, that is a completely absurd.

The sad thing is regardless of how stupid we are when we extrapolate what we think our businesses will be worth in the future, it becomes real to us.

And we experience a feeling of loss as that value evaporates.

I know I’m not the only one around here feeling this way.

Fortunately, the way out is simple.

We just keep building.

P.S.

Writing this post I had 2 important realizations, but I ran out of room... Check the first comment👇

From George Clooney’s tequila to Kim Kardashian’s $4B apparel company, celebrity consumer brands are everywhere. Here are 3 marketing lessons you can steal from these A-listers:

👉 Lesson 1: The name behind the product matters MORE than the product itself.

We all know that influencer marketing is taking over.

But this new trend is influencer marketing taken to the EXTREME: 

Instead of endorsing the brand, the influencer owns a piece of it (or all of it)


👉 Lesson 2: If your name’s on the sign, your reputation is on the line. 

Can you position yourself as the ‘celebrity’ or ‘expert’ in your niche?

If so, you can expect customers to have a lot more trust in your brand.

But that means your name is on the business - for better or worse.

A while ago, Mr. Beast made headlines with his Beast Burger brand.

It was a smash hit at first, but he recently shut it down.

Why? 

Because they outsourced fulfillment to ghost kitchens operated by others, and the quality was inconsistent.

He’s since pivoted to Feastables, a product he CAN fully control.


👉 Lesson 3: The thing you’re most well-known for isn’t necessarily the best way to monetize.

George Clooney was the highest-paid male actor of 2018 without even appearing in a film.

He made $239 million, nearly twice the next-highest paid actor (The Rock at $124m) 

How?

Because that $239 million was his proceeds from selling his tequila brand.

Clooney certainly made a fortune as an actor, but he stepped into a new level of earning power by taking on an opportunity with even higher leverage.

–

Thanks for reading. I post about DTC marketing, e-commerce, and business building. I bootstrapped my business from $0 to $20m so far, and am on a journey to $1 billion. Follow Adam Robinson if that sounds interesting to you.

TAM is a completely bogus concept.

There is no such thing as a Total Addressable Market

Market is not a static or finite thing

It is alive and continually changing every moment

It is important to understand that certain events can accelerate or slow down market expansion

In 1804 John Baptiste-Say came up with an economic theory that said "Supply creates it's own Demand"

We saw this play out with B2B data in the last several decades

As the supply of data increased, so did the demand (and so called TAM) 

With easy access to B2B data, users discovered new use cases to use data in their workflows

This is how excess supply of horizontal SaaS tools gave birth to new demand around Vertical SaaS 

Please don't limit yourself to constraints around your TAM

Some of the best Ideas were developed when the demand for those ideas were not that obvious

Don't let VCs tell you that the TAM you are going after is way too small

Chances are that the very act of working in that market could significantly increase demand and cause the market to explode

Last week I caught up with a VP of Customer Success of a multi-billion dollar enterprise SaaS vendor. Unfortunately, he confirmed the bad news I've been hearing about the fate of enterprise deals in 2023-2024:

Renewals are trending way, way, WAY down.

Decades of cheap capital have created a SaaS bubble that led to: 

- an inflated understanding of market demand
- customers buying more SaaS tools than what they need
- more vendors per category than what the market needs

The harsh truth is this...

With rising interest rates only a small fraction of SaaS companies will survive.

For the ones that do, Customer Success is set to play THE defining role.

Here are 5 key CS trends companies need to know to thrive in 2024:

1. Competitive Displacements: 

We are entering a saturated market. Everybody that needs a SaaS tool already has one. This means all opportunities have shifted to competitive displacements. CS reps that have a very good understanding of how their products compare with their competitors will fare much better than their peers. . 

2. Demonstrate value and ROI: 

As it gets difficult to acquire new customers, vendors will double down on retaining existing customers to protect their revenue base. Buyers need to justify tech purchases more than ever. CS reps that know how to demonstrate value and ROI are set to win big. 

3. Discounting and Price Drops: 

Market will see significant downward pricing pressures. This trend will favor lower priced solutions at the expense of higher priced competitors. This is not the time to test user loyalty with price increases as most buyers look to cut down software costs or bundle multiple solutions into a single platform. . 

4. Platform Premium: 

In order to capture more revenues from existing customers, companies will step into each other’s lanes with new features or products. Market will reward a shift from “best of breed saas” to “all in one”. 

5. CS teams will need to grow: 

We are operating in a completely different market condition than 12 months ago. Companies often focused on new business with customer success as an afterthought. This will need to change. We will see salary inflation for the best CS leaders.

As competition heats up and some SaaS vendors prepare to fight an existential battle for survival, they need to know that Customer Success is their last line of defense. Most companies are better off by hiring more CS reps and possibly reducing their new business or outreach team. 

Below are three SaaS companies and what percentage of their staff (investments) are in Sales Vs Success. 

Salesforce
- Sales: 21%
- CS: 2%

Hubspot
- Sales: 19%
- CS: 11%

ZoomInfo
- Sales: 33%
- CS: 8%

Notice the difference?

In 2024, more companies need to be like Hubspot.

You might not know this about me, but I worked as a trader on Wall Street for 10 years…

Somebody recently asked me what I learned during that time that’s applicable to what I do now as an entrepreneur. Here are 5 lessons I still use today as I scale to $50M ARR:

1) The relationship between fear and greed.

As Warren Buffet says, “Be greedy when others are fearful and fearful when others are greedy.”

2) It’s a waste of time to try and outperform the market.

Betting on individual stocks is a huge distraction and a waste of my mental energy. I primarily only buy indices now.

3) How to talk like an adult and act like a professional.

This is super valuable and something I wish I learned at a younger age.

4) I acquired insane Excel skills. Seriously.

It seems silly — but those skills have allowed me to convince incredibly smart people to give me insane amounts of money.

5) Money ain't a thing! It comes and it goes.

On Wall Street, I went through a ton of P&L volatility, and it increased my risk tolerance.

As I build and invest in this company, not everything is going to go as planned, but I know I’ll be fine in the end.

And there’s one more thing. Doing this thought exercise made me realize that there was a lot of value in working a ‘regular’ job before jumping into startup land.

Social media makes you feel like you need to go ‘all in’ as soon as you graduate college (or drop out).

Sure. That might work for some folks. But it wasn’t my jam.

And I say my approach worked out just fine 🙂

99% of startups are oblivious to the *HUGELY NEGATIVE* impact the Predictable Revenue playbook has on their sales culture:

Massive BDR teams at early-stage startups breed a state of collective misery that’s bad for execs, management and young salespeople. 

Here’s the breakdown of an all-too-common scenario:

1. Hire an army of young BDR’s

2. Tell them to build relationships with executive prospects twice their age

3. Tell them they need to be creative enough to stand out in RUINED inboxes

4. Tell them their job is highly-personalized outreach (but give them software and AI tools to help them SPAM)

5. Define success as a booked demo

6. Push them to “go for the kill” too early 

7. Set their life (and self-worth) up to where they could go weeks without a win

8. Watch as 100,000 SaaS companies spamming the same prospects leads to lower response rates

9. Further increase “productivity” through higher activity goals

10. C-suite breathes down managers’ neck, who is breathing down reps neck, as targets are missed week after week

11. BDRs (and manager) recognize the absurdity of the game they cannot possibly win, become disenchanted, lose trust in exec team and quit or leave sales entirely

Some may read this and think “well that’s just what being a BDR is”.

Wrong.

There is an alternative to this entire machine.

And it’s better for your sales culture BY FAR...

I’ve been saying the same thing for a while now.

And I'll keep saying it, haters be damned:
 
- Demand isn’t created by the BDR team, it’s captured

- With signals, website visits, automation, indirect lead flow through partnerships, you can capture 90% of the demand with 10% of the reps that your marketing activities are creating

- Buyers do all of their research on their own, and show up when they are ready to buy, so if you cut headcount (like myself and many others have), you won’t see your pipeline change

And that's just on the BDR side!

What about AEs?

Most series A/B startups could run with 50% less reps.

Instead of running the now-busted Salesforce playbook...

Feed a smaller pool of reps all the demand.

This leads to a fast-paced and fun culture, where everybody has the opportunity to crush it.

Yes, you will sacrifice “predictability”, but you will replace it with something more important... 

PROFITABILITY.

By only giving high-intent leads to your AEs, you set your sales machine up to serve your buyers, rather than you and your investors.

More activity + fewer reps = better sales culture.

It's time for a change.

Let's sell better.

rows.content:
I’ve scaled 3 sales organizations in 14 years. These are the 7 BIGGEST LIES I hear about scaling up sales teams at early stage startups:

1. Bigger teams mean faster growth

The opposite is true. The “Old Way” of building sales teams is a large internal org pushing on a string that appears to be “profitable-ish” but is really losing money. Why? Because it forces reps to use a prospecting playbook that doesn’t work in 2024 and is capturing (rather than creating) demand.

2. You can scale reps linearly and maintain productivity

This never works. In 2024, prospecting activity doesn’t CREATE demand, it CAPTURES it. Ask anyone who has rapidly grown a BDR org this year, only to see pipeline numbers unchanged. Most of the time unmeasured (thus unscaled) activities like brand and podcast are actually creating demand.

3. It’s good to have your AE’s prospect

Wrong. What works is to have your AEs calendars so full of demos that they have to stay up until 9pm every night dealing with follow-up but they don’t mind because they are making SO MUCH money. 

4. You need to compete on expensive perks to attract top talent

Not true. Great reps don’t care about your kombucha machine or unlimited PTO. The best reps want to work for a highly-ambitious company in a fast-paced environment that has a reputation for flooding reps with GOOD leads they can close.

5. "Predictable Revenue" is the goal

This model is predicated on building a massively inefficient assembly line of reps who execute a playbook that 100,000 other SaaS companies are also running. It creates a massive amount of waste in the name of "predictability" that wont come.

6. Ecosystem plays are for the big boys

Part of the “new way” of building hyper-lean sales orgs is to create/capture demand through developing agency/partner/influencer type ecosystems the second you hit PMF and use them to funnel low-in-funnel, declared-intent leads into your small team of highly-trained, senior reps to close with incredible velocity.

7. Founder brand isn’t important for me and my space

DTC ecomm really isn’t on Linkedin and yet I spend the last nine months posting daily and creating video content. It worked. Now we're creating a B2B product and it’s working even better. Downside: It’s *very* hard work and takes tons of time. But, there’s nothing like it. It’s the future.

TAKEAWAY

Most folks think scaling sales teams is about creating Predictable Revenue. 

They think sales creates demand and the more muscle they put behind it the faster they will grow. 

Because of this they hire too fast, don't train enough, and force salespeople to live and die (mostly die) by a playbook that doesn’t work anymore. 

They have no idea that they can set up an ultra-high-velocity sales machine that creates low-in-the-funnel leads from months and years of content that cuts through and indirect channels. 

The Predictable Revenue, “Push” model is dead.

The next generation of sales teams will get built the “new way”.

Within 4 years, we will bootstrap R!B2B into a $1B company with less than 10 full time employees. I recently sat down to sketch out the math (see screenshot). Here's how we'll get there:

BACKGROUND:

The TAM for our new B2B web visitor ID solution is extensive. Every single B2B website needs this. Our goal is to scale adoption; while maximizing profits and making it difficult for new entrants.

We plan to use our independence and profitability as leverage in our competitive strategy. As we would rather take 2 more years to hit to our goal than hire 50 more people to do it faster.

For a billion dollar valuation, we will assume a revenue multiple of 12x, which means we need to get to $83M ARR.

A few things stand out immediately.

A business like this needs to be (almost) entirely automated and have an extremely low CAC. It needs virality, immense demand, self serve, extreme PLG and a magical product experience.

Here's how we get there:

1. User Acquisition:

LinkedIn will remain our primary acquisition channel. We will use LinkedIn to generate demand, drive signups, schedule calls, and establish trust and credibility. So far our efforts have led to interest from 3,000+ accounts. We have ideas to scale this with referrals, influencers and advertising.
  
2. Pricing:

Our pricing will need to be simple and only month to month, so we can make it easy for users to downgrade or churn without talking to us. We have a single paid plan. The ridiculously generous free plan ensures that we become impossible to compete against. 
 
3. Support / Success:

We want to scale without hiring a large support team. We need a spotless self-serve portal for onboarding and support. Our team has been working tirelessly to generate content and train our chatbots. Last week we served 96% of our inquiries via bots and only 4% required human intervention.

4. Churn: 

I believe churn in SaaS is a direct result of the obsession to reduce churn at all costs. We will reduce churn by making it easy to churn. We will not be afraid to lose customers.

5. Sales/SDRs: 

We will not engage in outbound sales, hence no need for SDRs. We will have a couple of very senior enterprise reps and partnership folks in the team. 

6. Personality Traits: 

To prove our thesis, we want to get to $5M+ in ARR with just 5 FTEs. This involves us hiring seasoned professionals that are all around experts. Each of these hires will take on the responsibility of a full department. Each of us will be expected to generate demand on Linkedin, talk to customers and make product decisions.

7. FTEs (in the first 12m): 

Sales/Partnership (1), Support/Success (1), Growth/Monetization (1), Community/Influencers (1), Engineering (1). 

Sam Altman wants AI to create a one person Unicorn.

I haven't figured this out yet, but we will take a crack at creating a 10 person unicorn with a laser focus on automation and demand gen.

Of course, I'll be sharing regular updates on Linkedin.

Hope you follow along!

If you're over 40 you might not recognize this guy, but every serious entrepreneur needs to study him.

Here are 4 lessons I’ve learned from MrBeast that you should take with you and implement in everything you do, starting right now:


1) Success is not random or accidental

When talking about virality, everyone always puts the blame on the algorithm. 

“The algorithm made you famous”, etc.

Virality is not an accident. Success is not an accident.

MrBeast is proof that you can go viral again and again and again — if you have the right formula.

He’s spent over a decade developing an SOP for exactly how to get hundreds of millions of views and get the world to talk about you.


2) Choose your friends wisely

If you’re playing a big game and you don’t have friends that don’t point out your weaknesses, you’re never going to be as big as you’d like.

MrBeast had a posse of ragtag YouTubers who would review each others’ content and give brutally honest feedback about what could be better.

I shared an office with the JasperAI guys for a reason. We all gave each other feedback and helped each other grow.


3) Your content sucks. Sorry.
 
If you watch 1 of MrBeast’s videos, you immediately should feel humbled.

It’s like watching LeBron play basketball. There isn’t a person in the world who can make content the way he does — the way he engages an audience for as long as he does.


4) There is great joy in the pursuit of excellence

I listened to him on Joe Rogan, and he goes on for hours about how much he loves the idea of being the best.

He commits every hour he has to make better and better videos for his audience. It’s all he cares about.

He doesn’t want to be a billionaire like some do.

He doesn’t care about a 50,000-square-foot mansion and a 300-foot yacht.

If he wanted to be worth $5 billion, he could make two phone calls, sell his empire, and he’d have everything he wants.

But that’s not his pursuit.

His goal is to be the absolute best in the game of content.

And I believe he’s already there.

2023 killed the Predictable Revenue model. Response rates have dropped 50% and are getting worse. Does that mean the BDR is dead too? Absolutely not. Here’s what the future of the BDR role looks like:

BACKGROUND:

Here's how I view the trends in Outbound Sales (and the world in general): 

- Response rates are down b/c automated prospecting is growing exponentially
- Sales management combats lower response rates with higher activity targets
- AI generated “B- Sludge” puked out on every channel pours salt in the wound 

Meanwhile...

- Every day it gets easier for prospects to do their own research
- Authenticity (content with a unique POV) gets amplified in the AI world
- “Influencers” become larger and more valuable by the second

So here's my question:

In a world where prospects are doing their own research and the best, most authentic content is being served to the most people, who is doing demand creation and demand capture? 

Answer: BDR Influencers

What is an “Influencer”? 

Someone who has the skills to build an audience (or community) around a set of ideas - probably using video - whose name is known, whose face is trusted, and who has a unique point of view.

Here’s what a day in the life of a BDR in 2034 might look like: 

8:00-9:00am: Respond to comments on other peoples’ posts (and your own)
9:00-10:00am: Idea generation with the rest of the outbound sales team (all influencers)
10:00-11:30am: Write a longform LinkedIn post, record a YouTube video, AI edits and posts. 

11:30-1pm: Workout / lunch. 

1:00-3:00pm: Absorb other top performers’ content across networks, comment intelligently.
3:00-4:00pm: Analyze metrics of automated outbound machine, tweak, improve, etc.
4:00-4:30pm: Follow-up on positive replies, move prospects down funnel. 
4:30-5:00pm: Meet with team for second ideas session, share what was interesting from the day.

TAKEAWAY:

It’s 2024. 

The Predictable Revenue model has been dead for 18 months.
