I bootstrapped my startup to $22m ARR in 4 years. People tell me they would LOVE to bootstrap rather than take VC money, but they don’t know how. If you're at $0 MRR, here are 4 ways you can fund your startup:

1. EXCLUSIVELY Friends and Family.

The key here is to not let any institutional money into your angel round, and explain that you are intending to grow a solid, profitable software company. Go to the people who would fund a restaurant if you opened one. People who are betting on YOU as a person, not the idea or company.

2. Start a consultancy or agency to fund your SaaS.

SaaS is hard because you (usually) have to start at SMB and work your way up over time. It takes a LOT of $15/mo payments to pay salaries. Small consultancies or agencies are much easier to get to cash positive and will help you acquire some of the basic skills you need. 

Mailchimp, my favorite SaaS ever, started as an agency. Nathan Barry funded ConvertKit by selling eBooks. Russel Brunson funded Clickfunnels with InfoProducts. The list goes on.

3. Keep your job.

This is a little Gary Vee of me, but you can work nights and weekends to get an MVP and some initial customers off the ground. I would recommend not cutting off your income and going all-in on something until you see signs of product-market fit. Remember, it will take longer than you think!

4. Fund it with your (or your rich spouse’s) savings.

I happened to save a couple million bucks in my 20’s trading credit default swaps at Lehman Brothers. I realize that this didn’t happen to most people, but some people do have rich family members!

🚨 A word of warning... This is the MOST dangerous option, because however much money is available for a startup will get consumed by the startup (and more). If you are a first timer, there will likely be little to show for it in the end.

TAKEAWAY:

Building a SaaS startup is HARD.

It’s better to start your career as an entrepreneur selling something else.

Services and info products can help you hone basic skills like providing and charging for services, keeping customers happy, and collecting payment.

Once you crush another space, it may be time to turn to SaaS.

When you do, I hope you remember you wanted to bootstrap.

Because once you get on that VC treadmill, there is no getting off.

Kiss profitable growth goodbye.

99% of early-stage SaaS founders think they need VC capital to get to the next level. They’re wrong. What they ACTUALLY need is better product. Here’s my 7-part breakdown of what founders get wrong when they raise money:

1. They don’t realize word-of-mouth is the ONLY thing that matters

If your product isn’t growing on its own through word-of-mouth, you’re already dead, you just don’t know it yet. If it is, there are a million ways to speed it up. Sure, VC money may help with that, but it can't create what doesn't exist.

2. They don’t know what real product-market fit feels like

Trying to explain what PMF feels like to someone who hasn’t felt it is like trying to explain to a fish what it’s like to walk on the land. One day of true PMF is better than 100,000 words describing it. I know because I’ve now spent years on both sides.

3. They lie to themselves about their crappy products

So much of our identity and ego are tied to our amazing products and businesses that it’s *very* difficult to realize when you DON’T have PMF. You see founders who have been able to raise and raise again without true PMF, which makes everything look bigger, but now as the tide goes out, we’re seeing a lot of naked people.

4. They hire too many people before they have a repeatable sales model

I made this mistake several times - most recently in early 2023. Fortunately for me we had a ton of positive cashflow, but if we didn’t, this all-too-common urge would have led me to go out and raise money, only to burn through it all and end up back at the same place.

5. They get FOMO because their startup competitors are raising big rounds

This is the second dumbest mistake we all make. We don’t realize that STARTUPS DON’T KILL STARTUPS, they kill themselves. In almost all cases startups would have been better off keeping their head down and focusing on product than raising rounds because their “competition” did.

6. They think it will help them hire and close bigger deals

This is another LIE investors tell you to get you to transact. Do you know what will help you close bigger deals? A better product and a better sales process. What will help you hire better people? The reputation of having incredible PMF and great execution.

7. They want to feel rich

This is the DUMBEST mistake we all make that investors use against us. Even if we take zero or little secondary, and give investors preference with all sorts of controls, a big valuation makes us FEEL good about our beautiful business, even though it means nothing.

TAKEAWAY:

Institutional capital isn’t necessary to level-up a SaaS.

A great product will catapult you higher than you can imagine.

The problem is that most founders have no idea what a great product looks like

Cheap, abundant capital has kept mediocre SaaS alive for far too long.

Want me to show you what a great product looks like? 

Watch this video…

Then try NOT to join the waitlist here: https://lnkd.in/gknvUTM3

You build a much stronger foundation when you bootstrap

2. Always have a few experiments running that can be 1000x-ers.

Companies stop growing because the founders settle

5. Attend events

6. Spend aggressively, but reallocate quickly

I'm aggressive with spending money on growth

But as soon as the data says it's not working, cut it quickly and reallocate to something else

7. Keep making your core product better.

In the long run, this is the #1 most important thing

Having a great product is a cheat code that makes every other part of running the business easy

I bootstrapped 2 startups over the last 10 years. Here's the 5 non-secret secrets to scaling revenue when you don't have big VC money:

- You need to be working on your next “S” curve 
 
2. Keep making your core product better
 
- You can always get faster, easier, quicker time-to-value

- Your work is never done 
 
3. Come up with even more ways to deliver perceived value
 
- Hit people over the head with the value you generate
- Make sure they are seeing at it the same way you are
- There are other ways to provide value than $$$ 
- Can you educate them? Entertain them? Make something beautiful?
 
4. Be the leanest possible version of your current stage
 
- More people doesn’t mean faster - it usually means slower
- Lean has SO many benefits, culturally, financially, otherwise
- I don’t know how many times it will take me to learn this lesson
 
5. Invest in RevOps early
 
- You need to understand your metrics as you scale
- Where you deploy capital will soon become the most important thing
- I got this one completely wrong

You don't need to raise a billion dollars to build a great company.

In fact, sometimes that makes it much harder.

Ignore the pomp and circumstance.

Commit to the basics and then execute.

Every single day.

Dear SDRs and AEs, if you want to book a meeting with a B2B executive decision maker, here are 6 things you should NEVER do in your outreach:

1. Don’t send paragraphs about your solution, frankly they don’t care

2. Don’t share the number of users or awards you have, they really don’t care

3. Don’t share testimonials of your best customers, how does that help them??

4. Don’t invite them to a private event, they are way too busy

5. Don’t tell them you agree with their last post, they don’t believe you 

6. Don’t tell them you support the same sports team or love their school, they still don’t believe you

What you should do instead?

- Shift your focus from what you are selling to what problems the decision makers may be facing in their current role. Talk to others in their team to verify if possible

- Put in some effort into your outreach

- Send them an email outlining what you think may be their top priorities and how you can assist

- Convince them that you want to help solve the problems not just sell your solution

- Send them a few slide decks and a proposal of your solution 

- Ask for a 20 min call to review your proposed solution  

- Make the following promise before asking for a discovery call: (a) that you will use this time to not sell, (b) you will not use the call just to qualify them for future outreach, (c) you will commit resources to helping them with their priorities so they end up benefiting even if they don't buy your solution 

- Bring a senior AE or a decision maker to the call to demonstrate you respect their time

- Ask questions throughout the presentation and offer follow ups 

A lot of the AEs or SDRs will not make this required commitment 

The rest of you have an opportunity to differentiate yourself  

I don't see why any decision maker wont take this call  

If you win, you may end up having the first stab to the revenue.

If you lose, you may still end up developing a strong connection for the future.

When writing copy — it’s very easy to come off as desperate.

Instead:

Write like you’re writing to someone you’ve known for years.

It’ll put you in the mind frame of being comfortable with the way you write, which signals status and makes people respect you and trust you.

For example, I ‘could’ say:

“Hey there,
I’m Adam, the founder, and CEO of Robly!
Thanks for sending your first email with us. Myself and my team are happy to have you on board with us!
You are now a member of our family!
Don’t hesitate to ask me any questions and we’ll get back to you within 24 hours.
Yours truly,
Adam Robinson”

This is a “take me out of your system, I’m switching to Sendlane as we speak” email.

It’s trying too hard.

And it’s SO obvious that the purpose of this message is to be a little bit ‘too nice.’

It just feels like I’m about to ask for your credit card information. Yuck.

Write like you’re writing to a peer, and the person will feel like you’re a peer.

It’s a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Don’t be needy.

Don’t say too much.

And of course, have a little bit of fun with it.

That’s how you write high-converting copy.

Outbound sales tech vendors (like Salesloft, Outreach, ZoomInfo and Apollo) are stuck in a death spiral. Ironically, it’s their success that's killing them. 

Here's why the marquee B2B sales engagement/data firms have been cannibalizing the very industry they operate in and what comes next:  

1. It's the End of an Era

For a while dumb outbound worked. But now, everyone’s Inbox is wrecked. For 20 years companies have been running the Predictable Revenue Playbook, hiring teams of SDRs to blast messages. That’s why by the time you finish reading this post, I will have received another dozen unsolicited emails and phone calls that I will never read or respond to.

2. More activity is not the answer

Because of the increase in unsolicited emails, outbound has become much harder. Conversion rates, open rates, response rates, connect rates are all “down”, leading to a bigger increase in outbound activity. It's a vicious cycle.

3. Revenue Misalignment:

Companies that profit from increase in outbound activity will see decreased valuations as the industry eats itself up... unless they decide to reinvent and find new business models that ensure a decrease in outbound activity. 

4. ChatGPT Will Make It Worse:

With automated personalization, our ability to discern spam goes for a toss, leading to further decrease in response rates, conversion rates and open rates, thereby accelerating the death cycle.

So what’s the answer? 

Should we all stop doing outbound?

Far from it. 

We need to switch our approach and mindset. 

A decade ago, just sending bulk emails to decision makers was good enough. 

Then we used personalization to differentiate from the bulk outreach. 

Now personalization is becoming ineffective as well. 

In 2024, the key to outbound will be Signals, Triggers, Relevance and Context.  

For example: 

If you're starting a new campaign, don't define your audience as:

“VP of Marketing from $100M companies based in California”

Instead, look for:

 “VP of Marketing from $100M companies based in California that has: Visited my website, Met us at the event, Connected with my colleagues on Linkedin, demonstrated 3rd party intent, raised money, switched offices, 20+ new hires in sales team, social engagement, webinar attendees and as many more as you can find”.  

Outbound teams that have a Signals-first approach will win the future.

If Sales Tech companies are going to survive, they will have to reinvent themselves to ensure a decrease in dumb outbound and demonstrate an increase in contextual signals based outreach. 

Simply relying on their users to make this decision may not be enough.

Despite what you hear on Linkedin, the SDR role is NOT dead. 
By 2030, SDRs will be the most important team in any org. 
Here's what the future of the SDR role looks like:

In the last two decades, Sales has shifted from in person sales to mostly virtual and online sales. 

When SaaS started, most revenue came from net new businesses. 

Most of the demand for SaaS already existed and all you had to do was capture it before your competitors did. 

To help with this, companies hired a large number of SDRs.

A lot of the foundational salestech was built to accelerate the job of a SDR. 

But that was then...

Now, we are seeing the market shift from net new to competitive displacements. 

Which means almost everybody that needs tech already has it. 

SDRs and the role needs to evolve.

This means researching their prospects, identifying problems, proposing solutions and generating demand via actionable recommendations. 

Here's how this will change the SDR role:

SDR Teams in 2020:

- Young, inexperienced staff
- Not very familiar with Product, customer accounts or the market fit
- Not a thought leader in the space
- Focus on brute force outreach - phone or email
- Demand Capture (Tactical role)
- Generalized Role
- Only help top of the funnel

SDR Teams in 2030

- Senior, experienced staff with Analyst, Product, Consulting or Sales background
- Powerhouse of information. Intimately familiar with product & customer domains. 
- Thought leader in the space and trusted by prospects
- Signal and Trigger based outreach. Social, Events and Webinar channels to engage with prospects 
- Demand Creation via Problem Identification and Solutions Exploration  (Strategic role) 
- Specialized Roles (Competitive Intel, Key Account Intel, Signals, Solutions and Business Case)  
- Help throughout the funnel and deal cycle. 

SDR teams are not going away

The way we identify opportunities will change.

But if you are a SDR today, you have a bright future ahead. 

Play the long game. 

Choose a market and become an expert in that domain

Ignore the naysayers on Linkedin.

SDRs aren't going anywhere.
rows.hook: Despite what you hear on Linkedin, the SDR role is NOT dead.

I got my nuts kicked in during 1H23, but still somehow managed to grow Retention.com (profitably) from $15,000,000 to $20,000,000 ARR.

Here are the 6 biggest startup lessons I learned trying to go as fast as possible… and running into a brick wall:


1. No matter your revenue numbers, run a tight ship or the cash will dry up. 

Coming into 2023, I was desperate to get the brand EVERYWHERE. I sponsored newsletters, events and podcasts with no clear ROI. We hired as many people as we could as fast as we could (with zero regard for titles and comp packages). And I watched us go from generating $700k free cash to almost $0 for six straight months. That was all so dumb. I hate not making money. We fixed it this quarter. 


2. It’s far better to have a company with less employees and flood them with activity than to have a ton of people with a bunch of spare capacity (even if it means sacrificing some top-line growth).


3. Other people's playbooks are inspiration rather than prescription. 

I made the mistake of assuming that since the large Shopify apps like Klaviyo and Yotpo were able to make the BDR model work, that we would be able to do the same. WRONG. Every business is different. What worked for them isn’t necessarily going to work for us.


4. Organic social media is an effective method for generating awareness, but you have to be intentional about it. 

Last October I started posting on Linkedin every single day. The GOOD NEWS is we generated a ton of attention. The BAD NEWS is most of those people had no idea what we do. Now, I'm working on building the exact audience we want and creating content specifically for our buyers, rather than chasing followers.


5. To remain bootstrapped, we need to have higher ROI standards. 

We can’t spend the same amount of cash with the same output as companies who have raised $50-100M. We have to be more creative with how we do events, sponsorships, sales, literally everything.


6. Never forget who you are. 

I want to run a business that I look at and say “that’s an awesome f*cking business”. So, what does that look like? High revenue per employee. Insane monthly cash flow numbers. A culture that is fast-paced and addicted to activity. And healthy growth...between 50-100% per year. In Q1, we were the opposite of all this. But, we’re getting back to who we are. By the end of the year, we'll check each one of those boxes.

Looking back, the videos were ridiculous.

Just get started.

Put your message out there. 

Try to cut through the noise and catch some attention.

Be silly, try things other's wont, and innovate.

You can refine it later, but put V1 out there and see how the market reacts.

Don't overcomplicate it.

You'll never "be ready".

Just go for it.

I’ve been getting hate on LinkedIn because people think I’m saying outbound sales is dead. So let me be clear... Outbound sales is NOT dead! But the old “Predictable Revenue” model used by most SaaS companies is. 

Here are 6 reasons why we need a new outbound playbook for 2024:

1. Inboxes are completely destroyed

My co-founder texted me this morning and asked how I can possibly manage all of the prospecting emails that we get blasted with every day. The answer? I can't. 99.9% get deleted or ignored. 

2. LinkedIn inboxes might be even worse

Despite LinkedIn’s attempts to control the spam on the platform, my inbox here is just as bad if not worse than email. I had 4,200 incoming connection requests in the last 3 weeks and 70% of the new messages I get are pitches.

3. The number of SDRs has grown exponentially 

Predictable Revenue was a GREAT book (I read it many times) and it birthed an SDR industry on the back of the idea that pipeline generation can be accomplished through assembly-line tactics, and more bodies = more rev. This was true. It's no longer the case.

4. Automation tools and $12 domains made everything worse

People have replaced the ideas of resonance and relevance (quality) with VOLUME (quantity) as their primary goal of an outreach program, which combined w/ #3 has led to #1.

5. AI tools are sweeping the leg

Every day more and “better” messages are being created by large language models, getting stuck into #4 by #3, leading to #1

6. Teams got scaled too big because you can measure their output

A booked demo can be measured, so if you want more of them, you add more bodies. My argument is that you can capture the same amount of demos with 20% of the bodies.

TAKEAWAY:

In 2023, buyers aren’t responding to cold outreach like they used to. 

I know a dozen founders who have scaled back their BDR teams and have seen no change in pipeline generation (me included).

Why? 

Because in the Predictable Revenue days, demand was created by SDRs, because the channels available to them weren’t ruined.

In today’s world, SDR’s are (mostly) an expensive and inefficient way of capturing existing demand.

The new playbook for building SaaS revenue machines in 2024 involves creating content, driving indirect leads through ecosystem and partners, and running a super-lean in-house sales team whose outreach is driven by inbound and high-value intent data.

Outbound is alive and well...

But SDR's prospecting cold leads IS dead.

The Two Opposing LinkedIn Audience Building Strategies (explained in 60 seconds):

THEIR WAY: 

- Create posts around generic topics that LinkedIn loves…
- Work-life balance, hiring, mental health, LinkedIn leadgen, AI, checklists
- Ghostwriters are used (most of the time)
- Join engagement circles or hire engagement service to “get in feeds” 
- Post viral content over meaningful content (think memes)
- Have no intention about who the actual members of your audience are
- Do not reply to comments on your own post
- Stay away from work in public, share only wins but not losses
- Use someone else or AI to reply to other peoples’ posts
- Do not analyze quality of your own audience
- The goal is to grow followers to the highest number possible

OUR WAY: 

- Create the best hook possible for that given post
- Write every line so that the reader will be compelled to continue
- Wrap up the post with something coy to create a dopamine hit
- Zero involvement in engagement circles or artificial post inflation
- Affinity is built through true thought leadership and meaningful content
- Know exactly which audience each post will reach (Founder, Sales, Marketing)
- Create talking head videos for most posts to build a stronger connection
- Be wildly transparent about the journey, share numbers and mistakes
- Answer every single comment yourself
- Have high percentage of your audience in the ICP (75% for me)
- Goal is to drive quantifiable sales outcomes (booked demos, signups)

TAKEAWAY:

Agencies tell you they can ghostwrite and grow your followers with just 1 hour of your time a week. 

They can, and they will. 

It’s one way to start building your brand, and you can see SOME benefit.

Here’s the problem... 

The best case outcome is that you’re “well known”. 

I believe the power of LinkedIn is the opposite. 

If you create the best content, and figure out how to reach your ICP, you can become “known well”, which is a far more powerful level of trust.

Trust = brand. 

In 2024, brand is built one post (and one comment) at a time.

Just 12 weeks post-launch, RB2B crossed $600k ARR. Sounds great, right? Tomorrow we're going to make a move that will cut our revenue by +50%. Here's why I couldn't be MORE EXCITED about it:

BACKGROUND:

- We “accidentally” launched our person-level identity product on March 1
- We tried to give the leads and a push to slack away for free
- We wanted to charge $495 for integrations, but you can parse the slack block
- Our free-to-paid conversion rate is only 1.3%

I have written a few posts about how our pricing is broken. 

- It’s broken for smaller businesses because it’s too expensive 
- It’s broken for larger businesses because we don’t have an ICP filter yet
- It’s broken for everybody because no one knows what to do with the leads

The solution (thank you LinkedIn) is:

- Give the product away for free to 85-90% of the market
- Cap the free plan, force larger businesses to pay for leads
- Build the ICP filter as quickly as possible

Here’s the first PROBLEM with that plan:

We currently have 110 paying customers.

In order to avoid confusion - and do the right thing - we’re going to:

- Drop people down in price who fall into a lower plan
- Not jack the price up on people who JUST started paying us $495

Here’s the second (much LARGER) problem:

- 35% of our 110 customers are going to drop from $495 to $119/mo
- Another 30% are dropping from $495 to $249/mo

That’s going to decimate our ARR.

Especially because I don’t have the confidence to raise prices at the high-end yet, even though I have a very strong feeling that most of our highest-volume customers are getting value well beyond $495.

So why am I excited? 

1. We’ve spoken to 100s of users. I believe this pricing change, combined with the two-touch sales motion we’re putting in place could 5x our conversion rate.

2. I think we can implement PLG for low-value users at these lower price point and get touch-free conversions (but … they will be very high churn)

TAKEAWAY:

$600k ARR in 12 weeks has been nothing short of amazing.

Having to then make a move that will take revenue down by 50% feels terrible.

I’m not sure my younger self could stomach a move like this one.

(For anybody $500k-$1m ARR - could YOU chop it 50% and sleep at night?)

Early on Santosh and I declared that at RB2B we would not make decisions optimized for revenue.

Instead, we would optimize for: 

1. User growth 
2. Low time-to-value
3. Eliminating friction

Looking back, I think my younger self was playing not to lose.

No I want to play to win.

When you have the ability to look past revenue and optimize for user base and viral expansion…

That’s the global domination mindset.

I asked the President of the fastest-growing Shopify store on the planet (with a $150M run-rate) what the biggest problem with DTC email marketing was. His answer is packed with insane insight. 

I spoke with Ben Yahalom, the President of True Classic last week.

Here's what he said: 

“I don’t think brands realize how much of a *SIGNAL GAP* there is between Meta and Klaviyo. Apple has been clamping down on the ability to track people. First it was iOS14, which crushed the ability for Meta to track people across websites. Then, as of a couple months ago, Apple made it so that Meta and Klaviyo could only track people for seven days MAX. 

The problem is that there are a bunch of things happening on the Shopify store (like cart abandonments) that due to Apple’s changes, aren’t making it to Meta and Klaviyo. The easiest thing to do to improve performance in Email Marketing is to focus on doing whatever you can to close the *SIGNAL GAP* between Shopify and Klaviyo.”

So important he said it twice...

The SIGNAL GAP.

That's the biggest problem facing DTC email marketing.

So...

How do you solve the signal gap? 

1. Build a 1st party cookie pool through server-side tracking
2. Facilitate cross-device identification

The fastest growing Shopify store on the planet is focused on closing the SIGNAL GAP.

Are you?

Last week Clark Barron wrote a hit piece about rb2b.com, making four serious accusations. Here's why he's wrong and my point-by-point response:

1. This is a wholesale assault on data privacy and will lead to a dystopian future

2. Our technology skirts existing privacy legislation in the US

3. That by operating exclusively in the US, we are doing something wrong by not subjecting our technology or its users to GDPR

4. I am preying on “SAAS bros that are too naive and dumb to have any ethics yet” who are “growth obsessed lunatics”

This is one side of the data privacy argument, and while I believe that they are untrue, I respect those who hold these beliefs.

Here are my responses:

1. This is a wholesale assault on data privacy. 

Google and Facebook know who is on your site - the exact individual - and charge you for the privilege of targeting them. Why should small business and startups not be able to make money off the same information? This is what our customers think. It’s hard for extreme privacy advocates to believe this, but it’s true.

2. Our technology skirts the existing privacy legislation in the US. 

This is factually untrue. Our technology is 100% compliant with all federal and state rules and regulations. Clark states that it’s “technically” legal in the us. That concept doesn’t exist. Either something is legal or it isn’t. I am a law abiding citizen, so are our customers. If this becomes illegal, we will stop doing it. If it were to become legal in Europe, we would do it there too. 

3. We are doing something wrong or exploiting a loophole by not operating in Europe.

We don’t operate in Europe because GDPR says that we cannot. If GDPR said we could, we would operate there. If the US, or a state, says we can’t do this, we will stop. This is not exploiting a loophole. We are operating legally in jurisdictions that permit it. 

4. I’m preying on “SaaS Bros” who are too stupid to know what I’m doing.

First of all, I am a SaaS bro. I created a product for myself. It’s valuable to me and my business. When it started working, we gave it to other people. They thought it was valuable also. Our customers aren’t naive. They just believe something different. This is a political debate, akin to many hot button issues in the US.

TAKEAWAY:

We sell polarizing technology. 

The very definition of “polarizing” is that it divides people into sharply contrasting sets of beliefs.

And like with anything polarizing, there is a loud vocal minority who disapprove of what we're doing.

That's OK.

Because one fact remains unchanged...

Our technology is 100% compliant.

The rest of the heated debate is just that... debate.

Which I welcome.

New tech is bound to attract detractors.

If you do not agree with me, I respect that. 

I’m not trying to change your mind. 

I just want you to know that many, many people disagree.

And that is their right.

Calling them idiots isn't going to win you any friends.

Word-of-mouth is like a cheat code for your business.

It can have customers knocking at your door, wanting to pay $10K per month on annual contracts (speaking from experience here).

But how do you generate it? Here are 3 simple strategies:

1) Create a WIN-WIN-WIN offer

The person referring wins. The new customers win. You win.

2) Be ultra-generous with refunds

I believe in ‘karma’ when it comes to this stuff. If someone’s asking for a refund, just give it to them quickly. It will come back to you down the line.

3) Systematically give out gifts to people who help you

If someone refers us a deal, I’ll send them a pair of AirPod Max’s. A $530 gift.

Again, I believe it will come back around to us.

Is there anything that you’ve done that has helped accelerate word of mouth? Let me know in the comments or DMs.

In 2020, my startup went from $0-$1M ARR with a controversial growth hacking strategy. Here's the highest ROI Facebook ad we ran and the story behind the social campaign that saved the company:

BACKSTORY:

In early 2020, Covid had just hit.

The world had gone into lockdown.

My SaaS was in its infancy and we had a handful of large event clients cancel contracts overnight.

50% of our revenue disappeared.

I didn’t know if we were going to survive.

Then I had a crazy idea.

I noticed more people taking selfie videos and posting them on Instagram.

So I thought... What if I could make a weekly 60 second selfie video every week with my wife that was:

- Amusing
- Had a different background
- Answered the top 3 sales questions

We did a couple of these “It’s Adam and Helen again, week [X] of lockdown” with masks around our necks, in a different part of our house.

They did okay, but with this video, I had a breakthrough.

Facebook LOVES controversy.

I knew I needed to lean into it however I could.

Fortunately for me, there are some very controversial aspects about our core product.

We identify anonymous web traffic and can resolve them to email addresses, even if someone doesn’t fill out a form.

There is a very loud minority of people who think this practice is horrible.

Not only that, I figured out that they will call you a SCUMBAG, a CRIMINAL and a THIEF in the comments.

Facebook LOVES that even more!

So, what did I do?

I leaned into it.

We created ads that I KNEW they would hate.

When the ads went live people started attacking me and I fired insults right back at them…

…from the BRAND account!

This made their heads explode.

My idea was that we didn’t have a brand to destroy, so who cares.

The pissed off people would write another novel length comment back, I’d fire back at them, and meanwhile, this type of inflammatory dialogue is Facebook’s favorite thing ever, and the ad would absolutely crush.

What happened next?

I created new ads based on the inflammatory comments from the last post.

The campaign took on a life of its own.

People WERE anticipating the ads every week.

And new customers and leads rolled in.

This whole process ended up lasting less than a year.

The ads eventually just stopped working.

But the company was saved.

And we hit $1M ARR shortly after.

–

Disclaimer: I would NEVER do anything like this at our current stage.

We actually do have a brand to destroy and an image to uphold.

I just want you to know how hard it is to go from $0-$1M.

And what you have to be prepared to do to get there.

$1-$10M is easier.

$10-$20M is easier than that.

But $0-$1M???

That’s the hardest thing there is.

Get creative or die.

Two weeks ago 🏄‍♂️ Scott Leese told me, “Outbound sales, as we know it, is dead.” Here’s why Scott thinks he’s only got 3-4 years left as a sales consultant (and what the future of B2B sales looks like):

1. The trend in response rates is going one way… DOWN.

The biggest objection I get when I say “the Predictable Revenue model is dead” is “YOU'RE AN IDIOT because you have a $25k ACV and outbound sales never should have worked for that anyway.” 

It’s undeniable response rates are down 50% the last 18 months. Let’s say that wiped out my $25k deal and now the floor is $50k. What do you think happens over the NEXT 18 months? 

Response rates will be down ANOTHER 50%. So now we’re at 100k floor. 

What about 18 months after that? Down ANOTHER 50%. 

Now we’re at a $200k floor for outbound. 

How many reps employed today sell something under $200k? 

Almost everyone.

2. Usage of traditional channels is going one way… DOWN. 

Scott and I both have our ringers off 24/7 and don’t use the phone at all. We both only read emails from people we know, and don’t even look at emails from people we don’t know.

Wait for the next generation. Scott has a 14 and 16-year-old, who literally NEVER use email, don’t text, and communicate with Snap and Insta DM only. 

We’re currently seeing cracks in the foundation, but soon a generational change will lead to collapse.

3. Fewer buyers are interested in speaking to salespeople every day.

Scott told me that he just purchased a $1.1m investment property in Chicago without speaking to a single person. He brought up that Amazon is crushing every mom and pop store because you can sit on your couch, press a few buttons, and get anything you want. 

Old dogs on LinkedIn (and I’m 43) insist people want to talk to people. 

I think they’re wrong.

TAKEAWAY:

Outbound Sales, as we know it, is on the brink of collapse.

It’s not IF, it’s a matter of WHEN. 

What’s the future of B2B sales look like?

We’re entering an era where sales teams will act more like editorial teams.

It’s a NEW MODEL centered around creating MAXIMALLY AUTHENTIC content that meets the buyers on the platforms they’re living on.

Teams will be much smaller, with WAY bigger reach. 

They’ll be scaling human-to-human connection.

Sales teams will have one “builder” who will constantly be working on the machine that listens to signals from the content engine and nudges prospects down the funnel, capturing them when they’re ready to buy.

Sales cycles will be shorter because the awareness, education, and nurturing will be virtually zero-touch.

These teams will be lean, hyper-efficient, and fun to work for, because reps are basically artists who spend most of the day creating and only speaking to prospects when they’re ready to buy.

The sales leaders of tomorrow will either be able to: 

1. Build audience over organic social media
2. Engineer scalable signal-based selling machines

If you can’t do one of those two things, you’re walking the plank.

I gave my 4th keynote of Q224 at SaaSFest. As I came down from the stage, a CMO of a $40M ARR SaaS asked me, “How many leads do you get from doing all these talks?” His jaw dropped when I told him the truth: 

“I have no idea.” 

I proceeded to explain to this CMO that: 

- 75% of work week is spent on content, podcasts, keynotes, and webinars
- I have no idea what any individual thing I spend my time on is doing 
- I am optimizing for “human-to-human connection”… which can’t be measured

Here’s how the rest of the conversation went down: 

CMO: 75% of your time is spent on content? Aren’t you the CEO of two startups? How can you make that happen? 

ME: It’s giving more back to me than anything ever has. I have a great team who handles what I would normally do. Plus, we’re bootstrapped. No board, no fundraising cycles.

CMO: What do you mean you have no idea what the impact is?

ME: I mean exactly that. I spend 5-8 hours per week on random peoples’ podcasts. I have literally no idea what is coming from that. I can see the analytics of a LinkedIn post. I have no idea what digging into my deepest pain and sharing it with the world is doing. I have no idea what spending an extra hour per week recording video is doing. We have a weekly live webinar called Inbound-Led Outbound. I have no idea if or how that is translating into any type of users or revenue. I’m trying to do a bunch of keynotes. I do not know or care if anyone in the audience is signing up. 

CMO: What do you mean you are “optimizing for human-to-human connection?” 

ME: I create content to maximize humanity and authenticity. I am bringing them along on my journey. I’m sharing things that no one else is willing to share. I’m putting my face out there, so people feel like they know me and how I speak. I’m making the 3rd season of a fu*king DOCUSERIES about it all. You can’t measure the success of ANY of that. 

CMO: If you can’t measure it, why are you doing it?

ME: Because I believe that the most powerful forces in the universe cannot be measured.

CMO: [HEAD EXPLODES]

TAKEAWAY:

People love to measure things. 

Problem #1 with measuring things is that you start optimizing for those things. 

Problem #2 is that the most powerful things - H2H connection, in my case - can’t be measured.

If I started trying to measure different parts of my plan, the content I put out would look and feel completely different than it does today. 

Would I have more followers? 

Maybe.

Would I have more random people (not in my ICP) commenting “100%” and “Fire” on my posts? 

Absolutely.

Would I feel known and trusted by an increasingly large percentage of the individuals in my ICP every day? 

No way!

What I’m doing is driving a much deeper, more powerful type of trust. 

But it’s a type of trust that can’t actually be measured.

One thing’s for sure though. 

Trust = brand.

In 2024, brand is built one post at a time.

After 5 months of getting smacked by the slowdown, crushed by churn and devastated by downsizing, I am *finally* confident Retention.com has turned the corner. Here’s what I’m proud of (and not so proud of) that happened in August: 

Proud of:

- We crossed a major milestone - $20m ARR in Baremetrics
- We’re back in the black! Out of the PAINFUL breakeven period
- We are building an increasingly deep understanding of the 60-day contraction problem that was the major headwind since April and cleaning up the core business
- We have made a handful of pricing changes that we believe will change pricing from a headwind to a tailwind
- We are in beta for a $77/mo PLG product aimed at smaller Shopify stores
- We have big early enthusiasm for our product for B2B sales teams (DM me)
- We have a lean and mean, super high velocity sales motion and reps who are drowning in demand and the size feels great
- I have figured out how to write some viral Linkedin posts that could REALLY help with our B2B demand generation

Not so proud of:

- I was hoping to report our monthly growth rate was increasing again (it didn’t)
- We got smacked by a huge legacy publisher contraction and non-core churn that put us back at the 3-ish% total topline growth rates we have been seeing
- We don’t have the analytics yet to look at the core annual subscription rev which we know looks great from Salesforce but can’t see yet
- I HATE the messaging on our website, which is totally my fault
- Our RevOps isn’t yet at the state where we need it to be, despite pushing hard
- Despite massive progress on the customer journey, it is clear that we are under-resourced post-sale, which is leading to some sub-optimal customer experiences

Biggest Opportunities: 

- Santosh is starting full-time today! He’s going to help us improve operational rigor, own the PLG motion on the DTC side, and help with many strategic aspects of the B2B biz
- We hired Charlie to help us with our product marketing, which has been a massive gap
- By the end of September we will be able to look at analytics by revenue type
- We should be getting valuable customer feedback on the B2B product and PLG DTC product that should help us with targeting and messaging
- I will be further honing my Linkedin skills to create maximum awareness through founder brand in the new B2B universe we will be targeting
- We should start generating $350k+ free cash as the months go on (phew!)

August wasn’t as good as I wanted it to be. 

I truly hoped to report a higher growth rate from a higher total revenue number. 

While I can’t report that, I do believe that we’ve turned the corner. 

We’re back on track to be the lean, mean, very profitable and rapidly scaling company that I have always sought to create.

Sometimes it’s the darkest before dawn.

Hang in there, keep building.

Will 6sense have to do a massive Twitter-style layoff by 2026? Here’s my take on why 6Sense is a “Fake Unicorn” and MY detailed 23/24 P&L (so you know where I’m coming from):

To set the stage: 

Last month 6Sense put out a press release about crossing $200m ARR.

They said they grew revenue +40% last year, and I hear they are shooting for +30% this year.

What the article DIDN’T say is that: 

1. 6Sense has raised a total of $526m to create that $200m ARR 
2. The last $100m was Venture Debt in June of 2023 - the legalized equivalent of loan sharking
3. I hear that they are going to BURN $25m this quarter

And as a kicker, the plan is to IPO next year.

As you can tell from looking at MY P&L, none of this makes sense to me. 

Unless I am doing the math wrong, 6Sense’s “Rule of 40” is currently -10.

I believe that 6Sense is in a very dire situation.

Here’s the THREE THINGS 6Sense can do to survive, and what will happen if this plan fails.

___

BACKSTORY:

In the fall, I was an outsider to B2B. 

I started asking people about the landscape of ABM tech. 

The first thing I heard was: 

“6Sense created a ‘Dark Funnel’ narrative that hypnotized the CMO community. They all bought the tech. The dirty little secret is the tech just doesn’t do what they say it does. Hardly anyone makes money.” 

That sounds strange to hear for the first time.

But when you say it to someone who has been in B2B for a while, you watch as heads nod.

Another weird thing is the fact that their G2, Glassdoor, and Gartner presence is 95% positive, but when I post ANYTHING about 6Sense it elicits a 95% negative response.

Here is what you will NEVER hear when you ask around:

“6Sense is a great product.” 

___

So 6Sense is burning uncontrollably and needs to pull a rabbit out of their hat to survive.

What would I do if I were in this position?


Step 1: 

I would fly around to industry events and CMO meetups to deliver the following message: 

“We figured it out. We’re crushing it this year with OUTBOUND.  And it’s ALL BECAUSE OF OUR OWN TECH!!!!”

The community of CMOs eats the message up. 

Finally there is a solution to the SaaS Pipeline Crisis.


Step 2: 

As the community turns into pipeline, I would oversell an unattainable dream.


Step 3: 

I would send all customers early renewal notices stating that the price of 6Sense is about to increase by 3x. 

If the recipient loses their mind (like yours truly), I would offer flat extensions. 

If they did not, I would get the knives out and butcher whoever I could.

____

6Sense may be able to hit their 2024 goals by: 

- Spreading the narrative that they figured Outbound out (and it’s their tech)
- Overselling EVEN MORE than in prior years, and 
- Raising prices on current customers with a ferocity never seen before

Even if they do, where does that put their “Rule of 40”? 

Somewhere between 0 and 10?

Is THAT an IPO profile in 2025? 

But what if, and here’s the REAL kicker…

I recently interviewed the former President of Kajabi, Jonathan Cronstedt, who took the company from $6M to $100M ARR and a $2B valuation in just 5 years.

When you build a company that big, you learn a thing or two about attracting quality talent and keeping them satisfied.

What Jonathan taught me was that an employee's satisfaction is directly tied to how deeply they connect with the company’s values and vision.

This is where people derive meaning and purpose from their work.

And we’re seeing the consequences play out in real-time.

We need an entirely different go-to-market playbook, which recognizes that demand is created differently than in the days of Salesforce.

We need incentives to change - from investors down to execs down to sales leaders - that stop reinforcing this behavior and leads to over-hiring and under-growing.

We need to understand that revenues will be less “predictable”, but we get to trade predictability for profitability, job stability, and happy salespeople.

It’s time to do things in a new way.

Today I'm taking a break from my normal GTM posting to answer an important question. Did Houthi rebels cause the recent LinkedIn, Facebook and Instagram outage? And what is the risk for US internet? My (long) investigation:

BACKGROUND: 

A week ago, it was reported that three cables under the Red Sea that provide internet have been cut by the Houthi rebels in Yemen.  The internet cable connected Europe to the Middle East and India. Because of this 25% of traffic between Asia and Europe was redirected to other networks causing immense congestion and delays.

Can this happen to the cables coming into the US ? 

- If you look at the map of submarine cables, you see there’s no 1-2 cables that can be cut to disrupt internet service in the US. Several cables would need to be cut in Atlantic and the Pacific
- US internet traffic can be routed through Canada or Mexico if cables are cut 
- In a situation like this the costs will rise but Satellite providers can allocate additional bandwidth causing minimal disruption
- Furthermore, most content and servers in the US for tech companies are located within the country. So any disruption outside will not cause a problem to our local services 

How easy is it to cut a submarine cable? 

- Not easy at all! It’s much easier to do DDoS attack than destroy cables. 
- You have to cut the cable 6000m under the sea (deepest any human has dived has been 240 meters). So this is not a job for a lone terrorist!
- Cables are pretty tough to cut. They were designed to tolerate seismic activity and withstand hostile environments and extreme temperatures.
- A motivated player with state support can definitely cut a submarine cable 

What is the connection between the LinkedIn outage with this undersea cable ?

- The disruption is certainly not limited to social only, other service providers including Google have been down as well 
- All these service providers likely have servers in the US. However, to deal with the Red Sea issue, they must have re routed their global traffic causing stress to their network causing the outage 
- There is a small possibility that these two incidents were unrelated and the outage was a result of a cyber attack or a human error like the one that caused the outage in 2021 in meta 

International laws are the weakest link in addressing this problem:

- In Feb 2023, two Chinese vessels severed cables in East China Sea. While There is no direct evidence they did this intentionally, Taiwanese officials claim this was part of Chinese harassment. 
- For cables that are sabotaged in international waters, there is currently no  regime to hold the perpetrator of damage responsible.

IN SUMMARY:

Did the Houthi's cause the LinkedIn outage?

It's unclear! But likely...

Will we continue to face disruption to global internet services?

Absolutely.

As the number of states and proxies on global conflict increase, the likelihood of such incidents happening are going to steadily rise.

Five years ago, I was stuck. We just couldn’t get past $3M ARR.

An opportunity came up that would help me get the leads that I was chasing forever.

This guy had been let go of another company and was putting together a program that his former company had created.

He was under a non-compete but we thought we were fine to move forward because of how non-competes worked in California. A few months later, the former company sued us and we quickly learned that everything was NOT fine…

Here are 4 critical lessons I learned from that experience:

✅ If you don’t want to get sued, respect non-compete agreements.
✅ In America, anyone can sue you for anything. Why? Because it’s America, baby!
✅ When you’re new to the startup business world, it can feel a bit like a David vs Goliath scenario. Be very careful when poking the bear, especially if that bear is a Goliath.
✅ If you ever do get sued, get out of the situation ASAP. Even if it means settling for more than you’d like. It’s not worth the mental pain and anguish.

Hope me sharing my experience helps you avoid a situation like that.

In 2012, when I joined ZoomInfo as the VP Product, Growth & Strategy, they were stuck at $9M ARR. When I left 5 years later, we were at over $80M ARR.

Here’s the 5-step GTM playbook we used to get unstuck and build the foundation to scale:

Step 1: Develop contrarian products that satisfy unmet demand

- Most companies can't convince themselves to radically innovate
- In 2012, data companies were selling CSVs, no one was investing in product
- We took massive risk and doubled down on building products to streamline data delivery
- We started to "look different" from the space
- Sometimes it's better to "look different" than "be better"

Step 2: Focus on SMB or lower end of the market

- Market disruption always happens at the low end
- As a small company, it’s difficult to compete for your competitor’s best customers
- Instead aim your efforts at the customers your competitors would give up without a fight
- We focused on the SMB and lower mid market with a self-serve product at a low price
- Everyone else was fighting for the more lucrative enterprise customers

Step 3: Increase Prices, Decrease Churn, Add Features Rapidly

- We rapidly developed features that gave GTM teams ammo for upgrades
- With new products, we could add a new line item in the invoice and post growth with relative ease
- New features also gave us the reason to reach out to customers to talk about upsell
- All this was predicated on our ability to develop a sustained product roadmap with a strong understanding of the impact on GTM and our ability to attach growth initiatives to every small feature release

Step 4: Intentionally Design Market Expansion for Virality

- Nonlinear growth comes from getting the inbound engine started early
- At first, we went after the spray and pray approach with some automation, which worked well
- However, our revenues exploded when we started getting strategic with TAM and went after market niches, especially the ones that were ignored by other B2B data vendors
- This allowed us to dominate multiple small verticals and as we got popular within those verticals it resulted in word of mouth - virality, inbound inquiries and increased retention contributing to the non linear growth

Step 5: Cultivate a Leader's Mindset

- Startups are often fighting just to stay afloat - this creates chaos, panic & unrest in organizations
- By switching the mental model from a survival mindset to a leader's mindset, you can switch from a perpetual struggle for revenue growth to attempting to decimate competitors
- You switch from being a price follower to becoming a price setter in the long run
- This mindset provides a purpose, a better decision making framework, and results in a much healthier business and work culture

TAKEAWAY:

Markets are always evolving, and every market can be disrupted.

Any business can get unstuck.

The specific plays required to disrupt the B2B data market would be different today, but the ZoomInfo playbook's principles are timeless.

I bootstrapped 3 startups in 13 years. Here are the 3 BIGGEST failures of my startup career:

1. “Robly Authorized Partners” (2017)

My first startup Robly was email marketing software. 

We were stuck at $3m ARR for 5 year and I had no idea what to do. 

Our original GTM motion was marketing to Constant Contact customers. 

In 2017, Constant Contact was acquired by Endurance and they killed a boots-on-the-ground program they invested 10’s of millions of dollars in called their Authorized Local Expert program shortly thereafter. 

Soon after, one of the senior leaders reached out to me with an idea.

We attempted to absorb the program and failed miserably. 

It turns out it was a great program as a branding play for a company as large as Constant Contact, but didn’t make sense from a unit economics perspective for a company as tiny as ours. 

To add insult to injury, I got sued for hiring the former leader during his non-compete. 

2. Lead(.)com (2018)

I hired my now co-founder Diana Ross to do some consulting for me to figure out how I might get my $3m ARR SaaS un-stuck. 

She believed that there was space above Mailchimp and below Salesforce Marketing Cloud to create and market a mid-market Email Newsletter app. We spent a year building it, and I did a deal with a friend in the domain space to lease the domain Lead(.)com. 

We were going to “launch” at the Traffic & Conversions Summit in 2018, having almost finished the platform. We pulled a big stunt that involved promo girls in Lead(.)com clothes walking around to everybody at the conference (a mostly male demographic) asking them, “How big is your list?” 

No one cared. 

I was devastated, having wasted a year and a million bucks of salaries building software that we literally just threw away.

3. Retention.com and the “Billion Dollar Challenge” (2023)

In late 2022, we honed in on our ICP. We started scaling up our go-to-market engine and everything was flying, WAY faster than expected. I was confident that we had a unicorn on our hands. 

So confident that I made a 2 season docuseries called “Billion Dollar Challenge”, declaring that we would hit $50m ARR (up from $15M) by the end of the year. 

We oversold, over-hired, and our churn ended up being WAY worse than I thought. Instead of $50m ARR, we ended up hitting $22m.

You may say that growing from $15-$22m ARR (bootstrapped) is still really good, especially in 2023, and you would be right, however...

When you publicly call your shot at $50m…

And you confidently make a docuseries about the journey… 

And you end up with UNDER HALF the ARR… 

That’s an epic fail. 

But, you know what they say. 

What doesn’t kill you makes you stronger.

Keep building.

In 14 months, I bootstrapped my SaaS Startup from $10M-$20M ARR (half the time it took me to go from $1M-$10M ARR). Here's my 6-step framework for scaling up without raising VC money:

Step 1: Bring on an advisor to give us the unicorn playbook

- I needed help from someone experienced for the next phase
- Santosh put ZoomInfo and Apollo on the unicorn path
- He acted as an advisor for 12 months
- Then joined us full time as COO

Step 2: Grow the team

- We got to $10M ARR with six full-time employees
- We needed people and processes to push to the next level
- We started with go-to-market, then built out an engineering and product
- We (sadly) went too far too fast… we were 55 at one point, now we’re 45

Step 3: Build an in-real-life sales motion

- We sell to primarily large Shopify merchants
- They tend to buy at at dinners, events, and shows
- We hired a partnership team to build an agency and affiliate motion

Step 4: Build out a proper product and engineering team

- Tate had built the entire app, Anne and I had done product
- It was incredibly fast and surprisingly high quality, but high key-man risk
- We hired Michael to learn the product and app before we hired engineers
- We now have a very strong team in product and engineering

Step 5: Dial in reporting and RevOps.

- This still hasn’t completely happened yet
- We went from spreadsheets to Salesforce starting last summer
- We’re attempting to have Salesforce be the source of truth
- We have a complicated business to report on (annual deals w/ opt-out dates)
- We continue to make progress… but still have no idea what our CAC/LTV is

Step 6: Expand TAM, keep building cool stuff.

- We’re going downmarket, in beta with a $77/mo Shopify app. 
- We’re going upmarket, uncapping our $5k unlimited deal, getting SOC.
- We’re going B2B, in beta with an individual-level ID product for sales teams

TAKEAWAY:

What got you here won’t get you there.

You can only get so far with a team of highly productive individual contributors.

But, with the foundation we put in place we 2x'd revenue with a small increase in headcount.

Happy to answer questions in the comments! 👇

TL;DR

Step 1: Bring on Unicorn Advisor
Step 2: Grow the team
Step 3: Build IRL sales motion
Step 4: Build out engineering
Step 5: Dial in RevOps
Step 6: Expand TAM

P.S.

If you’re interested in beta testing our new B2B product, DM me.
